Nintendo is ending Google and Apple sign-ins early next year
The company is asking users to set up a password or a passkey for their Nintendo accounts.
Nintendo will discontinue Google and Apple log-ins early next year, so you may want to update the way you sign into your account soon. Starting on January 26, 2027, it will no longer be possible to sign into your Nintendo account, or to create a new one, with Google and Apple as a log-in method. In addition, it is also ending the My Nintendo Platinum Points mission that rewards you for linking your Google with your Nintendo account.
The company had made the announcement in a support page, where it also said that the exact end time of Google and Apple sign-ins depend "on the progress of the system change work." Nintendo is asking users to set up a password or a passkey before January 26. To set up a passkey, go to the Accounts page, sign into your account, choose Sign-In and Security Settings, select Passkeys and then Edit. From there, you can choose Register New Passkey to start signing into Nintendo with your device's authentication method.
Nintendo didn't say why it's removing Google and Apple sign-ins, and whether it has security concerns with them. Whatever Nintendo's reason for it, you may want to get your log-in sorted if you want uninterrupted access to your games and to the eShop.

- Jensen Huang has resigned as NVIDIA's president and CEO after 33 years, with CFO Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO.
- NVIDIA appointed former Synopsys executive Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever board chair following Huang's departure from the board.
- NVIDIA will consider internal and external candidates for its next CEO, while its Q3 FY2027 earnings report remains scheduled for November 17.
Jensen Huang resigns as the president and CEO of NVIDIA, ending his 33-year run at the chipmaker he co-founded. NVIDIA announced the leadership change on November 12, 2026, confirming that CFO Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor.
Huang has also stepped down as a member of NVIDIA’s board, effective immediately. The company appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever board chair. Jones previously served as CEO and executive chairman of Synopsys and has more than 30 years of experience in technology and venture investing.
Jensen Huang’s NVIDIA Resignation As President Comes Amid Controversy
Huang’s departure follows a period of scrutiny surrounding reports of two extramarital relationships, including one involving a businesswoman reportedly suspected by US intelligence officials of having ties to Chinese intelligence. Huang previously acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to NVIDIA employees.
The controversy also raised questions about possible national security concerns and NVIDIA’s business relationships in Asia. The company’s board had launched an independent investigation on November 8, saying it had no reason to believe that NVIDIA secrets or national security had been compromised. Reuters also reported that the board had been considering Huang’s future before the resignation announcement.
Huang co-founded NVIDIA in 1993 and led its transformation from a graphics chipmaker into one of the world’s most important companies in AI and accelerated computing. The company became central to the AI boom following the growing demand for its GPUs after the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.
Colette Kress Takes over as Interim NVIDIA CEO
Colette Kress will continue serving as NVIDIA’s executive vice president and CFO while taking on the interim CEO role. She joined the company in September 2013 and has led its finance organization through a period of major growth.
Before joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance positions at technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft. The board said it has confidence in Kress and the existing leadership team, adding that the company’s operations, customer commitments, and product roadmap will continue without interruption.
NVIDIA will consider both internal and external candidates as it searches for a permanent CEO.
The company is still scheduled to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on November 17, followed by an earnings call. NVIDIA says its leadership transition will not interrupt its operations or product roadmap.

Nebraska rushed Medicaid work rules. Then a cancer patient was told he'd lost coverage
Eli McCreary of Omaha, Neb., said he had recently been diagnosed with kidney cancer when he got a call from a local hospital run by CHI Health. He said he was informed that he wasn't insured anymore under Medicaid — and that the hospital would cancel his appointments unless he paid out-of-pocket.
McCreary, who was 64 at the time, said he phoned a call center for help. He said he was told his benefits under Medicaid, the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities, now required that he have a job.
"You're required to do work to stay on," McCreary said a representative told him. "And you haven't fulfilled your work requirement."
For decades, McCreary said, he has battled drug addiction. A substance use treatment program discharged him in March, and in June he was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney, according to documents reviewed by KFF Health News. He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
"I don't understand what job I can get," McCreary said. "I can't walk. I can hardly breathe. I can't move around. What job am I going to get?"
McCreary said he canceled a CT scan and other tests at the hospital, which is part of CommonSpirit Health, the nation's largest Catholic health system. He also delayed a cancer-related appointment with a physician who travels back and forth to Omaha. "I missed my window of opportunity with him for another month," he said.
Taylor Miller, a spokesperson for CHI Health, declined to answer questions about McCreary's experience. In an emailed statement, she said that "CHI Health is committed to helping patients understand their health care coverage and access to care, including available financial assistance resources."
Determined to be the first state to enforce Medicaid work requirements under President Trump's signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Nebraska launched the new rules May 1 — eight months before most states are set to do the same. With their newly elected majorities in Congress, Democrats have said they plan to repeal the changes to Medicaid in their first 100 hours in office in January. But it is unclear if they will be successful, because Trump could veto it.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen said in December that state officials "certainly appreciate President Trump and his whole administration for delivering this key reform." Pillen spoke alongside a videoed-in Mehmet Oz, the Trump administration official overseeing Medicare and Medicaid.
"We're excited to be able to be the first to make it happen," the Republican governor said.
Laura Strimple, a spokesperson for the governor, didn't respond to requests for comment. Jeff Powell, a spokesperson for Nebraska's Department of Health and Human Services, said its rollout "has been very successful." He pointed to state data showing 86% of affected applicants met the requirement or qualified for an exclusion and 93% of existing enrollees kept their coverage.
Health clinics and organizations advocating for poor and working-class Nebraskans say the rollout has been rife with problems — many due to poor training and inadequate staffing.
The high price of cutting benefits
About 70,000 adult Medicaid recipients in Nebraska are subject to the work requirements. They must prove they're working or participating in a similar activity for 80 hours a month, unless they qualify for an exemption. State officials and consultants advising them have said the May 1 date was challenging to meet.
To deploy the law's Medicaid coverage restrictions, Nebraska budgeted millions of dollars for government contractors, according to state documents KFF Health News obtained via a public records request. Documents from Nebraska's health department outline $8.2 million in contractor costs to enact Medicaid changes, including work requirements and more frequent checks for whether people still qualify.
Nebraska operates the information technology system that determines who in the state qualifies for Medicaid, unlike most states, which outsource the work to companies under contracts often worth hundreds of millions of dollars. But Nebraska's health department nonetheless relies on the private sector to help administer its Medicaid program.
The $8.2 million in costs span two years. They stem from two companies that Nebraska uses to increase agency staffing: Public Consulting Group, based in Boston, and Atlanta-based Covendis, which supplies information technology staffers.
One of the companies has praised Nebraska's implementation of work requirements. A post on Public Consulting Group's website quotes senior consultant Latanya Michaux.
"I really cannot brag enough about how well Nebraska handled this requirement," Michaux said, crediting the firm's "incredible relationship" with the state.
Covendis executives did not respond to requests for comment. Powell said the health department "uses contracted staff when hiring a state employee is either uneconomical or impractical because of time constraints, or when the role requires highly specialized skill sets."
Advocates who work with Medicaid enrollees in Nebraska say that participants are confused and don't know whether the rules apply to them. These advocates say enrollees also have gotten inaccurate information. In December, Pillen said the state "won't be adding workforce" to implement the work requirements, a decision those advocates have criticized. Pillen in July also instituted a government-wide hiring freeze.
Nebraska listed at least half a dozen contractors costing more than $250,000 each, including one person whose compensation exceeds $1.8 million, the documents show. Nebraska submitted the records to federal Medicaid regulators as part of a routine process to secure federal money. Powell said the funding requests "may not reflect actual expenditures."
Sarah Maresh, a program director with the social justice advocacy nonprofit Nebraska Appleseed, said the amounts were "shocking."
"When you put in complicated policies like this, there are large corporations making money behind the scenes," Maresh said. "This just further confirms that it's happening in Nebraska quietly."
Confusion and longer wait times
The Medicaid work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and other changes shepherded by Republicans will curtail insurance gains that came from the Affordable Care Act, also known as Obamacare. The GOP tax and spending law, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over a decade, adds reporting requirements and restrictions that make it harder for people to stay enrolled.
As of early July, most denials related to the work requirements among Nebraska adults applying for Medicaid were due to unsubmitted paperwork, according to internal documents from Nebraska's health department that KFF Health News obtained through a public records request. The state wrote this was "expected."
State data shows that average wait times at a Nebraska health department call center nearly doubled between May and July, going from about 13 minutes to 26 minutes, before declining in August. In interviews, advocates for Medicaid enrollees said they've encountered people who have waited on the phone for hours.
Nebraska received more than 101,000 calls in August, a 66% jump from May.
"If people are working, they just don't have time to be sitting on the phone to go through all of this stuff," said Kenny McMorris, CEO of the Charles Drew Health Center, a federally qualified health center in North Omaha. He said roughly half of Charles Drew's 13,385 patients are on Medicaid, and of those, 42% are subject to the work requirements.
"You can leverage the technology, but you still got to have people there to help," McMorris said.
Then there are experiences the official data may not catch, like what happened to McCreary — saddled with figuring out what happened with his Medicaid benefits amid a health crisis, and whether it was even true that he had to work to keep them.
McCreary had heard about the Medicaid work requirements but didn't know they might apply to him. Powell confirmed McCreary was eligible for Medicaid because of the ACA — putting him in the population subject to work requirements.
His ordeal underscores the fallout from being caught in confusing government systems and silos that aren't obvious to the public.
"This cancer ain't going to stop just because I ain't got insurance," he said. "It's going to keep working on me."
When he received the call from the hospital about his coverage, "I was really in despair," McCreary said. Eventually, he said, he called for help.
Nebraska's health department runs AccessNebraska, a call center for help with safety net benefits such as Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as food stamps. But the number McCreary recalls dialing ended up not being AccessNebraska — it was for a different call center, one for SNAP accounts that Nebraska outsources to a private company. Powell said the state has no record of McCreary calling the health department.
McCreary said the worker didn't have a good explanation for why the Medicaid work requirements would apply to him. Before his health deteriorated, McCreary worked as a driver for an asphalt services company. He said he worked "until I couldn't do the job anymore."
"I really had hoped to work longer," he said. "I kind of enjoyed that job."
Attorneys and policy professionals who work with people on Medicaid and other public benefit programs said that McCreary's substance use treatment, lasting four months starting in November 2025, and other health conditions should have exempted him.
The federal law outlines categories of exemptions, such as being too sick to work. People who are considered too ill include those who have a serious medical condition or a substance use disorder.
Nebraska's health department said it sent tens of thousands of letters, text messages and emails to inform enrollees about the new requirements. According to state documents, Nebraska said it would "implement enhancements" to its computer system and online portal, including allowing people to submit documents online and having "clear, plain-language" enrollee notices. McCreary, however, doesn't have an account on Nebraska Medicaid's online portal, preferring to handle things over the phone or in person.
He also said it's possible he missed letters from Nebraska Medicaid about his coverage.
"I don't know if it's my fault or not," McCreary said.
The Cornhusker State's experience could be a harbinger of things to come. Next year, work requirements will apply to millions of adult Medicaid enrollees in more than 40 states.
The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has estimated the policy will lead to 5.3 million more people being uninsured in the U.S. by 2034.
"We definitely had fun"
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid changes are the most complicated in years — changes that government benefit experts say will strain and exacerbate long-standing problems with state technology systems for health benefits.
"It's already a shaky system, and now you've added more burdens on top of that," said Gelila Selassie, director of health advocacy for the nonprofit Justice in Aging.
Nebraska and federal officials, as well as consultants advising the state, detailed the difficulties and successes with the state's May 1 launch during an August panel discussion at a national conference in Oregon.
"They said, 'We're going to go live May 1.' To which CMS said, 'Oh, my God!'" Brent Weaver, an official who specializes in Medicaid IT at the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, said about Nebraska.
Nebraska officials knew "they weren't as agile as they probably would have liked to have been," Weaver said, "but they didn't let that stop them."
"If they fail, we looked at it as a failure," he added in comments that broadly praised the state's approach.
CMS did not answer questions from KFF Health News about Nebraska's rollout and Weaver's remarks.
In Nebraska, a group of 60 people held hours-long meetings three days a week that were "very exhausting," Michaux, of Public Consulting Group, said during a different session at the conference.
"Our calendars were cleared, and that was the focus," Michaux said.
Because CMS had not yet issued regulations outlining key details such as how people could get exemptions — it would do so June 1 — Nebraska officials said they had to rely on the law's broad language to make initial decisions.
"We had to get comfortable being uncomfortable," Jacob Kawamoto, a deputy director at Nebraska's Medicaid division, said at the conference.
Public Consulting Group said it worked with the state to develop new guidance and "process guides" — materials for Nebraska eligibility workers with instructions on how to process Medicaid applications or renewals. Training materials for Nebraska caseworkers reviewed by KFF Health News refer to those guides.
"The training was very robust, and the process guides were very robust," Michaux said.
Maresh disagreed with that characterization. "There are gaps" in the state's training materials, she said, and caseworkers "are confused" about work requirements.
Public Consulting Group also helped the state institute changes to Nebraska's Medicaid IT system, according to the company. "We are preparing for future updates and enhancements," Michaux said.
In response to questions, Public Consulting Group spokesperson Alyssa Brown said the company "has supported Nebraska Medicaid via a broad range of consulting services since 2019, including work on federal and state compliance initiatives." She said Michaux "discussed" the process guides at the conference but Nebraska developed them. Similarly, Brown said the company did not develop training.
Federal taxpayers will largely bear the costs of implementing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid policies in Nebraska and elsewhere. Congress allocated $200 million in one-time funding to states. Under federal regulations, the U.S. government picks up most of the tab for state IT system changes, paying as much as 90% of the cost.
"Even though it was not so easy," Michaux said at the conference, "we definitely had fun standing up the Medicaid work requirement program."
Public Consulting Group's employees, Brown told KFF Health News, are "passionate about public service and helping our clients improve the lives of the people they serve."
Dropping Medicaid enrollment
As of August, roughly 1,100 Nebraskans had been denied benefits because of Medicaid work requirements. Most denials were because people did not respond to requests for information.
Nebraska's total Medicaid enrollment has declined by roughly 4,600 people since May, a drop of 1.4%, according to an August report.
As for McCreary, the Nebraska health department's Powell maintained he experienced "no lapses in coverage" and said he was disenrolled from Medicaid after turning 65. Despite what McCreary said he was told, Powell said Medicaid work requirements weren't the reason: He aged out of Medicaid and into Medicare before they could be applied to him.
Selassie, from the nonprofit Justice in Aging, said McCreary's care shouldn't have been disrupted.
McCreary is now enrolled in Medicare, and Medicaid covers some of his health costs. He was able to reschedule his canceled appointments.
"The cancer has grown so much," he said.
He had surgery in early November to remove his right kidney.
KFF Health News correspondent Samantha Liss contributed to this report.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony.
Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group.
After years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities in 2002. He was freed a few months later and secured refugee status in 2004, but was arrested again in 2024 after it was revoked.
On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture after he slipped out of detention.
The fugitive held a senior position in the Red Brigades, a radical Marxist organization responsible for attacks from 1969 to 1980, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”. The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.
Security footage showed Bertulazzi dropping from a building into a public road as cars drove past.
A detective tracking the former member of the Red Brigades reportedly told La Nación that Bertulazzi rappelled down from the fifth floor using a harness.
“First, he removed his electronic ankle monitor and placed it in a tube filled with pork, along with a blood pressure monitor to maintain the temperature. He then climbed on to a roof and, using a rope, lowered himself five meters until he jumped onto a vacant lot behind the building where he lived, and then scaled a metal gate to reach the street,” the detective said, according to the publication.
The footage, which indicated the time was 6.01am on 10 November, showed a possibly shaken Bertulazzi sitting down to rest for a few moments.
Police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data and headed to the house, where they found the device discarded and Bertulazzi nowhere to be found.
Argentina approved his extradition to Italy in July 2025 after the country’s supreme court rejected a final appeal.

The makers of Kaali Kheti have unveiled the trailer of the upcoming psychological horror film, headlined by Jackie Shroff and Sharad Kelkar. Set against an eerie rural backdrop, the trailer offers a glimpse into a village where the fields hold disturbing secrets and farming becomes central to a terrifying chain of events.
Kaali Kheti trailer: Jackie Shroff and Sharad Kelkar explore a terrifying world of psychological rural horror
Moving away from conventional horror settings, Kaali Kheti explores an unusual premise by placing agriculture at the heart of its narrative. The trailer introduces a village living under the shadow of an unexplained force, with the land appearing to have a life of its own. As the mystery surrounding the fields unfolds, the atmosphere grows increasingly unsettling, hinting at a supernatural presence that has taken control of the village and its inhabitants.
Jackie Shroff and Sharad Kelkar lead the film, with both actors appearing in intriguing avatars. Shroff brings his distinctive screen presence to the mysterious world of Kaali Kheti, while Kelkar adds further gravitas to the narrative. The trailer offers glimpses of their characters without revealing too much about the secrets surrounding the village.
Rather than relying entirely on familiar horror tropes, the film appears to build its tension around the relationship between the villagers, their land and the mysterious events unfolding around them. The agricultural setting also lends the story a distinct identity, with the fields emerging as a central element of the horror.
Written and directed by Haris Imtiyaz Khan, Kaali Kheti is produced by Sana Khan under the banner of BlackCanvas Studio. The film also features Neha Sargam, Virendra Saxena and Shaji Choudhary in pivotal roles.
While the trailer provides a glimpse into the unsettling world of Kaali Kheti, it leaves several questions unanswered about the force haunting the village and the secrets hidden beneath its fields. The film is scheduled to release theatrically on November 20, 2026.

Chennai breathes far cleaner air than Delhi. A study that followed 12,064 adults in the two cities put the typical yearly level of fine particles around Chennai homes between 2010 and 2016 at 40.2 micrograms per cubic metre, just above the national standard of 40, against 101.5 in Delhi. In both cities, the dirtier a person’s air, the likelier they were to develop type 2 diabetes.
The World Health Organization’s theme for World Diabetes Day, on November 14 this year, is early action. The sixth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6), carried out in 2023-24, found 17.8% of women and 20.9% of men aged 15 and above had high blood sugar or were on medicine for it, up from 13.5% and 15.6% per cent in NFHS-5, conducted in 2019-21. In Chennai district, nearly 3 in 10 women fall in the group.
That said, there are limitations to this data: NFHS teams prick a finger at whatever hour they visit, so people may or may not have eaten, and a reading above 140 milligrams per decilitre counts as high. One such reading cannot diagnose diabetes. However, what is most routinely blamed for the rising burden of diabetes in the country -- and it is rising -- are weight and diet. And while these are significant factors, dirty air is rarely blamed. Perhaps it’s time it is.
The outdoor evidence
Siddhartha Mandal of the Centre for Chronic Disease Control in New Delhi and his colleagues used satellite and weather data to estimate daily levels of fine particles, called PM2.5, near each participant’s home.
Over a median of almost five years, 743 people developed type 2 diabetes. Each extra 10 micrograms in a person’s yearly average accounted for a 22% higher risk, after the researchers allowed for age, socio-economic status, tobacco and alcohol use, diet and exercise. Studies in richer, cleaner countries have put the rise at 7 to 11%.
A 2024 global review of 46 studies also linked PM2.5 and the coarser PM10 to type 2 diabetes. Its authors point mainly to inflammation and oxidative stress (damage from reactive oxygen), which blunt the body’s response to insulin, the hormone that moves sugar into cells. The Global Burden of Disease project puts about a fifth of the healthy years lost worldwide to type 2 diabetes in 2019 down to PM2.5, about 14% from outdoor air and 6% from household smoke.
Smoke in the kitchen
Between 2018 and 2021, researchers from the Madras Diabetes Research Foundation tested adults in 30 villages of Cheyyur taluk in Chengalpattu district as part of a project called TREND.
All but 208 of the 13,877 adults lived in homes cooking on traditional fuels such as firewood or kerosene. Diabetes was more common among them, 14.2% against 12%, and more common still, 16.5%, in homes without a separate kitchen. Among women, traditional fuel use was linked with 80% higher odds of diabetes of diabetes, after the researchers allowed for age, weight, family history, education and income.
One round of testing, however, cannot prove what causes diabetes, and the group using clean fuel was small. Even so, a 2022 review of nine studies with 45,620 people found that those who cooked with solid fuels had 46% higher odds of diabetes. However, in homes that burned only biomass like wood or dung, the link was too weak to be certain.
Short of gas, short of data
The NFHS used to report cooking fuel and blood sugar from the same homes. Clean fuel, mostly LPG, reached 58.6% of homes in 2019-21, up from 43.8% in 2015-16, as the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana distributed connections. Even at that pace, about 3 homes in 10, mostly in villages, would still have cooked on fuels such as wood, dung and kerosene by 2023-24. The NFHS-6 fact sheets, released on May 29, leave this figure out. The Health Ministry has said this, and other missing statistics are being monitored through dedicated national surveys and administrative databases; however these other surveys do not take blood samples, leaving possible connections unable to be made.
Much of India’s LPG comes from abroad. About 90% of those imports pass through the Strait of Hormuz, which the West Asia war choked in early March, leading to shortfalls across the country. Poor homes, though, used little gas even before the war. The average Ujjwala household bought 4.71 cylinders in 2025-26, and about one in seven in Bihar bought none, the Petroleum Ministry told the Lok Sabha. The ministry has since cut subsidised refills from nine a year to four, about half of what a family cooking only on gas needs, as per figures cited by think tank, the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW).
Every return to the wood stove brings back smoke tied to diabetes, and even a month of dirtier air nudged up blood sugar in the Delhi and Chennai study, a worry for anyone already living with the disease. As long as India’s kitchens depend on imported gas, the next war or blockade can push them back to wood, and more people towards diabetes.
The Kerala puzzle
If dirty air alone drove the numbers, the least polluted States would sit at the bottom of the survey’s tables. A satellite study of 2024 pollution by independent research organisation, the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), put Kerala among the seven States and Union Territories with the cleanest air. Yet Kerala has the highest share of women with high blood sugar of any State or Union Territory, 28.9%, according to NFHS-6. Meghalaya, where CREA found every district above the national pollution standard outside the monsoon, has the lowest of any State, 7.1%. Kerala also has the oldest population of any State, and diabetes grows more common with age. This complicates the picture.
What could help, would be more data, and long-term studies that could tease apart the effects of air, with those of age, weight, diet and access to doctors, of the same people.
The NFHS, though, could provide answers sooner than any new study. The Health Ministry has said that a more detailed NFHS-6 national report will be released, though it is not clear if this will include cooking fuel numbers. If the report and household data include cooking fuel, researchers could compare blood sugar in homes using wood and gas, taking age and weight into account, and use data from before the shortage as a baseline. The Petroleum Ministry already tracks Ujjwala refills by State, and could publish this information monthly for every district.
It remains to be seen, however, if the data will materialise. Until then, India remains the country with the highest burden of diabetes, and one of the highest levels of air pollution.
(Dr Margubur Rahaman is a public health researcher at MAMTA Health Institute for Mother and Child, New Delhi. margubur48@gmail.com; Ankit Mishra is an ICSSR Doctoral Fellow at the Govind Ballabh Pant Social Science Institute, Prayagraj. ankitmishrakoraon@gmail.com)

Gurugram bans coal, wood-fired tandoors at hotels and eateries under revised GRAP norms to curb pollution
Under the revised provisions of the GRAP issued by the CAQM, only equipment powered by electricity, gas, or other approved clean fuels may now be used.
District Magistrate and Gurugram Deputy Commissioner Uttam Singh has issued orders to prohibit the use of coal and wood as fuel in tandoors at all hotels, restaurants, and open-air eateries across the district in an effort to combat air pollution.
Under the revised provisions of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) issued by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM), only equipment powered by electricity, gas, or other approved clean fuels may now be used in these establishments. This order is effective immediately, an official said.
ALSO READ: How CPCB’s defence of Delhi's Diwali AQI undercuts its own case
According to an official statement, the district magistrate has directed the Municipal Corporation of Gurugram, the Municipal Corporation of Manesar, the relevant officials of the Haryana State Pollution Control Board, and other concerned departments to ensure strict compliance with these orders.
All sub-divisional magistrates will also coordinate with the respective municipal bodies and enforcement agencies to ensure the effective implementation of these orders.
ALSO READ: Secondary organic aerosols biggest contributor to Delhi pollution on Wednesday: IITM
The district magistrate has requested that officials conduct regular inspections, take action against any violations, and submit daily reports detailing inspections, violations, and actions taken.
He has also appealed to the general public and the operators of business establishments to cooperate with the administration in this campaign to reduce air pollution.
Operators of hotels, restaurants, and eateries must strictly refrain from using prohibited fuels and ensure that only equipment utilising approved, clean-burning fuels is used in their establishments.

Avery has been writing fan fiction for about six years, now mainly focused on the gay hockey romance Heated Rivalry. Until last month, it all lived in one place—Archive of Our Own. Then, on October 29 the fan fiction behemoth went dark due to a “security incident.” Within days, Avery was alarmed to find her works on mirror sites she hadn’t posted them to.
“To me it’s a security risk,” Avery, who did not want her real name used due to fears of backlash on social media, tells WIRED via DM. “One bad actor could put malware in that drive.”
She emailed the sites—Squidgeworld and AO3.Life—and the stories were removed, though she’ll never know if she has found every copy online. (AO3.Life has since been taken down, and Walter Hopgood, president of Squidge.org, which hosts Squidgeworld, told WIRED it removes works that are posted without an author’s permission.)
Avery’s problem is one shared with many fanfic authors since the team behind AO3 announced the site will remain offline for up to four weeks.
Hosting more than 18.8 million fan works across hundreds of thousands of fandoms, AO3 is among the most visited websites in the world. When it went down, some fans started freaking out over the “AO3 apocalypse.” Within days, readers who had saved stories on their own device placed them onto shared libraries on Google Drives. But finding alternatives has caused friction in the community, as some authors are unhappy with the way their works are being distributed without their permission, breaking fanfic norms and exacerbating fears about AI scraping.
One of the many drives to pop up was the Archive Salvation Google Drive project, a collective of fan fiction downloaded from AO3. It faced criticism after launching, though a spokesperson tells WIRED it offered ways for authors to ask for their work to be removed. But it’s since been hacked and is no longer accessible, according to a November 3 statement on a moderator’s TikTok, though the group behind it is still sharing fanfics in a closed Discord server.
“We continue to acknowledge the controversies of such drives but also want to acknowledge the joy this has brought readers and the authors who submitted their fics to us,” the statement said, adding, “our drive was controversial and very public, so the hacker is most likely someone who stands against drives like this in general.”
Avery doesn’t mind her work circulating in private drives or being asked for copies of their work for fans to read—her concern is with her work being uploaded to giant drive libraries.
But she says AO3’s breakdown has revealed entitlement among some readers, who’ve messaged her demanding to know where her fics are now available. “I just can’t wait for AO3 to go back up so that people can go back to normal,” she says. “It’s left a sour taste in my mouth.”
“Writers hating their readers this much will kill fandoms actually,” one user wrote on X in response to an artist expressing frustration about people who “don’t contribute anything to the fandom” weighing in on how work is shared. Another X user accused the same artist of being “self-righteous” and “entitled.”
Avery says some readers seem to feel authors’ feelings “are secondary to the readers.” “It feels like AO3 going down made so many people so crazy that they couldn’t get their fix, and I think the authors are most outspoken because it’s our work.”
Riley, a writer with over 90,000 followers across X and Instagram, ran afoul of some fellow authors when they shared a Google doc cataloging some of the drives compiling fanfic on November 2. Some people claimed it was a privacy violation and could put AO3 users at risk of doxing. “It’s about basic respect,” one user wrote, while others demanded their fics be removed from the list.
Riley, who did not want their real name used for fear of receiving more backlash, made their X account private soon after.
“I did not anticipate the potential harmful effects of me compiling the document of stories, which is why I deleted it,” they tell WIRED.
Meanwhile, Ellipsus, a collaborative writing platform with an anti-AI stance that was founded in 2022, has seen a boom in interest since AO3 went down. Allegra Rosenberg, an Ellipsus employee and writer, says that new sign-ups are up more than 500 percent since the outage began and views of its public reader links—the ways in which authors can share work—have increased heavily.
What Ellipsus offers is control. Authors can control who can see their work and how they can interact with it. They can turn on comments, and readers can leave kudos (called “props” on Ellipsus), as well as custom fonts and themes. Rosenberg says the company noticed that many of the users were fan fiction writers and adjusted features for them before the outage, for example, a button that exports work directly to AO3.
”We know that people want a space to not only write but share new writing, in a way that feels safe for them,” says Rosenberg.
Another reason the outage has felt so fraught is that the world of fan fiction has broken containment, becoming mainstream in part due to shows like Heated Rivalry and the adaptation of former fan fictions such as Alchemised by SenLinYu, which was originally published on AO3, into bona fide novels.
“It’s the Tik-tokification of fanfic,” Avery says.“Everyone wants a snippet and a graphic and a one shot, and they can share it on Twitter, and then suddenly a thing I wrote years ago goes viral. Fan fiction never used to go viral.”
Rosenberg, who is writing a book on fandom, thinks that so much of the backlash comes from a mismatch between how big the community actually is and how small it still feels to many. The giant drives and libraries drew outrage due to their scale and a fear from many fans that their stories could be taken down. That fear has a real history within fandom spaces.
“In the ’90s and 2000s, there were cease-and-desist notices and takedown controversies on Fanfiction.net and LiveJournal that led to AO3’s founding,” Rosenberg explains. “So there is this shared history and memory within fandom culture as a whole when it comes to fan fiction.”
The demand for fan fiction does not come only from people active in fandom circles. It also comes from people who are seen as casual fans—those who are not as invested in the wider fandom. Fan fiction operates on norms where people ask permission, and there is a tolerance for a certain level of informal sharing. The AO3 outage has tested these norms and has exposed the lack of practical protection an author has once their work is posted. Readers are doing what they have always done—sharing work that they love. However, the burden of this sharing is uneven, as authors fear losing track of their own work.
“I think this whole AO3 going down thing has reminded people that the internet is forever for better or for worse,” Avery says. “Long after I die, if we still have the internet, my fics will float about even without AO3.”

Rescue Ends in Brooklyn After 8 Die in Building Collapse
The Fire Department said the search for victims on Flatbush Avenue was over, while city investigators began looking into an excavation occurring next door.
After a night of frantic searches through the rubble of a Brooklyn building collapse that killed eight people, New York City officials announced on Thursday that they were ending their rescue efforts, concluding there were no more victims.
Eighteen other people, including four firefighters, were injured in the collapse and its aftermath at 1321 Flatbush Avenue. Two children who were cousins were among the eight killed, according to an internal police report. Three were construction workers.
The tragedy shattered the heavily immigrant neighborhood and set off a city investigation into excavation at the construction site next door at 2625 Bedford Avenue.
The collapse occurred around 4 p.m. on Wednesday. James Williams, who works at a deli across the street, said he had been hearing an incessant loud hammering noise every few minutes from the construction site on Wednesday afternoon. He went outside and saw bricks falling from 1321 Flatbush, a three-story apartment building. “I’m like, Oh hell, what is going on?” he said.
He watched as the building started to crumble, its front and side sliding away, and a check-cashing shop that he frequented underneath all collapsing into the open construction site next door. He saw clothes and a microwave oven thrown into the dust-filled air. He heard people scream.
The first firefighters arrived within a minute, followed by more from around New York City and from New Rochelle, N.Y., in Westchester County. The search and rescue efforts involved about 250 personnel in all.

UPDATED with latest company comments: Microsoft is continuing to investigate widespread outages affecting Outlook email and other services offered through its 365 platform.
The tech giant issued a string of social media posts Thursday acknowledging that users had been reporting issues with access, throwing a major wrench into business communications across sectors. Enterprise and business customers of Microsoft 365 were experiencing problems connecting to email via the Exchange server as well as accessing other services. The U.S. is one of the main regions affected, but Microsoft says it potentially poses a problem across the world.
As the outage dragged into the end of the work day, the tech giant put out a less-than-encouraging status report. “We’re continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” the company wrote. “Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss.”
Watch on Deadline
Workers are “fully isolating a portion of our service infrastructure, restarting the affected components, and gradually reintroducing traffic to confirm our services remain stable,” the company went on to say. “We’re also analyzing traffic patterns across our entire service infrastructure and evaluating whether isolating traffic within each region may allow affected regions to recover independently.”
After the initial issues with email, word surfaced about users unable to connect with Teams, Azure, OneDrive, Copilot and other offerings. The home page of outage detection site DownDetector was filled almost entirely by Microsoft alerts.
“We’re investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas,” the company posted at around noon ET on Thursday. “While we’re working to mitigate impact, we’ve confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region.”
Microsoft later clarified, “We’ve determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.”
A status hub designed to provide service updates cited “an unexpected increase in a specific type of service traffic to determine whether it’s contributing to the elevated load. In parallel, we’re evaluating options to redirect traffic to alternate infrastructure to expedite relief.”
Media companies were among those across all business sectors whose activities slowed to a crawl due to the tech glitch. Employees at Amazon Prime Video, Skydance and NBCUniversal and other companies confirmed to Deadline they were in the dark.
There were no immediate indications of a possible cause, though online speculation touched on factors like digital downloads of Grand Theft Auto VI pre-orders or hackers looking to make a statement. Still other theories sought to connect the outage to the day’s other momentous tech news: the ouster of Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of Nvidia. Huang was forced to resign after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and amid reports of affairs with executives at his own company.
The origins of Microsoft 365 date to the early 2010s, when the company was ramping up its efforts to transition its Office programs Word, Excel and PowerPoint to the cloud. After a meteoric rise as a software maker in the 1980s and 1990s, Microsoft weathered some lean years after a federal antitrust lawsuit and a sluggish initial response to the advent of the internet. Under CEO Satya Nadella, Microsoft has successfully pivoted into cloud computing and, more recently, AI en route to a multi-trillion-dollar market valuation.
Shares in Microsoft have thus far not been affected by the outage, finishing Thursday’s trading day up a fraction to $523. The company’s stock, along with those of a dozen or more large companies placing heavy bets on AI, will come under increasing scrutiny on Wall Street in light of the Nvidia news.

Nomura Holdings is exploring the sale of its crypto business Laser Digital Holdings, after losses at the Zurich-based entity last year pushed the brokerage’s entire European operation into the red.
Japan’s largest securities firm is talking to potential buyers including Marex, which is evaluating the deal, according to people familiar with the matter. No final decision has been made, and Nomura could end up selling it to another party or holding onto the business, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is private.
Spokespeople for Nomura and Marex declined to comment.
The talks come after severe crypto market swings caused significant enough losses at Laser to drag Nomura’s European operations to a quarterly loss. Management acknowledged the “considerable volatility” of crypto-related earnings and moved to tighten risk controls. The development was a setback for Nomura’s CEO Kentaro Okuda, who highlighted Laser last year as part of the firm’s efforts to capture “future business opportunities.”
Founded in 2022 and led partly by longtime Nomura veteran Steven Ashley, Laser provides trading and asset-management services to institutional investors, as well as making venture-capital investments in crypto startups. It’s one of a few Nomura offshoots focused on digital assets. Others include Boostry and Komainu, which specialize in tokenizing financial products and custody services, respectively.
Late last year, Laser poached a trio of derivatives traders from Mike Novogratz’s Galaxy Digital, and more recently obtained a license to provide cryptoasset exchange services in Japan. In May, it received conditional approval for a U.S. national trust-bank charter.
Marex offers a suite of digital-asset tools including execution, clearing, financing and structured products. In October, the company expanded its offering with the launch of a new over-the-counter rolling spot crypto product for institutional clients.
The wider digital-assets market has been stuck in a prolonged slump. Bitcoin, the largest token, is today trading below $74,000, more than 40% off its peak. The value of cryptocurrency transactions in Japan, including margin trades, more than halved from a year earlier in the first nine months of this year to ¥17.2 trillion ($108.5 billion), according to data from the Japan Virtual and Crypto assets Exchange Association.
Line Xenesis, the crypto unit of Japanese internet company LY, in which Nomura took a minority stake in 2019, shut its Line Bitmax cryptocurrency exchange in June.
Still, Japan is moving toward allowing exchange-traded funds that invest in cryptocurrencies, with the first products potentially listing as early as next year. That could benefit asset managers that put ETFs together as well as brokerages that distribute them. The government also plans to lower the tax rate on gains from cryptocurrency investments.

Noida Metro extension to landmark museum project and more: A look at key cabinet decisions
The Cabinet approved a hike in fertiliser subsidies, a ₹2,390-crore Noida Metro extension amid other key decisions
Centre on Wednesday approved a series of key decisions spanning fertiliser subsidies, metro connectivity, heritage preservation and entrepreneurship. The four major decisions include a 64.3% increase in the fertiliser subsidy budget for the 2026-27 Rabi season, approval for the Noida Metro Aqua Line extension, funding for the Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum and the continuation of the Stand-Up India Scheme for five years until March 2031.
Here are the four key decisions:
1. Fertiliser subsidy budget raised by 64% to ₹62,370 crore
The Union Cabinet approved a subsidy budget of ₹62,370 crore for phosphatic and potassic (P&K) fertilisers for the 2026-27 Rabi season, marking an increase of 64.3% over the ₹37,952 crore allocated for the previous season.
Deep Dive
The increase of ₹24,418 crore comes amid disruptions in the international fertiliser market following the US-Israel attacks on Iran in February. Restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global fertiliser trade, have further affected the market.
The revised subsidy allocation takes into account trends in international fertiliser prices and input costs.
2. Cabinet clears ₹2,390-crore Noida Metro extension; Blue and Aqua lines to get new link
The Cabinet also approved an 8.449-km extension of the Noida Metro's Aqua Line at a cost of ₹2,390 crore on Wednesday, paving the way for improved connectivity between the Delhi Metro network and Noida and Greater Noida West.
The project is aimed at improving access to commercial, residential and institutional hubs along the route.
The extension will have five elevated stations and connect Noida Sector 51 to Greater Noida Sector 4.
A key feature of the project will be an interchange facility with the Delhi Metro's Blue Line at Noida Sector 61. This will provide commuters with an additional connection to the wider Delhi-NCR Metro network.
3. ₹3,230 crore for Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum approved
The Union Cabinet ₹3,230 crore">approved ₹3,230 crore for the development of the Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum in New Delhi's North Block and South Block.
The project is scheduled for completion by March 2031 and will showcase India's civilisational history spanning 10,000 years.
The museum will be developed in the two nearly century-old heritage buildings that have served as the seat of the Union government. The project will involve the adaptive reuse of the existing structures to create the national museum.
4. Cabinet approves continuation of Stand-Up India Scheme until March 2031
The Union Cabinet also approved the continuation of the Stand-Up India Scheme for another five years, until March 31, 2031.
The scheme aims to promote entrepreneurship among women, Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) by providing financial assistance to 2.5 lakh additional entrepreneurs over the next five years.
Since its launch in April 2016, the scheme has facilitated loans to more than 2.75 lakh entrepreneurs belonging to these categories, a government press release said.

Why a US-Russia showdown left Morocco celebrating
- Published
Morocco has welcomed the end of a decades-long UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, after a diplomatic showdown between the US and Russia left the Security Council unable to agree on its future.
The council failed on Friday to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (Minurso) after Russia vetoed a US-backed proposal. A rival Russian draft to extend the mission also failed to secure enough votes.
The decision raises questions about the future of Africa's longest territorial dispute and the fragile ceasefire between Morocco, which claims Western Sahara, and the Polisario Front which has been fighting for the territory's independence for more than 50 years.
Here is what you need to know.
Why is Western Sahara disputed?
Western Sahara, on Africa's north-west coast, was a Spanish colony until 1975. It has significant phosphate reserves and valuable fishing grounds along its Atlantic coast.
As Spain prepared to withdraw, both Morocco and Mauritania claimed the territory.
The International Court of Justice found historical ties of allegiance but no territorial sovereignty that overrode the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination.
Morocco's then King Hassan II responded by organising the Green March. On 6 November 1975 about 350,000 Moroccan civilians entered the territory in a mass demonstration intended to put pressure on Spain.
Days later, Spain signed the Madrid Accords with Morocco and Mauritania, agreeing to transfer administrative control. Morocco took the northern two-thirds and Mauritania the southern third. The agreement did not settle the question of sovereignty.
The Polisario Front, an independence movement founded in 1973, opposed the deal. It saw it as replacing Spanish colonial rule with Moroccan and Mauritanian control.
Mauritania renounced its claim in 1979, but Morocco continued fighting Polisario.
Algeria became Polisario's main regional ally, providing military support and hosting its leadership and thousands of Sahrawi refugees in camps near the city of Tindouf.
The North African country says its position is based on the right to self-determination, while Morocco sees Western Sahara as an integral part of its territory.
Morocco and Algeria fought a brief border war in 1963 over disagreements about territory inherited from French colonial rule. Their relationship has remained tense, with Western Sahara at the centre of their dispute.
What was the UN's mission role?
After 16 years of fighting, Morocco and Polisario agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991, with the territory divided by a sand wall, or berm, to keep the rival forces apart.
The UN established Minurso to monitor the ceasefire and organise a referendum on the territory's future. Sahrawis were meant to choose between independence and integration with Morocco.
The vote was scheduled for 1992 but never took place. The two sides could not agree on who would be eligible to participate, with disputes over voter identification becoming a major obstacle.
In 2007, Morocco put forward a proposal for autonomy, which would see Sahrawis managing their internal affairs, while Rabat retained control over defence and foreign relations.
The Polisario Front and Algeria rejected the plan, insisting on a referendum that included independence as an option.
Years of UN-sponsored negotiations failed to produce a breakthrough.
The ceasefire broke down in November 2020, when Polisario said it was resuming armed struggle.
But following a long diplomatic campaign by Morocco, the UN Security Council voted in 2025 in favour of a resolution backing the autonomy plan as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.
While most Sahrawis live in the part of Western Sahara controlled by Morocco, tens of thousands are estimated to be in refugee camps in Algeria.
What happened at the UN?
The US proposed extending Minurso's mandate for another year, but its draft went beyond the usual renewal.
It would have removed the word "referendum" from the mission's name and made Morocco's autonomy proposal the sole basis for further negotiations.
The draft received the support of 11 of the Security Council's 15 members, including France and the UK but Russia vetoed it, arguing that it was too favourable to Morocco.
Russia then proposed extending Minurso's mandate without changing its terms. That draft also failed, receiving only two votes in favour.
Minurso's mandate expired at the end of Saturday, 31 October. The UN said the following day that the mission had entered a liquidation period, with a reduced team overseeing the transfer of military equipment and other assets.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination must be respected and warned of the risk of renewed hostilities.
The Polisario Front condemned the US proposal. Its representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing it, saying it would "torpedo the foundations of the UN peace process" and threaten regional and international peace.
Morocco, meanwhile, said the mission's personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days, arguing that Western Sahara issue should no longer be considered by the Security Council.
Minurso had 155 military personnel and was expected to cost $62m (£46m) in the financial year beginning in June, according to a UN report.
Why is Morocco celebrating the end of the UN mission?
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew Minurso's mandate.
In Laayoune, the territory's largest city, footage showed people celebrating, waving Moroccan flags and displaying portraits of King Mohammed VI.
"The decision is an opportunity for Rabat to challenge what it sees as an international mechanism that has failed to resolve the dispute," Issam Laaroussi, a Moroccan expert in international relations, tells the BBC.
He said Morocco would now have more room to push its autonomy proposal and shift negotiations away from a referendum on independence towards autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty.
The decision does not, however, change Western Sahara's legal status or amount to international recognition of Moroccan sovereignty.
Western Sahara remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, while the African Union officially recognises its independence, as the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR).
But the decision comes after several countries backed the position of Morocco, which in recent years has made securing international support for its claim a central part of its foreign policy.
In 2020, the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of an agreement to establish diplomatic relations between Morocco and Israel.
France also backed Morocco's autonomy plan as the basis for resolving the dispute in 2024.
Morocco rejoined the African Union in 2017, more than three decades after leaving its predecessor, the Organisation of African Unity, in protest at the SADR's admission.
Since returning, Rabat has sought to build support for its position from within the organisation. At least 10 African countries have opened diplomatic missions in the territory in support of Rabat.
"Morocco is not necessarily seeking to abandon the UN process, but to change the framework for negotiations and draw greater support from regional organisations," says Laaroussi.
Addressing a special joint session of parliament on Monday, House of Representatives Speaker Ahmed Touizi hailed the end of Minurso as a victory for the country's diplomacy.
He said the country should now move from "managing the dispute to implementing its autonomy plan under Moroccan sovereignty, while pressing ahead with development projects in the territory."
Could this lead to a renewed war?
The fear is that Minurso's departure could lead to renewed fighting.
The mission has monitored military developments and helped reduce the risk of escalation.
Aid organisation Oxfam warned that losing its monitoring and de-escalation role could undermine stability, with serious consequences for civilians.
Laaroussi admits that the mission's departure could create security gaps.
"Minurso's departure does not create the original conflict, because the conflict is already there, but it could aggravate an already fragile security environment," he says.
The UN decision has also fuelled nationalist rhetoric online.
Several Moroccan users have shared AI-generated images of themselves in military uniform, declaring their readiness to fight for Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara.
In Morocco, Western Sahara is widely regarded as a national cause. Political parties that are often divided on other issues are united in supporting the country's claim to sovereignty over the territory.
Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita has said the end of the mission does not mean the end of the ceasefire, and that Rabat remains committed to it "within respect of its security and sovereignty."
Polisario has not said what it will do next.
Any resumption of fighting could well draw in Algeria, as tensions with Morocco remain high.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), both countries significantly increased military spending last year, with SIPRI citing their dispute over Western Sahara as a key driver.
Algeria spent an estimated $25.4bn, more than four time Morocco's $6.3bn.

Ex-NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang is set to testify before Congress this month
House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast said the hearing will take place before Thanksgiving.
Jensen Huang might have stepped down from his roles at the top of NVIDIA, but he won't be sliding out of the spotlight just yet. The company's former CEO and president is set to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving, according to House representatives.
House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast said Huang agreed to testify on Wednesday — hours before NVIDIA announced his resignation with immediate effect — after lawmakers threatened him with a subpoena. It appears the hearing will take place behind closed doors (which is unfortunate, because that's likely to be some spicy testimony). However, Mast expects it to be filmed and transcribed, according to Bloomberg. The House's Intelligence and China-focused committees will join the Foreign Affairs cohort for the hearing.
"Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but NVIDIA is a very important company to the United States of America," Mast said. "I don't want to see anything hurt in NVIDIA, but he has some very serious questions to answer."
NVIDIA has been in turmoil after it emerged over the weekend that the company was investigating Huang over an affair to which he admitted, allegedly with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating the situation as well.
On Wednesday, it was reported that Huang had another affair, this time with Kimberly Powell, an NVIDIA executive who reported to him. The company's board met later that day to determine Huang's future. Colette Kress, NVIDIA's executive vice president and chief financial officer, is stepping in as interim CEO while the company seeks a permanent successor.
Meanwhile, the Department of Justice is reportedly investigating Alice Huang, the alleged spy, to determine whether entities associated with her were involved in attempts to smuggle Super Micro Computer products to China. The DoJ is also said to be taking the lead in an investigation into her former company, the Singapore-based Megaspeed International, over alleged smuggling of US-made chips into China in defiance of export restrictions. The company said it would cooperate with the probe.
Officials in Singapore opened an investigation into Alice Huang, Megaspeed and associated individuals last year. The Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement on Thursday that she was barred from re-entering the country after police determined she knowingly offered up inaccurate information to downplay her role in Megaspeed. However, they "concluded that there was insufficient evidence to establish that Huang had committed any offences relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated." The investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals is ongoing.

12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న 4వ జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లో పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను తగ్గించడం/మాఫీ చేయనున్నారని చెబుతూ ఒక వీడియో సోషల్ మీడియాలో విస్తృతంగా ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న 4వ జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లో పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను తగ్గించడం/మాఫీ చేయబడతాయి.
ఫాక్ట్: ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను మాఫీ చేస్తున్నట్లు జాతీయ లేదా రాష్ట్ర లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీలు ఎక్కడా ప్రకటించలేదు. అయితే, 2026లో కర్ణాటక, బీహార్, ఒడిశా వంటి పలు రాష్ట్రాలు పెండింగ్ చలాన్ల చెల్లింపులో రాయితీని కల్పించాయి. తెలంగాణ, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ రాష్ట్రాలు గతంలో ఇలాంటి రాయితీలు ఇచ్చినప్పటికీ, డిసెంబర్ 2026లో జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లో మాత్రం ఎలాంటి రాయితీని అధికారికంగా ప్రకటించలేదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా ఈ విషయం గురించి జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లను నిర్వహించే నేషనల్ లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీ (NALSA) అధికారిక వెబ్సైట్ను పరిశీలించగా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న దేశవ్యాప్తంగా పలు రాష్ట్రాలలో లోక్ అదాలత్లు నిర్వహిస్తున్నట్లు తెలిసింది. దీనిలో భాగంగా విచారణలో ఉన్న సివిల్, క్రిమినల్, చెక్బౌన్స్ కేసులు, కాంపౌండబుల్ ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్ కేసులు, మోటారు వాహన ప్రమాదాలు, కుటుంబ తగాదాలు మొదలైనవాటిని రాజీ మార్గం ద్వారా పరిష్కరించుకునే అవకాశాన్ని ఈ లోక్ అదాలత్లు కల్పిస్తాయి. అయితే, పెండింగ్ ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను 100% మాఫీ చేయనున్నట్లు ఇందులో ఎక్కడా పేర్కొనలేదు.
ఇదే విషయమై తెలంగాణ స్టేట్ లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీ (TSLSA) వర్గాలను సంప్రదించగా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న తెలంగాణలో జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లలో ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లకు మాఫీ/ డిస్కౌంట్ ఇస్తున్నట్లు తాము ఎక్కడా అధికారికంగా పేర్కొనలేదని స్పష్టం చేశారు.
అంతేకాకుండా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లలో తెలంగాణ వ్యాప్తంగా పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను రాయితీపై చెల్లించే అవకాశం కల్పించడం లేదని తెలంగాణ పోలీసులు కూడా మాకు ధృవీకరించారు. మార్చి 2026లో కూడా ఇటువంటి వార్తలే వచ్చినప్పుడు వారు దీన్ని ఖండించారు. మరోవైపు, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీని, పోలీసులను సంప్రదించగా వారి స్పందించలేదు. అయితే, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ పోలీసులు కూడా పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లపై రాయితీ కల్పించే విషయం గురించి ఎక్కడా అధికారికంగా ప్రకటించలేదు.
అయితే కర్ణాటక, ఒడిశా, బీహార్ వంటి పలు రాష్ట్రాల్లో 2026లో ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లకు రాయితీ కల్పిస్తూ సెటిల్మెంట్ చేసుకునేందుకు వీలుగా ట్రాఫిక్ పోలీసులు లోక్ అదాలత్లను నిర్వహించిన సందర్భాలు ఉన్నాయి. గతంలో హైదరాబాద్ ట్రాఫిక్ పోలీసులు కూడా ఇలాంటి లోక్ అదాలత్లను నిర్వహించారు. 2016, 2017 సంవత్సరాల్లో హైదరాబాద్ ట్రాఫిక్ పోలీసులు గోషామహల్లో లోక్ అదాలత్ నిర్వహించి, 50% రాయితీతో పెండింగ్ చలాన్లను చెల్లించే అవకాశం కల్పించారు. అయితే, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లలో తెలంగాణ, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ రాష్ట్రాల పోలీసులు లోక్ అదాలత్ ద్వారా ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లపై రాయితీని కల్పించే పథకాన్ని అధికారికంగా ప్రకటించలేదు.
చివరిగా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరిగే జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లో పెండింగ్ ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లు 100% మాఫీ అవుతాయని సోషల్ మీడియాలో జరుగుతున్న ప్రచారంలో నిజం లేదు.

BSE SME listed Veefin Solutions has migrated to the main board of the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and the BSE, more than three years after its SME IPO. Veefin's shares opened for trade on the BSE mainboard at ₹249.75 (2.5% higher than previous close) and at ₹250.84 on the NSE. Veefin’s market capitalisation as of 13:20 IST stood at ₹633.76 Cr ($67.61 Mn). Shares of Veefin were trading 1.2% higher at ₹249 apiece on the BSE and 1.2% higher at ₹246.65 apiece on the NSE around 13:30 IST. Veefin listed on the BSE SME platform in July 2023 at ₹86.05, a near 5% premium from its IPO price. The company's ₹46.73 Cr IPO comprised about 57 Lakh shares, with equal parts of fresh issue and offer for sale shares. Its mainboard debut comes on the heels of the company solidifying its financial position over the recent quarter. Its operating revenue for the first half of the ongoing fiscal year (H1 FY27) doubled to ₹238.8 Cr while its consolidated net profit zoomed 127% YoY to ₹24.9 Cr. Veefin reported a 127% year-on-year (YoY) increase in consolidated net profit to ₹24.9 Cr in H1 FY27 from ₹11 Cr in the corresponding period last year. Net profit was also up 9% from ₹22.8 Cr in H2 FY26. In Q2 FY27, Veefin's net profit rose 61% sequentially to ₹15.3 Cr from ₹9.5 Cr in the preceding quarter. Operating revenue increased 9% sequentially to ₹124.7 Cr from ₹114.2 Cr, while total income stood at ₹125.7 Cr. The company also reported a deal pipeline of around ₹920 Cr alongside its half-year results. Around 84% of the pipeline comprises opportunities from banks and financial institutions outside India, with Southeast Asia emerging as a key market. The mainboard listing is expected to widen access to Veefin's shares among retail and institutional investors. Unlike the fixed trading lots on the SME platform, the main boards allow investors to buy and sell shares individually. Veefin Bets On AI Employees In a statement, the fintech SaaS company said that it will now look at expanding beyond fintech with an AI platform that enables businesses to deploy digital employees for defined roles. Alongside the listing, the company announced a rebranding from veefin.com to veefin.ai, reflecting the growing role of AI in its products and growth strategy. Its next growth opportunity is through the Veefin AI Operating System (AIOS), a platform designed to help businesses create, deploy and supervise AI employees for defined roles. Veefin has developed more than 1,000 reusable AI skills and has started deploying AIOS internally across three functions: customer implementation, customer support and software testing. The company is using these deployments to improve productivity and build experience before offering the platform to customers. The company sees an opportunity to cross-sell the platform to its current customers and reach enterprises beyond the financial services sector. “We listed on the SME platform three years ago as a supply chain finance technology company. We come to the main boards as a multi-product company whose revenue has more than doubled in the past year, and with many more investors able to take part in what we build next,” Gautam Udani, vice chairperson, cofounder and COO of Veefin Group, said. Founded in 2020 by Udani and Raja Debnath, Mumbai-based Veefin develops lending, supply chain finance and transaction banking software for banks, NBFCs, fintech companies and enterprises. The company began with supply chain finance and has since expanded into trade finance, cash and liquidity management, loan origination, loan management, collections, and corporate and retail digital banking. Its customers use its technology through complete applications, platforms or individual components integrated into their own systems. Veefin has also expanded through acquisitions and strategic investments, including stakes in digital marketing firm White Rivers Media, generative AI startup Walnut AI and lending enablement platform EpikInDiFi. The mainboard transition follows a similar move by E2E Networks, which made its BSE mainboard debut in June after being listed on the NSE since 2018. E2E took the direct listing route to list its shares on the BSE.

Is honesty always the best policy? When to speak up — or stay silent
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Should you tell your partner how you really feel about their casserole? Offer a colleague feedback about their subpar interview performance? Let a stranger know she has toilet paper on her shoe?
Life Kit
How honest should you really be? Tips for sharing good and bad news
Sometimes the hardest part about talking to other people isn't finding the right words to say — but deciding if you should say anything at all, says social psychologist Vanessa Bohns.
"There are times when honesty is the best policy," she says. "On the other hand, honesty is not the best policy if whatever we say is going to be honest without any instrumental value."
Bohns is the author of Should I Say Something? The Science of What to Share—and What to Keep to Yourself, published in October. The book provides research-backed strategies to help you figure out when to share the truth or a personal opinion. It also offers advice on when to share good news, say sorry or be vulnerable.
There's a reason why giving difficult feedback or even loving criticism can feel like a dilemma. "It pains us to embarrass or hurt other people," Bohns says. So we don't tend to like doing it. In fact, there's a name for the phenomenon — the MUM effect, or minimizing unpleasant messages.
But with care and intention, it's possible to make informed choices about when to speak up or stay quiet, no matter how small or big the situation. Bohns shares three questions to ask yourself before sharing an opinion.
Is this information helpful?
When you decide to tell someone something, remember you're sharing two things: the message itself, and the fact that you are choosing to speak up at all, Bohns says.
People often spend far too much time worrying about the content of their messages, she says. "But the choice of saying something at all communicates so much. It says, 'I see you. I care about your suffering. I want to help you in some way.'"
So, before telling your boss/spouse/mother-in-law how you really feel about that new haircut, Bohn says to consider whether your feedback is actionable.
Honesty is only the best policy if your opinion is going to help someone "perform better or avoid embarrassment or learn something about themselves." If your feedback is mean-spirited, unrelated to the matter at hand or simply can't be enacted, you're probably better off holding your tongue.
For example, flat-out telling your roommate the cake she baked for your birthday tastes terrible? That's just mean. But if she bakes that same cake to enter into a baking competition? It would be mean not to offer her some feedback!
Would I want to hear this?
Just because you don't want to share the truth doesn't mean the person on the receiving end shouldn't or wouldn't want to hear what you have to say.
A 2022 survey, for example, found that people consistently underestimate others' desire for feedback. In the study, researchers put visible smudges of lipstick, chocolate or marker on their faces. Then, without acknowledging those smudges, they went out on the street asking random people to participate in a survey on a different topic.
Less than 3% of the survey participants spoke up, even though the smudges were something the researchers "clearly could have done something about and would have wanted to know," says Bohns.
So, if you choose to stay silent when your new co-worker keeps mispronouncing the name of the company CEO, for example, reflect on your own motivations. "Are you being kind, or are you avoiding your own discomfort?" writes Bohns in her book. Speaking up may help your colleague in this instance.
Do they want your feedback?
Has anyone ever given you advice about a topic you knew more about than they did? Or misjudged how much you knew based on how you looked?
When in doubt, don't assume you know what information the other person wants or needs from you. Pre-assessing how valuable the truth is to someone else, or their ability to handle it, can quickly make well-meaning feedback sound patronizing, writes Bohns in her book.
So just ask the other person if they want the feedback you have to share. "Give them the autonomy, then respect their decision, whatever it might be," she says.
