The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.
The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.
“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”
Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.
Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.
Associated Press contributed to this report

Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies.
Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories
- UK | Ministers are considering changing the law to force the entertainment industry to better protect women and children in the wake of the revelations over David Walliams and the conviction of Russell Brand.
- Climate | The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.
- US midterms | Democrat Scott Colom has become the first Black senator in Mississippi to be elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.
- Europe | Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
- Technology | Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.
In depth: Everything we know (or don’t) about the Nvidia affair
Last month, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, the former executive of a Singapore-based computing company, Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia; it buys the extremely valuable chips they produce, which are essential for powering AI, and rents computing space to Chinese companies. The US government had already been investigating whether Megaspeed could be flouting US restrictions and smuggling chips into China – allegations that both Nvidia and Megaspeed deny.
US intelligence officials, who had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, eventually concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who had been passing on information to Beijing. The intelligence behind this assessment is classified, so we don’t know exactly what they found – or which intelligence body was conducting the surveillance. Nvidia said Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected”, but on Sunday, Huang admitted in a letter to his employees that he had been having an affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children,” he said, adding that he was “deeply sorry”.
Nvidia’s valuation is inextricably linked to Huang. By yesterday, $430bn (5.5%) had been wiped off its share price, and in the early hours of this morning, that figure ballooned to about $600bn following reports that Nvidia’s board was deciding whether to oust Huang (you can follow the latest on that here). The company has appointed outside counsel to review the pair’s relationship and says it has no reason to believe that secrets or national security were compromised.
The most interesting aspects of this story are the questions we can’t (yet) answer. Did Nvidia’s board know that US intelligence suspected Alice Huang was a spy? What evidence led US intelligence to conclude she was spying for China? What information could she have passed to Beijing? And …
Who is Alice Huang?
Reporters and sleuths on Chinese social media have been trying to get to the bottom of who the Megaspeed chief really is. On Tuesday, the Financial Times published an interesting report (£) about Alice Huang’s backstory. She was born in the rural area of Hunan, worked as a journalist at China’s state broadcaster, then at HSBC and the investment bank Citic Securities. In 2015, she joined an investment management company Hexi.
There, she met financier Kang Wei. The two became romantically involved, and together they reinvented themselves as AI entrepreneurs. In 2023, Huang and her business partners acquired Megaspeed, a Singaporean subsidiary of a Chinese gaming company, which she and Wei aimed to turn into a datacentre business. According to the FT’s report, the two pitched investors on their ability to secure access to Nvidia chips.
Nobody knows exactly when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, when their relationship became romantic, or what information she might have passed to Beijing while it was going on. The earliest picture of them together is at an after-party following a tech trade show in Taipei, taken in 2024. As Aisha Down and Dan Milmo pointed out earlier this week, Jensen Huang is close to Donald Trump, so it’s possible that Alice Huang could have gained glimpses into US AI policy as it was being formed, into Trump’s thinking on AI, or into Nvidia’s company strategy. But without seeing the evidence, all this is speculation.
What does this reveal about Chinese espionage?
The US has been historically cautious about allowing AI chips to end up in Chinese hands. In 2022, Joe Biden’s administration introduced the Chips and Science Act, which restricted the sale of US chips in China, banning the export of most Nvidia chips. “The Chinese have a very strong pedigree for industrial espionage and copying other nations’ technologies,” Steve Tsang, the director of the SOAS China Institute, tells me. “They’ve been doing this for decades. And now it’s no longer engines they’re interested in, but AI.”
Both the US and China have an interest in gathering intelligence about each other’s AI firms. What’s more remarkable is the possibility that the Chinese spy agency, the MSS, could have recruited Alice Huang as a “honeytrap” to ensnare Jensen Huang – a method fraught with risk, which seems more reminiscent of 1970s spy fiction than contemporary counterintelligence (China, for its part, has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a spy).
“The facts clearly aren’t established, but it seems more likely that if Alice Huang was working for Beijing, the MSS would have recruited her after they became aware of her relationship with Huang, not before,” Nigel Inkster, the former director of operations and intelligence for the British Secret Intelligence Service, tells me.
China has built a large intelligence gathering operation: the MSS is now bigger than the CIA, and various national security laws mean that Chinese nationals can be required to provide assistance to the Chinese state. “You have a lot of people who can be co-opted into intelligence gathering, all of whom can be tasked with different requirements,” Inkster says. “Business delegations travelling abroad can be tasked with gathering information. So can visiting academics.”
“The big question, to my mind, is whether the Chinese intelligence agencies have actually been willing to deliver unwelcome information to the party leadership,” Inkster adds.
What approach has the US taken?
Jensen Huang is the most influential figure in the US AI industry outside major labs such as Anthropic, and has cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump. He’s successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen regulations on AI and roll back restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China (last year, Trump controversially approved the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chips directly to China in exchange for the federal government taking a 25% cut). Huang was present at the White House twice last month: once for a state dinner with Xi Jinping, and again for a meeting of tech and AI executives.
Huang’s close relationship with Trump could help explain why the president has so far played down concerns about Chinese espionage, appearing remarkably ambivalent about the recent allegations. The president was reportedly briefed last year about US intelligence conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, and in spring this year, his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, supervised the drafting of a classified memo warning that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with a Chinese spy. In May, Trump issued a last-minute invitation to Jensen Huang to board Air Force One in Alaska and join a delegation of executives bound to China. A US government official told reporters at the New York Times that when Rubio learned that Huang would be joining the trip in Alaska, he briefed Trump on the memo.
But on Monday, Trump, who is due to meet Xi Jinping later this month, said he had not known at the time of the trip about Huang’s relationship. He said the FBI had been investigating a matter relating to Huang, and defended the Nvidia CEO, describing him as an “honourable guy” who “built a great American company”.

Researchers from the Hoag Family Cancer Institute have made a potential breakthrough in the early diagnosis of ovarian cancer – a disease often detected after it has spread.
For decades, efforts to detect the cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumours. “We asked … what if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” said study leader Rajan Gogna.
Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. The study found that women experiencing these changes have elevated levels of a molecule called Tu-Stroma in their blood.
The study’s co-author Dr Esha Madan says the discovery “could transform how we approach prevention”.

A high-level meeting chaired by Minister for Local Self-Government K.M. Shaji in Thiruvananthapuram on Thursday sought a report from the Ernakulam District Collector on the temporary relocation of 78 families of P&T Apartment Complex at Mundamveli and the feasibility of potential permanent rehabilitation packages.
District Collector G. Priyanka has been asked to submit the report within a fortnight. The Keralam government will take steps to implement ‘Family Sustainability Mapping’ across the State to identify, at an early stage, children living in high-risk environments, Minister for Women and Child Development Bindhu Krishna has said.
Speaking at a press conference to announce the Ujjwala Balyam Awards on Wednesday (November 11, 2026), she said a decision regarding the mapping was reached during a meeting convened following the death of a two-year-old child in Alappuzha recently due to suspected malnutrition.
The circumstances of families and children will be assessed with the cooperation of schools, Anganwadis, local self-government institutions, District Child Protection Units, healthcare workers and the police. Children facing risks such as malnutrition, neglect, domestic abuse, child labour, begging, school dropouts, substance abuse-related issues or various forms of exploitation will be identified and necessary protection and rehabilitation will be ensured.
“Child protection efforts should not be limited to intervening only after abuse or exploitation has already occurred. The government’s objective is to proactively identify high risk situations and ensure timely protection for children. Coordinated action among various departments and institutions will be strengthened to prevent issues such as sexual abuse, physical and mental abuse, neglect, child labour, child begging, human trafficking and online exploitation,” she said.
Activities will be jointly coordinated by departments including the Department of Women and Child Development, the Health Department, the Police, and the Local Self Government Department. This will enable the strengthening of existing child protection systems as well as the proactive identification of risks and the implementation of preventive measures. The Minister stated that the active participation of society is essential to ensure a safe childhood and equal opportunities for every child and to create an environment in which they can grow up with self confidence.
Ms .Krishna said that a total of 52 children from 14 districts have been chosen for the Ujjwala Balyam Awards for showcasing exemplary talent in arts, sports, literature, science, social work, environmental protection, information technology, agriculture, waste management, humanitarian activities, crafts, sculpture and acts involving extraordinary courage.

Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.
The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
The skulls are believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians in the country that received more enslaved Africans than any other during the transatlantic slave trade.
Each was brought back in a padded box inside a reinforced suitcase, carried on flights by Brazilian diplomats after a four-year campaign to recover the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in the US.
Brazilian researchers from local universities will now try to learn more about who the two individuals were.
The skulls will not be displayed in museums or have their images released, and the Brazilian government has pledged that they will be buried with funeral rites as soon as the identification process is complete.
“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.
The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022, and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.
In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.
“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.
Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger, poverty, gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police.
During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.
“It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.
It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.
The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.
The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.
Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.
Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking.
The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.
“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.
Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.
“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

Brain implant company Synchron has paused clinical trials of its second-generation device after it failed to perform as expected in initial study participants, WIRED has learned.
The Brooklyn-based startup, a competitor to Elon Musk’s Neuralink, is also undergoing a restructuring, which includes eliminating jobs and scaling back its footprint in New York while building up a team in San Diego to support the development of an entirely new device.
Synchron is one of several companies developing brain-computer interface technology meant to allow people to control digital devices by reading brain signals and translating those signals into output commands. The company has touted its technology, dubbed the Stentrode, as minimally invasive since it does not rest in the brain itself or require brain surgery.
Instead, the stent-like mesh tube is inserted into the jugular vein at the base of the neck, then guided with a catheter to sit on top of the brain’s motor cortex. The company’s first-generation Stentrode connected using an external wire resting on a user’s chest. Ten volunteers across the US and Australia received that device and were able to send emails, text, browse the internet, and do online shopping and banking with their thoughts. Synchron has also enabled volunteers to control an Amazon Alexa and Apple’s iPad and Vision Pro without using their hands or voice.
Synchron’s second-generation device has fewer electrodes and is fully wireless, using Bluetooth to connect. The company launched a multisite trial in the US earlier this spring with sister sites in Australia and Canada to evaluate the newer Stentrode, and some participants have already had it implanted. Those sites have recently paused enrollment, however, because the device is not working as intended, according to sources familiar with the trials who asked to remain anonymous.
In a statement to WIRED, Synchron says it voluntarily paused enrollment “after identifying a performance issue involving the lead, the cable that carries signals from the Stentrode to the implanted electronics.”
“The issue does not involve the Stentrode itself and no safety issues related to the device have been identified. The pause was a company decision, not an FDA-directed action,” the statement continues.
The company says it has since brought lead design and manufacturing in-house. Instead of fixing the lead alone, Synchron says it is upgrading the whole Stentrode system and will resume trial enrollment once the hardware upgrades are complete.
“We will continue to support participants with Stentrode devices across their lifetime. Our commitment to their care and well-being remains unchanged,” Synchron says.

Two of the five US trial sites that WIRED was able to reach confirmed that recruitment is on hold at those locations. A coordinator at one site said the pause was not safety-related and was due to Synchron taking a look at the device to make sure the company is getting the readouts it is looking for.
These trials are key to Synchron advancing the Stentrode into a larger pivotal trial, which is needed for the US Food and Drug Administration to grant marketing approval.
“We still have strong confidence that it has the potential to be a first-line therapy,” CEO Tom Oxley says of the Stentrode.
Synchron’s website and LinkedIn page show around a dozen job openings in San Diego, including electrical and mechanical engineers, microchip designers, and materials scientists. The San Diego team will be designing and manufacturing the upgraded lead and Stentrode, as well as a separate device that the company has not yet revealed that will go “beyond the blood vessels altogether,” according to its website. Oxley previously told WIRED that the company was planning to develop a device that reaches multiple brain regions at once, which could allow more complex and natural functions beyond moving a cursor or making a mouse click.
The brain-computer interface field is expanding rapidly, with money pouring into companies pursuing both implanted devices and wearables. Synchron was estimated to have a nearly $1 billion valuation after closing a $200 million funding round last fall. It is backed by Khosla Ventures and the venture firms of Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos.
Neuralink was reportedly valued as high as $42 billion in secondary market transactions as of this summer. The company had an early problem with its implant in 2024 after it malfunctioned in its first volunteer, Noland Arbaugh. The coin-sized device sits in the skull and has 64 tiny, flexible wires that are threaded into the brain. A few weeks after Arbaugh received the device, several of the wires came out of his brain, leading to a loss of cursor control. Neuralink was able to compensate for the lost threads and restore control by modifying its recording algorithm.
Recent advances in artificial intelligence are fueling the development of brain-computer interfaces since AI models can read brain patterns faster and more accurately than traditional algorithms. Merge Labs, a brain-computer interface company cofounded by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, came out of stealth in January with $252 million in funding. OpenAI provided some of the funding, and the two companies are collaborating on AI models.
While these devices have shown incredible promise for people with severe motor disorders, they remain experimental. Synchron’s setback shows just how far the field still has to go before these systems are commercially available for patients.

Draft electoral rolls for SSR published in 13 states, 3 UTs; UP to release on Nov 17
Bihar’s list adds about 1.3 million electors over its post-SIR roll, while Tamil Nadu’s count rises to 57.7 million but remains below its pre-revision total.
Draft electoral rolls were published on Thursday in 16 states and Union territories as part of the Election Commission of India (ECI)’s Special Summary Revision (SSR) 2027, marking the start of a month-long window for claims and objections.
Originally slated for 17 states and UTs with January 1, 2027, as the qualifying date, Thursday’s rollout covers 13 states —Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttarakhand, West Bengal —and three UTs —Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep and Puducherry — after Uttar Pradesh deferred its draft publication by five days to November 17.
Voters across these regions have until December 11, 2026, to submit claims and objections ahead of the final roll publication on January 4, 2027. The window for UP voters will now run until December 16.
The qualifying date is the cut-off by which a person must have turned 18 to be eligible for enrolment in a given revision.
Also Read | Delhi SIR: Form 6 applications cross 3L-mark after draft roll excludes 47.5 lakh voters
The draft rolls published on Thursday show modest net additions to rolls that were pruned heavily during the SIR.
In Kerala, the draft roll has 27,360,254 names, against 26,953,644 in the final post-SIR roll, a rise of about 0.4 million. The state had 27.8 million voters before the SIR began.
In Manipur, the draft list has 1,994,357 electors, about 33,700 more than after the SIR, which deleted 0.189 million names and added 56,871. In Goa, around 43,000 voters were added and at least 11,000 deleted. Assam, where a Special Revision was held instead of the SIR, recorded a net increase of 218,771 electors, taking the roll to about 25.2 million, including 287,233 electors aged 18-19. Rajasthan’s draft roll has 52,667,416 registered voters.
Tamil Nadu is still well below its pre-SIR strength. It had 64.1 million voters before the SIR. This number dropped to 56.7 million electors when the post-SIR rolls were published. As per the draft SSR rolls published on Thursday, the state has 57.7 million electors.

In Bihar, the draft roll lists 75.5 million electors. This is about 1.3 million more than the post SIR number of 74.2 million electors.
Thursday’s publication marks the formal opening of the public revision phase under SSR 2027, the first routine roll update in most of these states since the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
A senior ECI official told HT, “This is in line with the ECI notification issued on October 15. SSR is a routine process and the exercise will proceed as usual and in accordance with the Representation of the People Act (1950).”
The SSR, which is an annual exercise, uses the existing roll as its starting point, generally carrying forward existing voters’ names to the draft roll. The exercise will be carried out in every state after the SIR is completed.
First-time voters can fill Form 6 to get included in the voter list. Advance applications will also open for those turning 18 on April 1, July 1 or October 1, 2027.

Under the SSR, officials start with the existing roll, publish a draft and invite claims and objections.
Booth-level officers verify new applications, and EROs decide on them before the final roll is published. In the SIR, however, electors are largely asked to fill enumeration forms and the roll is rebuilt from those forms, requiring voters to establish their eligibility.

Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the US Congress. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast confirmed that the Nvidia founder agreed after senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him. The development comes as Nvidia announced Huang’s immediate resignation as president, chief executive and board member following reports of an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China.
“Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,”
 Mast told reporters at the US Capitol, a Bloomberg report claims. 
“I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.”
When is Jensen Huang expected to testify
Huang is expected to testify under oath before the Thanksgiving holiday later this month, according to the report. The session appears likely to take place behind closed doors, although Mast said he expected it to be recorded on video and transcribed.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee will participate alongside the House’s China and Intelligence panels. A final date for the testimony was not specified in Mast’s remarks. 
Mast’s comments also referred to his disagreements with Huang over export controls, the rules governing sales of sensitive technology to other countries.
What Nvidia said about Jensen Huang’s resignation
While reports described Huang as being ousted, Nvidia’s announcement said he had resigned as president, CEO and a member of its board, effective immediately.
The company named executive vice president and chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive. She will continue in her finance role until the board decides on a permanent replacement, which will involve both internal and external candidates.
Kress joined Nvidia in September 2013 after nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft. The board also appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair.
Shortly after Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation, US President Donald Trump suggested that Apple executive chair Tim Cook should take over as the company’s permanent CEO, an NBC News report claimed.

US set to host Quad Leaders Summit in Manila next week
India, the US, Japan and Australia are expected to announce new initiatives on economic security and strategic infrastructure at the Quad summit in Manila.
Quad member states are expected to unveil several deliverables, mainly focused on economic security and strategic infrastructure, at the leaders’ summit that is expected to be held on the margins of the Asean Summit in Manila next week, people familiar with the matter said.
The upcoming Quad Leaders’ Summit — the first gathering of the leaders of India, Australia, Japan and the US since September 2024 — is set to be hosted by the US, the people said on condition of anonymity. India was set to chair the leaders’ summit in 2025, but its efforts to arrange the meeting last year were hampered by a lack of clarity over US President Donald Trump’s travel plans.
The deliverables expected to be unveiled at the upcoming summit were finalised at the Quad foreign ministers’ meeting on the margins of the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta on October 31, the people said. The foreign ministers’ meeting resulted in several outcomes, including the provision of technical and financial aid worth more than $85 million to support access to trusted artificial intelligence (AI) technologies across the Indo-Pacific.
Economic security will remain an area of focus for the Quad, even as the grouping continues its work on critical technologies, maritime domain awareness and strategic infrastructure across the Indo-Pacific, the people said.
The people also pointed to the significance of the US hosting the Quad Leaders’ Summit in Manila amid continuing tensions between China and the Philippines. Beijing and Manila have had a series of testy exchanges since last month, when the Chinese envoy reacted strongly to Philippine defence secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr’s description of China as a regional “troublemaker”.
The envoy responded by saying that the Philippines should be grateful to have a neighbour like China, adding that “if we want to use force, we may easily win”. This was followed by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos saying that the envoy’s remarks sounded “very much like a threat”.
However, there is still a lack of clarity on the timing of the Quad Leaders’ Summit, which is expected to be held later in the day on November 17, following the East Asia Summit, the people said. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to arrive in Manila on the afternoon of November 16 and leave early on November 18, the people said.
The upcoming summit will also mark a departure from the practice of holding such meetings only in Quad member states.

Telangana to introduce 10+2 system in all state-run schools from 2027-28 to prevent dropouts, says CM Revanth Reddy
Under the proposed new structure, education will be divided into three stages: primary, secondary and senior secondary.
The Telangana government will introduce a 10 plus 2 education system in all the state-run schools from the next 2027-28 academic year, extending school education up to Class 12 on the lines of Kendriya Vidyalayas, chief minister A Revanth Reddy announced on Wednesday.
Currently, school education till Class 10 is overseen by the School Education Department, with the 10th-grade Secondary School Certificate (SSC) public examinations conducted by the Telangana Board of Secondary Education. The next two years are called Intermediate Education and are governed separately by the Board of Intermediate Education (BIE).
Under the proposed new structure, education will be divided into three stages: primary education from nursery to Class 4, secondary education from Classes 5 to 8, and senior secondary education from Classes 9 to 12, all governed in a single system.
What CM Reddy said
At a review meeting held with education department officials at the Marri Channa Reddy Human Resources Development Institute, the chief minister said the decision was aimed at reducing student dropouts after Class 10 and ensuring continuity in education, particularly among girls and students from disadvantaged communities.
Revanth Reddy directed the department officials to make all necessary arrangements for implementing the new system from next year as part of a broader initiative to overhaul the state's education sector.
He said the government's objective was to provide quality education from the nursery level to university and equip students with the knowledge and skills required to compete in the modern world.
Revanth Reddy emphasised that students should develop proficiency in languages and communication skills by the time they complete Class 12.
“They should also be given opportunities to pursue subjects of their choice after the senior secondary stage and develop expertise in their respective fields,” he said.
The chief minister expressed concern over the increasing number of students dropping out after Class 10, particularly girls and children belonging to Dalit, tribal and minority communities.
“Extending schooling up to Class 12 within the same education system would help address the problem by ensuring uninterrupted access to education,” he said.
He pointed out that institutions such as Kendriya Vidyalayas, Navodaya Vidyalayas and Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas, which provide education up to Class 12, record comparatively lower dropout rates.
Officials briefed the chief minister on progress in preparing the proposed education structure, which covers the entire learning cycle from nursery to intermediate education.
The meeting also discussed the implementation of the 10+2 system in 18 other states nationwide. The Telangana government has decided to introduce the system with the stated objective of improving access to quality education, reducing dropouts and providing students with better academic and career opportunities.

A video showing smoke and flames gushing from a multi-storey building is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows a massive fire at Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, caused by an AC blast in a flat on the 21st floor. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals show a massive fire at Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, caused by an AC blast in a flat on the 21st floor in November 2026.
Fact: While a fire accident took place at Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, after an AC unit exploded in June 2026, the viral visuals are AI-generated. Gautam Buddha Nagar Police Commissionerate clarified in a post on X that the information being circulated was misleading and baseless. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
Upon conducting a relevant keyword search using the details mentioned in the viral claim, we found reports from June 2026 stating that a fire broke out in a flat on the 21st floor of Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, at around 8 AM, following an AC unit explosion. According to reports, six fire engines rushed to the spot after receiving information about the incident, and firefighters brought the fire under control after about 30 minutes (here, here, here).
However, we also found reports dated 10 November 2026 stating that an AI-generated video of a fire sparked panic; 20 fire brigade teams arrived, but found nothing (here, here). According to these reports, a video claiming to show a fire caused by an AC blast in a flat on the 21st floor of Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, went viral on social media. Following this, the police and fire brigade teams were alerted and rushed to the location. However, they found no fire at the site.
Moreover, the Gautam Buddha Nagar Police Commissionerate clarified in a post on X that the information being circulated was misleading and baseless. It also stated that a case had been registered under relevant sections against the person responsible for creating and sharing the misleading information, and that strict legal action was being taken.
We also verified the viral video by running it through AI detection tools, HIVE AI and SynthID.
To sum up, an AI-Generated fire accident video is falsely linked to AC Blast at Noida’s Aranya society.

Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED.
An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.
“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.
One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”
The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment.
Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email.
Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO, and former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips.
It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.
Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.”
Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

The young politicians with African roots making history in the US midterms
- Published
"JD [Vance], habibi (my love)".
It was an unlikely greeting to hear at a Democratic Party victory rally after the US midterm elections.
Abdul El-Sayed, 42, born to Egyptian immigrant parents, playfully addressed Vice-President JD Vance, who had campaigned against him but will now swear him into office in January as Michigan's new Senator.
The US-born Democrat spent much of his campaign fending off attacks from conservative media and President Donald Trump, who accused him of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed rejected the allegations.
"My name is Abdul Rahman Mohammed El-Sayed," he said in an Egyptian Arabic accent to the cheering crowd at his victory rally. His Arabic Muslim name was a target for many of his opponents. He is set to become the first Muslim senator.
El-Sayed ran a social media-first campaign, with TikTok edits showing him speaking directly to young voters, tapping into Gen Z humour, and sporting friendship bracelets.
The former public health administrator's campaign centred on a progressive agenda, including Medicare for All, affordable housing and curbing corporate influence in politics. He has also been a vocal critic of US military aid to Israel.
But El-Sayed was not alone. From an Ethiopian-born Gen Z congresswoman to candidates with Nigerian heritage, several other politicians with African roots won in this year's midterms.
The elections, held halfway through a president's four-year term, decide who represents Americans in Congress, as well as in thousands of state and local offices.
At 29, Melat Kiros became the first Gen Z woman elected to the US Congress.
Born in Ethiopia, she arrived in the US as a baby and grew up in Denver. She had never held elected office before defeating a 15-term incumbent in Colorado's 1st District in the Democrat primary before winning a landslide in Tuesday's election.
Kiros, like El-Sayed, campaigned on issues that have become central to young progressive voters: the cost of living, universal childcare and Medicare for All.
Endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, she has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and ending US military aid to Israel.
Her outspoken criticism of Israel's war in Gaza has attracted controversy. Kiros has said her criticism is directed at the Israeli state, not Jewish people.
She was fired from a top New York law firm in 2023 after she refused to take down an open letter to dozens of law firms who had urged law school deans to crack down on antisemitism on campuses as students engaged in pro-Palestinian protests.
Kiros condemned antisemitism, but warned the law firms, including the one she worked for, against conflating "such bigotry with the geo-political question of Israel's legitimacy".
She said she started thinking more seriously about politics in general after being fired.
Adrian Boafo, meanwhile, a second-generation Ghanaian-American, will represent Maryland's 5th Congressional District after succeeding veteran Congressman Steny Hoyer, who retired after a political career spanning more than four decades.
The 32-year-old was born in Virginia and raised in Prince George's County, Maryland. His parents immigrated to the US from Ghana.
Boafo's route to Congress began in local politics. He served on the Bowie City Council before becoming a Maryland state delegate in 2023. He also worked for Hoyer before eventually winning the race to replace him.
His campaign focused on the cost of living, childcare and protecting federal workers, a major issue in a district close to Washington DC and home to thousands of government employees.
In his victory statement, Boafo said representing his constituents had "never felt more urgent", pointing to federal job cuts, rising costs and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
Among those returning to Congress is Somali-born Ilhan Omar, 44, who won a fifth term despite an ongoing federal investigation.
Federal agents searched her Washington home in October as part of an investigation into her immigration paperwork. Omar has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.
First elected to Congress in 2018, Omar became the first Somali-American and one of the first Muslim women to serve in the chamber. She has also been a frequent target of President Trump, who has repeatedly criticised her and other Somali immigrants.
Trump has previously used derogatory language to describe some African countries, including Somalia. In October, his Yemeni-born adviser Amer Ghalib said the president would refrain from using such language.
Others made their breakthroughs in state and local politics.
Junior Ezeonu was born in Nigeria and moved to the US as a young child. By 27, he had already become Grand Prairie's youngest city council member before winning a seat in the Texas State House.
Then there is Carol Kazeem, 34, a Pennsylvania state legislator of Nigerian heritage who has retained her seat at District 159. At least four candidates with Nigerian heritage won in the 3 November midterms.
For some young Africans watching from across the Atlantic, these victories have offered a glimpse of what a new generation of voters could achieve at home.
On social media, users have shared the election results as a source of inspiration, particularly in Nigeria and Kenya, where major elections are due in 2027.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

Indian security personnel carrying batons and shields and accompanied by riot control vehicles surrounded the site of a planned opposition protest in Delhi on Sunday that is set to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Authorities warned of traffic diversions ahead of the protest march and rally that will be led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi. The opposition says it expects hundreds of thousands of people to participate in what it says will be a major challenge to the prime minister, Narendra Modi, and his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta party have held near-daily demonstrations since last month demanding that the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, step down over the voter list revision that critics say favours the BJP.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.
The opposition parties have announced they will hold a nearly 1.5km march on Sunday from central Delhi to the Ramlila Maidan, a ground that is the designated site for their protest rally.
Visuals from news agency ANI showed riot control vehicles and dozens of security personnel armed with batons and shields outside the rally venue, where announcements were being made urging people to ensure smooth traffic movement and cooperate with police officials.
Delhi traffic police said a “large gathering” was expected at the venue, and traffic regulations and diversions would be implemented “as required”.
“People have started coming to participate in this rally ... we have ensured proper arrangements at the venue, and arrangements are also planned on the route of the march that will happen in a few hours from now,” senior police officer Rohit Rajbir told ANI.
The protests demanding Kumar’s resignation erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported in September that his two deputies had raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The change, which began last year, removed over 130 million names from voter lists, including 28 million who died, 63 million who relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party – allegations the poll panel and BJP reject.
