Consumer tech focussed venture capital firm Fireside Ventures has seen a second exit from its leadership and investment team in two weeks. Prayag Mohanty, principal at Fireside Ventures, who led its early-stage bets, has quit the firm, Inc42 has learnt from multiple sources. His exit follows a bigger leadership change at Fireside Ventures. Earlier this month, the firm said that cofounder and partner Vinay Singh has stepped down after nearly a decade at the firm. Responding to Inc42's query, Fireside Ventures confirmed Mohanty’s exit. "Prayag Mohanty is moving on from his role of Principal at Fireside Ventures. We value his contributions made during his time with us, and wish him the best in his future endeavours," Fireside said in a statement to Inc42. Another Blow For Fireside Mohanty joined Fireside Ventures as a Principal in January 2020. He was one of five principals listed on the firm's investment team, alongside Ankur Khaitan, Shuchi Pandya, Varun Varma and Ankita Balotia. As a principal leading Fireside’s early stage investments, Mohanty fronted several of the firm's seed stage bets over the past year, including a ₹8 Cr round in Gurugram-based men's personal care brand Unbound, a ₹20 Cr round in Noida-based Oroos Confectionery and another ₹8 Cr seed round in kids wellness startup Wellopia. In earlier media reports, he was quoted as saying that Fireside Ventures is ramping up investments in pre-product-market-fit and even pre-revenue startups through a co-investment model with other funds and angel investors, with 8-10 such deals in the pipeline from the new third fund. Before Fireside, Mohanty had spent about seven years as a principal at IvyCap Ventures from 2013 to 2020, and was involved in deals for listed jewellery giant BlueStone, BiryaniByKilo and Vinculum. The key departures come less than a year after Fireside announced the final close of its Fund IV at ₹2,265 Cr (about $253 Mn) in December 2025. With Singh’s exit, the firm is being led by founder and managing partner Kanwaljit Singh and cofounders and partners Kannan Sitaram and Dipanjan Basu. The fund drew commitments from LPs including the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), Investment Corporation of Dubai, HarbourVest, Waterfield and Fidelity International. In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament building.
Fact: The video does not show the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament. It shows a pro-Palestine activist replacing the German national flag with a Palestinian flag on a flagpole outside the Reichstag building, which houses the German Parliament (Bundestag), in Berlin on 08 November 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) featuring visuals similar to those seen in the viral video. According to these reports, the incident took place outside the Reichstag building, which houses the German Parliament (Bundestag), in Berlin on Sunday, 08 November 2026.
The reports (here, here) state that a 22-year-old pro-Palestine activist climbed a 30-metre-high flagpole in front of the Reichstag building at around 11:30 am, removed the German national flag, and replaced it with a Palestinian flag.
The group ‘Peacefully Against Genocide‘ claimed responsibility for the incident, stating that the action was a protest against the German government’s pro-Israel policy and its silence on alleged human rights violations in Gaza.
According to a press release issued by Berlin Police on 08 November 2026, two people who allegedly assisted the 22-year-old activist were detained and later released after their identities were established. The Palestinian flag was subsequently removed with the assistance of the Berlin Fire Brigade. Police also launched an investigation into suspected offences, including insulting state symbols, damaging government property, trespassing, and violating Berlin’s assembly law.
To sum up, the viral video shows the Palestinian flag hoisted outside the German Parliament, not the Israeli Parliament.

Congo's Ebola cases have crossed 11,000 cases in another development that shows the severity of the outbreak.
Also Read: Congo’s Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases as authorities race to slow spread in African countries
The latest Health Ministry data on Wednesday (November 11, 2026) showed 11,042 people have been infected by the deadly virus that has now killed 5,387, nearly half of those infected, in the country's deadliest outbreak.
Since the outbreak was declared mid-May, Congolese authorities have struggled to contain it due to a series of factors including conflicts and a health system crisis.
The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no known vaccine or treatment and has spread to the eight of the country's 26 Provinces.
Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first discovered in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa from 2014 to 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current outbreak already ranks second, and has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared compared with the West Africa outbreak. Health officials declared the outbreak in May, but medical evidence suggests infections were occurring months earlier.

An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.
The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.
"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen, a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."
The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.
"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.
Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.
"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.
Researchers have been searching for a drug to lower Lp(a)
Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).
So Nissen and his colleagues gave 8,350 adults who already had heart disease either a placebo or a drug called pelacarsen, which cuts Lp(a).
The drug did suppress Lp(a) levels by about 78%, the researchers showed. But after five years, that drop didn't translate into saving people from suffering cardiovascular complications.
"Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," says Nissen, who presented the first details about the study at an American Heart Association meeting in Chicago Saturday and published more specifics in the New England Journal of Medicine and the NEJM Evidence.
Drugmaker Novartis, which sponsored the study, announced last month that the study results hadn't met its goals but without releasing specifics.
In a statement, Novartis said the study "provides meaningful evidence" about the relationship between Lp(a) and heart disease and may "help inform future approaches to cardiovascular management." "Progress in science depends on pursuing challenging questions and studies [like the pelacarsen study] play a crucial role in moving the field forward, even if the results are not what we had hoped for," the company said.
What went wrong?
The failure of the drug to help patients is stunning because so many scientists, doctors and drug companies hoped Lp(a)-lowering drugs would provide the next major weapon in the fight against cardiovascular disease, which kills more than 900,000 Americans each year.
"I think it's a big deal because the expectation was so high that this would end up being positive," says Harlan Krumholz, a Yale University cardiologist. "And so it was really jarring to see this."
Researchers are scratching their heads about what went wrong.
It could turn out that high Lp(a) doesn't actually cause heart attacks and strokes, but instead is a marker for something else that increases the risk.
There could be other reasons for why the study failed.
"Maybe you need to treat longer. You may need to treat earlier, before people have advanced hardening of the arteries," says Roger Blumenthal, a cardiologist at Johns Hopkins University.
Another possibility is that Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only help people with higher Lp(a) levels.
"Maybe a higher Lp(a) should have been required for entry into the trial," says David Maron, a Stanford University cardiologist who serves as the president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.
The pelacarsen study could also have failed because Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only benefit people whose blood pressure and bad cholesterol weren't as well controlled, several experts said.
Another explanation could be that there's something about pelacarsen, the experimental drug, that doesn't produce a benefit.
It's possible other Lp(a)-lowering drugs might.
Several other drugmakers, including Amgen and Eli Lilly, are testing other experimental Lp(a)-lowering drugs. The results of those trials are expected to become available over the next few years.
"The take-home message is the story's not over," says Karol Watson, a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. "It's kind of just starting."

A Mumbai-based man's account of his cook's monthly earnings of ₹1.05 lakh has sparked a discussion about income, financial security and conventional measures of professional success. The cook reportedly earns through assignments across multiple households and by catering to film crews during night shoots. He is now planning his first international holiday with friends, with Thailand as the destination. In a LinkedIn post, Manuraaj Garg compared the cook's financial circumstances with those of some of his MBA-educated friends. He highlighted how multiple sources of income, a limited commute and relatively low expenses have shaped the cook's approach to money. Garg detailed the cook's earnings from different assignments. The cook charges ₹18,000 for preparing meals twice a day at Garg's home. He earns another ₹16,500 from a flat in the same building and ₹38,000 from a larger family nearby for cooking and managing kitchen-related work. The cook also works at a film set on Friday nights, preparing food for the crew during night shoots. “Friday nights he’s at a film set – feeding a unit through a night shoot, dal-chawal at 1 am while the hero does retakes: ₹7,500 a night,” Garg said. Garg added that the cook's wife earns ₹45,000 a month, taking their combined household income to approximately ₹1.5 lakh. Comparing these earnings with the financial realities of some of his MBA-educated friends, Garg said higher salaries do not necessarily translate into equivalent disposable income once taxes, equated monthly instalments (EMIs) and childcare expenses are accounted for. “What’s actually left for the month is often his number – without the paper.” Garg also drew attention to the difference between the cook's earnings and the formal employment structures followed by salaried professionals. “His money has never met the system. No Form 16, no TDS, no CTC breakup, no 'variable component'. Not because he’s hiding – the system was simply never built to see him,” he said, adding that what the cook earns is what he gets to keep. The cook's work is spread across four employers, all within a two-kilometre radius. According to Garg, this arrangement allows him to diversify his income rather than depend on a single employer. Losing one assignment would affect only a portion of his earnings. Garg also said the cook regularly receives enquiries from prospective employers willing to pay more for reliable service. He contrasted this with the experiences of some of his IIT-educated friends, who sometimes struggle to receive responses from employers even after completing multiple interview rounds. Another difference, Garg noted, is the cook's approach to spending. He does not face the same pressure to maintain an expensive lifestyle or meet social expectations around cars, schooling and appearances. “His financial advisor is one sentence: 'Arre pagal hai kya, bahut mehenga hai.' My friends’ financial advisor is also one sentence: 'Chalo yaar, let’s do it,'” Garg wrote. Despite his relatively cautious approach to spending, the cook does have an indulgence: the latest iPhone Pro, which he purchased on EMI. Garg said he otherwise avoids unnecessary expenses and is careful about his spending. The 34-year-old is now preparing for his first international holiday with friends. The planned Thailand trip will also mark his first flight and his first passport. Garg recalled sharing travel tips with the cook, including recommendations to visit Maya Bay, sample street food and rent a scooter. Their conversation, he said, briefly moved beyond the employer-employee relationship as they exchanged travel stories and holiday plans. “For ten minutes, nobody was anybody’s employer – just two boys talking Thailand,” he wrote, adding that his wife eventually asked them to return to their respective work. Concluding his post, Garg questioned conventional ways of measuring financial well-being. “He is not poor. He is not rich. He is something our spreadsheets don’t have a column for: a man whose maths still works,” he said. Through the account, Garg highlighted how multiple income sources, manageable expenses and personal spending choices can shape an individual's financial circumstances beyond the conventional measures of salary and job titles. One nice thing about discovering exoplanets is that, once you work out how long their orbits take, they continue to show up like clockwork. The timing is so regular, in fact, that we can use variations to detect the gravitational influence of additional planets in the same exosolar system. And the precise timing is useful in that we can rely on it to point telescopes at the system when we know some of the light we detect has passed through the planet’s atmosphere.
Except when we can’t.
On Monday, researchers reported on an exoplanet that simply stopped showing up. TOI-2535b is a hot Jupiter-sized planet we’ve been observing as it transits between its host star, TOI-2535, and Earth for about seven years now. But it recently stopped showing up, and researchers suspect that’s due to an unseen companion orbiting in a different plane.
Big changes
TOI-2535 is one of the many stars with exoplanet candidates identified by TESS, the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite. It’s a K dwarf, meaning it’s somewhat smaller than the Sun. And TESS found signs of a Jupiter-sized planet orbiting it every eight days, an orbit close enough to make TOI-2535b a “hot Jupiter” exoplanet. At that point, there was nothing especially unusual about it.
But a closer look at the data showed two very strange things. First, the timing of when its transits occurred could shift by as much as six hours, a substantial variation for an orbit this brief. That’s typically a sign of gravitational interactions with another planet; depending on the details of that second planet’s orbit, it may slow the first one or accelerate it through a transit more quickly. Since the second planet doesn’t show up in TESS data, it appears to orbit in a slightly different plane, so it doesn’t pass between its host star and Earth.

- Bandipora-Gurez, Mughal Road, Srinagar-Leh Highway closed
- Wet Spell Likely to Continue Till Friday; Temps Likely to Drop 6-8°C
Srinagar- Fresh snowfall in the higher reaches and rainfall across the plains brought a chill to Kashmir on Thursday, disrupting traffic on several key roads, including the Bandipora-Gurez Road, Mughal Road and Srinagar-Leh Highway, as the Meteorological Department forecast more rain and snow across Jammu and Kashmir.
Under the influence of an active Western Disturbance, several higher reaches of the Valley, including Gulmarg, Sonamarg, Zojila Pass, Margan Pass, Drass, Machil Valley and Jumagund in Kupwara district, received fresh snowfall.
The plains of Dawar in Gurez Valley also witnessed the season’s first snowfall, officials said.
Razdan Pass in Bandipora district recorded around six inches of fresh snow, while approximately two inches accumulated at Peer Ki Gali along the Mughal Road in Shopian district.
Following the snowfall and slippery road conditions, vehicular movement on the Bandipora-Gurez Road, Mughal Road and Srinagar-Sonamarg-Gumri Road, which connects Kashmir with Ladakh through Zojila Pass, was suspended.
The Border Roads Organisation’s 56 RCC has launched snow-clearance operations at Razdan Pass to restore connectivity along the strategic Bandipora-Gurez road.
Meanwhile, the plains of Kashmir, including Srinagar and parts of north and central Kashmir, received rainfall, bringing down daytime temperatures and intensifying the chill.
The wet weather also triggered a landslide along the Uri-Baramulla National Highway at Rajanwani in north Kashmir, disrupting vehicular movement and leaving commuters stranded.
Officials said debris and boulders accumulated on the road following the landslide, bringing traffic to a halt. Road clearance operations were initiated to restore movement.
According to the Meteorological Department, an active Western Disturbance is affecting Jammu and Kashmir on November 12 and 13, bringing light to moderate rainfall in the plains and moderate to heavy snowfall in higher reaches.
Director Meteorological Centre Srinagar Mukhtar Ahmad said several mountainous areas were likely to receive significant snowfall under the influence of the weather system.
The higher reaches of Kupwara, Bandipora and Ganderbal districts are likely to witness moderate to heavy snowfall, while mountainous areas of south Kashmir, the Pir Panjal range and Chenab Valley may also receive fresh snow.
Popular tourist destinations, including Gulmarg, Sonamarg, Pahalgam and Doodhpathri, are also likely to experience snowfall.
In the Jammu region, Poonch and adjoining areas may receive moderate to heavy rainfall, while other parts are expected to witness light to moderate precipitation. Thunderstorms, hailstorms and gusty winds are also likely at isolated places.
The MeT department has forecast a fall of 6-8 degrees Celsius in daytime temperatures across Jammu and Kashmir during November 12 and 13.
A brief spell of light rain and snowfall at a few places is expected on November 14 and 15, while generally dry weather is likely from November 16 to 20.
The anticipated snowfall could affect traffic movement on several high-altitude roads and mountain passes, including Zojila, Razdan Pass, Sadhna Pass, Sinthan Top, Margan Top and Peer Ki Gali on the Mughal Road.
Authorities have advised commuters and travellers to avoid travelling on affected roads until further notice and follow official traffic advisories. Travellers, transporters and tourists have also been advised to plan their journeys in view of the possibility of disruptions on mountain passes and hilly roads.
Farmers have been advised to safely store harvested crops during November 12 and 13 to prevent possible damage from rainfall.
Meanwhile, the Mechanical and Hospital Engineering Department (MHED), Division Anantnag, conducted mock drills of snow-clearance machinery across Tehsil Kokernag to assess operational preparedness ahead of the forecast wet spell.
SRINAGAR RECORDS 17.3°C
Meanwhile, according to the latest weather data issued by the Meteorological Centre Srinagar on Thursday, Srinagar recorded a maximum temperature of 17.3°C and a minimum of 5.6°C.
Qazigund recorded a maximum of 16.7°C and a minimum of 5.8°C, while Pahalgam recorded a maximum of 14.5°C and a minimum of 2.7°C.
Kupwara recorded a maximum temperature of 17.3°C and a minimum of 3.7°C, while Kokernag recorded 15°C and 6.4°C, respectively.
Gulmarg recorded a maximum temperature of 9.9°C, while the minimum settled at minus 0.6°C, making it the coldest among the weather stations in the Kashmir division.
Among other automatic weather stations, Bandipora recorded a maximum of 19.9°C and a minimum of 6.1°C, Baramulla 18.1°C and 6.4°C, Shopian 16.8°C and 2.2°C, while Sonamarg recorded 11.9°C and 2.6°C, respectively.
The maximum rainfall recorded was 7.5 mm at the AWS Gulmarg station, according to the weather bulletin.
In the Jammu division, Jammu city recorded a maximum temperature of 27.6°C and a minimum of 15.3°C.
The MeT department has advised people, particularly those travelling through higher reaches and mountain passes, to remain cautious and follow weather and traffic advisories in view of the prevailing conditions.

Pakistan’s former Prime Minister Imran Khan was taken to hospital in Islamabad late on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) for medical treatment and returned to prison, sources said.
Khan, who is imprisoned in Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi, had an eye check-up at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), one of the officials said on Wednesday (November 11).
“He had some blood pressure issues ... and was given required treatment last night. He has been shifted back to his prison cell,” the person said.
The cricketer-turned-politician has faced multiple corruption charges since he lost power in a no-confidence vote in 2022, and has been in prison for more than three years. All of Khan’s convictions bar one have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing and says the charges are politically motivated, a claim the government denies.
Khan’s lawyers say the 74-year-old’s health has deteriorated in prison and that he has lost significant vision in his right eye.
It is the first known instance of Khan being taken to hospital for treatment and returned to jail since August, when his hospital visit was cut short.
A Pakistani court has also ordered jail authorities to allow Khan’s legal team to see him and his wife, his party said.
His party’s deputy chairman, Shah Mehmood Qureshi, was also taken to hospital in the eastern city of Lahore from a jail in the same city on Tuesday (November 10). He remains in hospital.

While this claim spread in 2026, the actual incident happened in 2020.
A claim is spreading online that a bald eagle attacked a $950 "government drone" in midair, sending it crashing into Lake Michigan.
Social media users shared the story on Facebook and Reddit, prompting Snopes readers to search the website to determine whether a bald eagle had, in fact, launched a successful attack against a foreign object in its airspace.
This story is true — although it happened years ago, not in 2026. It is also worth noting that while some posts online appear to show a bald eagle flying at a drone, there is no actual footage of the incident, according to the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy, or EGLE — the agency whose drone lost to the eagle.
Michigan state officials confirmed the eagle's assault in an Aug. 13, 2020, news release titled, "Shoreline-mapping EGLE drone sent to watery Lake Michigan grave by U.P. bald eagle." (U.P. is a reference to Michigan's Upper Peninsula.)
Here's how that release began:
An Upper Peninsula bald eagle launched an airborne attack on a drone operated by a Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) pilot last month, tearing off a propeller and sending the aircraft to the bottom of Lake Michigan.
The brazen eagle vs. EGLE onslaught took place near Escanaba in Michigan's Upper Peninsula on July 21 when EGLE environmental quality analyst and drone pilot Hunter King was mapping shoreline erosion for use in the agency's efforts to document and help communities cope with high water levels.
King had completed about seven minutes of the mapping flight — his fourth of the day in the area — when satellite reception got spotty. He pressed the "Go Home" recall button. The drone dutifully turned, reacquiring a strong satellite feed.
King was watching his video screen as the drone beelined for home, but suddenly it began twirling furiously. "It was like a really bad rollercoaster ride," said King. When he looked up, the drone was gone, and an eagle was flying away. A nearby couple, whose pastimes include watching the local eagles attack seagulls and other birds, later confirmed they saw the eagle strike something but were surprised to learn it was a drone. Both King and the couple said the eagle appeared uninjured as it flew from the scene of the crime.
The release also confirmed that the drone was "a $950 Phantom 4 Pro Advanced" and shared data indicating that the eagle tore off a propeller, as many of the claim posts said (emphasis ours):
Data from the flight records detailed the drone's final moments:
- The eagle strike occurred 7:39.7 into the flight roughly four-tenths of a mile from King and 162 feet above the water
- Its speed instantly dropped from 22 mph to 10. Within a half-second the flight record shows the beginning of downward spiral along with "excessive spinning" warnings
- In the next 3.5 seconds the drone sent 27 warning notifications including one indicating a propeller had been torn off
- Gaining momentum as it fell, its last communication came at 34 feet above the water, falling at 30 feet per second, or 20.4 mph.
Per the release, King and the unidentified couple searched for the drone, "but hours of scouring the shoreline were fruitless." An unmanned aircraft systems coordinator with the state agency, Arthur Ostaszewski, also attempted to find the drone using a kayak, snorkeling gear and "telemetric data from the flight that pinpointed exactly where the drone hit the lake." He, too, was unsuccessful, even after walking a grid pattern for two hours — "like I was playing Battleship and wanted to cover the entire board," he said.
A week later, however, a team of Michigan state employees — which the agency cheekily dubbed in a news release as the Willful Eagle Trauma Team Engaged in Retrieval, or WETTER — managed to uncover the drone in almost the exact same location after "the previously murky water had cleared due to shifting winds and currents." EGLE shared a few pictures of the recovery effort on X, then known as Twitter:
The agency noted that the drone was not recording at the time of the bald eagle's assault, meaning that there would not be any footage of the fight over airspace.
Michigan officials speculated that the attack could have been "a territorial squabble with the electronic foe, or just a hungry eagle."
"Or maybe it did not like its name being misspelled," EGLE said, poking fun at its agency acronym.
At the time, EGLE said it was considering steps to try to prevent a repeat attack, including adding a design to make the drones look less like seagulls. Snopes found no evidence of any bald eagle drone attacks since EGLE's incident in 2020, however, so this may have just been a one-time thing.
EGLE also said the Michigan Department of Natural Resources was unable to issue a citation or violation notice to the "rogue eagle."
"Unfortunately, there's nothing we can do," the agency's spokesman said. "Nature is a cruel and unforgiving mistress."

IIT Kharagpur becomes first IIT to offer MD programmes approved by national medical body
IIT Kharagpur become the first IIT to offer postgraduate medical courses recognised by NMC, introducing 12 MD seats across six specialisations.
Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur in West Bengal has become the first IIT in India to introduce postgraduate medical degree programmes recognised by the National Medical Commission (NMC), offering 12 MD seats across six specialisations for the 2026-27 academic session, the institute announced on Thursday.
“The Institute undertook the prescribed regulatory process with the NMC, including submission of applications, documentation of academic and clinical facilities, and fulfilment of the applicable requirements in March 2026. The process culminated in permission for the six MD programmes for the academic session 2026–27,” director of IIT Kharagpur Suman Chakraborty said.
The programmes will be offered at the institute’s Dr B C Roy Multi-Speciality Medical Research Centre, with admissions through the second round of NEET-PG 2026 counselling from November 10 to 23, according to the announcement. Fees of the PG medical course and stipends paid to students will be on the lines of AIIMS.
“The postgraduate medical programmes are supported by the in-house expanding clinical infrastructure of Dr. Shyama Prasad Mookerji Superspeciality Hospital - new Hospital of IIT Kharagpur, together with the South Eastern Railway Hospital, Kharagpur, under the established institutional partnership. This arrangement provides the clinical training ecosystem for the approved postgraduate programmes, in accordance with the applicable NMC requirements,” Chakraborty said.
The six specialisations are general medicine, radiology, physiology, pathology, community medicine and biochemistry, with two seats in each discipline. The programmes will be available for eligible candidates through the Medical Counselling Committee’s (MCC) online counselling process.
MCC is the government body responsible for conducting online counselling to allot medical and dental seats based on NEET scores.
The move marks the entry of an IIT into postgraduate medical education and is aimed at bringing clinical medicine closer to engineering, artificial intelligence (AI), biomedical sciences and translational research.
IIT Kharagpur said in a statement that the programmes would provide opportunities for medical students to engage with research across areas such as AI-assisted clinical decision-making, advanced medical imaging, computational pathology, biomedical devices, molecular diagnostics, precision medicine and population health.
The institute added that its existing strengths in microfluidics, bioengineering, healthcare diagnostics, AI, computational sciences and translational medical technologies would provide a foundation for the interdisciplinary approach.
Chakraborty said the institute’s objective was not limited to training specialist doctors but also included developing medical professionals capable of addressing healthcare challenges through research and technology.
“India’s first IIT is now taking a historic step towards shaping the future of medical education. Our vision is not simply to train specialist doctors, but to create an ecosystem where clinical excellence meets engineering ingenuity, artificial intelligence and translational research,” he said.
“We want our medical graduates to be not only outstanding clinicians, but also innovators capable of addressing some of humanity’s most pressing healthcare challenges,” Chakraborty added.
He said the first batch would be pioneers of a new academic journey, with the institute aiming to nurture doctors who can combine clinical understanding with scientific discovery and technological innovation.
Established in 1951, IIT Kharagpur was the first institute in the IIT system. Its entry into postgraduate medical education comes in its 75th year and is part of its broader ambition to expand the role of technological institutions in addressing healthcare challenges.
The institute also said that it has identified research-driven learning and international academic exposure as elements of the proposed academic environment.

- The claim that a video shows two Muslim New York Police Department officers taking away a woman's dog for disturbing the peace, supposedly in the interests of enforcing the Islamic teachings known as Shariah, is still under investigation.
- We contacted the NYPD to ask questions and request an incident report to independently confirm several details, including to fully verify the woman's purported charge or charges. We also filed a formal request to receive officers' body camera footage and will update this story if we receive further information.
- The person who says he recorded the video told Snopes he knew of "no evidence" regarding the claim the officers were Muslim, or that Shariah or the Islamic faith played any role in the incident at all.
- The video made the social media rounds as a 3-minute clip with dramatic background music, showing NYPD officers questioning and detaining a woman walking her dog. At least one officer grabs hold of the dog's leash and also grabs the woman's arm. The clip's onscreen captions read: "Sharia is starting in NYC" and "Muslim police taking dog for disturbing the peace."
- A viewing of the original 16-minute video revealed that the officers didn't appear to actually take away the dog, and that they apparently charged her with disorderly conduct.
In early November, people shared a video allegedly showing two Muslim New York police officers taking away a woman's dog for disturbing the peace, supposedly as their way of enforcing Shariah (Islamic law).
Shariah serves to guide the moral and religious practices of Muslims, such as prayer, pilgrimages, fasting, charitable donations and personal virtue.
As a prime example of the rumor, on Nov. 8, an X user posted (archived) the 3-minute clip showing an incident that apparently began moments earlier. Two NYPD officers stand on a street corner at night, with one of the officers alleging that the woman, who identifies herself as a nurse who recently had surgery on her foot, was standing or dancing and recording a video "in the middle of the street" and wouldn't move to the sidewalk, blocking the officers' vehicle.
The officer grabs the woman's arm, briefly takes her dog's leash and tells her that if she doesn't identify herself, they will arrest her and take her "to prison," adding, "We'll take the dog, too." He then grabs her arm again.
The clip's soundtrack features dramatic music as the action takes place.
The onscreen caption reads, "Sharia is starting in NYC," and "Muslim police taking dog for disturbing the peace. Oh wait for that dog ban boy oh boy."
Reverse image searches found others sharing the same video and captions on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and X (archived), as well as clips with similar (archived) claims (archived).
The video appears authentic in that someone on the scene genuinely recorded it and did not create it with artificial intelligence.
The brief clip shared on social media omits 13 minutes of the original 16-minute video (archived), which shows that while one of the officers did briefly grab the dog's leash, it doesn't appear he actually took away the animal — nor did he or the other officer mention the dog as a problem. The longer, raw video not only lacks the dramatic music heard in the shorter clip but contains no mention of religion or Shariah at all.
TikTok user @nuyoricannomad, who said he recorded and first posted the raw video, told Snopes he knew of "no evidence" regarding the claim of the officers' religion playing a factor in the incident.
Pending more corroboration, Snopes hasn't added a fact-check rating to this article. We contacted the NYPD to ask questions and to request an incident report. We also filed a formal request to receive the police body camera footage. We will update this story if we receive further data.
People reposting the video with mentions of Shariah and a "dog ban" appeared to be playing on the exaggerated notion that Muslims hate dogs and view them as unclean. The stereotype apparently originates from an overgeneralization not from the Quran, but instead from the hadith, a narrative record of the sayings or customs of the Prophet Muhammad and his companions.
Video location and citation
In our interview with @nuyoricannomad — who wished to not be identified by name — he said he recorded the video around 3 a.m. Nov. 8. The incident occurred on the northwest corner of Second Avenue and East 39th Street in Manhattan's Murray Hill neighborhood.
According to @nuyoricannomad, both he and the woman, who he indicated is his friend, were walking north and using the East 39th Street crosswalk on the west side of Second Avenue. "We were walking slowly but she had recent surgery," he said, referencing her foot, which she briefly mentions in the clip (at 8:55).
At about the same time, the officers were traveling by car south on Second Avenue and attempting to make a right over the same crosswalk and onto East 39th Street, similar to the turning white SUV visible in this Google Street View image (archived).
Regarding charges for the woman, @nuyoricannomad said, "The citation was written for disorderly conduct." That charge, which Snopes is attempting to independently verify, would line up with a moment in the video in which one of the officers appears to make a phone call and mention disorderly conduct (at 3:30), possibly referencing New York state law's descriptor of obstructing vehicular or pedestrian traffic.
What the full video shows
The full video appears to begin moments after the incident started. One of the officers grabs the woman's arm and she tells him to stop touching her. He also takes her dog's leash for a brief period of time, tells her she will go to prison if she doesn't identify herself and says he'll take her dog, too. He doesn't clarify whether he's joking about taking the dog to prison or seriously warning he'll take her dog away if they take her into custody.
At least one person standing nearby tells the officers he's calling 911 to ask for a supervisor to come to the scene. One of the officers tells that person to stand back and says, "You can do whatever you want." (A user posting one popular Instagram video (archived) about the incident falsely claimed the officer said not "You" but "We," as in, "We can do whatever we want.")
The woman identifies herself as a nurse and challenges the officers' version of events. For example, one officer says, "You were in the middle of the street taking video." She responds, "I did not make a video." He then tells her she's being detained, saying, "You are not free to leave right now."
The woman says she had the right to walk across the crosswalk with a walk signal (at 6:25 and 8:10). We haven't yet been able to independently confirm the status of the traffic signal.
One of the officers alleges he, with the other officer in his passenger seat, was turning right and that the woman and others were in their way (ar 9:30). In that moment, he doesn't challenge the woman's claim she had the right of way with a walk signal.
Later in the video, an apparent police supervisor arrives and tells one of the officers to place @nuyoricannomad and another pedestrian under arrest if they interrupt the officers' investigation again (at 12:20).
The video ends with one of the officers appearing to hand a citation to the woman, who then appears to be free to leave with her dog and friends.
As to what started the incident, @nuyoricannomad told us that "at no point were we just standing on the crosswalk or 'dancing,'" referencing the officer's allegation that the woman had been dancing (at 8:55).
"The point of the video was to show how the cops mishandled the situation and escalated to a point that was not necessary," he said.

ED attaches Rs 2.78 crore assets of former Kolkata cop in land-grab case
The Enforcement Directorate attached properties linked to former Kolkata Police officer Santanu Sinha Biswas. The action intensifies the probe into alleged land grabbing, corruption and money laundering.
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Thursday provisionally attached immovable assets worth Rs 2.78 crore belonging to former Kolkata Police deputy commissioner Santanu Sinha Biswas in a money laundering and corruption case involving alleged strongman Sona Pappu, officials told news agency Press Trust of India.
The assets, which the agency described as proceeds of crime, include three flats in Kolkata and a plot of land in Kandi in Murshidabad district. They belong to Biswas, his family members and associates.
Biswas held several important positions in Kolkata Police during the previous Trinamool Congress government. He also served as the officer-in-charge of Kalighat police station, under whose jurisdiction former chief minister Mamata Banerjee's residence is located.
The ED arrested Biswas in May in connection with an alleged money laundering case linked to a land-grabbing racket. He is currently in jail.
“The ED investigation has revealed that the proceeds of crime were generated through illegal activities, including extortion, grabbing of real estate properties and unauthorised building construction through entities controlled by Biswajit Poddar alias Sona Pappu, Jay S Kamdar and associates,” the agency said in a statement quoted by PTI.
Biswas is accused of receiving financial benefits running into several crores of rupees from private entities and businessmen in exchange for extending illegal favours while in office.
“During his tenure as the officer-in-charge of Kalighat, he developed a close association with Jay S Kamdar and assisted him in illegal activities. Kamdar enjoyed massive clout within the police establishment through his association with Biswas,” the statement said.
“Biswas directly and indirectly acquired, concealed and possessed proceeds of crime to the tune of at least Rs 2.89 crore,” it added.
Kolkata Police has separately registered a case against Biswas on its own initiative under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
Biswas has been accused of colluding with Sona Pappu and businessman Jay Kamdar in an alleged racket that illegally occupied several valuable plots of land in Kolkata over an extended period.
According to the allegations, Biswas used his position in the police to intimidate and harass vulnerable landowners into surrendering their properties. The ED has claimed that the alleged syndicate grabbed land in different parts of Kolkata and generated proceeds of crime worth at least Rs 50 crore.
In July, the ED filed a charge sheet in the land-grabbing case, alleging that it had found evidence directly implicating Biswas in the misappropriation of around Rs 3 crore.
The latest action covers assets worth Rs 2.78 crore as the ED continues its investigation into allegations of money laundering, corruption and land grabbing involving Biswas and his alleged associates.

The West Bengal government will appoint coordinators in the wards of Kolkata Municipal Corporation and Howrah Municipal Corporation if the stay on civic polls is not lifted by the Supreme Court, West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said on Thursday (November 12, 2026).
The Calcutta High Court on October 6 restrained the West Bengal State Election Commission from issuing any notification for the upcoming KMC elections based on newly redrawn wards until a pending petition challenging the delimitation exercise is decided.
Addressing a gathering in Howrah District, Mr. Adhikari accused Opposition parties of obstructing the electoral process, and alleged that residents had been deprived of elected civic representation and proper municipal services for years.
“Those who are likely to lose their security deposits in the elections are the ones obstructing the process,” the Chief Minister said. He said that similar to proposal at KMC, coordinators will be appointed for each ward in Howrah Municipal Corporation (HMC) if elections are not held in time. According to sources, BJP leaders are likely to be appointed as coordinators across KMC and HMC.
Mr. Adhikari said that his government would approach the Supreme Court with a Special Leave Petition (SLP) seeking that the stay on holding civic polls be lifted. According to the Chief Minister, officials have limitations and cannot provide civic facilities for a long time.
Elections to the HMC have not been held since 2013, and for almost a decade officials have been providing services to the people of the civic body. The Trinamool Congress run board at Kolkata Municipal Corporation was dissolved weeks after the Bharatiya Janata Party government came to power. Mayor of KMC Firhad Hakim and other councillors resigned and the State government appointed an administrator to run the affairs of the largest civic body in the State.
The Calcutta High Court on Friday (October 6, 2026) restrained the West Bengal State Election Commission from issuing any notification for the upcoming Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) elections based on newly redrawn wards until a pending petition challenging the delimitation exercise is decided.
The West Bengal government had passed a legislation in the State Assembly on August 12, redrawing the wards of the KMC and HMC increasing the number of wards from 144 to 209 and 50 to 68 respectively. The Opposition parties have alleged the State government and its agencies have resorted to gerrymandering while undertaking delimitation of wards in order to secure partisan advantage to the ruling political party in West Bengal on the premise of previous electoral results.
The BJP government in West Bengal was keen on holding elections to KMC and HMC. In fact, the BJP leadership had started the process of selecting candidates. Mr. Adhikari has on several occasions, expressed their preference to hold civic body elections in Kolkata and Howrah by the end of November or early December this year.

Who is the suspected Chinese spy at centre of the Nvidia investigation?
US chip giant Nvidia has said it is investigating reports that its CEO Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who had been the managing director of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
The New York Times reported that US officials suspect Alice Huang has been working for China's spy agency to collect intelligence.

57th IFFI to be held in Goa from Nov 20, adopts ‘Stories Without Borders’ theme
The theme emphasises cinema’s role in bridging cultural and geographical differences through diverse stories and shared human experiences
The 57th edition of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) will be held in Goa from November 20 to 28. The festival will follow the theme “Stories Without Borders”, highlighting cinema’s ability to connect audiences across cultures and geographies.
Curtain-Raiser Press Conference
The festival’s highlights, key programmes and major attractions will be unveiled at a curtain-raiser press conference in Goa on Friday.
Who Will Attend the Event
Goa chief minister Pramod Sawant will attend the event along with secretary to the Union ministry of information and broadcasting Chanchal Kumar and chairperson of the National Film Development Corporation (NFDC) G Krishnakumar. Filmmaker Ashutosh Gowariker, who is the festival director for the 2026 edition, will also be present.

IFFI’s Role and Programme
IFFI is one of the country’s major international film festivals which provides a platform for filmmakers from India and abroad to showcase their work and promote an understanding of different cultures through cinema. The 2026 edition is expected to feature a diverse selection of Indian and international films, reflecting the festival’s expanding global participation.
The theme, “Stories Without Borders”, emphasises cinema’s role in bridging cultural and geographical differences through diverse stories and shared human experiences.

VS Hospitals has introduced a new 2D digital mammography system to strengthen breast cancer screening and diagnosis.
The AMULET SOPHINITY system from Fujifilm uses a high-resolution detector with a pixel size of 50 microns, allowing detailed imaging of breast tissue, including tiny microcalcifications, which can sometimes be an early indicator of breast abnormalities.
Mammography uses low-dose X-rays to examine breast tissue and can help identify abnormalities that may not be detectable through physical examination. The new system has intelligent exposure control, which adjusts X-ray exposure according to breast composition while maintaining image quality. AI-based positioning support is designed to assist in accurate positioning and consistent image acquisition.
The equipment takes approximately five seconds for standard image acquisition and 12 seconds for high-resolution imaging. It also has features such as flexible positioning, intelligent breast compression and automatic decompression to help reduce discomfort during the examination.
Speaking at the launch, S. Subramanian, Chairman and Managing Director of V.S. Hospitals, said early detection was important in breast cancer care and that mammography played a key role in identifying breast abnormalities.
The hospital will offer free mammography screening to underprivileged people throughout November 2026. Those seeking to avail themselves of the screening can contact the hospital at 7448850500.

RIP, Nvidia under Jensen Huang.
Several bouquets of flowers and at least one candle were photographed outside Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Thursday after Huang resigned as CEO.
The founder and longtime chief executive resigned Thursday morning in the midst of a scandal involving one confirmed extramarital affair and two reported others, and a board investigation into whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence operation.
On Thursday, several bundles of flowers sat against the Nvidia company sign in front of the company's headquarters. A man was also photographed adding a white candle in a glass jar in front of the sign.
The apparent tributes to the tech executive highlight just how influential Huang had become as he helped Nvidia grow into one of the world's most valuable companies and a leader in the AI boom.
Huang and his signature leather jacket had become largely synonymous with Nvidia, and he was one of the most visible figures in the AI revolution.
Nvidia's future without Huang remains uncertain. Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO, was announced as interim CEO while the company searches for a replacement.
As of Thursday, the stock was down 13% since Friday's market close, before Huang's admission of infidelity and the board's investigation were announced.
Following Huang's resignation, leaders in the business and tech world weighed in on what his absence will mean for Nvidia.
On Thursday, workers carrying Nvidia's signature green badges and backpacks seemed to be going to work as normal amid the shake-up.

In tough weather conditions, World Cup Finals gold medallist Dhiraj Bommadevara and Asian Games champion Kumkum Mohod displayed their strong resolve to claim top spots in men’s and women’s recurve qualification rounds, respectively, on the inaugural day of the National Archery Championships at the Parade Ground in Shillong on Thursday.
Dhiraj scored 680, comprising 24 Xs, the most by a mile, and 14 10s. Kumkum recorded 677, consisting of 10 Xs and 26 10s, to improve upon her previous career-best total of 671.
The fickle weather switched from being sunny and warm to cloudy and windy before a bout of drizzle tested the archers thoroughly. The action was called off owing to bad light even before the day’s schedule could be completed.
Dhiraj, who reached here at 10 p.m. on Wednesday night, recovered quickly to score 343 in the first segment before a change in schedule forced an unusually longer break of more than an hour. He returned to shoot 337 in the second segment and took the top spot by a slim margin of one point.
“Because of the fluctuating weather, I got to learn so much in one day. One side of the ground is open, while on the other side there is a huge mountain wall. Whenever there was wind, it was difficult to guess. Happy to have tackled the tricky conditions well,” said Dhiraj.

Delhi's air quality improved marginally to enter the 'poor' category on Tuesday (November 10, 2026), with the AQI settling at 299, Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data showed.
On Monday, the day after Diwali, the capital's average Air Quality Index (AQI) stood at 376, in the 'very poor' category. The improvement was observed due to wind speed picking up.
According to the CPCB, an AQI between 0 and 50 is classified as 'good', 51 and 100 as 'satisfactory', 101 and 200 as 'moderate', 201 and 300 as 'poor', 301 and 400 as 'very poor', and 401 and 500 as 'severe'.
On Tuesday, 23 monitoring stations in the city recorded 'very poor' air quality, with Pusa Road recording the highest AQI at 385, followed by Chandni Chowk at 381.
AQI readings were available for 57 of Delhi's 59 monitoring stations.
Safdarjung, Delhi's base weather station, recorded a minimum temperature of 15.7 degrees Celsius.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast moderate fog during the day and the maximum temperature is likely to settle at 28 degrees Celsius.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

Cash App founder's killer gets 16 years to life in prison
Bob Lee died from multiple stab wounds in 2023.
Two years after his conviction for second-degree murder, Nima Momeni, the tech consultant found guilty of killing Cash App founder Bob Lee, has been sentenced. San Francisco Superior Court Judge Alexandra Gordon handed him to 16 years to life in prison.
Lee was instrumental in the development of Cash App while serving as chief technology officer at Square. He was also an engineer at Google from 2004 to 2010 and was involved in the development of Android. Lee was later the chief product officer at crypto payments company MobileCoin and helped the World Health Organization launch its mobile app during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Murder and misinformation
In April 2023, Lee was found bleeding in a doorway on an empty downtown San Francisco street after being stabbed in the hip and heart. He managed to call 911 but died after being taken to a hospital.
Following the killing but before an arrest was made, some of Big Tech's loudest voices were quick to frame it in terms that supported their biases. "Many people I know have been severely assaulted" in San Francisco, Elon Musk tweeted, suggesting that "even if attackers are caught, they are often released immediately." Investor Jason Calacanis chimed in, calling those running the city "incompetent lunatics," while claiming the city was devolving into "utter chaos." (San Fransisco has a comparatively low crime rate, and has seen its homicide rate fall over the last four years.)
As it happened, this had nothing to do with governmental incompetence or random acts of violence. Lee was involved with Momeni's sister and had been partying with the two on the night of the murder. Prosecutors said Momeni killed Lee after learning that the Cash App founder had introduced his sister to drug dealers who abused her. Momeni's team claimed he acted in self-defense after Lee lunged at him with a knife. Lee was found to have cocaine, ketamine and alcohol in his system.
The judge rejected Momeni's request for a new trial. His lawyers say they plan to appeal.

BOUGAINVILLE DISPATCH
A Sweaty, Muddy Jungle Trek to a Famed World War II Wreck
Seven Chinese tourists, a dozen villagers and a couple of journalists forded streams and bushwhacked to the downed plane of Isoroku Yamamoto, the Japanese admiral. Machetes proved handy.
Halfway through the morning, I’m being tossed around like a popcorn kernel in the back of a troop carrier playing an eclectic medley of Backstreet Boys and Papua New Guinean jams.
We’re traveling along what feels more like a collection of loose rocks, arranged to be roughly vehicle width, than a road. I’ve lost count of the number of river crossings, including one where the water lapped a few inches from the car’s windows. And this is during a dry spell.
Our caravan is headed for an unlikely tourist destination deep in the jungle on Bougainville Island, an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea in the Solomon Sea.
The piecemeal remnants of a Mitsubishi G4M1 — Betty, as the planes were code-named by the Allies in World War II — have remained for some 80 years at the crash site of Japanese Navy Adm. Isoroku Yamamoto. This is the spot where Admiral Yamamoto, mastermind of the Pearl Harbor attack, archvillain to Americans in the war, a respected and memorialized figure to the Japanese, met his end in 1943.
Bougainville was occupied by the Japanese in early 1942, in the months after Pearl Harbor, as the Imperial Navy pushed into the South Pacific, with Admiral Yamamoto at the helm. In April 1943, Allied forces intercepted and deciphered Japanese communication on the admiral’s travels, and American P-38 Lightning fighters gunned down his plane over southern Bougainville, a feat the Americans triumphantly dubbed Operation Vengeance.

Five new miniature frog species found in eastern Himalayas
- Published
Scientists have discovered five new species of tiny horned frogs in India's eastern Himalayas, more than doubling the number of known species in the group.
A team of scientists from University of Delhi and Harvard University made the discoveries after five years of fieldwork, identifying the frogs as members of the Jingophrys group.
Among them is Jingophrys tanogogo - or the snail-eating horned frog - the first frog known in India to feed on snails and the first member of its family recorded with such a diet.
The research suggest the Himalayas have played a much larger role in frog evolution than previously thought and highlight the region as an overlooked hotspot for biodiversity.
The Himalayas, stretching from tropical forests to alpine meadows, are among the world's richest biodiversity regions.
Despite drawing interest from scientists and researchers, many parts here have not been fully explored.
The state of Arunachal Pradesh particularly has emerged as one of its least-studied regions.
Dr Sonali Garg, who led the study at Harvard University's Museum of Comparative Zoology, said the research highlights how significant evolutionary changes can go unnoticed in little-studied species.
The study - called two-fold hidden diversity of diminutive horned frogs (Megophryinae: Jingophrys) - was conducted by Garg along with her colleague James Hanken and Delhi University's SD Biju, Tage Tajo and Radhakrishna Upadhyaya K.
It was published on 11 November in the Royal Society Open Science journal.
"Some of the new species are extremely secretive and found in remote forests only during a short breeding season," says Biju.
Researchers say further studies will have to done to better understand their biology and conservation needs.
DNA analysis showed the horned frogs rapidly diversified into multiple species in the eastern Himalayas as the mountain range rose and the Asian monsoon took shape over millions of years, helping drive the evolution of the region's plants and wildlife.
The researchers said in a statement that local tribes gave them essential field support and knowledge that helped make the discoveries possible. Some of the species were named after these communities.
The Tanii horned frog (Jingophrys taniitatii), for instance, is named by combining the name of the Tanii tribe in the region with the word 'tatti' - frog in the local Apatani language.
The new species have been named Jingophrys taniitatii (Tanii horned frog), Jingophrys tanogogo (snail-eating horned frog), Jingophrys siangensis (Siang horned frog), Jingophrys hrdy (Hrdy's horned frog) and Jingophrys wularsoni (Wu-Larson's horned frog).

A 45-year-old woman allegedly lost Rs 49.2 lakh in an online trading fraud after being lured by a fake Facebook video featuring Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, police said.

India to supply 100 more ambulances to Sri Lanka under $5.28 million grant
The grant was signed and a Memorandum of Understanding was exchanged in the presence of Union health minister J P Nadda.
India on Wednesday signed a pact with Sri Lanka to supply 100 additional ambulances to the island nation's emergency service with grant assistance of USD 5.28 million, the Indian mission here said.
The grant was signed and a Memorandum of Understanding was exchanged in the presence of Health Minister J P Nadda.
The India-assisted ambulance services were initially launched in July 2016 in Sri Lanka's Western and Southern Provinces under a grant assistance of USD 7.5 million. It included the provision of 88 ambulances, their operational expenditure for a year and the setting up of an emergency response centre.
In July 2018, it was expanded country-wide by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and then Sri Lankan Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe, with an additional grant of USD 15.02 million, covering 209 ambulances, their operational expenses and training costs.
The latest expansion will add 100 ambulances to the existing fleet of 322 vehicles operated by the country's free emergency ambulance service, known as 1990 Suwa Seriya.
The service was established following a request by the Sri Lankan government during Modi's visit to the island in March 2015.
It is estimated to respond to 1,000 to 1,200 patient-transfer calls daily, providing free emergency medical transport across the country.
In a post on X, the Indian High Commission in Sri Lanka called it a "shining example of India–Sri Lanka development partnership delivering tangible benefits to people".

In Maine, a new approach to practicing medicine in the sky
Clipboard in hand, pilot Will Bradbury stands near a helicopter at LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters. He's running down emergency landing tips with his crew.
"If we need to get out quickly because of smoke or fire, just watch the terrain so that you're not walking uphill into the rotors," he reminds flight nurse Denise Saucier and paramedic Brian Merklin.
The team is getting ready to take off on a medical transport flight. Saucier folds herself into the compact helicopter. She's worked for the air ambulance service for seven years and still calls it a dream job.
Dream job or not, the life of a flight clinician is hard and, given the headwinds slamming rural healthcare, getting harder.
Since 2015, demand for medical flights in Maine has doubled. In 2025, LifeFlight crews flew 3,031 flights, more than one every three hours. This year, demand is up another 10%.
Nationwide, air medical services are filling the gaps left behind as rural hospitals close, convert to outpatient-only rural emergency hospitals, or stop offering unprofitable services like labor and delivery.
And, as Medicaid cuts estimated by the Congressional Budget Office at $911 billion over ten years take effect, it's going to get worse. Hundreds more rural hospitals or maternity departments are at immediate risk of closing. With every closure, medical care gets further away.
And, increasingly, ground ambulance stations, many of which are also struggling to keep their doors open, can't meet the need. That leaves flight clinicians like Saucier and Merklin seeing more patients every day.
"We're seeing this across the board. The need for air medical services is increasing year over year," says Nicholas George. He runs the ETHOS Database, a national tracking system for air medical programs.
When the rural health care system breaks, EMS — on the ground and, increasingly, in the air — is the backstop.
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Healthcare of last resort
Every week or two, Saucier finds herself on a flight to one of Maine's thousands of islands. Occasionally, crews even land in the state's vast forests and mountains, then take snowmobiles to reach patients.
But "scene calls" to roadside — or trailside — accidents are less than 10% of LifeFlight's transports. (They're a higher percentage in urban areas.)
Most are interfacility transports, like today's. They'll stabilize a patient at a small, local hospital and fly them to a larger, better resourced one.
Saucier glances out the window for hazards. The view still reminds her of the role the organization plays in Maine, one of the country's most rural states.
"You go so long of a distance without seeing any houses, any roads," Saucier says. "It really hits home how rural Maine is and how necessary EMS is in the state."
And the pressure is on air ambulances as ground services in Maine are increasingly strained. The system is so fragmented that patients can fall through the cracks. Last year, a woman in a small northern Maine town died while the county dispatch center called 10 ambulance services. None responded.
Air ambulance services, though, come with unique challenges, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. It's been difficult to retain staff with the medical expertise to treat everything from heart attacks to injuries to fragile newborns, and who can stick with the demanding job without burning out.
Almost a quarter of ground-based EMS workers leaves the field every year. While there's no comprehensive staffing data for air medical services, flight clinicians face a slew of unique stresses, including dangerous conditions; long shifts and unpredictable hours; ever-increasing training and certification requirements; and significant mental health burdens. And then there's the pay, which is low throughout emergency medical services.
For years, LifeFlight retained only 60% to 70% of its workers, says CEO Joe Kellner.
"This is a really hard job," Kellner says. "By their job description, they are seeing people on their worst day, over and over again."
Training elite clinicians
This year, for the first time in nine years, LifeFlight is nearly fully staffed. One of the nation's handful of independent nonprofit air medical companies, LifeFlight has taken an innovative approach to the problems that plague the industry, including a combination of better training, higher pay and in-house mental health support.
Mike Abernethy, an EMS expert and retired emergency medicine professor at the University of Wisconsin, considers the company one of a handful of model programs for the industry. LifeFlight of Maine is a nonprofit, unlike much of the industry, which is dominated by for-profit businesses with reputations for charging exorbitant prices.
"There's just absolutely no comparison in the aviation and medical quality of these programs" versus an average for-profit air medical business, Abernethy argues.
When Kellner, a paramedic himself, became CEO in 2023, he began addressing the recruitment and retention problems. What LifeFlight calls the "Critical Care Academy," a six- to eight-month orientation program, is intended to address both issues.
Emergency critical care advances quickly. So most clinicians need regular education, both to remain successful on the job and to get hired in the first place.
On another day at headquarters, four instructors sit in a claustrophobic control room. Through a window looking into what appears to be a hospital room, paramedics Daniel Horne and Brad Alleger are undergoing an annual skills assessment, a simulation of a real-life medical crisis.
Dr. Dave Saquet turns on a mic and coughs. "It's hard to breathe," he whispers urgently. "It hurts everywhere."
His voice seems to be coming from the patient — a breathing, bleeding mannequin lying on a hospital bed.
"What happened to you?" Horne asks.
"My house was on fire," Saquet chokes out.
A wall monitor displays the patient's vital signs — which Saquet is manipulating on his laptop.
Medics and nurses here do simulations often, both to pass the Critical Care Academy, and also to stay up to date on occasional but critical events, like emergency births, newborn resuscitation, and burns. Before the assessment ends, the paramedics will have tried and failed to intubate the patient. After that "failure," they performed an emergency procedure to enable breathing, switching from the mannequin to a pig trachea.
Because it's hard to find recruits qualified enough for the rigorous training, the company also started a mentorship program for people considering applying. Some even attend the academy, gaining skills even if they'll never work for LifeFlight.
Success comes slowly: Recently, LifeFlight hired one of last year's mentees.
Experiments
Kellner instituted an unusual change that he says even nurses endorse: LifeFlight raised paramedics' pay to match flight nurses' compensation. Industrywide, paramedics make less. That keeps costs down, which is why pay equity is rare. Kellner believes the change has helped with recruitment.
Another experiment: LifeFlight hired a full-time mental-health counselor.
EMS workers' rates of post-traumatic stress injury, anxiety and depression are more thanfive times higher than the average American's.
"That has led people to leave this profession," Kellner says.
That was true for paramedic Brian Merklin, who was working for a different service in Nevada during the pandemic.
"We got hit really hard," he says. "The crews were just flying nonstop. We did four-day shifts, so for 96 hours we were just going, going, going."
About a third of the staff quit, he says. "They were getting air medical service plus COVID, right in the teeth."
Eventually, Merklin too needed a break. He left the profession for a few years. Then, when he felt the urge to fly again, he found LifeFlight.
Today's trip
The helicopter, which took off from Bangor, lands on a community hospital's rooftop helipad. Merklin and Saucier hurry to the patient's side. Most LifeFlight patients are unconscious or too ill to consent to share their stories, so the details are private. The injuries are shocking. If this patient doesn't get to a trauma center quickly, they might die.
Merklin and Saucier are unfazed.
But it's this kind of incessant trauma exposure that makes mental health support for first responders so invaluable.
Merklin serves on a peer support team.
"There's a lot of lip service paid … to the cost to your mental health in this profession. But this is the only place I have ever worked that actually provided support," he says. "I would love to see it take hold in other areas."
If counseling keeps two or three people from leaving, it's a wise investment, Kellner argues: "The cost of training somebody new into our organization is about $100,000."
As both air and ground EMS become even more essential, the task is to recruit and keep more people like Merklin and Saucier.
Because, if hundreds more hospitals do close, highly trained EMS workers may be the only people standing between patients dying and getting the care they need.
Elaine Appleton Grant's reporting was supported by the National Institute for Health Care Management.

Violence erupts in Bangladesh as ousted PM's supporters stage protest
- Published
Police in Bangladesh have fired tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse supporters of the deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who are demanding her return to the country.
A police vehicle was set on fire in Gopalganj district, where the banned student wing of Hasina's Awami League party clashed with security forces.
Nationwide protests by pro-Hasina activists started a day after the former leader said she had requested a passport to return to Bangladesh from exile in India.
The demonstrations by the student wing, called Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL), are seen as the first organised show of force by Hasina's supporters since she was ousted in August 2024 following a huge uprising against her rule.
Traffic was disrupted in some parts of the country as protesters tried to set up roadblocks using burning tyres.
Several passenger vehicles were also set on fire in various parts of Bangladesh in the run up to the protest.
A 60-year-old driver of a passenger bus was killed by smoke inhalation after people set fire to the vehicle in the city of Faridpur early on Tuesday.
Elsewhere, about 200 protesters briefly blocked traffic on the 6.2km (4 mile)-long Padma bridge across the Ganges, that connects the capital Dhaka with the south-western region.
Bangladeshi local media said dozens of crude bombs exploded in the past few days in Dhaka and elsewhere.
"Any attempt to worsen the law-and-order situation or create instability through any conspiracy within the country from across the border (India) will not be allowed to succeed," Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.
"Our supporters were not responsible for the violent incidents. They were carried out by unknown miscreants. We believe in peaceful protests," a senior leader of the BCL, who is now in exile in a foreign country, said.
Hasina fled to neighbouring India two years ago following a massive uprising, bringing an end to her 15-year reign.
Opposition parties accused Hasina of jailing political rivals, supressing dissent and overseeing widespread human rights abuses. She always denied the charges.
The United Nations has estimated up to 1,400 people were killed, most by gunfire from security forces, during the anti-government protests in 2024.
The activities of the Awami League were banned soon after she fled the country and it was not allowed to contest the February general election.
A special Bangladeshi tribunal last year sentenced her to death in absentia after being found guilty of crimes against humanity.
She has denied all the charges, calling the trial "biased and politically motivated".
Despite the death penalty threat, Hasina said she wanted to return to Bangladesh in December and requesteded the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi to issue her with a passport.
But the Bangladeshi government said the country would not provide a passport to her and called her "a terrorist".
"She is a fugitive criminal. We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's junior foreign affairs minister, said.
"Should we treat her like an ordinary commercial traveller and tell her to come and visit her in-laws' residence?" Kobir asked.
A state prosecutor in Bangladesh on Tuesday said the verdict would be executed if she came back, saying she had missed the opportunity to appeal.
Awami League leaders allege that in the past two years hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces.
Dhaka officials reject accusations that Awami League supporters are being systematically targeted.
