Social media giant Meta has once again come under the radar of Indian authorities over alleged child sexual abuse material (CSAM) prevalent on Meta-owned platforms. Now, National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) member Priyank Kanoon has urged the women and child developement (WCD) ministry to look into the financial relationship between the social media giant and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). Citing advocacy group Legal Rights Observatory, Kanoongo reportedly said that UNICEF is trying to offer its help to Indian authorities in the ongoing government probe into the child sexual abuse material (CSAM), sold as ads, on Meta platforms. Speaking with news agency PTI, Kanoongo flagged that Meta has given ‘millions of dollars” to UNICEF and continues to fund the organisation. He argued that this financial relationship could create a conflict of interest, particularly because UNICEF is engaged in child-protection work while Meta faces allegations involving exploitative content on its platforms. In a letter written to WCD secretary Anil Malik, he called for a probe into the financial ties between Meta and UNICEF. Kanoongo also raised concerns that UNICEF could end up serving Meta’s interests rather than supporting child protection. He also urged the government to ensure that Meta is not allowed to use UNICEF as a “shield to evade accountability”. “Therefore, there is a concern that this organisation, which is supposed to work on the issue of child sexual exploitation material while receiving funding from Meta, might end up serving Meta's interests. The activist group has expressed apprehension that this organisation could potentially work in favour of Meta's interests,” Kanoongo reportedly said. The NHRC member said that he has already brought the matter to the attention of the WCD ministry, external affairs ministry, home affairs ministry and the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre. He also urged Indian authorities to keep the alleged conflict of interest in mind while conducting investigations and taking enforcement action. The concern, he claimed, was that allegations of vested interests being served through financial funding should not turn out to be true. This comes a months after a BBC Eye documentary, aired in July, allegedly found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting CSAM in India. As per Kanoongo, the NHRC has already identified about 100 such instances. The aftermath saw the Centre pull up the social media giant and summon the company’s top leadership. The government also directed Meta to strengthen CSAM detection, increase human oversight of moderation and improve safeguards for content in Indian languages and local contexts. Earlier reports suggested that government was considering waving off Meta’s “safe harbour” protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000. This could have potentially forced the company to face greater legal liability in cases of CSAM or other illegal content being posted on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. Post this, the social media giant agreed to report instances of child sexual abuse to the local law enforcement agencies in September. Days later, Meta also said that it has introduced LLM-driven systems to identify “signposting” within ads to counter predators who advertise illicit material in ways that can evade automated detection. The social media juggernaut also claims to have deployed AI-driven sweeps to uncover missed CSAM material and integrated “red-teaming” AI agents to strengthen detection mechanisms.

How good is Hamilton and how long can he stay in F1? - Q&A
- Published
McLaren's Lando Norris converted pole position into a race win at a wet-dry-wet Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday.
Max Verstappen came through the field to take second after starting at the back of the grid because of an engine penalty, while his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar was on the podium in third.
Mercedes sealed the constructors' championship for the first time since 2021 at Interlagos following a fourth-place finish for George Russell and fifth for new world champion Kimi Antonelli.
Here BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
Lewis Hamilton has just completed his 400th F1 grand prix, with more than 100 of these races having him on pole position. There are drivers with a better pole percentage than this, so just how good is he and for how much longer can he stay at the top? - Clive
Lewis Hamilton is unquestionably one of the greatest Formula 1 drivers in history.
He's statistically the most successful - with the most race wins and pole positions.
He's tied with Michael Schumacher for the most championships with seven, and many would - and do - argue he should have eight, given the controversy of the mishandled final race of the 2021 season.
Greatness as an F1 driver is about more than raw statistics, but even so Hamilton has consistently proved to be at the very highest level, with a series of outstanding drives in races that will go down in history as some of the greatest ever.
Examples of those would be the 2008 British Grand Prix and the 2021 Brazilian Grand Prix, along with many others.
All of this should go without saying.
He's also won races in nearly all his seasons - the only exceptions being 2022, 2023 and 2025.
There is no question that, within the context of his remarkable career, Hamilton struggled relatively in the era of 'ground-effect' cars from 2022-25.
He was beaten by Mercedes team-mate George Russell in two of their three seasons together, and looked a shadow of his usual self against Charles Leclerc in 2025.
Those performances led some to question why a driver formerly famed and lauded for his adaptability did not seem as able to adapt to the driving style required of those cars.
And that, in turn, led to questions as to whether the fact he apparently could not was related to his age - he is now 41.
But with this year's cars, Hamilton is back in much more familiar territory, is performing extremely well again and is neck-and-neck with Leclerc.
Those questions about the four years from 2022-25 will remain just that, but there is no doubt Hamilton is sensitive to them. He has referenced them a number of times this year, including last weekend in Brazil, when the topic of his 400th race came up.
"I never ever thought that I would be reaching numbers like that," he said. "It's crazy because I still feel young, and regardless of the things that people say, you saw my pole last week, I still have the pace, I still have the speed and I still have the dedication, which is most important and the focus. For me, that number is kind of irrelevant."
Longevity in sport depends on many factors, and each athlete is different.
On the face of it, however, there is no obvious reason why, on an age front, Hamilton cannot continue for a good few more years - Fernando Alonso is 45 and is still performing at an extremely high level, as he proved yet again in Brazil at the weekend.
Hamilton has said he wants to race at least until F1 returns to Africa, which will not be until 2030 at the earliest, when he, too, will be 45.
For that, he will need at least one new contract, as his current one with Ferrari is believed to end next year.

We heard, and saw, a lot of 'yo-yo racing' in the first half of the season. This seems to have reduced. What has changed? - Ali
'Yo-yo racing' was a term coined at the start of this year for a new character of on-track battle in which cars swapped positions multiple times over a series of laps.
This was caused by the new power-units introduced this year, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power and are fundamentally energy starved.
The operations of these engines included 'overtake' and 'boost' modes.
'Boost' is a facility for a driver to demand extra electrical energy whenever he wants, as long as the battery has charge.
'Overtake' mode gives a driver following within one second of a car in front an extra 0.5MJ of energy recovery and deployment capability per lap.
At the start of the season, this - combined with the teams' and drivers' relative unfamiliarity with the new technology - led to a number of examples of yo-yo racing in the early grands prix.
This is where one driver has more electrical energy available, uses it to overtake, whereupon the driver behind now has more and overtakes back, and so on.
This has been less prevalent recently and there are two reasons for that.
Primarily, the tracks in recent weeks have been less 'energy-starved'. And the more energy-starved a car is at a track, the more likelihood there is for yo-yo racing.
The overtaking comes from the variation in energy levels, and being at tracks where drivers can't use all the energy they want all the time.
On top of that, drivers and teams have now been using the engines for a season and are much more on top of how to use them, and therefore how not to leave themselves vulnerable.
At the same time, rule changes have been introduced since the start of the season to reduce the impact of energy starvation, such as imposing energy limits on tracks where it is a major issue. This flattens out the peaks and troughs in energy availability.
And into next year and beyond further steps are being taken to make the engines more "normal" in operation - by changing the energy split to 60-40 in two steps by 2028.
This is almost certainly going to lead to the frequency of overtaking reducing, while the drivers become happier with how the cars feel to drive.
Whether the audience perceives that as better or worse racing remains to be seen.
What is the reason a driver like Esteban Ocon would want to stay in F1 as a reserve driver rather than commit to race elsewhere in a different series? All F1 drivers are very, very good, and presumably would be in demand, so why not compete elsewhere, win some races, be a hero? - Stephen
When it became clear that Ocon was not going to be retained by Haas next year, and that his options for a race seat seemed to have evaporated, the Frenchman was insistent that his F1 career was not over.
Staying involved in the sport as a reserve driver - if he can find a spot - is the best way to keep current in the sport.
It means a driver is available should either of the race drivers at whatever team he can land with be incapacitated.
It keeps him familiar with current F1 machinery through simulator sessions, and perhaps driving recent cars.
And it simply keeps his face around and in people's minds.
Go and race elsewhere, whether it's Indycar, Formula E or endurance racing, for example, and it's much easer to be forgotten, or for people to assume your time has come and gone.
Why hasn't Liam Lawson been confirmed for 2027 despite his brilliant driving this year? - Pete
The decision as to which two of the three drivers in contention to drive for Racing Bulls next year is in the hands of the Red Bull shareholders Chalerm Yoovidhya and Mark Mateschitz, and Red Bull's ultimate F1 boss Oliver Mintzlaff.
Lawson is in contention along with his current team-mate Arvid Lindblad and F2 front-runner Nikola Tsolov.
The old Red Bull way - under Helmut Marko and Christian Horner - would have been to jettison Lawson now on the basis he has had his chance in the lead team and is unlikely to be considered for another, and put in Tsolov as the next cab off the rank, so to speak.
The counter-argument is that leaves two unproven talents going against each other next year, which would leave Red Bull not knowing what they are looking at.
Better, this argument goes, to keep Lawson and Lindblad together next year for a fuller reading on Lindblad, with Lawson as a known-quantity benchmark, then drop whoever performs least well at the end of 2027 in favour of Tsolov.
In not so many words, Racing Bulls team boss Alan Permane made this second argument in Brazil at the weekend.
"Red Bull's had a very successful young driver programme," he said, "and I don't want to be critical of it, but I think if you guys are critical of it, maybe sometimes the drivers haven't been able to have enough time to settle, or maybe some snap decisions have been made.
"We're trying to apply a little bit of science, and that takes some time.
"So we are looking at everything and studying, analysing, and time is on our side. We're not in a rush to do anything, and I'm very confident the right decision will be made.
"I realise it's frustrating for our drivers. I realise it's frustrating for everyone else, but we want to get it right, and we will get it right."
Interlagos consistently produces thrilling races. Should F1 be doing more to preserve racing at 'classic' circuits? - Nathan
F1 faces a difficult balancing act with the calendar.
It wants a truly global world championship. It wants exciting racing that engages audiences. It wants a good mix of circuit types for variation and interest. And it wants to make money.
When it comes to 'classic' race tracks, that's not always an easy equation to solve.
The main reason is that the classic tracks are often in countries that are not able or willing to pay the big-money fees.
The same model and restrictions do not apply in autocracies that want to use races for national self-promotion, hence they can and do tend to pay bigger fees.
But F1 is well aware of the importance of classic circuits, and it wants to ensure it keeps the best of them.
As a consequence, F1 does make compromises that ensure the likes of Monaco, Silverstone, Spa and Suzuka stay on the calendar, even if not every year any more in the case of Spa.
At the same time, the sport makes a considerable effort to make new tracks as interesting as possible. Some are more successful than others, but that's always going to be the case.
Take Las Vegas, for example. It is far from the greatest track in terms of driving challenge, and was hardly likely to be given it is made up of streets in an American city, but it makes up for that with spectacle and kudos.
As for forthcoming permanent circuits, former F1 driver Alex Wurz - the designer of the new tracks in Qiddiyah, Saudi Arabia, and Rwanda, which are both due to come on to the calendar in the next few years - has done his level best to ensure they are fulfilling and challenging for drivers and promote good racing.

Statewide government hospitals recorded a total of 1,387 inpatient admissions during this period. The admissions included 956 for accidents, 321 for minor injuries or assaults, and 110 for burn injuries. One burn-related fatality was recorded, involving a child under the age of 15.
No adult deaths due to burns were reported during this timeframe.
Demographic data for burn injuries shows that men formed the largest group of victims, with 92 treated as outpatients and 76 admitted as inpatients.
Children under 15 were the second most affected demographic, with 48 outpatients and 17 inpatient admissions. Adult women accounted for 19 outpatients and 17 inpatients. In total, hospitals saw 159 outpatients and 110 inpatients for burn cases.
The Thanjavur Government Medical College Hospital recorded the highest patient volume for burns, accidents, and minor injuries, treating 36 outpatients and admitting 87 inpatients.
Other major medical centres handling the bulk of the emergency caseload included the Madurai Government Medical College Hospital with six outpatients and 84 inpatients, and the Chengalpattu Government Medical College Hospital with 85 inpatients.
The Periyar Nagar Government Hospital recorded one outpatient and 64 inpatients, while the Thoothukudi Government Medical College Hospital treated 46 outpatients and 13 inpatients.

Have you heard of the names Kadambini Ganguly and Anandibai Joshi? Considered India’s first female doctors, these names have often been looked past in the pages of history and even medical textbooks. Today, let’s talk about the story of Kadambini Ganguly — India’s first practising lady doctor.
It was in 1861 that Brahmo reformer and headmaster Braja Kishore Basu had a daughter. She was named Kadambini Basu. Young Kadambini, despite hailing from a community that did not necessarily support women’s education like many others at the time did, received an education at the Brahmo Eden Female School and later at the Hindu Mahila Vidyalaya.
As the daughter of someone who organised and fought for women’s emancipation, Kadambini went on to study in college and became the first woman to pass the University of Calcutta entrance examination. In 1882, she passed the examination for the Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree along with Chandramukhi Basu from the University of Calcutta, making her and Chandramukhi the first female graduates in the country.
Entry into medicine
Wanting to study medicine, Kadambini decided to enrol at the Calcutta Medical College after graduation. She was, however, believed to have been unable to receive the BMC certificate due to a shortage of a couple of marks. She did receive the GBMC (Graduate of Bengal Medical College) degree, though, in 1886. Thus, she became the first Indian woman to be allowed to practice Western medicine.
Around 1888, Kadambini started working at the Lady Dufferin Hospital for a monthly salary of 300 rupees. She had even gone to Nepal to treat British royalty. Along with pursuing medicine, she was also politically quite vocal and active. Around 1899, Kadambini was one of the first women delegates elected to the Fifth Session of the Congress in Bombay and the next year, she won to become the first women speaker at the Congress.
She also served as the president of the Transvaal Indian Association, founded by Gandhiji’s colleague Henry Pollock. She was a member of the Women’s Conference held in Calcutta and even presided over the General Brahmo Samaj session in Calcutta.
A doctor, wife and mother
Around 1883, Kadambini married Dwarakanath Ganguly (thus the change in name from Kadambini Bose to Kadambini Ganguly in many documents). Dwarakanath Ganguly was a Bengali Brahmo reformer, educator, journalist, and pioneer of women’s rights in British India.
She was a mother to eight children and is often said to have been deft in needlework. She became a practising doctor while equally devoting herself to family and household affairs, an action which was deemed impossible by many in the era.
Despite having being burdened with domestic chores, like most women of that time, Kadambini still managed to smash the glass ceilings and societal stereotypes in both her professional and personal life.
A name which should not be forgotten in the course of time, Dr Kadambini is a reason many of us are able to pursue our passion — in medicine and in life.

- According to experts, there is no evidence former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill said any variation of the quote, "Americans can always be trusted to do the right thing, once all other possibilities have been exhausted."
- Israeli politician Abba Eban, who died in 2002, appears to be the first to have said a version of this quote in the late 1960s, albeit with a reference to "nations," rather than "Americans."
- Historical records and reports indicate that people began attributing the quote to Churchill in the 1980s, long after his death in 1965.
For years, people have claimed that former U.K. Prime Minister Winston Churchill said, "Americans can always be trusted to do the right thing, once all other possibilities have been exhausted," or similar iterations of this quote.
One example of it was posted on Reddit as early as 2010 (archived).
The rumor recirculated on social media following the results of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, seemingly in response to the Democratic Party winning control of both the House and the Senate.
Members of Congress, journalists and even a webpage of America's National Churchill Museum have also attributed this quote to Churchill.
(X user @fakedansavage)
There's just one problem: It has not been possible to find any evidence proving Churchill ever made such a statement.
A 2016 blog post by The Churchill Project of Hillsdale College, which is dedicated to accurately recording the politician's legacy, reads:
We have been unable to discover [the quote] in any transcript, memoir, or published or private writings, speech, or correspondence. This is not to say that Churchill didn't have that sentiment from time to time.
In 2013, NPR ran an audio story about how often U.S. members of Congress cite this unsubstantiated Churchill quote. Per the public broadcaster, Sen. Mark Warner, D-VA, used the line so regularly that "his staff decided to put it on a plaque or some other memento."
"But when they went to research the origins of the line, they came up empty, despite blood, toil, tears and sweat," NPR said.
Richard Langworth, editor of a 2008 book called, "Churchill by Himself: The Definitive Collection of Quotations," reportedly told NPR something similar:
"I wish I could substantiate that he said it. But so far, I cannot," says Richard Langworth, editor of the journal Finest Hour, published by WinstonChurchill.org.
Langworth has combed through millions of words written by and about Churchill and found no evidence that the former prime minister ever said that about America.
This phenomenon of attributing snappy quotes to Churchill and other notable figures of history is so common it has a name, "Churchillian Drift." Nigel Rees, former host of the BBC's now-defunct "Quote... Unquote" radio quiz show, first coined the term to describe "the process whereby the actual originator of a quotation is often elbowed to one side and replaced by someone more famous."
Where did the quote actually come from, then?
As fact-checking blog Quote Investigator reported in 2012, the earliest version of this saying appears to come from a comment made by Israeli politician and diplomat Abba Eban, per a 1967 New York Times article — though he did not mention "Americans":
Commenting that the passage of time offered the best hope of an end to the problems of Israel and her neighbors, he said: "Men and nations behave wisely when they have exhausted all other resources."
Eban also repeated this sentiment in a United Nations speech.
The first time this quote was used to reference Americans appears to be in a U.S. congressional hearing in 1970, when Bernard F. Hillenbrand — the first executive director of the National Association of Counties, a nonprofit that represents county governments across the U.S. — attributed the quote to an anonymous "Irishman" (see PDF Page 43):
And indeed, we often know how to do things by the philosophy that was expounded by another Irishman I know. He said that you can depend on Americans to do the right thing when they have exhausted every other possibility.
Quote Investigator reported that by 1980, people were crediting Churchill with the quote, according to the pages of an academic journal and a Harvard Business School bulletin that are not available online.
In 1985, U.S. Department of Agriculture then-Secretary John Block also attributed a variant of this quote to Churchill during a Senate hearing (see PDF Page 69):
Winston Churchill once said, "You can always count on Americans to do the right thing after they have tried everything else."
Churchill died in 1965, meaning historical records indicate the quote was only attributed to him after his death.

A video circulating on X, bearing the logo of M World, purports to show Russian foreign minister Sergey Viktorovich Lavrov saying that India is merely an oil-trading partner to Russia and that the two countries share only a commercial relationship. In the video, Lavrov is also heard claiming that India has no right to interfere in Russia’s foreign policy or advise Moscow on matters concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States or any other country.
Supreme Court advocate and activist Prashant Bhushan shared the video on his X account (@pbhushan1), which he later deleted. In his post, he criticized the Indian government and questioned what kind of advice external affairs minister S Jaishankar gave to Russia.
Another X account, Diya Kapoor, also shared the video with the similar claim of Sergey Lavrov drawing clear boundaries about the relationship with India.
🚨🇷🇺🇮🇳 RUSSIA DRAWS A CLEAR LINE!
“India is a trading partner, nothing more. We supply oil, and India pays for it. This commercial relationship does not give New Delhi the right to dictate or interfere in Russia’s foreign policy.”
Sergey Viktorovich ⚠️🌍 https://t.co/uX1x0adl0G
— Diya kapoor (@DiyaKapoor113) November 2, 2026
Some X accounts also shared this video with the claim of Sergey Lavrov dismissing India.
Fact Check
After a closer examination of the video, the movements of Sergey Lavrov while speaking appear unnatural and seem out of sync with the audio. This suggests that the clip may have been edited or manipulated. Using this as a lead, we performed a Google reverse image search on several keyframes from the video and found a video with the same background and clothing uploaded by M WORLD on October 31.
A comparison of the two videos shows that Sergey Lavrov’s clothing, background, head movements, and hand gestures are the same, with only the audio being different. Even the ‘M World’ YouTube channel logo appeared in both videos, confirming that the original video had been digitally manipulated. Both videos also feature the exact same glitch at the same moment.
In the original video, Sergey Lavrov is seen refusing the reports from Ukrainian officials claiming that Russian President Vladimir Putin refused to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and stating if Zelenskyy wants a direct meeting, he must travel to Moscow, where Russia will guarantee his safety and security.
Media outlet DW News posted the original video on October 31 showing the conversation about President Putin and Ukrainian President Zelenskyy meeting.
Furthermore, the official X account of the Russian Embassy in India, Russia in India (@RusEmbIndia) has also debunked the video. “Please stop copying silly AI fakes,” it said in a comment to the X post by Diya Kapoor.
@DiyaKapoor113 Please stop copying silly AI fakes
— Russia in India 🇷🇺 (@RusEmbIndia) November 3, 2026
Union government’s official MEA fact check account, too, flagged the post as fake.
Fake Alert!!! 🚨🚨🚨
The video of the Russian Foreign Minister being used in this post is fake! https://t.co/jpEX6qu19p
— MEA FactCheck (@MEAFactCheck) November 3, 2026
To sum up, the viral video claiming that Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov publicly dismissed India’s diplomatic standing is completely false and an AI-generated deepfake. The original footage contains a briefing regarding Russia-Ukraine relations, and there is no mention of India.
Twinkle Shrivastav is an intern at Alt News.

The Nvidia scandal has wiped away $1T in value. What that means for your investments
Chipmaker's massive weight in stock indexes can have far-reaching impacts
Nvidia's stock dove again on Thursday as the massive affair and alleged spying scandal led longtime CEO Jensen Huang to step down, forcing investors to question what the company's future would look like without him.
Shares in the AI chipmaker plunged by 14 per cent after the stock market opened following Huang's resignation as CEO and a board member, before climbing back up and closing the day down 4.3 per cent.
The broader market mostly escaped the Nvidia fallout, with major indexes dipping to only moderate losses to finish the day.
Michael Dehal, a senior portfolio manager at Dehal Investment Partners, says the appointment of chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO likely helped pull Nvidia stock back up.
"That quick resolution on a temporary basis was reassuring to investors," Dehal said.
But this has still been a major slide for a company which first reached a $5 trillion US valuation a year ago and has lost more than $1 trillion US of that in the wake of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang has admitted to having an affair but did not say whether it was with Alice Huang, the woman U.S. intelligence services allege is working for Beijing. He is alleged to have had another affair with a vice president within the company who reports directly to him, according to a report published by the New York Times on Wednesday.
It's unwelcome news to industry-watchers who are now re-evaluating Nvidia's worth without its seemingly irreplaceable leader and co-founder.
And such big swings can impact investments and retirement funds held by many Canadians too, say financial planners and money managers.
As one of the most valuable companies in the world, Nvidia makes up a big part of major stock indexes, where companies with bigger market values are given more weight.
Because of its size, the Santa Clara, Calif.-based company makes up about six per cent of the S&P 500, and about nine per cent of the tech-heavy Nasdaq.
Dehal says a lot of Canadians hold index funds through exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which track those major indexes, meaning they may be exposed to big swings in Nvidia's value. Mutual funds may also be tech-heavy, but might be more diversified since they are actively managed by professionals.
A screen on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange displays news about Nvidia's stock price in New York, on Monday. (Yuki Iwamura/Associated Press)
Those indexes have become dominated by tech companies in recent years as the AI boom has made other companies like Apple, Microsoft and Google's parent company Alphabet more valuable. With tech outfits now making up an estimated 40 per cent of the S&P 500, certified financial planner Zainab Williams says investors who have parked their money in basic ETFs might be exposed to big changes in tech stocks — AI in particular.
"People often hold so many different ETFs and they feel that they are well diversified," Williams said. But if those ETFs are made up of a lot of the same companies, "you are exposing yourself to the same type of volatility."
Portfolio manager Michael Dehal says Huang's quick exit from Nvidia was 'reasuring to investors.' (Submitted by Michael Dehal)
Some industry analysts worry the Nvidia scandal could ripple throughout the broader tech market because of the company's role in the AI buildout.
With an estimated 80 per cent market share for its chips that power everything from AI data centres to ChatGPT or drones, the company is an integral player in the industry. It's also poured money into funding other AI companies, bankrolling the likes of Anthropic, Toronto-based Cohere and the cloud computing outfit CoreWeave.
Because Huang was a driving force behind those financing deals, Dehan says whether Nvidia keeps funding other tech companies is an open question, and could be a short term drag on other AI firms.
But he and other investors expect the tech sector won't take a major hit. In fact, tech companies like Broadcom and AMD that make their own chips made gains on Thursday, picking up some of the slack left behind by Nvidia, according to the president of Murray Wealth Group, Jamie Murray.
"The money's still there, it's still going to be spent. And we don't really see this slowing down everything, just maybe a shifting of the deck chairs," Murray said.
Outside of tech stocks, Dehan says those with a diversified portfolio shouldn't worry — but it does drive home the importance of not putting all your eggs in one basket.

Williams says the situation could serve as a reminder for investors to "look under the hood" of their investments to get a better sense of whether they might be exposed to certain industries or companies.
"If what happened [in the] last week really gave you heart palpitations, take a look at what you can start doing to reduce some of that exposure and to look at investing in different countries, different sectors," Williams said.

A little-known law could upend the dairy industry
California grants animals a right to exercise. Will the state finally enforce it?
Deep-blue, regulation-happy California is not usually imagined as factory farm country. But the state leads the US in agricultural output, and it is, by a wide margin, America’s top producer of dairy, one of the most brutal sectors in our food system. And it turns out that one of the most foundational, most disturbing practices found in modern dairy farming may already be illegal under a California animal cruelty law — but state officials have shown little inclination to look into it.
At any given time, 9 million to 10 million dairy cows populate farms across the US, and California is home to 1.7 million of them, the vast majority of whom are raised on mega dairies. Because cows, like other mammals, must give birth to produce milk, dairy farming is organized around continuous cycles of pregnancy, birth, and lactation. Dairy cows typically give birth around once a year; their calves are then promptly taken from them. Depending on their sex, the calves will eventually join a milking herd or be raised for beef.
But whatever their ultimate market destination, the overwhelming majority of baby cows born in the dairy industry, in California and nationwide, spend their first few months of life housed alone, in individual crates or enclosures. Many of them look like this:
Earlier this year, I wrote at length about that practice. These wooden crates provide each calf about 13 square feet of living space, less than one-tenth the size of a typical parking spot. “We’re talking roughly the size of a coffin,” Vanessa Shakib, a lawyer and co-founder of the Los Angeles-area nonprofit Advancing Law for Animals, told me. Confining calves in this manner is not dissimilar to the use of gestation crates in the pork industry — tiny metal enclosures where pigs barely have room to move. Gestation crates have sparked intense national controversy that’s reached the halls of Congress and the US Supreme Court. But the extreme confinement of dairy calves has not received anywhere close to as much legal and political scrutiny.
In California, there’s an obvious legal problem with calf crates. The state has a plain-English law, Section 597t of its criminal code, that mandates that confined animals be provided an “adequate exercise area.” Though it doesn’t define what constitutes such an area, Shakib and other farm animal advocates argue that it strains credulity to believe the minuscule, barren crates provide one. The practice “is squarely at odds with the plain meaning of the words,” Shakib said.
But California has never enforced that law against calf crates in the state’s powerful dairy industry, where millions of newborn calves have been kept in extreme confinement (nor, apparently, has the law been enforced against any factory farm). It’s a prime example of agricultural exceptionalism — the doctrine running through American legal and political culture, as Vox’s Kenny Torrella has written, that effectively absolves agribusiness from having to play by the same rules as everyone else.
Shakib and her organization are now hoping to change that.
They’re leading a lawsuit against Hettinga Dairy, a Southern California farm that has kept thousands of calves in individual crates, alleging that it’s violating Section 597t. If the case succeeds, it could create a blueprint for similar challenges statewide, and even spark a broader reckoning within America’s dairy industry.
The case that could transform how dairy calves are treated
Advancing Law for Animals just filed suit on behalf of the Caru Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, a California animal protection nonprofit seeking a court ruling that the calf crates violate state law. The case names Hettinga Dairy and related defendants in connection with a San Jacinto, California, facility that specializes in raising calves. The most recent available records from California’s State Water Resources Control Board report the farm’s animal population as 4,200 calves.
Such facilities, often known as “calf ranches” or “calf nurseries,” have become increasingly central to the US dairy business — as we wrote earlier this year, they “raise calves on dairy farms’ behalf during the fragile infant stage in which they’re too young to bring in any revenue.”
Caru SPCA (which is formerly known as the Animal Legal Defense Fund Cruelty Prevention Unit) flew drone cameras over the Hettinga facility earlier this year to document the calf housing there, filming the small wooden crates that are common in California and the Southwest, typically providing less than 15 square feet of space per calf. Many dairy farms and calf ranches use a different, plastic hutch design that provides more space, but the smaller wooden hutches remain widespread.
Calves typically spend about two months in these hutches before being moved into larger group pens; the lawsuit alleges that Hettinga keeps them in crates for around nine weeks.
“Calves are trapped for months, even in summer heat, unable to stretch their limbs or move freely,” the lawsuit alleges. Under 597t, “animals have a statutory right to minimal movement, and Defendants systematically violate that right daily, creating immense and ongoing suffering.”
That San Jacinto farm is part of a broader network of dairy farms and calf-raising facilities linked to the Hettingas, a prominent dairy family whose farms collectively confine thousands of calves and cows across California, according to state public records. Most consumers have never heard of Hettinga, nor of the hundreds of other industrial dairies and calf-raising farms across California that operate largely out of public view. But the Hettingas also have a presence on grocery store shelves: According to the brand’s website, the family also owns Sarah Farms, a mass-market milk label in the Southwestern US.
Vox emailed a list of questions about the allegations in the lawsuit to multiple contacts associated with Hettinga businesses. An employee at GH Processing, a Hettinga family-associated dairy plant in Arizona, confirmed receiving the email and said she would pass it on to colleagues in California. No one responded to Vox’s questions by publication time.
A representative from the California water board told Vox that the 2024 annual report for the San Jacinto calf facility identified Hein and Ellen Hettinga as the farm’s operators. But state regulators have not received the 2025 report, which was due in January 2026, and could not verify the facility’s current ownership. Hein Hettinga, who built the family’s dairy empire, died in 2023; Ellen, his wife, is one of the defendants named in the lawsuit.
Dairy industry trade groups often defend calf crates, arguing that they allow farmers to provide each animal with individualized care and reduce their exposure to pathogens. Whether that’s true is contested — some industry veterinarians endorse that view, while others maintain that it’s based on a narrow view of calves’ well-being and that properly managed social housing need not harm their physical health. Even within the industry, there’s growing acknowledgement that isolation is harmful to calves, and that it would be better for dairy farms to transition to a different system.
A 2023 assessment of calf welfare from the European Food Safety Authority — the EU agency that provides scientific guidance on animal welfare — found “no locomotor play behavior possible” for calves given a space allowance of about 16 square feet each. A calf in such confinement “is expected to spend most of its time lying down because no other activities can be performed,” the review states. To fully express natural behaviors like galloping, jumping, and kicking, it recommends that calves housed alone be allotted 318 square feet each, and calves housed in groups be allotted 215 square feet each, though it notes that even smaller increases in space could meaningfully improve their welfare.
Guidelines from Calf Care and Quality Assurance, a US industry-created animal care program, state that “individually housed calves have a harder time coping with changes in housing and diet and may have cognitive and developmental disadvantages, including poor learning skills and deficient social skills.” Temple Grandin, the famed livestock scientist at Colorado State University, has written that “calves should be raised with other calves, not in isolation.” They are, after all, intensely social herd animals.
Regardless of the industry’s opinion on the practice, though, 597t makes no exception for livestock industry standard practices, the way some states’ animal cruelty laws do. “It doesn’t matter whether this defendant or whether the dairy industry believes solitary confinement of baby animals serves a useful purpose,” Shakib said. “California law here is crystal clear — it requires an adequate exercise area. Industry custom or convenience does not erase that requirement.”
California’s animal cruelty double standard
The ubiquitous confinement of dairy calves in tiny crates remains poorly understood by the general public, and even, to some extent, within the animal protection movement. That is because, for many years, animal advocates focused their campaigning against extreme confinement in the dairy industry on veal, the notorious specialty meat made from male dairy calves.
Those efforts helped bring about California’s Proposition 12, a landmark law passed in 2018 that bans certain forms of extreme confinement, including tiny crates that used to be the norm in veal production. Any veal raised or sold in California must now come from calves allotted at least 43 square feet of living space each. But the overwhelming share of California’s dairy calves are not raised for veal and thus get no protection under Prop 12, even as many members of the public may assume the problem of extreme confinement of calves has been solved.
In the last few years, however, a small wave of animal advocates have been drawing attention to the continued plight of dairy calves. The animal rights group Direct Action Everywhere (DxE) over the last year has documented and mapped calf confinement across California, including at Grimmius Cattle Company, the largest calf raiser in the state and the subject of Vox’s earlier reporting. This fall, DxE investigator Lewis Bernier obtained footage showing calves from a dairy farm that the group said supplies to Land O’Lakes being transported to Grimmius, where the newborn animals are raised in the same standard, approximately 13-square-foot wooden hutches. Land O’Lakes did not respond to requests for comment.
The crates aren’t the only problem
Beyond extreme confinement in crates, DxE’s investigations have surfaced allegations of overt abuse of calves — including animals being kicked, punched, and pulled by their ears and tails — at calf ranches and dairy farms throughout California.
Drone footage taken earlier this year at a dairy farm that DxE linked to Leprino Foods — a major cheese supplier that reportedly sells to Domino’s, Papa John’s, and Pizza Hut, among others — shows calves being kicked, pushed, pulled by their ears, and thrown to the ground. In one clip, a calf appears to be kicked in the face. One of DxE’s investigators followed a milk truck from that farm to a Leprino plant, the group said. Leprino Foods did not respond to requests for comment.
DxE has also captured drone footage of calf and dairy facilities that California records list as operated by members of the Hettinga family, separate from the one that is being sued by Advancing Law for Animals. At one of the calf ranches, in San Bernardino County, Robert Drummond, a member of DxE’s Los Angeles chapter, filmed handlers who appear to be whipping frightened calves and pulling them by their tails. Hitting calves and pulling them this way are both considered “unacceptable” handling practices by the industry’s own calf-raising guidelines. DxE reported those findings to the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department, which did not provide comment for this story.
An annual report filed with the California water board identifies Gerben Hettinga as the operator of that farm, a representative from the agency told Vox. Vox attempted to reach Hettinga using the email addresses and phone number listed for him in state records but received no response.
Advancing Law for Animals’ lawsuit is not the first time animal advocates have accused California’s dairy industry of violating 597t. “There’s a long history of animal activists and organizations trying unsuccessfully to enforce this law,” Will Lowrey, founder and legal counsel at animal advocacy legal nonprofit Animal Partisan, told me in an email. His organization has also sought enforcement of 597t in the dairy industry.
DxE has sent criminal complaints about calf crates, citing 597t, to eight law enforcement agencies throughout California; the group says that none of them have taken enforcement action. In March, the sheriff’s office of Tulare County, in the heart of the Central Valley’s dairy industry, rejected one of these complaints and stated in its reply to DxE that calf confinement did not violate the law because “the facilities reviewed do not raise calves for veal production.” But 597t doesn’t exclusively apply to veal; it applies to all confined animals. The sheriff’s office may have confused it with Prop 12. The office did not respond to a request for comment.
DxE has also met with California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office about calf confinement, and office staff asked the group questions about its investigative findings, DxE director of communications Cassie King told me. Responding to Vox’s request for comment about whether 13-square-foot crates are permissible under 597t, the attorney general’s press office said, “we cannot provide a comment at this time.” DxE plans to rally outside Bonta’s office in Sacramento this week calling for enforcement of that law against Grimmius Cattle Company. The group submitted a packet of documents to the attorney general, including a statement from more than a dozen veterinarians about the animal welfare harms of small calf crates.
“The California dairy industry seems inclined to act like [597t] doesn’t exist and no law enforcement officer, prosecutor, or judge that I have come across seems inclined to enforce the law as written,” Lowrey wrote to me. “It’s hard to imagine that this is for any other reason than deference to the state agriculture industry.”
The law enforcement officials that have rejected these complaints haven’t explained how calf crates could satisfy 597t’s requirement for an adequate exercise area; they largely sidestep the question altogether. For non-livestock animals, meanwhile, California has enforced the law more readily. A state appeals court recently upheld 597t convictions against two people who had continuously kept German shepherds in kennels measuring 48 to 50 square feet. For hundreds of thousands of calves kept in cages one-quarter of that size, though, the protections offered by California’s animal cruelty laws have proven illusory.
Police and prosecutors have broad discretion to decline to pursue criminal complaints, but a lawsuit like Caru SPCA’s may be harder to brush aside. The question will now be addressed by a judge, and California’s dairy industry could finally face an on-the-merits ruling on whether these crates are legal. “At some point, I believe a judge will find that the law says what it says and will decide that a California dairy keeping calves in hutches [is] in violation of Penal Code 597t,” Lowrey wrote. “It’s just a matter of time and maybe—hopefully—Caru v. Hettinga is that case.”
It’s understandable that state officials may hesitate to enforce a law that could upend a linchpin of the dairy industry, whose products are consumed by nearly every American and woven into virtually every corner of our food system. But animal agriculture has a long history of warning that animal welfare regulations will devastate its business, only to adapt when regulation takes effect.
And although California has earned its reputation for overly burdensome regulation in other domains, giving newborn calves enough room to move hardly seems like an unreasonable imposition (especially considering that dairy farming makes up only a tiny share of the state’s massive economy). Freeing them from this form of solitary confinement would amount to one of the most consequential animal welfare advances in California’s history. And it need not require passing any new laws — the state merely needs to hold the dairy industry to a standard already in place.

African writing award probe finds 'no evidence' winning story was AI generated
- Published
The Caine Prize for African Writing has said that after an internal review it has found no evidence that Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza had used generative AI to write his winning short story and confirmed him as the winner of this year's £10,000 ($13,000) award.
Ellah Wakatama, chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees, said the matter had been investigated following an article in US magazine The Atlantic with the headline, Yet Another Literary Prizewinner Seems to Be AI.
"From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human written," she said in a video posted on X.
The accusation had caused a social media uproar and Kundizeza had denied the allegation.
The Atlantic article by journalist Vauhini Vara alleged that AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.
Her allegations followed rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies.
Following the publication of her article last month, Vara had told BBC's Front Row programme that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".
The backlash on social media included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.
- Zimbabwean author denies using AI to write award-winning story 
  - Published14 October
Wakatama said the Caine Prize organisation had considered Vara's allegations "carefully and fairly".
"We chose to take a human-centred approach to the investigation. Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel, and the Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published," she said.
"It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author."
In a statement, the Caine Prize explained further that the analysis had been conducted by an independent cyber security and digital forensic investigator, external.
The day after winning the prestigious Caine Prize award earlier in October, Kundizeza had told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.
He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began.
