What's a Honey Trap? The spy tactic that helped topple Jensen Huang
One of the world's oldest spy tactics appears to have helped topple one of the world's richest men. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday amid revelations that he had an affair with a female client that U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese spy, according to the New York Times.
NPR has not independently confirmed the reporting by the Times, which said Huang also had an unrelated affair with a company executive who reported to him. The Chinese government has called the accusation of spying, "nothing but smears against China."
Using a romantic relationship to gather intelligence from foreigners – known as a honey trap – has a long history in China and beyond. The Chinese Ministry of State Security, the country's main civilian intelligence agency, routinely tries to recruit women and occasionally men for honey traps, according to former CIA officers and other U.S. officials familiar with Chinese spy craft.
Some target businessmen for industrial espionage or to gain insights into the economic and political strategy of foreign governments. Peter Mattis, a former CIA counter-intelligence analyst, said honey traps also serve as influence operations with spies trying to gain enough trust to shape the target's thinking about China.
'A whole of society approach'
"The biggest thing here that we should pay attention to is that the Ministry of State Security celebrates a tradition of getting inside the enemy's decision-making," said Mattis, president of the Jamestown Foundation, a national security think tank in Washington, D.C., that focuses on America's geopolitical rivals.
Nicholas Eftimiades, who spent more than 34 years with the CIA and Defense Intelligence Agency and now teaches at Penn State, said the honey trap is just one tactic among many that use ordinary Chinese citizens to gather information at home and abroad.
"Unlike the CIA, or MI6 or any of the other Western services, China has a 'whole of society approach,'" said Eftimiades, the author of Chinese Intelligence Operations: An Analysis of the People's Republic of China's Intelligence Services. "Chinese law supports this. The National Intelligence Law of 2017 requires citizens to cooperate with intelligence collection efforts."
A long list of honey traps
The Chinese government has employed honey traps in the United States and elsewhere in the West. In the 2010s, Christine Fang worked as a political fundraiser in California where she developed a physical relationship with Democrat Rep. Eric Swalwell before and after he became a congressman.
The FBI warned Swalwell they thought Fang was a spy. He denied doing anything wrong and she fled back to China.
In the 1980s and 1990s, the FBI paid Katrina Leung – a Los Angeles businesswoman – $1.7 million over 18 years to spy on China. However, Leung had affairs with two FBI agents and the bureau later determined she was a double-agent.
The most remarkable honey trap case dates to the 1960s, when a young French diplomat began a nearly two-decade affair with a male Peking opera performer, whom he thought was a woman. The story inspired the play and movie, M Butterfly.
The woman implicated in the Nvidia case, Alice Huang, is a Chinese businesswoman whose company, Megaspeed, was a major buyer of advanced chips from Nvidia. The Times reported the U.S. had her under surveillance and learned of her connections to Chinese state security through her communications.
Desmond Shum, a Hong Kong businessman and former China insider, says Alice Huang doesn't fit the usual profile in these cases. She appears to be what the Chinese call a "white glove" – or front-person for multi-billion-dollar commercial deals, which Shum says could have insulated her from the Ministry of State Security.
Shum doesn't think Alice Huang is a professional spy, pointing out that she hasn't been discreet on social media, posting photos from her visits to luxurious country clubs and fancy foreign destinations.
"A spy wouldn't do that," Shum told NPR from his home in the United Kingdom.
Isaac Stone Fish, a former reporter in China who runs Strategy Risks, a China-focused business intelligence firm, says the Ministry of State Security – or MSS – could have approached Alice Huang after it learned of her affair with the Nvidia head.
"One imagines that every time a Chinese person enters into a romantic relationship with a very, very powerful American, MSS notices that," Stone Fish said.
The stuff of spy novels and movies
Honey traps are a staple of spy novel and movie plots, including the Netflix series, Black Doves, The Americans on FX, Apple TV's Slow Horses as well as James Bond films, such as From Russia with Love.
In reality, when Chinese state security approaches women for these operations, it's embarrassing and humiliating. The tactic perpetuates racist, sexist stereotypes while casting suspicion on the vast majority of Chinese people, who have nothing to do with intelligence gathering.
In addition to China, many intelligence services have engaged in honey traps. The Russians historically used sex workers for blackmail and leverage. During the Cold-War, East Germany sent well-educated and well-mannered male spies – known as Romeos – to West Germany.
Mossad, the Israeli intelligence service, used honey traps from the 1950s into the 1970s in countries such as Egypt, Iraq and Iran. But investigative reporter Yossi Melman, who's written many books on Israeli intelligence, says the practice has dwindled as cyber spying and digital traps have proven more efficient.
The U.S. used sexual entrapment against the Soviets, but several former officials said the Americans now prefer to appeal to people on ideological grounds and provide financial carrots, such as money for college tuition or health care for a sick family member.
Even though countries repeatedly warn businessmen and government officials about the tell-tale signs of a honey trap, ego and vanity remain human weaknesses and men continue to succumb, said Eftimiades.
"Welcome to the male of the species," he said. "Is everyone aware of this? Yes. Does everyone think it'll happen to them? No. And, you know, and it happens all the time."

Sandpapergate: Australia Test captain Pat Cummins dismisses Usman Khawaja's claims over ball-tampering scandal as 'utter nonsense'
Usman Khawaja said in new book 'Sabr' that every Australia player was aware of ball-tampering scheme in Cape Town in 2018; current Test captain Pat Cummins, who played in the match, reiterated his denial of involvement and dismissed Khawaja's claims as "utter nonsense"
Friday 13 November 2026 00:11, UK
Australia Test captain Pat Cummins dismissed his former team-mate Usman Khawaja's claims as "utter nonsense" after the recently retired batter said in his autobiography that the whole side were aware of ball-tampering that took place on their 2018 tour of South Africa.
Khawaja made the revelations in his new book 'Sabr', which was released earlier this week, bringing the scandal back onto the agenda eight years after Cameron Bancroft was caught on camera using sandpaper on the ball while Australia were fielding.
Only Bancroft, then-captain Steve Smith and his vice-captain David Warner were punished, with each receiving lengthy bans as the rest of the Australian team and coaching staff denied knowledge of the scheme.
Cummins, who was a relatively junior member of the side playing in just his 13th Test match, in 2021 issued a joint-statement with fellow bowlers from the fixture Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon, in which they denied knowing that a foreign substance had been taken onto the field to alter the ball in order to try to make it swing.
"When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong. I've said that consistently for the last eight years," Cummins told reporters on Friday morning in Sydney having called the press conference himself on social media.
"I did not know that was happening, but Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that.
"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."
Following the publication of the book, Warner, who received a year-long ban from all cricket and a lifetime ban from leadership roles, said on Monday that Khawaja's version of events was "100 per cent accurate".
Cummins, who was appointed Australia captain in November 2021, criticised Khawaja for being "casual" with the lives of his former team-mates and Australian cricket as a whole.
"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations," Cummins said.
"In his book, Ussie has been casual with my life and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket."
Cummins, who appeared to become emotional at times in a press conference that lasted more than an hour, revealed that a video taken of him and his wife Becky in a heated discussion a day earlier had been prompted by her anger with Khawaja's actions.
Despite that and his clear disagreement with Khawaja's statements, Cummins said that he does not intend to pursue legal action.
"I did get advised this week that some of the things that've been said are probably defamatory, but I won't be doing that," Cummins said.
"You've got to move on. It's been eight years. We're moving on. So you got to draw a line at some point."
Cummins has been rested for England's white-ball tour of Australia, which resulted in him holding his press conference on Friday morning in Sydney just hours before the first ODI was scheduled to begin in Perth.
How have other Australian players reacted?
Cummins' extraordinary press conference came a day after Australia ODI captain Mitchell Marsh, who was also part of the team that toured South Africa in 2018, declined to comment on a series of questions about Khawaja's book.
Khawaja also claimed in the book that Australia experimented with lifting the seam on the ball during the 2017-18 Ashes at home to England, which they won 4-0 under the captaincy of Smith.
Starc, who had spoken to reporters on Tuesday, took a similar line to Cummins as he insisted that his recollections hadn't changed.
Starc, who is also not part of Australia's limited-overs side to face England, said of Khawaja's claims: "I haven't really paid much attention to it to be fair.
"There are differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process, at the time and since.
"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers but from where I stand my opinion hasn't changed, my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.
"As far as our statement said, we weren't aware of things being taken on the field. That's where I'll leave it.
"I will be sticking to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time eight years ago, so clearly there are differing versions from different people.
"We weren't aware of anything taken on the field to be tampered with. We saw it on the big screen in Cape Town.
"As far as the book is concerned, I haven't read it. I probably won't read it, so that's for Usman to elaborate on."

Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation.
The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians.
According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years.
The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort.
In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia.
A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022.
This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military.
Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said: “The Indonesian government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure that no Indonesians will be recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues.”
Indonesia, she added, was particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking.
Days later, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting its nationals that used social media and messaging apps to recruit victims.
The posts promised lucrative jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after the applicants travelled to Russia they were directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, with some deployed to conflict zones, police said.
The ‘I Want to Live’ governmental initiative was established in September 2022 by the coordination headquarters for Prisoners of War with support from Ukraine defence ministry and defence intelligence (HUR).
It was designed to allow active-duty troops, including Russian servicemen and foreign nationals recruited into the Russian military, to safely surrender and exit the battlefield.

Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?
- Published
After a shock announcement 10 months ago that the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) would be held every four years, the governing body of football on the continent has reversed course.
The Confederation of African Football (Caf) will instead retain the tournament's traditional biennial staging, with its president Patrice Motsepe saying the U-turn was based on "advancing, protecting and promoting" the interests of the African game.
The first indication that the frequency of Afcon was being reconsidered came at Caf's strategy conference in Cape Verde earlier this month.
Questions are now being asked about the decision-making process and what this means for the future of African football.
Why was the planned change controversial?
Afcon has predominantly been held every two years since its first edition in 1957, barring two three-year gaps in the 1960s and one year between the 2012 and 2013 tournaments.
On the eve of the 2025 finals in Morocco, Motsepe announced all that would change from 2028.
The South African said the shift to a four-year cycle was, in part, to help the global calendar "be significantly more synchronised and harmonised".
In recent years Afcon has been staged midway through the European club season, leading to recurring disputes over the release of African players.
Fifa general secretary Mattias Grafstrom was sitting aside Motsepe when the plan was announced, and critics highlighted that the scheduling change favoured football's world governing body more than the African game.
"I think the general sentiment around the continent has been that the two-year cycle has served the continent very well," Football Association of Zambia (Faz) official Sydney Mungala told the BBC.
"The idea of pushing it to a four-year cycle was a bit of a surprise, maybe a concern, to the bulk of the African federations."
- Afcon to return to two-year cycle after Caf U-turn 
  - Published21 hours ago
- Afcon to be held every four years from 2028 
  - Published20 December 2025
What were the benefits of the switch?
Afcon has developed into Caf's biggest revenue generator, with a profit of $114m (£85m) forecast for Afcon 2025, up from $75m (£56m) for the previous finals in Ivory Coast.
In its stead, an annual Africa Nations League involving all 54 countries on the continent was proposed. Motsepe described the ambition as creating a "world-class competition every year".
The idea was to move beyond Caf's heavy reliance on Afcon and develop a more sustainable commercial model which could support football development.
Yet the last time an ambitious alternative competition took place in Africa, it failed to deliver on its financial promise and was quickly ditched.
The Africa Super League, announced by Caf in 2022 to revolutionise continental club competition, and with projected annual revenues of $200m (£149m), was discontinued after just one edition.
Motsepe later acknowledged that commercial deals fell short of expectations.
"We didn't proceed as quickly because the partners that were giving us money were not giving us the deals we thought we would be happy with," he said.
Why the U-turn on Afcon?
The decision to move to a four-year cycle was taken at a meeting of Caf's executive committee last December - without being tabled at a general assembly where all member nations are represented.
"These kinds of decisions should be put to the general assembly, they should be debated and discussed for months at a time," Algerian journalist Maher Mezahi told the BBC.
"Afcon is the locomotive by which Caf funds all of its other competitions."
Caf subsequently asked its 54 associations to express a preference between proceeding with the four-year format or retaining the original schedule, and the executive committee eventually voted to restore the status quo.
Motsepe said the decision was in the "best interest of African football" and would contribute to the development and growth of the sport.
He also admitted misgivings about the new Nations League, with concerns it would require "several years" before it could make "the substantial financial and football development contributions" to help the continental game be "self-supporting".
How does Fifa fit in?
Fifa president Gianni Infantino first publicly proposed holding Afcon every four years in February 2020, an idea Motsepe rejected after he was elected as Caf president 13 months later.
That has not stopped the South African cultivating a close relationship with his counterpart and Infantino's drive to expand the Fifa World Cup to 48 teams - and in the process increase African representation at the tournament - has won him backing across the continent.
Yet the Swiss' position has been under threat since his plan to sell stakes in Fifa's competitions was leaked in July.
Since then Infantino has been busy shoring up his power base ahead of his re-election bid, including at Caf's strategy meeting this month.
"He came to Cape Verde to generate support, And, by and large, Africa gave him that support," Mezahi said.
"But I think they did that in a quid pro quo - they gave him the support in return for some concessions.
"And I think the main concession was the return of the Africa Cup of Nations [to a two-year cycle].
"It shows that Africa is willing to assert its influence and look after its interests, even in the face of the global game's interest."
- Infantino says he is backed by 'vast majority' 
  - Published6 days ago
- Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president? 
  - Published6 August
Why is Afcon revenue so important?
Afcon is Caf's financial lifeline, accounting for a substantial share of the governing body's income.
Morocco 2025 was projected to generate $192m (£143m), representing 66% of Caf's total revenue from competitions across men's, women's and age-group football.
For many FAs, Afcon's importance extends far beyond the tournament because they cannot always rely on consistent government or corporate investment.
"We have 11 [Zambian] national teams and only two are partly sponsored by government," Faz official Mungala said.
"The rest have to be supported from the FA's coffers. We actually fund some of these programmes from the support that we get from Caf and Fifa."
What about upcoming Afcons?
The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to be held in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July next year.
Yet, on a visit to East Africa in September, Motsepe called for a "heightened sense of urgency" in order to make sure stadiums and supporting infrastructure are ready on time.
The next Afcon will be held just one year later in 2028 - a decision Caf made when planning for the switch to a four-year cycle and which it as has decided to stick with.
An announcement on where and exactly when the finals will be held is yet to be made.
Subsequent tournaments will be held in 2031 and 2033 to avoid clashes with the World Cup.
The proposed kick-off date for the Africa Nations League, meanwhile, is September 2029.
Motsepe's latest statement suggests the new competition will also be held every two years - rather than annually as he initially announced last December – but that begs the question of how space will be found for the fixtures to be played in an Afcon year from 2031 onwards.
While debate continues around the game's congested calendar, Caf's U-turn on scheduling has at least protected the tradition of Africa's biggest sporting showcase.
It also exposes, however, the challenge of finding a workable financial model which benefits African football as well as the demands of the global game.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office has denied reports of a heated exchange with US President Donald Trump during a phone conversation over the weekend, which reportedly centred on the possibility of resuming military strikes against Iran.
According to a report by Hebrew-language outlet Ynet, cited by The Times of Israel, Netanyahu's office rejected the allegations, describing them as "Fake news, complete nonsense". The denial came after anonymous sources familiar with the conversation described it as particularly tense, with one source reportedly calling it a "shouting match from hell."
The Times of Israel also reported that a senior Israeli official confirmed the phone call had taken place. However, the official told Ynet that it was “very much not a difficult conversation.”
The denial comes amid reports that Netanyahu has repeatedly pressed Trump in recent days to launch another military offensive against Iran.
According to The Times of Israel, the Israeli Prime Minister has been urging Washington to consider renewed military action even as Trump weighs the possibility of pursuing a diplomatic solution against escalating military tensions.
Earlier in the week, Trump indicated that further military strikes against Iran were not immediately necessary.
However, The Times of Israel noted that Trump said on Thursday that the United States does not “need a deal with Tehran.”
Meanwhile, Defence Minister Israel Katz met today with IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir and other senior defence and security officials, asserting that all decisions made during the current transitional period of coalition talks are being handled "responsibly" and in complete coordination with the military.
The Times of Israel reported that Katz's office quoted him as saying, "Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, I and the IDF chief of staff see eye to eye on the Iranian issue in all its aspects, and we will continue to work together and do whatever is necessary to ensure the security of the State of Israel and protect its citizens."
The defence minister's office further noted that Katz emphasised during the assessment that "all decisions are made responsibly and in full cooperation between the political and military leadership," underscoring that "Israel’s security is the central consideration," according to The Times of Israel.
The Times of Israel added that these remarks come after Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot—who currently holds the mandate to form a new government—cautioned Netanyahu against deploying security forces in the absence of an immediate threat, following reports that the caretaker prime minister has been pushing for military strikes on Iran over the objections of defence officials.
Meanwhile, citing Hebrew media reports, Times of Israel reported thatPrime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has begun his security briefing with Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot.
The Prime Minister’s Office does not immediately confirm the reports.
This comes after Israeli media reported that Trump and Netanyahu engaged in a heated telephone conversation over the preceding days, which reportedly deteriorated into an acrimonious exchange amid ongoing disagreements regarding the course of the war with Iran.
According to reports from Israeli news organisations Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth, the Israeli leader repeatedly pushed for renewed military action, whereas the American President preferred allowing ongoing peace negotiations with Tehran to continue.
Netanyahu has consistently argued that Washington should resume strikes and actively pursue regime change within the Islamic Republic, while Trump has favoured maintaining economic pressure to secure diplomatic concessions from Tehran. The Israeli Prime Minister's Office rejected claims that the conversation became confrontational, describing the reports as "fake news".
Israeli news outlets Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth reported that Netanyahu repeatedly urged Trump to restart the war during the call. Trump, however, continued to back a diplomatic approach as talks with Iran progressed.
Sources quoted by both outlets described the conversation as having descended into a "shouting match from hell". A senior Israeli official confirmed that the two leaders spoke over the weekend but denied that any confrontation had taken place.
The latest reports emerged days after the Financial Times said Netanyahu had been telephoning Trump daily to persuade him to resume an all-out war. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving Prime Minister, is facing uncertainty over his position after losing seats in the general election held in October.

In a major change to screening guidelines, the American Cancer Society recommended on Thursday that American men between ages 50 and 69 at an average risk of prostate cancer should test their prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood levels every two years.
The prior guidelines, released in 2010, left testing for average-risk men to their discretion, after assessing cancer risk with a physician.
Similarly, PSA testing recommendations were strengthened for high risk groups — Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer. They are now encouraged to get PSA-based screening yearly starting at 45. Black men in particular disproportionately die from prostate cancer, and the guideline authors said they hope that increased surveillance will reduce the number of Black patients presenting with cancers at advanced stages.
Then, starting at 70, the decision on whether to continue screening becomes individualized as the balance of benefit and harm is not as clear after that age. Screening should be interrupted after 80, or in men who are not expected to live another 10 years.
The changes reflect recent findings that screening through PSA levels reduced disease specific mortality for certain men, bringing the indicator back into specialists’ good graces. Once a preferred biomarker to identify risk of prostate cancer, routine PSA screening had fallen out of favor — and was dropped from the guidelines in 2010 — for its lack of specificity, which resulted in many men undergoing follow-up procedures when they had no cancer, or very slow-growing tumors.
The U.S. Preventive Service Task Force, a federally appointed panel of outside experts, has not changed its guidelines since the new evidence became available in 2025, and continues to recommend against routine, population-wide PSA screening, suggesting instead individualized decision-making. But the panel, whose recommendations determine the preventive services that insurers must cover, has announced an upcoming update.
The cutoff for PSA levels to be considered high is established as 3.0 nanograms/milliliter or higher for men aged 45 to 69 years old. This is an important clarification, said James Eastham, chief of urology at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. “Most PSA blood tests in the United States, when they’re reported, say under 4.0 [ng/ml] is normal, but it really should be under 3,” he said. “I think [the update] will hopefully help primary care physicians refer folks a little bit earlier.”
To limit the risk of overdiagnosis and overtreatment, the guidelines also now recommend two elevated PSA readings, followed by an MRI scan and/or testing for other biomarkers of prostate cancer, with the aim of reducing the number of patients undergoing biopsies. “We just wanted to give a little bit of flexibility for folks who cannot easily obtain an MRI,” said William Dahut, chief scientific officer at the ACS and a contributing author of the guidelines, about including both biomarkers and MRIs as a possible step following elevated PSA levels. However, he noted that an MRI would still be recommended prior to biopsy, should a biomarker test come back abnormal.
Though there are a variety of biomarkers, the guidelines don’t recommend one over the other. Dahut said ACS researchers intend to look more closely at biomarkers to establish which may be more effective in predicting a more aggressive cancer.
“I think the new guidelines are certainly a balanced approach for early detection of prostate cancer,” said Eastham. “There have been many men undergoing unnecessary biopsies, and many low risk cancers that were subsequently overtreated,” he said. By recommending some steps between an elevated PSA and a biopsy, he said, the new recommendations reflect the evidence that while being a good biomarker, PSA alone would identify too many men as biopsy candidates.
Finally, the guidelines emphasize the importance of active surveillance in men with slow growing cancer: “If you screen more men, you’re going to find more men with early-stage disease, and we need to be strong in our position that that does not mean that you need to rush for therapies or that you need to have therapies at all.”
For Eddie Baynes, a 56-year-old prostate cancer survivor and advocate, the new guidelines “hit the nail on the head” when it comes to recommending routine PSA screening. As a Black man, he knew he was at higher risk of developing prostate cancer, yet it wasn’t until the fraternity he belonged to organized a screening event that he, at 52, started getting regular PSA tests with his bloodwork. Though routine screening wasn’t part of the ACS recommendation at the time, it led to a cancer diagnosis and a prostatectomy.
That’s why he’s been advocating for men to get PSA levels tested, and relatively frequently. With the new guidelines, men like him will start routine screening earlier than he did. “Part of my advocacy is getting tested more frequently. So now, just to have that announcement coming from the American Cancer Society, it just makes what I’ve been urging individuals to do for a while stronger,” he said.

ByteDance is reportedly working on its own AI agent
The Chinese company wants to compete with Meta’s Muse.
ByteDance wants to take on Meta's Muse with its own AI agent. The company is readying an AI assistant that could be revealed in "the coming weeks," Bloomberg reports.
The report doesn't detail what the agent will be called or how it will work, but says that it will "serve a similar role" to Meta's Muse. Muse has already drawn more than 10 million users and CEO Mark Zuckerberg has predicted the AI agent could generate more revenue per user than its existing "family" of apps. The agent is also expected to play a significant role in Meta's AI glasses, and the company has previewed a standalone "charm" for Muse.
It's not clear if ByteDance is also planning on incorporating its agent into hardware. The AI assistant is one piece of the Chinese company's strategy to compete with frontier AI companies. ByteDance cofounder Zhang Yiming recently told employees that it would likely take "until at least 2029 or 2030" for the company's AI efforts to catch up, Bloomberg reported. Within the AI space, ByteDance has been primarily known for its video generator, Seedance. Clips from the video model went viral on social media platforms earlier this year, which eventually drew legal scrutiny from US-based studios.
If the TikTok maker does introduce its own AI agent, it would also likely raise new concerns about data privacy and how much access personal agents should get. ByteDance didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Get in, loser: Broadway's newest 'Mean Girls' are ready to insult (and enlighten) you
What would it mean to become Miss Ghana 1986? Fame, fortune, perhaps rubbing elbows with '80s superstar Bobby Brown? For a group of six teenage girls at the Aburi Girls Boarding School, the answer is: everything.
The battle for the crown is at the heart of School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play, written by Tony Award-nominated playwright Jocelyn Bioh. The play is ending a Broadway run this week and celebrating with livestream broadcasts on The League of Live Stream Theater's website for a fee (but is free for high schoolers).
School Girls is set at a boarding school in Ghana in 1986. It follows Paulina, the school's queen bee and her crew, whom she frequently belittles and bullies over their looks.
"So, do you want to be fat-fat? Or fit? And popular." Paulina asks Nana, harassing her over eating porridge instead of an apple at lunch.
Ahead of a visit from a pageant recruiter to the school, Paulina's plans to win Miss Ghana go awry after a new transfer student arrives: Ericka from … Ohio!
Ericka exposes Paulina's toxic behavior and shows her up during a performance of Whitney Houston's Greatest Love of All. Ericka, being lighter-skinned than Paulina, sparks a clash between the school's headmistress and the pageant director over beauty and who would have the best chance of winning the Miss Global Universe pageant.
Paulina becomes the victim of circumstances that she cannot control.
School Girls explores the themes of girlhood and impossible societal beauty standards with humor and humanity.
Although its title references the Tina Fey-penned 2004 film, Mean Girls, famous for its pink-hued portrayal of the toxic side of high school girls, Bioh says she wasn't actively thinking about the movie when writing School Girls.
After completing the play and needing to settle on a subtitle, Bioh found herself reflecting on the themes: "I'm like we're dealing with things and ideas and feelings and emotions." She said that her friend, actress Danai Gurira, described it as feral teenage girls. "I'm like, that archetype is incredibly universal."
A perspective on colorism
Beyond the talk about tiaras, '80s fashion and praise for Judy Bloom, School Girls tackles the issue of colorism head-on.
Bioh says she knew it was a topic she always wanted to write about after her own long journey to own her beauty as a dark-skinned woman. "I just wanted to write something that felt like it could maybe shorten the journey for somebody else who maybe felt the same way I did. Especially as a young, impressionable girl."
While School Girls approaches the topic from the perspective of Ghanaian women and girls, Bioh says the play's message has resonated with people from different backgrounds, underscoring that colorism is a global issue.
"'Cause who has decided that this one standard of beauty is the standard of beauty for everybody? I think that's a problem," Bioh explains. "I don't have a solution other than to, you know, create a play that people can feel entertained by or perhaps be impacted by, and hopefully shift their implicit bias as they move through the world."
The cast of School Girls displays a vast array of talent: Denée Benton (Paulina), Lucia Aremu (Ama), Nia Otchere-Sarfo (Gifty), Jordan Rice (Mercy), Erin Morton (Nana) and Jasmine Amy Rogers (Ericka), just to name a few. While it is an all-Black female cast, the diversity of physical appearance is clear.
"The audience, even if they are not young Black girls who went to school in Ghana, they still see facets of themselves in these girls. I think that's where the heart and beauty of it lies." Bioh says.
Audience reaction
School Girls is now on Broadway nearly 10 years after its Off-Broadway premiere. She says it's been a moving experience to see how the show's message continues to stay with audiences long after they leave the theater.
"I had a DM from Jenna Fischer of all people, who went to see the play a few days ago, and literally messaged me again today to say she's still thinking about the play," she says. "You know, how cool that someone who I just absolutely adore and also think is, like, a comedic genius, but who likely has never had any sort of experience with colorism, is still thinking about what the play is saying and how much it moved her.
For those who get to experience School Girls, Bioh hopes you have a good time and walk away with a deep sense of empathy not only for the young girls but for the adult women too.
"I ask people to shift their ideas about things," Bioh says. "If you can just move it just a little teeny bit, then I guess, you know, I've done my job."

TOI correspondent in Washington: Thirty-five years after Mira Nair, then pregnant with Zohran Mamdani, brought Mississippi Masala to screen, exploring the unlikely romance between an Indian woman and a Black man in America's Deep South, America’s poorest state has scripted a plot twist that Hollywood might have considered improbable: electing its first Black US senator in more than 150 years.
In a remarkable real-life sequel, Democrat Scott Colom, a civil rights attorney, has defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, by a narrow 4600 votes margin to become Mississippi's first Black US senator since Reconstruction, when the beaten Confederacy was briefly undergoing a democratic transformation.
The symbolism is difficult to overstate: Mississippi has the highest proportion of Black residents of any American state, approaching 40 per cent. Yet the state has not elected a Black senator since Blanche Bruce, who entered the Senate in 1875 and served until 1881. Hiram Revels, the first Black American senator, had also represented Mississippi, in 1870. What followed was nearly a century of segregation, poll taxes, literacy tests, lynchings and violent resistance to Black political participation as Mississippi became synonymous with some of America's ugliest racial chapters.
There is an Indian connection to this history that goes beyond Nair's movie, which explored the unlikely relationship between Mina (Sarita Chowdhury), the daughter of Indian immigrants expelled from Idi Amin's Uganda, and Demetrius, an African American carpet cleaner played by Denzel Washington early in his career. In 1935, Howard Thurman, the African American theologian and civil rights intellectual who grew up in the segregated South, travelled to India with a delegation and met Mahatma Gandhi in February 1936. Their discussions about racial oppression, freedom and non-violence helped transmit Gandhian ideas into the American civil rights movement. Thurman subsequently influenced Martin Luther King Jr., who drew deeply from the Gandhian philosophy of non-violent resistance.
Even more strikingly, Indian freedom fighter and social reformer Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay spent 18 months travelling across America between 1939 and 1941. On a journey through the segregated South, she encountered the indignity of racial segregation on an American train in next door Louisiana, where a conductor challenged her presence in a whites-only carriage. Refusing to move, she recognised a kinship between the struggles of African Americans and Indians against systems of racial and imperial domination. Her observations, later recorded in America: The Land of Superlatives, offer a remarkable Indian perspective on the American South.
Colum is very much in that Gandhian mold. A civil rights lawyer, municipal judge, and three-term District Attorney, he was given no chance in the election considering Trump had won the state by a whopping 23 per cent in 2024 and Hyde-Smith had won her previous election by seven points. Virtually every poll had classified her seat as safely Republican. But he refused to budge.
In fact, such was Hyde-Smith’s hubris that she declined repeated invitations to debate Colom, sneering that he would not be able to fill a room if she was not present. Trump himself may have sensed some trouble though when polls showed the race narrowing in the final days, making his first visit to Mississippi in seven years to campaign for her. "I'm here because Cindy's doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can't take a chance,” he said.
On Wednesday, Colum took his chance and drove Hyde-Smith out of the Senate with a stunning victory that was built on kitchen table issues rather than bloviating about ballrooms. A 7th generation Mississippian, his campaign masterstroke was a 30-sec ad built around Hyde-Smith's response to complaints about soaring beef prices: consumers, she suggested, had plenty of other proteins to choose from. Colom's ad, echoing the “let-them-eat-cake” smackdown, featured incredulous Mississippians delivering the devastating rejoinder: rather than choose another protein, they would choose another senator.
On Thursday, Democrats were dancing in the aisles even as MAGA minions were panicking at the prospect of Colum becoming a “national threat” to the Republican Party as one Fox News commentator put it -- bigger than Democratic Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Colom himself offered a characteristically restrained response to suggestions that he could become a national political star: Mississippi first; no masala please.

In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that all men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA test.
Men at average risk should get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, according to the new guidelines released Thursday.
Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years.
Men ages 70 to 74 should consult their doctor on continuing screening, while those 75 and up are not recommended to get screened.
The new guidance departs from ACS’s previous iteration, published in 2010, which made no universal recommendations for routine screening. Men at age 50 were recommended to use shared-decision making with their doctors on whether or not to get tested. The recommendation was similar to that from the US Preventive Services Task Force, a federal panel that regularly evaluates evidence and makes recommendations on such preventive medical care. (The USPSTF is currently working on an update to its prostate cancer screening recommendation, though it should be noted that the panel has recently been overhauled by anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and new members are reportedly rife with conflicts of interest.)

When Ashok Kumar lost his job in 2019, the H-1B visa holder had 60 days to find a new employer willing to sponsor him. He pulled it off, but he's worried his next job search could be even harder.
This week, Business Insider reported that IBM is ending visa and green card sponsorship for most roles in its consulting division. The company cited evolving skill availability and client needs as reasons for the move.
Kumar, a tech lead at a large corporation, said he's concerned that more companies could follow IBM's lead.
He's among several tech visa holders who told Business Insider that immigration policy uncertainty and concerns about job security are influencing their career decisions and long-term plans. Some worry about their ability to stay in the US or find new jobs, while others remain focused on the opportunities available to them.
IBM's decision comes amid other developments affecting foreign tech workers. In October, the Trump administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe, and six major IT services companies from the Permanent Labor Certification program, a key step in the employment-based green card process. The move prevents the companies from submitting new applications or moving forward with pending ones.
The administration said the move was aimed at stopping companies from misusing the program to favor foreign workers over American workers. The administration has also sought to impose a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas, though federal courts have blocked the measure.
Kumar's employer wasn't among the companies suspended from the PERM program, but the news added to his concerns about the future of immigration sponsorship. He said friends he discussed it with shared similar concerns.
"Everyone was worried about their future," he said
'You can do everything right'
One Microsoft employee is preparing for her final attempt at the H-1B visa lottery, but she's already worried about what comes next.
The worker said she initially ignored Instagram reels that friends sent her about the October PERM suspension. When she finally watched one, she was shocked to learn that Microsoft was among the companies affected.
Even if she's selected in the lottery, she worries that the PERM suspension could create another obstacle to securing a green card and staying in the US long-term.
"You can do everything right, build a career at a company like Microsoft, and still not feel secure about your future here," she said. Microsoft has disputed the administration's allegations that it misused the visa system.
For some foreign tech workers, the uncertainty extends beyond their careers. One tech worker on an F-1 STEM OPT visa said he's delayed buying a car because he doesn't know how long he'll be able to remain in the US. He also raised the possibility of moving to another country, such as Canada or the UK.
"My friends are indeed panicking and getting restless," he said.
Different reactions to immigration uncertainty
Not every foreign tech worker is equally concerned about their immigration future. Some pointed to the fact that the PERM suspension currently affects only a handful of companies. One Big Tech visa holder said he's not too concerned because he doesn't have long-term immigration plans in the US.
Others have tried to tune out immigration news altogether.
"It's exhausting to follow everything so I'm staying away from all of it," one tech visa holder said.
For Aman Goyal, a product manager on an H-1B visa, the uncertainty hasn't outweighed the opportunities he sees in the US.
Goyal, who came to the US in 2023, considered looking for work abroad after being laid off last year but ultimately landed a new role based in the Seattle area. He said visa challenges remain a concern as he considers his long-term future in the country, but he wants to make the most of his time in the US.
"I'm definitely interested in continuing to be here, meeting and building my network as much as possible, as well as learning about the next phases of AI as much as possible," he said.

Quick Answer
You can edit Instagram Reels on Mac using Claude AI and the free Instagram Edits app. Install Claude Code, enable the app’s MCP automation server, and connect both. Then use simple text prompts to create projects, arrange clips, add transitions, titles, and effects, and export finished Reels in 4K.
The wait is over. The Instagram Edits app is finally available on desktop, but only on macOS, as of this guide. Instagram Edits is my go-to app not just for editing Instagram Reels, but also a reliable free video editor with all the features and a simple design.
Although the app is designed for creators and competes with CapCut, it has been limited to Android and iOS so far. But a few months ago, Instagram announced a desktop version, and now it is finally here. Right now, the app is only available on macOS, with Windows and other platforms coming in future releases.
I have been using the app for the past couple of days. It is very similar to the mobile app and is also free to use, but it also features an MCP connection, which you can use to connect to any of your AI subscriptions, such as Claude, Codex, and Muse, and let AI edit your videos.
The desktop interface is slightly different and can be complex for beginners. It took me a while to get used to it, but I have created a detailed guide to get started.
I also created a guide on how to connect your MCP, like Claude, to Instagram Edits to edit your videos, and it covers everything about this feature, including common setup errors. This guide is for beginners, so each step is comprehensive and detailed.
Table of Contents
How to Connect Claude AI to Instagram Edits and Edit Reels on Mac
Before connecting your Instagram Edits app to the MCP server, ensure you have the following pre-requirements:
- A Mac with an Apple chip (M1 or newer) on macOS 15.1 or later. Currently, the Instagram Edits desktop app is only available for macOS, with Windows and Linux versions coming soon, but there is no expected release date yet.
- Download and install the Instagram Edits app from here
- A paid AI subscription for any model; you can also use the free AI model.
Part 1: Get Claude Code
Step 1: Open Terminal and type the command: claude –version, and press Return. If you see a version number, it means Claude Code is already installed on your device. You can skip to Part 2 to continue setup.
If you see something like zsh: command not found: claude, it means Claude Code is not installed on your device, or Terminal can not find it yet. Follow the next steps to install Claude Code on your Mac.
Install Claude Code: To install Claude Code, use the official Anthropic installer. To do that, open Terminal on your Mac and paste this command: curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Wait a few minutes, and then you will see a ” Claude Code successfully installed message in your terminal.
Check the setup notes below. If you see something like installation exists but ~/.local/bin is not in your PATH, it means the terminal still can’t find Claude Code yet.
Now follow the next two steps. If you don’t see such a note, you can quit the terminal, reopen it, and use this command to confirm that Claude Code has been successfully installed on your device: confirm claude –version. If you see a Claude version, it’s installed on your device. Then continue with part two.
Next, paste this command into the terminal and press Enter: echo ‘export PATH=”$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH”‘ >> ~/.zshrc
Next, paste this: source ~/.zshrc, and press Enter. Now type claude –version and press Enter. You will see the Claude version number. This means Claude Code is successfully installed on your device in the terminal
Part 2: Turn on Claude access in Edits
Next, you need to let Claude access your Instagram edits apps. First, ensure the Instagram edits app is installed on your Mac. If not, you can use the official download link here. Once installed, follow the steps below:
Step 1: Open the app on your Mac and sign in with your account. On the home screen, you will go directly to the Projects tab.
Step 2: Next, you can tap on your profile picture in the top right corner of the screen or click on the edit option in the menu bar at the top of the screen and then click on the settings
Step 3: Next, tap on the automation from the sidebar
Step 4: By default, automation is turned off. Now, from the automation settings, turn on the toggle that says Enable Automation Server.
Step 5: Under the Connect an AI Client section, click the copy icon next to the Claude code. This will copy the connection command with your access token. Remember, don’t share this command with others. In this case, I am using Claude code. If you are using Codex, tap the copy button next to Codex. The same goes for Muse.
You can also connect any AI model. Since it is a standard MCP server, any AI app can connect to the MCP server over HTTPS and can control edits.
Remember to replace <TOKEN> with the Access token from Edits > Settings > Automation, and keep Edits open with the automation server turned on
For Google Gemini CLI:
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli
gemini mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp
For Qwen:
npm install -g @qwen-code/qwen-code
qwen mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp
For DeepSeek, Grok, Mistral, Kimi, GLM, and most others, we can use OpenCode
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
{
“$schema”: “https://opencode.ai/config.json”,
“mcp”: {
“servers”: {
“edits”: {
“type”: “remote”,
“url”: “http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp”,
“oauth”: false,
“headers”: { “Authorization”: “Bearer <TOKEN>” }
}
}
}
}
Part 3: Connect Claude Code to Edits
Next, let’s connect Claude Code (or any AI model) to edits. Remember that you can only do this once.
Step 1: Now, paste the command you copied from the previous section into the terminal. You will see: Added HTTP MCP server metapilot-native
Step 2: Next, for Claude, paste this command: claude mcp get metapilot-native and press Enter. Under status, if you see Connected, it worked. If it says Failed to connect, ensure the edits app is running and follow the previous steps carefully.
For other models, follow these:
| App (models) | Connect command | Check it worked | 
| Claude Code (Claude) | claude mcp add –transport http –scope user metapilot-native http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” | claude mcp get metapilot-native | 
| Gemini CLI (Gemini) | gemini mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp | gemini mcp list | 
| Qwen Code (Qwen) | qwen mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp | qwen mcp list | 
| Codex (OpenAI GPT) | echo ‘export EDITS_TOKEN=”<TOKEN>”‘ >> ~/.zshrc && source ~/.zshrc && codex mcp add edits –url http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp –bearer-token-env-var EDITS_TOKEN | Run codex, then type /mcp | 
| OpenCode (DeepSeek, Grok, Mistral, Kimi, GLM and more) | No command. Paste the opencode.jsonc block from my last message into the folder you run OpenCode in. | opencode mcp list | 
| LM Studio (local Llama, Gemma, Qwen, DeepSeek R1) | No command. Program tab, then Install, then Edit mcp.json, and paste the JSON block. | Look at the Program tab | 
| Cursor (any model it offers) | No command. Paste the same JSON into ~/.cursor/mcp.json. | Cursor Settings, then MCP | 
Part 4: Start Claude Code
Now go to the folder where the videos are saved to edit them using Instagram edits. I recommend that you store all the videos in the Movies folder so it is easy to access in the future. In this case, I stored all my files in the Movies folder on my Mac. Now, once you have access to the folder, follow the steps below.
Step 1: To use Claude, go to the folder using the CD command. For example: cd ~/Downloads or cd ~/Movies. In my case, cd ~/Movies. Next, once you are in the folder, Type Cluade and press Return.
Step 2: Claude will ask whether you trust the folder you provided. Use the down arrow and select I trust this folder, and press Enter. It asks only once, and once you give permission, you can store all future videos in this folder for edits.
Step 3: To check, you can type /mcp and press Enter. It lists the apps Claude Code is connected to. metapilot-native with a green tick means Claude can control Edits.
Step 4: Go to the metapilot-native option and press Enter to see more details. You can use the down or up arrow to navigate between the options.
Part 5: Make your first Reel with Claude
Now let’s use Claude to create my first reel. In this case, I asked Claude to edit a 50-second coffee reel from five clips. In your case, you can store all the clips in the folder. First, test the connection again. Once done, follow the steps below.
To test the connection, go to your folder and type list my Instagram edits projects and press Enter. You will see metabolist native and the table of all your edit projects.
Step 2 : Now you can ask Claude to make edits for the Instagram reel video. You can manually create a new project, add clips, and point Claude to the project title and edit your videos, or you can ask Claude to create a project, add clips, and edit your first reel. I recommend giving Claude the full location of your clips and the title.
Step 3: That’s it. Claude will now create a new project and add Sunclips. You can open the Instagram Edits app to see the changes.
Step 4: Once you’ve loaded the clips, you can ask Claude to add transitions between them and also add titles, sound effects, and much more. In this case, I’m asking Claude to add the title “Morning Coffee” in big white text for two seconds and then add smooth transitions between the clips.
Step 5: Once you’ve made the edits, you can also ask Claude Core to export the clips in 4K, and it does it for you.
Step 6: Once the video is exported, Claude notifies you of the length, format, and size. You can open the same folder to see the clip. Claude also notifies you where the clip is stored and its title.
Let AI Handle Your Video Editing
This is how to connect Claude code using Instagram Edits MCP. For now, the Instagram Edits app is only available on macOS, and you can connect any AI model to make edits.
Since Claude requires a subscription, you can try a free AI model if you have one. You can also run any free AI model locally and ask it to edit, but the quality may vary and may not be as good as frontend models.
Since this guide focuses entirely on Claude Code, we are also creating a separate guide on how to connect other free AI models, including Google Gemini (which comes with a free Jio AI offer), DeepSeek, and other models.
If you have any issues while connecting Claude Code, let me know. If you prefer a video guide, we have also created one that you can check out above.

French Open champion Mirra Andreeva stormed past Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 6-0 to reach the last four of the WTA Finals on Wednesday as Elina Svitolina kept her bid on track with a three-set win over Karolina Muchova.
Russian 19-year-old Andreeva held her nerve after falling behind 4-1 in the opening set -- winning the last 11 games to seal the round-robin victory in just 62 minutes.
“Oh my God, I’m even happier than I was after my first match,” Andreeva said. “I feel like I can play another two matches, I’m so full of energy. I’m so pumped up. I’m so happy.”
Andreeva, whose three titles this year include her maiden major at Roland Garros, is making her singles debut in the elite season-ending event.
The world number three seemed to be feeling the nerves in the early going against second-ranked Sabalenka.
Irked that she had given up a break with a double fault, she was able to flip the switch, dealing handily with Sabalenka’s big serves and pushing the Belarusian star back with her own big groundstrokes.
Andreeva crucially kept momentum on her side with a break for a 3-0 lead in the second set.
Sabalenka, trailing 0-40, saved three break points, but Andreeva gave herself another with a swinging volley winner and grabbed another break when a Sabalenka forehand flew just long.
The increasingly demoralised Sabalenka had no answer. After the Belarusian smacked a backhand into the net to give her opponent match point Andreeva polished things off with a service winner.
It was another disappointing performance for the 28-year-old Sabalenka, whose three wins this season include prestigious back-to-back victories at Indian Wells and Miami but no Grand Slams.
“She definitely played great tennis,” Sabalenka told reporters. “The good thing is that I still have a chance to qualify. The bad thing, that I’ll need some time to recover after I don’t even know how many games in a row I lost.”
Making her sixth straight Finals appearance, Sabalenka can still advance if she beats Svitolina in their final round-robin match on Friday.
Svitolina roared back from a set down to beat Muchova 3-6, 6-2, 6-2.
Ukrainian veteran Svitolina lifted the WTA Finals trophy in 2018 but hadn’t been back to the elite season-ending event since 2019.
She got off to a rocky start against Muchova, who broke Svitolina three times in the opening set.
Trailing 2-1 on serve in the second Svitolina found her range, winning five straight games to force a third set.
“I was not happy with the first set,” Svitolina said. “I didn’t play as well. I just made some adjustments, tactical adjustments.
“I think it helped me also to be more aggressive, because I was too passive in the first set,” Svitolina said.
Muchova’s second round-robin defeat coupled with Andreeva’s victory means the Czech was eliminated from semifinal contention.

Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen. These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen’s purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google’s ecosystem use.
With Google’s recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company’s products.
Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

The incoming Democratic chairs of key committees have taken a new step toward investigating the most-favored nation drug pricing agreements between drugmakers and the Trump administration, STAT reports. The drug pricing deals are expected to be a top health care oversight priority for Democrats once they take the majority in January. Earlier this year, the top Democrats on the Senate Finance Committee and the House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor committees requested that companies disclose the details of the deals they struck to tie Medicaid drug prices to levels in peer countries.
The Trump administration last year came up with a plan to combat high drug prices, making European governments pay more, and the result so far is that drug prices in the U.S. remain high and there are fewer new drugs in Europe, The Wall Street Journal says. There has been a 27% drop in new drug releases across European countries over the last 17 months, compared with the same period before President Trump announced the plan, according to new data from market-research firm GlobalData. Online travel aggregator (OTA) Yatra swung to the red and reported a consolidated net loss of ₹78.4 Lakhs in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27). In contrast, the travel tech platform has reported a net profit of ₹14.3 Cr in Q2 FY26 and ₹33.9 Lakhs in Q1 FY27. The losses came despite the company raking in ₹1.7 Cr in one-time deferred tax benefits during the quarter. The bottom line was primarily impacted as the company’s revenue from operations tanked 39.1% to ₹213.6 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹350.9 Cr in Q2 FY26. However, on a sequential basis, Yatra’s top line rose 13.7% from ₹187.9 Cr in the preceding quarter. The OTA attributed the losses to the “challenging operating environment”, lower MICE (meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions) volumes, and the reorientation of the MICE vertical towards smaller corporate group programmes. “... Our year-on-year profitability was impacted primarily by MICE, which faced an exceptionally strong comparable quarter last year and a tactical shift towards smaller corporate group programmes amid prevailing uncertainty…,” said Yatra CEO Siddhartha Gupta. Including other income of ₹4.4 Cr, Yatra’s total income stood at ₹218 Cr in Q2 FY27. Meanwhile, total expenses for the quarter under review declined 35% to ₹219.9 Cr compared to ₹339 Cr in Q2 FY26. The company also incurred an additional tax expense of ₹59.3 Lakh during the quarter. Revenue less service cost (RLSC), which is essentially the gross margin, declined 0.2% to ₹125.5 Cr in Q2 FY27. As a result, EBITDA declined 47% YoY to ₹13.2 Cr, while EBITDA margin stood at 10.48%during the quarter under review. In a statement, the company’s gross bookings grew 6% YoY and 3% QoQ to ₹2,165.5 Cr in Q2 FY27. During the quarter, Yatra said that it added 54 new corporate customers with an estimated annual revenue potential of ₹203.5 Cr. “We continue to make progress on our strategic priorities, including expanding into the SME and mid-market segments through Travel Pro, strengthening our expense management offering through RECAP, expanding hotel supply and leveraging AI-led automation. These initiatives are helping us broaden our addressable market and build a more scalable business, positioning us for sustainable growth and improved profitability over the medium term,” added Gupta. Yatra’s US Entity On Nasdaq’s Radar Separately, the travel tech platform’s US-listed entity, Yatra Online Inc, said that it has received a letter from Nasdaq after its shares traded below the exchange’s minimum $1 closing bid price for more than a month. This has effectively put the travel tech company on a compliance watch. The company said that the notice does not immediately delist the company’s shares from the Nasdaq Capital Market. However, the OTA said that it has been given a timeline of 180 days, until May 10, 2027, to regain compliance. To do so, its shares must close at $1 or higher for at least 10 consecutive business days, even though Nasdaq may require up to 20 consecutive days in certain cases. If Yatra fails to meet the requirement by May next year, it may qualify for an additional 180-day compliance period. This would require the company to meet Nasdaq’s other continued-listing thresholds and formally notify the exchange of its intention to cure the deficiency. A reverse stock split is among the options available to lift the share price. Yatra said it may consider such a move if necessary, but cautioned that there is no assurance it will regain compliance. Nevertheless, Yatra said it intends to closely monitor its closing bid price and may evaluate available options to restore compliance. The notice highlights the pressure facing the travel-tech company’s US-listed shares. As of 1:13 AM IST, shares of Yatra Online Inc were trading at $0.77, down 18% in the past six months and nearly 57% lower on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. This comes as the US-listed Yatra Online Inc has been reporting increased net losses, compressed margins and falling revenues. Slowing growth in core verticals, market volatility and rising short-term trade-related borrowings have further led to the sell-off in the stock. But a sustained share price below $1 can further reduce liquidity, deter institutional investors and complicate future fundraising. Meanwhile, shares of India-listed Yatra closed Thursday’s trading session 0.94% lower at ₹81.03 on the BSE.

Missing 11-month-old baby rescued after being buried alive in a crate in South Carolina
- Published
An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father.
Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him.
The baby was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours.
The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery.
Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father.
The search for baby Koah began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house.
Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Koah.
Comer was seen travelling to multiple locations without the baby and was later arrested in Lexington County without Koah. A search party of 100 police and fire department officials were then sent to search for the child, the sheriff said.
He added that when they asked Comer where his son was, he "did not have much to say" about his whereabouts.
Koon said that rescuers searched the woods near Comer's house and saw some "freshly disturbed dirt". As they began to dig, they heard a baby crying - something the sheriff described as "the most joyful sound you ever heard".
"The race was on. Everybody was getting down there trying to get him out," Koon added.
He said the crate was wrapped in a towel that probably provided enough air for Koah to survive for as long as he did, while the cold weather kept him from getting too hot.
"The crate was, probably, I'm guessing about a two-foot [61cm] by two-foot dog crate. So, I think, once that crate hit the ground, he was probably up at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground," Koon explained.
Of the parents' relationship, the sheriff said there were "obviously some issues". Comer had previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges, court records show.
Comer's mother, Patricia Comer, told NBC News that Koah's mother had full custody of him but allowed her to supervise while her son watched him. She said her son had watched the baby before unsupervised without any problems.
"Honestly, I'm his mother, and I never expected this from him," Patricia Comer said.

“Fifty-seven channels, and nothin’ on.”
Bruce Springsteen famously said those words during a concert and later in a song in the 1990s about the number of TV channels seemingly growing disproportionately to the availability of enjoyable content.
Within a few years, there would be hundreds of TV channels and still, some would argue in hyperbolic frustration, “nothing to watch.”
The advent of streaming services was poised as a potential solution to this problem. It granted viewers easy, on-demand access to thousands of movies and shows, which, theoretically, could ensure that viewers could always find something to watch.
According to a survey from Nielsen’s Gracenote, though, that’s not exactly the case today.
Gracenote, a Nielsen-owned content data business, surveyed 3,000 video streaming users in the US, Brazil, France, Germany, Mexico, and the UK who were at least 18 years old for its “2026 State of Play: Amid fragmentation frustrations, UX is the future of streaming” report. It found that many struggle to find something to stream. However, this is not necessarily because there’s nothing good on, but rather because they find it difficult to home in on good content on streaming services.
For example, over 51 percent of respondents said that “the abundance of content and [streaming] services is making it harder to find something to watch.”
Further, 19.2 percent of respondents said that, on average, they either “always” or “often” don’t know what to watch, can’t find anything, and then decide to do something else. And 27.4 percent of respondents said that, on average, they either always or often try to watch a specific program but end up not watching it because they couldn’t find it on streaming.
“Through the lens of catalogue size and streaming usage, connecting the 83.4 percent who don’t always know what they want to watch should be fairly straightforward, especially as companies increasingly use customer data to create personalized experiences that foster long-term engagement and loyalty. Audiences, however, aren’t finding what they’re looking for, and content discovery challenges are mounting,” the report reads.

Meta's Muse can now make calls on your behalf (if you have a paid subscription)
The AI agent can schedule appointments, make reservations and wait on hold for you.
Meta's Muse just got another ability that could make the AI agent feel a little bit more like an actual personal assistant. Muse is now able to place phone calls on your behalf, if you have a paid subscription.
With the change, Muse is able to call businesses to help with tasks like making reservations, scheduling appointments and other "calls you don't want to make," Meta's Chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said in an update. The feature is available to those who have paid for a separate Muse subscription, which comes with additional tokens and some extra features.
Some users who have had access to the feature already have reported that Muse has been able to handle phone-related tasks with relative ease. Moltbook creator and Meta Superintelligence employee Matt Schlicht shared a recreation of a phone conversation his agent had with a Volvo dealership last month, noting that it was able to wait on hold in order to get the info he needed.
My muse called Volvo for me to see when the next available appointment is.
You can listen to the phone call here.
I have it do multiple calls like this every day (I'm still trying to get better and better at leveraging muse).
My muse called, waited on the line for 15 minutes,... pic.twitter.com/bosH1tyW1R
— Matt Schlicht (@MattPRD) October 9, 2026
Interestingly, in the call shared by Schlicht, Muse doesn't explicitly identify itself as an AI agent though it notes it's calling his behalf and that it's transcribing the call. That may be enough for some straightforward tasks, but there's always a chance these types of calls could go off the rails or the person on the other end hangs up when they realize they're speaking with an AI.
Meta has been steadily churning out new features for Muse, which has already drawn more than 10 million users, according to the company. People can also now assign a dedicated email address to their agent in order to loop it into important emails without giving wholesale access to their inbox.
The company isn't the first to experiment with phone-calling abilities for AI. Google has introduced a number of similar features over the years, including "Call For Me" for Pixel phones and Instinct recently introduced a "Concierge" feature for its agent that's meant to handle more complex calls.

Rwanda's army team removed from Africa league after US sanctions, NBA says
- Published
The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in March.
The NBA had previously said the Rwandan army-funded Armée Patriotique Rwandaise (APR) club would not participate in the 2026 Basketball Africa League (BAL).
However this is the first time the NBA has revealed the reasons behind the APR's removal.
The association was responding to complaints by two US senators, who sent a letter asking them to reconsider their partnership with the Rwandan team. The US placed sanctions on the Rwandan army, accusing it of fuelling the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March.
The senators said the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights".
Last week, the US also imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its support for the M23 rebel group which has seized control of large parts of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies backing the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
Rwanda is an official BAL partner and pays the league to host its finals at the 10,000-seat BK Arena in the capital, Kigali.
The BBC has asked Rwanda for comment.

In the letter to the NBA dated 23 October, Democratic Senator Jeffrey Merkley and Republican counterpart Marsha Blackburn gave the association until 2 November to give a written response regarding its continued partnership with Rwanda.
"What is the NBA red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses?" the senators asked.
Among other queries, they also questioned how the association could "reconcile its continued partnership with Rwanda with its purported commitment to justice".
In its response, NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum said the Rwandan team "had been withdrawn" from the BAL following the sanctions imposed earlier in the year, American sports website ESPN reports.
The NBA said the APR basketball club would remain barred while the US sanctions are in place.
The APR is one of Rwanda's top basketball teams and represented the country in the BAL in 2024 and 2025, when it came third. It was replaced by the RSSB Tigers this year.
The BAL is a pan-African basketball league established and co-organised by the NBA and the basketball's world governing body Fiba.
It is a professional league featuring 12 club teams from across the continent.
Rwanda has hosted all but one of the league's final and playoff matches since the inaugural match in 2021.
The NBA reportedly receives millions of dollars annually from the country for the marketing and partnership rights.
DR Congo has repeatedly condemned Rwanda's high-profile international sports deals, including with the NBA, European football clubs and Formula 1, asking them to end their campaigns.
It argues that these help Rwanda clean up its global image, while the conflict continues in eastern DR Congo.
