ChatGPT maker OpenAI has introduced local inference and data processing for its APIs in India, adding to its efforts to expand the commercialisation of ChatGPT in its largest market. For context, local data inferencing allows businesses to ensure that both API requests and the computing required to generate responses take place within India for supported workloads. It is initially available for the GPT-6 Luna model and extends OpenAI's existing data residency options in the country. OpenAI's India enterprise head Nitin Bawankule pointed out that local inference gives businesses greater control over where their data is processed and could help more organisations move from experimenting with AI to deploying it in their day-to-day operations. "Some Indian businesses have not fully deployed AI for important work because they need the information involved to be processed within the country," Bawankule said. To use the new offering, customers need to create a new API project, select India as the location for both data storage and processing, and use the corresponding India regional endpoint. With the launch, India joins Australia and Japan as the latest markets where OpenAI has introduced API inference residency. Global AI Giants Push For Data Localisation In India Data localisation has emerged as an important consideration in enterprise AI adoption. While global AI models offer advanced capabilities, businesses handling sensitive information require a greater understanding of where their data is going. Storage and processing of data before model deployment is something that cannot be compromised from a security perspective for banks, financial institutions and government agencies. For these clients, data residency and infrastructure requirements can limit the use of international frontier AI models in production environments. OpenAI is not the first international AI company looking to address India's data localisation requirements. In August, Anthropic announced plans to bring in-country inference for its Claude AI models to India through Amazon Bedrock, AWS' managed service for building generative AI applications. The move was aimed at addressing data residency and infrastructure requirements that have kept banks, financial institutions and government agencies from deploying international AI models in production. Anthropic has since made similar data residency capabilities available for certain models on AWS Bedrock. For Indian AI startups such as Sarvam AI, locally hosted inference has also been an important differentiator when competing with global AI players. However, the entry of OpenAI and Anthropic into this segment could narrow that advantage as international companies begin offering similar capabilities in the country. For OpenAI, data inferencing is another piece of its India revenue. The AI giant has established a strong hold on the Indian market, where more than 10 Cr people interact with ChatGPT on a weekly basis. The company is looking to monetise its India holding. In November, a rumor spread that activists anonymously placed a golden statue of U.S. President Donald Trump rubbing his foot on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., referring to him avoiding the draft during the Vietnam War because he allegedly had a bone spur.
The claim and photographs of the supposed statue circulated on social media, including on Facebook and Reddit. An X post (archived) shared two images and said "The satirical monument, installed just ahead of Veterans Day, mocks Trump's Vietnam War draft deferment for bone spurs":
One of the photographs showed an epigraph at the base of the statue that read:
We honor the service and sacrifice of our commander in chief, Donald J. Trump. He's a soldier in spirit, who marched to the front lines of dodging the draft, armed with a perfect diagnosis of bone spurs.
We salute a leader who knows you can't spell sacrifice without "I," and a warrior who reminds us that sometimes when you're called to stand up, it's best to just sit down and rest your feet.
"I can be very military." — President Donald J. Trump
"The foot soldier," another inscription at the bottom said.
Meanwhile, Snopes readers searched our website, seeking confirmation that the statue was real.
It was. The statue appeared in a series of photographs on the reputable image bank Getty Images. Further, the organization responsible for putting it up confirmed it had in an email to Snopes. For this reason, we rated the claim true.
It also appeared on video news reports, including one by WUSA, a CBS affiliate in Washington:
The report said the statue was the work of an organization known as The Secret Handshake, an anonymous collective that also made the "Best Friends Forever" statue of Trump and late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein holding hands.
"We did put up the Bone Spur statue," The Secret Handshake told Snopes in an email.
The statue evokes the draft deferments Trump benefited from in the 1960s, during the Vietnam War. His disqualification in 1968 cited a medical reason, without providing details. In 2016, his campaign said it was because of bone spurs.
Three years later, Trump's former lawyer Michael Cohen testified that the president had not shown medical records proving the reason for his disqualification, according to a transcript of his testimony to the House Committee on Oversight and Reform:
Mr. Trump tasked me to handle the negative press surrounding his medical deferment from the Vietnam draft.
Mr. Trump claimed it was because of a bone spur. But when I asked for medical records, he gave me none and said that there was no surgery. He told me not to answer the specific questions by reporters, but rather, offer simply the fact that he received a medical deferment. He finished the conversation with the following comment. ''You think I'm stupid? I'm not going to Vietnam.'' And I find it ironic, Mr. President, that you are in Vietnam right now. And yet, I continued to work for him.
The statue is a humorous take on the suggestion that Trump allegedly dodged the draft without providing a real medical reason for not serving his country in Vietnam. It appeared on the National Mall on Nov. 9, two days before Veterans Day.
For further reading, Snopes has reported on other statues that derided Trump, including one that showed him naked in the European Parliament.

2 dead, 4 critically injured after building collapses in New York City
Firefighters dig through rubble of 3-storey building that fell at edge of construction site
Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-storey building in New York City's Brooklyn borough on Wednesday after it collapsed at the edge of a construction site, killing at least two people and trapping others beneath the wreckage.
Firefighters were called to the scene in the Flatbush neighbourhood at about 4 p.m. News helicopter footage showed dozens of firefighters scouring the debris, with a group homing in on one area and appearing to use a saw to cut through the wreckage.
At least 17 people were hospitalized with injuries, including four in critical condition, officials said during a news conference.
New York City Fire Department (FDNY) officials said their search-and-rescue operations would continue into the night. "We do not know how many people were missing overall," said the FDNY's chief of department, John Esposito. It was unclear whether people might still be trapped.
"This has been an incredibly challenging and fast-moving situation, with precarious wreckage to navigate and dangerous voids beneath the surface," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "This type of rescue is exactly what the FDNY trains for."
Firefighters search through the rubble on Wednesday. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)
About 250 firefighters were working at the scene, Mamdani said.
At about 6:30 p.m., firefighters pulled a dust-covered person — still alive and moving — out of a hole they had dug into the rubble pile, hoisting them up on a stretcher and rushing them to a waiting ambulance.
The building that collapsed — a mixed-use structure with apartments sitting atop businesses — had been perched at the edge of a lot where another one-storey building had been torn down for a construction project. The site was being excavated, and the building that fell down filled the construction pit with bricks and wood.
New York City's buildings commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, said that at the time of the disaster, construction workers were on site doing excavation work adjacent to the building that collapsed.
A wall was shorn off an adjacent Brooklyn building, exposing a bedroom and closets filled with clothing inside. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)
Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing.
A drone hovered over the site as firefighters dug by hand, tossing chunks of rubble aside. Rescuers also used dogs to sniff for survivors. As darkness fell, firefighters used flashlights to illuminate the area where they worked.
New York's fire commissioner, Lillian Bonsignore, said the rescue teams were performing "dangerous and perilous" work. "Every move is choreographed," she said.
One firefighter sustained minor injuries, fire officials said.
First responders rescue a person from the rubble of the collapse. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)
Phone and email messages seeking comment were left with the architect, property owner and general contractor listed in city records as being associated with the construction project.
One resident of the collapsed building, Anderson Velez, told the New York Post he was at work when his wife called and said she and their two children, aged 7 and 2, were trapped in the wreckage.
"She called me when the building collapsed while she was inside with rubble on top of her. She was screaming for someone to help get my son out and then the call cut off," he said.
Velez said he later learned that his family had been pulled from the rubble alive.

Recently listed furniture rental company Rentomojo reported a 62.6% year-on-year (YoY) decline in its profit after tax to ₹18.2 Cr in the quarter ended September 30, 2026 (Q2 FY27) from ₹48.6 Cr in the year-ago quarter. The decline was largely due to a deferred tax credit of ₹32.8 Cr recognised in the year-ago quarter, compared with a deferred tax expense of ₹6.2 Cr in Q2 FY27. On a sequential basis, the company’s net consolidated profit zoomed 133% from ₹7.8 Cr in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 52.8% YoY and 12% QoQ to ₹142.1 Cr in the quarter under review, driven by growth in customer orders, live subscribers and rental inventory. Including other income of ₹1.7 Cr, total income for the quarter stood at ₹143.8 Cr. Total expenses increased 53.2% YoY to ₹119.8 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹78.2 Cr in the year-ago period. Employee benefit expenses rose 38.3% to ₹19.5 Cr, while finance costs increased 46.7% to ₹9 Cr. The company said its normalised profit after tax, excluding exceptional items and deferred tax adjustments, increased 52.2% YoY to ₹24 Cr from ₹15.8 Cr in Q2 FY26. Normalised EBITDA also grew 52.7% to ₹58.8 Cr from ₹38.5 Cr a year earlier. Subscriber Additions, Higher Utilisation Drive Growth Rentomojo expanded its omnichannel network to 96 experience stores across 14 cities by the end of September, compared with 67 stores a year earlier. Customers ordered 3.8 Lakh gross items during the quarter, up 45% higher than last year's quarter. Besides, the company’s live subscriber base grew 42.5% to approximately 3.2 Lakh, while live item inventory increased 44% to 10.5 Lakh. Average occupancy grew by 61 basis points to 85.9% while average revenue per item (ARPI) increased 4.6% YoY to ₹1,650. The company also reported higher asset utilisation. Assets procured in the FY17 cycle generated cumulative revenue equivalent to 5.3X its original value, with around 54% of the cohort continuing to generate revenue. The FY18 cohort had generated 4.71X its original value, with 59.2% of its items still generating revenue. For context, higher utilisation of its rental assets allows the company to generate repeat revenue from its asset base. Purchase displaced, which measures the estimated retail value of consumer purchases replaced by customers choosing to rent furniture, grew 61% YoY and 8% QoQ to ₹446.9 Cr. This was the company’s second quarterly results following its public market debut in September after it raised ₹1,255.6 Cr from an initial public offering. The company said it had utilised ₹90 Cr, or 63.7%, of the ₹141.4 Cr net proceeds allocated to the IPO's stated objectives as of September 30. This included the complete utilisation of ₹70 Cr earmarked for debt repayment, ₹8.1 Cr towards warehouse and experience store lease rentals, and ₹11.9 Cr for general corporate purposes. Commenting on the performance, founder, chairperson, managing director and CEO Geetansh Bamania said the company would continue focusing on subscriber growth, better asset utilisation and technology while maintaining profitability, cash generation and returns on capital. Shares of Rentomojo ended today’s trading session 3.30% higher at ₹610.9 apiece on the BSE.

The world is no longer safe for frozen H2O.
New research published in Science on Thursday shows that the conditions that have kept ice, frozen soil, and snow stable are slipping away due to the burning of fossil fuels—and the implications are grave for the entire globe.
The climate of the past 12,000 or so years has been remarkably steady. That’s allowed for all kinds of wonderful things to happen, like human civilization flourishing. But rising temperatures are pushing the climate outside that envelope, and the new research looks at what the team behind the new findings has called the “safe operating space” for the icy, snowy landscape known as the cryosphere.
The scientists looked at changes to polar sea and land ice, mountain glaciers, permafrost, and snow cover over the past 12 millennia to analyze conditions that have allowed both civilization and other ecosystems to thrive. They then identified boundaries on those conditions that, if crossed, would upend the stability and safety humans have enjoyed for millennia.
The results show an “accelerating and partly irreversible loss of cryospheric integrity.” Arctic and Antarctic sea ice have both fallen outside the safe operating threshold, as have snow cover and the area of permafrost—frozen soil laden with carbon. While land ice hasn’t yet fallen out of its safe space, it’s on the brink. And because of warming that’s already been locked into the climate system, it’s likely to also fall outside the threshold in the coming centuries.
While it may feel like the Antarctic ice sheet or permafrost covering Alaska are distant concerns, they’re anything but. The West Antarctic Ice Sheet, which a growing body of evidence shows is nearing the brink of irreversible decline, has enough ice to raise sea levels by 11 feet (3 meters). Permafrost, meanwhile, holds trillions of tons of carbon dioxide. Any degradation means that CO2, as well as even more potent methane, could end up in the atmosphere, accelerating global warming even further. Other examples of major risks abound, including how melting Greenland land ice could slow down or even collapse the ocean conveyor belt that helps keep Europe temperate.
“The consequences of a changing cryosphere extend beyond regions where ice and snow are disappearing,” says Albert Noström, a climate researcher at the Stockholm Resilience Center who co-authored the new paper.
Dipping outside the safe operating space doesn’t mean that the world will see 11 feet of sea level rise in the next year, a trillion-ton CO2 eruption, or a Day After Tomorrow scenario. But it does mean that the odds of crossing dangerous tipping points are rising.
“As we scratch 1.5 [degrees Celsius] and go above it, we are just really gambling with potentially triggering some of these Earth system tipping points,” Noström says. The safe operating space framework also “takes a broader perspective” that assesses slower changes over time and “how far, in this case, the cryosphere is moving away from the conditions that have supported a relatively stable Earth system,” he adds.
Cutting emissions is the most obvious and straightforward way to stop the cryosphere from sliding further outside our comfort zone. But there are a growing number of proposals to pursue more radical interventions that could protect the world’s ice. Scientists have already draped glaciers in the Alps in blankets during the summer to prevent melting. Other researchers have explored techniques to pump cold sea water to the surface to help thicken ice and modeled whether a manmade barrier could stabilize the West Antarctic Ice Sheet.
These geoengineering approaches have the potential to be costly, and there’s no guarantee they would work. They’d also do nothing to stop the root cause of warming: burning fossil fuels. Noström says emissions cuts are the most urgent way to protect ice and snow (and ourselves), but with the cryosphere sliding into a more dangerous space, “in principle, we shouldn't put the lid on” research for more far-flung interventions.
“The safe operating space is a precautionary framework,” he says. “It ensures that we try to stay as far downstream from the point where these really potentially existential or huge consequences and risks can happen.”

This Beirut family has sold falafel for 100 years, through war and crisis. It has no plan to stop
The Tabbara family has been making falafel in Lebanon for over a century
BEIRUT -- For more than a century, the Tabbara family has been serving up falafel to Beirut’s residents.
Their business, which predates Lebanon’s founding, has survived two world wars and a series of local conflicts in the small Mediterranean nation.
Now, a fourth generation is getting ready to take over the modest shop, where customers can get $3 sandwiches of small, doughnut-shaped patties of deep-fried ground fava beans wrapped in flat Lebanese bread with pickled cucumber, tomatoes, parsley, thick tahini sauce and homemade dark red-hot pepper paste for the spice lovers.
“I have clients spread all over the world,” 82-year-old Mohammed Tabbara said as a European customer waited for a sandwich in Beirut’s busy Hamra district that's packed with cafes, clothing shops and two major universities.
“They all come to eat falafel because they know the flavor and the taste,” Tabbara added.
He is passing down the culinary craft to his 40-year-old son, Ziad Tabbara, a former accountant who has spent the last six years working full time with his dad.
“This is a flavor that made history and heritage passed down through generations,” said Ziad Tabbara, who as a child helped his father in the shop during summer vacations.
Ziad has no children of his own to pass on the tradition to — a sore point with his father who wants to see him married with children.
Beirut was still part of the Ottoman Empire when Ziad's great-grandfather Kamel Tabbara opened the family’s first falafel shop in the city’s central Bab Idriss district in 1914. It would be six years before the state of Greater Lebanon was established after World War I.
Kamel passed the business to his son Ahmad. Since 1950, the business has been mostly run by Kamel’s grandson Mohammed. It was around that time that the family moved its business from central Beirut. The current shop in a narrow street has been in place since 1979.
“I have been through 40 wars,” Mohammed Tabbara said, referring to two civil wars, Israel's 1982 invasion of Lebanon, multiple Israel-Hezbollah wars, and several conflicts involving Palestinian groups and the Syrian army.
Mohammed Tabbara, who began working with his dad at the shop when he was just 6 years old, still mans the counter, taking orders from clients and assembling sandwiches. Always smiling, Mohammed knows many customers by name. Some have been getting falafel there for decades.
Beirut is known throughout the Middle East for its cuisine, from fine restaurants to street food.
Small falafel spots can be found throughout Lebanon. A sandwich is a filling, affordable meal for people in a nation that's been experiencing a historic economic meltdown since 2019, rooted in decades of corruption and mismanagement.
Mohammed Tabbara's shop is decorated with two photos of him: A black-and-white one taken in 1966 and another taken two years ago in which he wears his trademark skull cap.
He takes pride in the shop's cleanliness. They change the cooking oil every day and wash the vegetables with vinegar and salt.
Jean Matta, 60, works in the neighborhood and has been eating falafel at Tabbara since 1992. “It’s crunchy, tasty and clean,” Matta said.
Ziad has learned his father's special secret recipe for falafel, which is made of Australian fava beans, soaked in water the night before, then ground before being mixed with salt and an array of spices, including coriander. Mohammed said chickpeas, used in many falafel recipes, are heavier and take more time to digest than fava beans alone. He also said he was the first in Lebanon to introduce a falafel patty covered with sesame seeds and with a hole in the middle, making it well-cooked inside and crunchy on the outside.
“The sandwich you take from here is light and 100% healthy,” Mohammed said as he wrapped a sandwich while his son dropped falafel patties into a giant frying pot.
“God willing, I will continue to offer the same flavor,” Ziad said.

Pat Cummins says Khawaja’s claim ‘complete and utter nonsense’
Cummins says he was “genuinely shocked” this week amid the comments in Khawaja’s book. He went on:
When he says we all knew, if [by] that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he’s 100% wrong. I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening …
He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That’s complete and utter nonsense.
Cummins goes on to say he believes Khawaja’s book has “been casual with my [life] and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket”.
More than once, Cummins used the phrase “the dark arts” to describe what is more euphemistically known as “ball management” on the cricket field.
A theme that emerged from the press conference is that around 2018, teams all over world cricket were seeking every possible advantage in working the ball: keeping it shiny and hard initially so that it would swing conventionally, and then roughing it up once it got old, so that it would ‘go’ reverse.
Cummins was asked about the dark arts: “Why not? Let’s get into it,” he said.
“I had heard superglue on brandings, so you shine the ball there. I’ve heard zippers, I’ve heard superglue on gloves, the keeper’s gloves so you can catch it. I have heard nail polish, layers and layers of nail polish. I bite my fingers, so I would be terrible but growing [a nail] out and make it super hard and using that. I’ve heard, obviously, the Murray Mints as one.”
(The Murray Mints is a reference to former England bat Marcus Trescothick who revealed in his autobiography that, during the 2005 Ashes series (which England won) he would suck on Murray Mints in the field, and use his sugary saliva to shine the ball to keep it swinging.)
Cummins spoke about sandpaper itself, saying it is common for cricketers to carry it in their kitbags.
“It’s actually, again, quite a normal thing. We carry sandpaper, normally for the batters; they rough up their bats. But we actually use it for balls as well around training. You face a lot of reverse swing, so the batters want to face it and practice it in the net.
“We’ve scratched balls on concrete, I’ve seen someone use a Stanley knife, I’ve seen sandpaper used. So, all the methods are very normal around training, so again I think it comes to [the claim that] ‘there must have been a grand plan’ because for the non-cricket, maybe for the non-international player, it sounds absurd, and it is absurd to take sandpaper on the field, but trying to give a bit more context – it is a part of the change room.
“We may have been doing it around training, but there is a leap to then think it’s okay to take it on feel, but maybe not, perhaps as big a leap as some people may think.”
Cummins ‘couldn’t disagree more’ that Khawaja was overlooked as Test captain because of skin colour
Recapping some of the elements of Pat Cummins’s marathon press conference:
Cummins said the most serious allegation raised by Usman Khawaja in Sabr was not the sandpaper incident at Newlands in 2018, but his allegation that he (Khawaja) was overlooked as the Australian test captain - in the wake of the sandpaper crisis – because he was not white.
Khawaja wrote it was a “kick in the guts” that Tim Paine, the wicketkeeper only recently returned to the Test team, was appointed interim captain after Smith was sent home from Cape Town.
Khawaja wrote:
I was a natural selection for interim captain, but was overlooked. I knew why. One reason was that I’d been a main protagonist during those pay disputes with CA and the board – and the board was who appointed the captain. On that basis alone, they probably weren’t going to give it to me.
But the second – and, I believe, more important – reason was that they weren’t ready for a brown Australian cricket captain, even as an interim. You may be thinking, How do you know this? It’s because the chairman of selectors had told a journalist I know very well that ‘Uzzy doesn’t “have” what we want in a captain. He doesn’t display the right stuff.’ I was pretty sure I knew what that meant. I didn’t fit the old-school Aussie mode or have the right skin colour for the job.
Cummins addressed that directly in his press conference:
“I think of all the things I’ve read this week, I think that’s actually the most serious. To think the job that I hold is quarantined from people based on their skin colour, that’s a pretty big statement. I think if you’re going to say that, I think you’ve got to have some evidence, and I just don’t think that’s the case.
“So again, I agree with Uzzy on a lot of things, but I disagree. I tell him that I disagree and him saying that if you’re Australian captain you have to be a certain skin colour, I couldn’t disagree with that statement any more.”
Cummins won’t be taking any legal action. He says:
I mean, I did get advised this week that some of the things that have [been] said are probably defamatory. I won’t be doing that. You got to move on. It’s been eight years.
We’re moving on, we are moving on. You got to draw the line at some point. I won’t be doing that.
‘Maybe we should have done a better job of explaining’
Cummins maintains he will stay until the questions finish, noting the presser has gone on for over an hour. He adds:
Maybe we should have done a better job of explaining over the years. Perhaps the public does deserve it. We are Australian property. But it is a really difficult one.
Cummins: ‘there’s a lot of nuance’ in what bowlers do to the ball
Cummins is speaking now about the nuance of ball politics.
The details matter because I can totally understand if you hear and have a passing interest in cricket and you see that sandpaper has been taken on to the field; I can see why it is jarring.
There’s a huge spectrum here of right and wrong, but there’s a lot of nuance. You are allowed to shine a ball. You are allowed to apply saliva. Not any more, but you were. But you cannot apply too much, you cannot load it up.
… There’s a lot of nuance and we take each extreme, I will shine it with a bit of saliva and maybe I have some sugar in my mouth. You can see how the boundaries get pushed a bit.
Cummins is getting asked a lot of detailed questions about the episode, but he says some of the fine-tuned inquiries are difficult to speak to as they took place almost a decade ago.
This is a hard thing to talk about because a lot of what we are referring to is eight and a half years ago and was dealt with, and I think the world is a better place for going through it. I think it’s in a much better spot.
This press conference is approaching 45 minutes. Cummins says he’ll stay until journalists had exhausted all of their questions, and then hopefully move on permanently from the rehashed controversy.
Cummins says it seems the issue has been ‘sitting heavy’ on Khawaja
Cummins won’t say much about any exchanges he’s had with Khawaja this week, saying they’re personal conversations and he doesn’t want to “go into it”.
When asked why he thinks the revelations are coming out now, Cummins says:
It looks like it’s been sitting heavy on him for a while. It’s eight and a half years ago. I get that … Maybe this is Usman’s chance and he never really got over it at the time.
But he reiterates that he believes the claims are “irresponsible”.
Cummins said he’s been frustrated Khawaja’s book is relitigating an episode from more than eight years ago, adding it had reopened trauma for some:
It’s eight and a half years, we have moved on.
We’ll keep saying it but, again, these are people’s lives. It was traumatic for some of them. They have had to work through quite a bit to get out the other side.
So again, that’s why I’m really disappointed and frustrated this week … how it’s been dealt with so flippantly.
Cummins says he believes there was a proper way to handle the sandpaper incident, pointing to the Cricket Australia investigation shortly afterwards.
Cricket Australia’s chief executive, Todd Greenberg, told media this week there was not “any compelling reason” to revisit the investigation, even though there are “specific details” in Khawaja’s book “that contradict the versions that have been provided by others”.
Cummins goes on:
There’s a very proper way to do things and improve. I think that investigation was a proper way to do it.
Everyone was asked in the circumstances about a game very quickly after. So that’s for CA. I think you can maybe argue whether the judgements were fair, but what can you do? I got asked all the questions, answered them all fairly.
A reporter just asked about the difference in stories. Cummins replied:
That’s my story, so I think he’s wrong.
He went on to say there appeared to be a “few big leaps” in the book and Khawaja had been “vague” and acted in a “very casual matter”:
The details really matter in that difference. So perhaps there was conversations with Cameron Bancroft around taking sandpaper out and how to do it. That doesn’t mean that everyone in that dressing room knew what was going on.
‘There was no master plan around using illegal methods’
Pat Cummins:
There was no master plan around using illegal methods. I think that’s maybe something that hasn’t been spoken about enough. People assume you have gone from very legal methods to suddenly taking sandpaper and then there must have been some huge master plan.
That is not the case …
There’s no grand plan, there’s no team meeting, there’s no bowlers saying ‘this is what must happen’.
Cummins was asked how the ball looked at the time.
At that stage, you know, even the umpires had a look. We didn’t know it had been altered with sandpaper.
Balls get roughened up every time we play. So, you know, whether that’s from a foreign object or something that’s totally legal and part of the game. Sometimes it’s hard to know. But out there in the field I did not see anything on the ball.

Khawaja memoir ‘readable, surprisingly revealing, sometimes painfully frank’
GideonHaigh, writing for the Guardian this week, says the greatest shame of the controversy inflamed by UsmanKhawaja’s memoir, Sabr, is that “99% of those opining about it will never read it”.
They will experience it by quotes and summaries, magnified and distorted, elided and exaggerated, shaped by voyeurism and schadenfreude.
In fact, Sabr is a readable, surprisingly revealing, sometimes painfully frank book about a unique career.
Haigh says Khawaja was among the most talented batters in an Australian generation “when it was not in oversupply”, but points out he played in only 22% of the national team’s total fixtures over that period.
If he developed a carapace to deal with such endless disappointment, should that surprise anyone?
Sabr might mean patience or resilience in Urdu, but a strength of Khawaja’s testament is that he allows the impatience to show through.
It is a cranky book because, perhaps, a degree of crankiness is what it takes to come back and back and back, when one is never sure one’s abilities are appreciated and one’s face fits.
Starc statement: ‘we weren’t aware of things being taken on the field’
Earlier this week, Mitchell Starc denied claims made in Khawaja’s book.
Starc broke his silence to address Khawaja’s comments, saying he was not aware that sandpaper was used in the Test before Cape Town, nor during the Newlands match. The paceman said his recollection of the match had not changed from what the bowlers said in a statement issued in 2021, which denied all knowledge of the ball-tampering plan.
He said:
As far as our statement said, we weren’t aware of things being taken on the field, that’s where I’ll leave it. We weren’t aware anything was taken on to the field to be tampered with. We saw [the sandpaper] on the big screen in Cape Town.
As far as the book is concerned, I haven’t read it. I probably won’t read it. So that’s for Usman to elaborate on.

Srinagar- Security forces on Thursday resumed the search operation in South Kashmir’s Kulgam district to track down two terrorists, who attacked a CRPF post injuring three personnel, officials said.
Two heavily armed terrorists emerged from a dense cluster of trees and opened fire at a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) post in the South Kashmir district on Wednesday, injuring three CRPF personnel, one of them critically.
The two men disappeared into the forested area after the attack that took place around 2.15 pm near Mir Bazar, about 75 km from Srinagar and just a km from the strategic Jammu-Srinagar National Highway.
Immediately after the attack, security launched a massive cordon and search operation in the area to track down the terrorists.
On Thursday morning, the security forces resumed the searches, the officials said.
They said the forces have erected barricades and deployed armoured vehicles at several places in the district.
Checking and frisking of vehicles is being undertaken at the security check-points as a tight vigil is being maintained.
The security agencies are using human and technical intelligence to aid the operation, the officials added.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

Why a US-funded vaccine trial on babies was cancelled in Guinea-Bissau
- Published
A proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled following accusations that the trial was "unethical" and "neocolonial".
The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines.
Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy.
The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns.
Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries.
The BBC has asked the US department of health and human services for comment.
Here is what you need to know.
What was the trial?
The study was planned at the Bandim Health Project, a research centre that has operated in Guinea-Bissau since 1978.
It was designed to involve 14,000 newborns, with half receiving a hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth and the other half not being given the shot.
Bandim said the trial aimed to investigate whether the hepatitis B vaccine given at birth has broader health effects beyond preventing infection.
Previous studies in The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau have raised questions about a possible link to increased mortality.
Researchers argued that because Guinea-Bissau does not currently offer routine hepatitis B vaccinations at birth, despite WHO recommendations, they have a unique opportunity to study its effects before such vaccines are introduced in 2028.
But critics questioned the ethics of withholding the vaccine from some babies, particularly in one of the world's poorest countries, where the infection is widespread.
The Trump administration funded the proposed study, with the CDC awarding the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) $1.6m (£1.2m) in December 2025.
What did the WHO say?
Walter Kazadi Mulombo, the WHO representative in Guinea-Bissau, told the BBC they became concerned after receiving questions about the study and finding no publicly available protocol.
He said the main ethical concern was that the trial would withhold an intervention already proven to protect newborns against hepatitis B.
"The vaccine has been used for more than 30 years in more than 115 countries," he said. "A study that will withhold that intervention from other newborns is unethical."
He warned that babies could be exposed to the virus during childbirth if their mothers were infected, as well as later in life.
Nearly a fifth of the population of Guinea-Bissau are infected with hepatitis B, a viral infection that affects the liver.
Those infected during infancy are particularly likely to develop chronic infections, which kill up to 25% of people, mostly through liver failure or liver cancer, according to data published in 2020.
The WHO is working with the government to bring forward the birth-dose vaccine.
"The country had been expected to add it to its routine immunisation schedule in 2028, but officials are considering introducing it in the first quarter of next year," Mulombo said.
Guinea-Bissau currently vaccinates children against hepatitis B at six weeks, which means it is less effective.
Why did Guinea-Bissau reject the trial?
Guinea-Bissau's government prohibited hepatitis B vaccine trials involving children in January. At the time, it requested a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study.
Health Minister Quinhin Nantote said in October that the suspension remained in force and had not been overturned by the Council of Ministers after reports emerged claiming that the trial would be taking place after all.
"We were surprised to learn from media reports that the study might proceed," Nantote said. "We are outraged because even I, as the minister responsible for this sector, was not informed."
The dispute intensified after the SDU said a revised study protocol had received ethical approval "from the relevant authorities in Guinea-Bissau", which Nantote denied.
Dr Gavin Yamey, a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in the US, criticised the proposal.
"The proposed trial reeks of neocolonialism," he told the BBC, questioning why the research was not being conducted in Denmark.
His criticism centred on the decision to withhold a recommended vaccine from some newborns in a country where hepatitis B is widespread.
SDU dean Jakob Grauslund said the trial had never started, no babies had been enrolled and no vaccinations administered as part of the research.
Was the trial approved by anyone?
The SDU said it had received a separate, positive assessment from the university's own research ethics committee.
Grauslund said the university had sought an additional independent assessment, although Danish law did not require one.
He added that the relevant Danish statutory research ethics bodies were unable to undertake the review.
Following the approval from the SDU's ethics committee, Grauslund decided that the project could proceed.
He, however, stressed that this did not replace the separate authorisation required from Guinea-Bissau's authorities.
What has happened to the vaccines?
On 19 October, Guinea-Bissau's Judicial Police searched the Bandim Health Project's facilities in the capital, Bissau, and seized a batch of hepatitis B vaccines.
Police said the batch was intended for vaccinating children but did not disclose how many doses had been seized or the specific grounds for the investigation.
They stressed that the seizure did not, in itself, mean the vaccines were defective or unsafe.
The police have not explicitly said whether their investigation relates to the proposed trial, the importation of the vaccines or other circumstances surrounding the batch.
Grauslund said he could not comment on the seizure of the vaccines.
Who is funding the research?
The proposed trial was funded by the US government at a time of significant changes to vaccine policy under President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Kennedy.
Under Kennedy's leadership, a US vaccine panel attempted to end a longstanding recommendation that all newborns receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth, but a federal judge later blocked this, along with other changes to vaccine policy made by the Trump administration.
Critics have questioned whether the research could help support that policy shift, although the study's stated aim was to investigate potential effects of the vaccine beyond preventing infection.
Kennedy has praised the Danish researchers as "the deities of vaccine research", and cited earlier findings from their work in support of concerns about vaccine safety. A subsequent study by some of the same researchers, however, found no evidence of the previously reported effect.
There is no evidence that the proposed trial was designed to justify a change in US policy.

Quick Answer
Concat is a free, open-source CapCut alternative with offline AI captions, voice cloning, background removal, 100+ effects, and 4K exports. It runs locally, needs no account, and adds no watermarks. Available across major platforms, it’s promising but still in beta, with some rough edges.
When you think of video editing, CapCut is a popular name that would pop up. It has made short-form editing painless. However, it has now started to put more of its tools behind a paywall, and a few of them need an internet connection to work.
If you are looking for a way out, you have probably already seen OpenReel, the browser-based open-source editor, or gone through our list of the best free video editing software. This time we have something different. Concat takes a different route. It is a free, open-source editor that runs on your own computer and is loaded with features like captions, voiceovers, and background removal built in.
Table of Contents
What is Concat?
Concat is a video editor that is currently in beta. The idea behind its development is easy to understand: It wants to give people stuff that CapCut offers but for free, like auto-captions, text-to-speech, background removal, keyframes, effects, titles, and 4K export. Everything Concat has on offer comes without strings attached. You don’t need to sign up, no watermark stamped on your exports, and no premium tier waiting around the corner.
The other big difference is where the work happens. Concat does everything locally, on your machine. It is built on a native Rust engine with a GPU compositor, and the AI models it uses (for captions, voices, and cutouts) are downloaded once from the settings and then run offline. This means the raw footage that you upload never gets uploaded anywhere.
CapCut is still a great editor, and nobody is pretending otherwise. When we compared it with Instagram Edits, we pointed out that CapCut has the richer feature set, but also that some of its tools need a connection and that its template and music ecosystem is tied closely to TikTok, which owns it. And if you are in India, you already know CapCut is banned here. So, you have to download the modded version or depend on some ad-filled alternatives.
That is the gap Concat is trying to fill. Not a “lite” version of a big editor, but a free one that keeps the stuff you reach for every day and keeps it on your own PC.
Concat features that matter
The feature list is long. But here are the parts that stand out.
Auto-captions that work offline
Captions are quite important nowadays, as content is reaching every part of the globe. But it is a chore every Reels and Shorts editor knows too well. Concat handles them using Whisper, a speech-recognition model that runs locally. You pick a model size (you can choose larger models, which are more accurate but require a stronger machine), and styled captions appear straight on your timeline. No upload, no waiting on a server, and it keeps working without internet.
Text-to-speech and voice cloning
Concat gives you free voices for narration, which is handy for tutorials or faceless channels. You can also clone a voice from just a few seconds of recording. That’s nice to edit a flubbed line without re-recording a whole take.
Background removal
You might have removed people or objects from your images. For videos, most of the editors ask you to pay. But Concat lets you edit out people or objects from a clip for free. If the automatic cutout misses a spot, you can paint the mask manually.
Keyframes with a curve editor
With keyframes, you can animate almost anything over time: position, scale, rotation, opacity, volume, and the settings of effects. There is a built-in curve editor too. You can use this to make a zoom feel smooth instead of mechanical, something that a paid video editor offers.
100 effects, filters and transitions
Concat comes with about 100 effects, filters, and transitions. They are rendered by your GPU and show up live in the preview. This way you can see what you are doing instead of waiting for an export to find out.
Fast cutting and a proper timeline
You get everything like split, trim, ripple delete, merge, freeze frame, and speed changes. If you like clips snapping together without gaps, you can switch on a magnetic timeline. Additionally, you can stack as many tracks as you want for overlays and picture-in-picture, keep several timelines inside a single project, and use blend modes like screen, add, and multiply. Crop and flip tools are there as well.
Titles with real styling
You can change fonts, add strokes and shadows, and drop in a background plate behind the words. If you don’t have any ideas, you can start from the already available presets.
One-switch audio cleanup
If your video has bad audio because of a faulty microphone or nearby noise, it can spoil a good video more than bad lighting does. Concat has a simple toggle for noise reduction, voice enhancement, and loudness leveling. You can also change voice effects to chipmunk, robot, and telephone.
Export and performance
Now, the best part is that with Concat, there is no limitation on export. It supports H.264, HEVC, and AV1, up to 4K at 60 frames per second with 10-bit colour.
Which platforms does Concat support?
Concat is versatile and supports multiple operating systems:
- Windows
- macOS
- Linux
- Android
- iPhone and iPad
Moreover, the editor is available in 26 languages. Downloading and setting up Concat is simple. Here’s what you need to do:
- Open the official download page, which picks the right build for your device. You can also grab any version from the GitHub Releases page.
- Install it like any other app on your device.
- On Windows, your system may warn you because the builds are not code-signed yet. Click More info, then Run anyway.
- On macOS, if the system refuses to open the app, the project suggests running xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Concat.app in Terminal.
- Open Settings and download the AI models you want (captions, voices, cutout). After that, they work offline.
Concat vs CapCut
| Feature | Concat | CapCut | 
|---|---|---|
| Price | Free, no subscription | Freemium | 
| Who is behind it | Open-source project (AGPL-3.0) | ByteDance | 
| Internet needed | Only to download AI models once | Some tools need a connection | 
| Templates and music | Limited | Large library tied to TikTok | 
A few things to keep in mind
Concat is promising and has all the features you would need from a video editor that is trying to be an alternative to CapCut. But don’t forget that it is young, and there are a few caveats that you should know about.
- It is a beta. The repo had over 200 open issues at the time of writing this article. So, you may come across some rough edges. We would advise you not to trust it with a client deadline until you have tested it on your own projects.
- Unsigned Windows builds and the macOS quarantine step can feel sketchy to newcomers. But it is safe, even though they are expected for now.
- You do not get a stock library to lean on. You will need your own assets.
- iPhone users have extra work because you have to sideload it, and sideloading is not for everyone.
Once you have the clarity, you should give Concat a try and let its output help you decide if you should keep using it or not. Let us know in the comments below which editor you are currently using.

Ramayana – Part I, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, is witnessing advance-booking interest for its second Saturday, November 14. The Nitesh Tiwari-directed mythological epic has registered advance ticket sales worth Rs. 10.80 crores nett across all languages and formats, with 3,06,164 tickets sold across 13,438 shows. The figures provide an early indication of audience demand as the film prepares for its second weekend, a crucial period that will determine how strongly it can sustain its theatrical performance.
However, a closer examination of the language-wise and format-wise data reveals some fascinating trends, particularly the enormous contribution from 3D screenings and Tamil's emergence as the second-highest-grossing language. The Hindi version continues to dominate Ramayana's advance-booking revenue, collecting approximately Rs. 7.87 crores nett, accounting for 72.83% of Saturday's total. However, the competition among South Indian languages has witnessed another interesting development. Tamil has emerged as the second-highest-grossing language, with approximately Rs. 92 lakh nett in advance collections. Malayalam follows closely at Rs. 89.42 lakh, while Kannada has generated Rs. 59.80 lakh and Telugu Rs. 52.34 lakh. The difference between Tamil and Malayalam stands at just Rs. 2.58 lakh, making their competition particularly close. Tamil's performance is noteworthy because Kannada and Telugu had generally dominated the South Indian language-wise collections during Ramayana's opening week.
Perhaps the most extraordinary finding from Saturday's advance-booking data is the overwhelming dominance of 3D screenings. All 3D formats have collectively generated approximately Rs. 8.74 crores nett, accounting for an astonishing 80.90% of the total advance revenue. In comparison, non-3D formats have contributed just Rs. 2.06 crores, or 19.10%. This is a particularly significant development when compared with Friday's advance-booking figures, where 3D formats accounted for 72.69% of revenue. In other words, 3D's revenue share is approximately 8.21 percentage points higher in Saturday's snapshot than in Friday's.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday following reports of two alleged affairs. One reportedly involved a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of spying for Beijing.
"Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive officer, and a member of the board, effective immediately," Nvidia's offical statement read.
"Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry," it added.
According to the board, chief financial officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and is its fourth-largest investor with a stake of about 3.61%, will also step down from the board.
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to consider his removal, a person familiar with the matter said. The meeting followed reports earlier in the day alleging that Huang had also been involved in an extramarital affair with a senior company executive who reported directly to him.
Nvidia's full statement
Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, chief executive officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.
Colette Kress, current executive vice president and chief financial officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as executive vice president and chief financial officer while serving as interim chief executive officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent chief executive officer and will consider internal and external candidates.
Kress has served as executive vice President and chief financial officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.
The board of directors appointed Harvey C Jones as its first-ever chair of the board. Mr. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as chief executive officer and executive chairman of Synopsys.
“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, chair of the NVIDIA board of directors. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.
”
“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”
Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.

New Delhi, Nov 12: The Controller General of Defence Accounts (CGDA), Ministry of Defence, has rolled out an extensive outreach initiative as part of the Nationwide Digital Life Certificate (DLC) Campaign 5.0. Coordinated by the Department of Pension & Pensioners’ Welfare (DoP&PW), Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, the month-long campaign is being conducted across the country from November 1 to 30, 2026. As on November 11, 2026, over 20.48 lakh defence pensioners have successfully submitted DLCs, the highest contribution among all participating departments.
The initiative aims to facilitate seamless, hassle-free submission of DLCs for defence pensioners and family pensioners through advanced technology-enabled solutions. A key priority is ensuring that elderly, super-senior, and differently-abled pensioners complete their annual identification conveniently without procedural hardships.
Extensive Pan-India Mobilisation
To ensure widespread physical outreach and ground-level support, the Defence Accounts Department (DAD) has mobilised:
194 SPARSH Service Centres (SSCs) fully equipped to assist pensioners in generating DLCs and avail SPARSH platform services.
4.63 lakh Common Service Centres (CSCs), 13 partner banks / IPPB and 29 nodal officers to facilitate pensioners to generate DLCs.
Around 80 outreach programmes are being conducted across the country.
Mega Camps: A Mega Digital Life Certificate Camp to be organised in Kochi on November 23, 2026 offering on-the-spot assistance in generation of DLC.
Promotion of Face Authentication Technology
A focal point of Campaign 5.0 is promoting Aadhaar-based Face Authentication Technology via Jeevan Pramaan portal and mobile application, with more than 80% of the digital life certificates being generated through Face ID. This facility allows pensioners to authenticate their life certificate using a smartphone, eliminating the need for external biometric hardware.
Key advantages include:
Submission from Home: Enables pensioners to generate certificates from the comfort of their homes, cutting down travel time and eliminating physical visits to bank branches or defence offices.
Overcoming Biometric Degradation: Addresses difficulties faced by super-senior pensioners whose fingerprints have faded with the passage of time and advancing age.
Support for Differently-Abled Veterans: Provides significant ease of access for pensioners facing reduced mobility.
Digital Self-Reliance: Encourages pensioners and their families to adopt digital practices, building self-sufficiency for future annual submissions.
Building on Proven Achievements
The Defence Accounts Department has consistently driven high adoption in nationwide digital governance initiatives. During DLC Campaign 4.0 in November 2025, the DAD generated over 20.94 lakh DLCs, through its pan-India network of SPARSH Service Centers, Common Service Centres and partner banks.
Outreach under SPARSH has also expanded significantly, with 35.11 lakh defence pensioners onboarded as of October 2026, supported by 301 SPARSH Outreach Programmes and 204 Raksha Pension Samadhan Aayojans resolving over 8,000 grievances on the spot.
Reiterating its guiding principle ‘Right Pension to the Right Pensioner at the Right Time’, the Defence Accounts Department has urged to all defence pensioners and family pensioners to visit their nearest SPARSH Service Center, banks or one of the 80 outreach programmes during November 2026 to experience a hassle-free, fully digitised life certificate submission process.

Anthropic has a new target for Claude adoption: people who run the factory floor.
The company launched a new Claude for Manufacturers plugin on Thursday. It's a cluster of add-ons that make the company's AI tool better for quality engineers, technicians, and other workers who run production lines. Although it won't directly operate equipment — that's another initiative the company is researching — it represents another industry-specific foray by the AI company.
In the lead-up to its trillion-dollar initial public offering, expected next week, Anthropic has a playbook. To boost revenue and adoption of its AI models, the company is releasing tools and connectors tailored to different workers: there are Claude models for healthcare, financial services, legal, government, and more. The manufacturing release fits the same strategy.
"Manufacturing is complex and judgment-heavy work," Lauren Collett, Anthropic's enterprise go-to-market leader, told Business Insider. "And I think that as model capabilities have advanced, this is just a really, really great time for us to be looking at some of these more complex business processes."
She said Anthropic heard from manufacturing customers that they have "more work than their experienced people have time to get through," so part of the hope is that the plugins will speed up repetitive tasks.
Anthropic's launch includes 17 skills, which are ready-made Claude setups designed to complete specific tasks. The plugin for manufacturers also connects Claude to the design software Autodesk Fusion and to Infor, which can help businesses with procurement.
Anthropic is pitching to people who run factories
The manufacturing plugin's skills include quoting a new job, diagnosing a machine's breakdown, sourcing equipment from a supplier, and compiling production data. A skill gives Claude instructions, making it more likely that the AI system will finish what a person wants.
Collett said she hopes that the tools can reduce the "back-office toil" that slows businesses down.
For example, if a part fails inspection, Claude could automatically document what happened, check past reports or email histories for the same defect, rank the likely causes, draft the correction report, and then hand that to the job's quality engineer, Collett said.
She also said that over time, Anthropic would likely add more connectors to other software that manufacturers use, beyond the set in this launch.
Anthropic, after its smash hit with Claude Code, has been pushing the use of its tools for other knowledge work. Its pitch to investors for its IPO relies on the idea that many industries could adopt the company's AI tools.
"Experienced people are hard to find," Collett said, "and so there's a really big opportunity for them to get better leverage out of the folks that they have today, giving them more time for the decisions that need their judgment."

Real Madrid's Vinícius Jr sends surprise message to boy who lost his legs in Sudan's war
- Published
In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.
The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.
Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.
We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.
More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.
Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.
More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.
The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.
For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.
When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.
"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.
Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."
Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."
Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.
"Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".
Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.
Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.
Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.
"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.
She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."
Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.
Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.
"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time.
There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.
Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.
Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.
After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.
For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.
- 'I can't afford to save both twins': Sudan's war left one mother with an impossible choice 
  - Published16 October 2025
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.
"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."
His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.
As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.
He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.
For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.
The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.
Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine".
"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.
Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.
Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.
