A documentary is a film, too. But at the Oscars, it still hasn’t been fully embraced as one.
One of the breakout hits of the awards season is A24’s insanely entertaining “You Can See Everything” from directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, which had a surprise world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival in September and opened in theaters Oct. 16, grossing nearly $80 million at the domestic box office through its fourth weekend. Many professional pundits and awards enthusiasts are predicting the film will make history as the first documentary feature to land a best picture nomination. So we looked at the history of nonfiction films at the Academy Awards to see which movies have been embraced by the various branches and categories (some now defunct) over the years and what that history says about the film’s chances.
	Across 98 ceremonies, feature docs have earned a total of 33 nominations in categories other than documentary feature, according to the Academy’s own statistics. Three of them won statuettes.
Of the 14 nominations nonfiction films have collected outside their own race since 2013 (the 85th ceremony), 10 have come in best original song. 
The documentary feature category is decided by members of the Documentary Branch, which was formed in 2001 and, according to the Academy’s most recent figures, has 719 voting members, making it the third-largest branch behind Actors (1,202) and Executives (759). Preliminary voting runs Dec. 7-11, narrowing the field to a 15-film shortlist that will be announced Dec. 15. Members of the branch will then vote from that list in January to determine the five nominees, which will be revealed Jan. 21.
The Academy has 19 branches, and each nominates within its own discipline. At the same time, the entire voting membership chooses best picture nominees. Although Academy rules do not expressly prohibit documentaries from competing in other categories, nonfiction films rarely factor into races that presume fictional storytelling, including production design, costume design and acting. This year, A24 is pushing “You Can See Everything” in 11 categories, including best picture, director, supporting actress and documentary feature. Its awards site initially listed the film in the artisan races of production design (Alex DiGerlando and Rebecca Meis), cinematography (David Bolen), costume design (Katina Danabassis), film editing (Adam Locke-Norton), makeup and hairstyling (Stephanie Pasicov and Kerrie Smith), sound (Paul Hsu and Richard Carlos) and original score (Ari Balouzian). However, an updated version of the site no longer lists production design, costume design, makeup and hairstyling or sound. As Variety previously reported, Seyfried’s acting turn is eligible for the Oscars and Critics Choice but not for BAFTA, SAG (The Actor Awards) and the Golden Globes Awards.
No documentary has ever been nominated for best picture or best director. The closest came at the inaugural Oscars, when “Chang: A Drama of the Wilderness” (1927), the jungle drama shot on location in Siam by Merian C. Cooper and Ernest B. Schoedsack (the duo who would later make 1933’s “King Kong”), was nominated for unique and artistic picture, one of two top prizes handed out that night.
Two years later, “With Byrd at the South Pole” (1930), an account of Richard E. Byrd’s 1928-30 Antarctic expedition, won cinematography for Joseph T. Rucker and Willard Van Der Veer, becoming the first documentary to win an Oscar more than a decade before the Academy created a category for the form. A documentary category was introduced at the 1942 ceremony, with features and shorts competing together. The two were split into separate categories in 1944.
The writers branch took notice in the late 1940s, nominating Robert and Frances Flaherty’s story for “Louisiana Story” (1948), about a young Cajun boy and his pet raccoon and the story and screenplay of Sidney Meyers’ “The Quiet One” (1949), which blends real-life locations with staged scenes to tell the story of Donald Peters, a 10-year-old Black boy from Harlem grappling with severe emotional trauma. They remain the only two documentaries ever nominated for writing, with “The Quiet One” competing in the category then known as writing (story and screenplay).
Norman Foster’s “Navajo” (1952), about a young Navajo boy caught in a clash of cultures, made history as the first film nominated for both documentary feature and cinematography, with Virgil E. Miller cited in the black-and-white category.
The music branch embraced nonfiction scores early on and continued to do so for more than three decades.
Louis Gruenberg’s music for “The Fight for Life” (1940) opened the door, followed by Disney’s wartime hybrid “Victory Through Air Power” (1943) by Edward H. Plumb, Paul J. Smith and Oliver G. Wallace; the Cinerama showcase “This Is Cinerama” (1953) by Louis Forbes; Disney’s True-Life Adventures entries “Perri” (1957) by Paul Smith and “White Wilderness” (1958) by Oliver Wallace; the U.K. import “The Bolshoi Ballet” (1958) by Yuri Faier and G. Rozhdestvensky; and, finally, Gerald Fried’s work on “Birds Do It, Bees Do It” (1975), the last time a documentary score was recognized, more than 50 years ago.
The lone winner of score in that era was “Let It Be” (1970), which took home the original song score for the Beatles, giving the band its first and only Oscar.
Michael Wadleigh’s three-hour music chronicle “Woodstock” (1970) remains the gold standard for crossover recognition. Wadleigh’s concert landmark won documentary feature and earned nominations for film editing (Thelma Schoonmaker, years before her three wins for Martin Scorsese) and sound (Dan Wallin and Larry Johnson). Its three total nominations are still tied with “Flee” for the most ever received by a documentary.
	The second editing nomination came 24 years later, when Steve James’ “Hoop Dreams” (1994) was famously shut out of the documentary feature category at the 67th Oscars, even as the editors branch nominated Frederick Marx, James and Bill Haugse. The snub became one of the most notorious in Academy history and helped force a rethink of how the documentary branch selected its nominees.
The craft branches have largely closed their doors to nonfiction films since. No documentary has been nominated in cinematography since 1953, in sound since 1971 or in film editing since 1995.
If there is a side door for nonfiction today, it’s the original song category. Twelve documentaries have received nominations for best original song: “Mondo Cane” (1963), for Riz Ortolani and Nino Oliviero’s “More”; “An Inconvenient Truth” (2006), for Melissa Etheridge’s “I Need to Wake Up,” the only song from a documentary to win; “Chasing Ice” (2012), for J. Ralph’s “Before My Time”; “Glen Campbell … I’ll Be Me” (2014), for Glen Campbell and Julian Raymond’s “I’m Not Gonna Miss You”; “The Hunting Ground” (2015), for Diane Warren and Lady Gaga’s “Til It Happens to You”; “Racing Extinction” (2015), for Ralph and Anohni’s “Manta Ray”; “Jim: The James Foley Story” (2016), for Ralph and Sting’s “The Empty Chair”; “RBG” (2018), for Warren’s “I’ll Fight”; “American Symphony” (2023), for Jon Batiste and Dan Wilson’s “It Never Went Away”; “Elton John: Never Too Late” (2024), for Elton John, Brandi Carlile, Andrew Watt and Bernie Taupin’s “Never Too Late”; “Diane Warren: Relentless” (2025), for Warren’s “Dear Me”; and “Viva Verdi!” (2025), for Nicholas Pike’s “Sweet Dreams of Joy.”
Etheridge’s win came more than four decades after “Mondo Cane” opened the door, and “An Inconvenient Truth” also took documentary feature that night. Davis Guggenheim’s climate film remains the only documentary feature winner to also win an Oscar in another category, and it is the last documentary of any kind to win outside its own race.
The more telling number is this one: 10 of the 12 documentary song nominees came from films the documentary branch passed over. Only “An Inconvenient Truth” and “RBG” were nominated in both categories. For distributors of music-driven or celebrity-centered docs, the math is plain. The song campaign is often the more realistic path to the Dolby Theatre than the documentary race itself, as “American Symphony,” “Elton John: Never Too Late” and “Viva Verdi!” (a portrait of Milan’s Casa Verdi retirement home, with its nominated aria sung by Puerto Rican soprano Ana María Martínez) all demonstrated.
The other modern avenue runs through international feature, where a film needs its country’s official submission before Academy voters can weigh in.
Ari Folman’s animated documentary “Waltz With Bashir” (2008) broke through first, nominated for foreign language film for Israel at the 81st Oscars, though it missed documentary feature. A decade later, three straight years of history followed. North Macedonia’s “Honeyland” (2019) became the first film nominated for both documentary feature and international feature at the 92nd ceremony. Alexander Nanau’s “Collective” (2020) repeated the feat the following year and gave Romania its first Oscar nomination ever. Then Jonas Poher Rasmussen’s Danish feature “Flee” (2021) became the first film nominated in documentary feature, animated feature and international feature in the same year.
None of the three won anything.
“Honeyland” lost to “American Factory” (2019) and “Parasite” (2019), “Collective” fell to “My Octopus Teacher” (2020) and “Another Round” (2020), and “Flee” went 0-for-3 against “Summer of Soul” (2021), “Encanto” (2021) and “Drive My Car” (2021). Four ceremonies have passed since “Flee” without another documentary in the international lineup.
So what does nearly a century of history tell us about “You Can See Everything?”
For starters, the doors that have opened for nonfiction have mostly been in craft and music races and those are precisely the categories where A24 has trimmed and focused its campaign. The film has already swept the Critics Choice Documentary Awards, winning all five categories in which it was nominated. But the Academy has been a tougher nut to crack.
Best picture is a different animal. The documentary branch doesn’t decide it. The full voting membership, now more than 10,000 industry professionals, does. That cuts both ways. A film the documentary branch might view with suspicion, as it once did “Hoop Dreams,” can still find support among actors, executives and craftspeople who simply loved the movie. The music branch has already shown that pattern 10 times over, nominating songs from documentaries the doc branch passed over. It isn’t far-fetched to imagine “You Can See Everything” landing in best picture while missing documentary feature altogether, a scenario already being floated this season.
Variety’s latest Oscar predictions have “You Can See Everything” earning three nominations: best picture, supporting actress for Seyfried and film editing. Notably absent is documentary feature, a category in which many pundits believe its omission would rank among the branch’s most significant snubs, alongside such overlooked films as “Won’t You Be My Neighbor” (2018), “Jane” (2017), “Stories We Tell” (2012), etc. But even a fraction of that predicted crossover haul would rewrite the Oscar record books.
The first major test comes Dec. 15, when the documentary shortlist is announced, followed by Oscar nominations on Jan. 21. If “You Can See Everything” breaks through in even one of the Academy’s other races, it would mark a significant milestone for A24.
Because, hey, a documentary is a film, too.

Russian President 
Vladimir Putin
 on Thursday warned that any foreign troops deployed in Ukraine would be considered "legitimate targets", saying their presence would threaten Russia's security.
Putin made the remarks during a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner at the Kremlin in Moscow.
According to Reuters, Putin said European countries wanted to deploy troops in Ukraine after a peace agreement and added that Moscow would consider them legitimate targets.
"We said from the very beginning that the presence of any foreign troops on Ukrainian territory is absolutely unacceptable for us, because we believe it threatens the security of the Russian Federation," Putin said during the televised meeting, according to the Kremlin remarks reported by Reuters.
The meeting was attended by US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner, alongside Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov, defence minister Andrei Belousov and presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev.
Referring to the possibility of European forces entering Ukraine after a peace agreement, Putin said, "That after peace is concluded, they will immediately bring troops into Ukraine. 
What does that mean? We have already said that for us it is a legitimate target, meaning the war will immediately resume."
He also said Russia wanted Washington to work with European countries on the wider security arrangements. "I would like the United States to work with Europe so that the Europeans could decide whether they want peace or war," Putin said.
Putin further stressed that Moscow wanted a lasting settlement rather than a temporary pause in fighting, saying peace in Ukraine must be "eternal".
Kushner, during the meeting, told Putin that Russia and Ukraine had made progress in negotiations but remained divided over how to implement a peace agreement. He said the two sides had "agreed on many of the principles, but are still apart on some of the way to accomplish" peace, according to the Associated Press.
Kushner also raised the issue of European participation in future negotiations, telling Putin that European countries wanted to be involved in discussions on Ukraine's future security arrangements. Washington has been seeking a broader negotiating framework involving European governments alongside Russia, Ukraine and the US.
Witkoff, meanwhile, highlighted progress made during the recent US-mediated negotiations in Abu Dhabi, particularly the agreement on a major prisoner-of-war exchange between Russia and Ukraine. He described the development as an encouraging sign in the diplomatic process.
Before entering the Kremlin, Witkoff was asked whether the progress in negotiations meant peace was closer. "I hope so," he replied, according to Reuters.
The meeting followed two days of trilateral negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11. The talks resulted in an agreement on a prisoner exchange but failed to produce a breakthrough on territorial demands and post-war security arrangements.

In early November, an image spread online claiming to show U.S. President Donald Trump posing for a photograph with comedian Russell Brand, social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate, mixed martial artist Conor McGregor, former boxer Mike Tyson and former football player Lawrence Taylor.
The alleged photograph showed (archived) Trump with his thumbs up, surrounded by a group of men convicted or accused of committing sexual offenses. An X post listed the names of the men at the alleged gathering:
Every MAGAt in this picture has been accused, indicted, convicted of, or found civilly liable for sex crimes. Three are currently in jail.
Andrew Tate @Cobratate - Indicted/Charged with multiple counts or rape and human trafficking
Russell Brand @rustyrockets - Convicted of Rape
Donald Trump @DonaldTrump - Civilly Liable / A federal Judge stated he raped E. Jean Caroll
Mike Tyson @MikeTyson - Convicted of Rape
Conor McGregor @TheNotoriousMMA - Civilly liable for Sexual Assault
Lawrence Taylor @LT_56 - Registered Sex Offender. Arrest for sex with a minor.
Tristan Tate @TateTheTalisman - Indicted/Charged with multiple counts or rape and human trafficking
(X user @MAGAts_Exposed)
The above image is fake and was created by artificial intelligence. There is no authentic photograph from a reputable media outlet showing these men together, let alone any evidence or reporting that they had all met even without cameras present. Google Gemini detected a watermark showing that the image was created or edited using Google AI.
Snopes ran the image through Google Gemini's SynthID check, a tool that scans for watermarks embedded by artificial intelligence software. That scan detected a SynthID watermark and concluded, "this image was generated or edited with Google AI, and a SynthID watermark was detected."
To confirm whether an image contains a SynthID watermark, readers can upload a photo to Google Gemini and ask, "Does this image have a SynthID watermark?" We should note, the absence of a SynthID watermark doesn't automatically mean an image is authentic, as it could have been created using other AI tools.
There are numerous signs that the image is AI-generated, namely that all the men's faces are blurred and it is of very poor quality. A video camera behind Brand is flashing light toward the photographer, creating an unnatural glow.
Using Google's reverse image search tool, we also found no reputable media outlets reporting on such an image. If such a photograph was real, it would be more widely disseminated.
The individuals in the above image have cultivated both distant and close ties to the Trump administration. The Tate brothers, who have been charged with rape and trafficking, among other criminal offenses, are connected to Trump allies, with Andrew participating in a Twitter Spaces livestream with Donald Trump Jr. As of this writing the Tates are being held at a Miami detention center without bail. Tyson, convicted of rape, has made public appearances with Trump.
Brand, who was convicted of rape and sexual assault, has appeared at numerous high-profile events led by Trump allies, including a Turning Point USA event and a Make America Healthy Again event. In November he was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison. McGregor, who was found liable of sexual assault in a civil case, has visited Trump at the White House and praised the president. In 2025, Taylor, a registered sex offender, was appointed a member of Trump's Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition.
Snopes has covered numerous fake images of Trump, including one of Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein on a private jet, and another one of them on a boat.

Nvidia announced the resignation of Jensen Huang after nearly a week of rolling revelations alleging romantic, extramarital relationships with multiple women, including one speculated to be an agent of the Chinese government.
The departure of Nvidia's showman of a CEO will inevitably shed more light on his closest collaborators at the chip company. One executive poised to exert influence in the post-Huang era is Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing.
The 48-year-old's contribution to Nvidia is hard-coded into the company's history. He's been working alongside Huang since 2004, when he started building the company's breakthrough software, called Compute Unified Device Architecture.
Back then, the team had two people and two libraries. Today, CUDA supports more than 900 libraries and artificial intelligence models. Each library corresponds to an industry using Nvidia technology.
Especially in light of Huang's departure, Buck's influence is just beginning. CUDA is the platform from which Nvidia jumped to, at one point, 90% market share in AI computing. CUDA is how the company defends its moat.
It's the heft of Buck's contribution that has led industry analysts and onlookers to repeatedly cite Buck in discussions of a possible successor to Huang, even long before one was needed.
One architecture to rule them all
Dion Harris, Nvidia's senior director of high-performance computing and AI factory solutions, sometimes forgets that he's in the room with the Dr. Ian Buck. Then it hits him that his boss, and friend, is a computing legend.
Since Buck's undergrad days at Princeton in the late 1990s, he had been focused on graphics — a particularly punishing field within computer science with no obvious connection to AI at the time.
"Computer graphics was such a dweebie field," said Stephen Witt, the author of "The Thinking Machine," which details Nvidia's rise from obscurity to the world's most valuable company.
"There was a stigma to working in computer graphics — you were maybe some kind of man-child if this was your focus," Witt said.
While pursuing his Ph.D. at Stanford, Buck connected multiple graphics processing units to push them to their limits. He had interned at Nvidia before pursuing his Ph.D., so he was familiar with the GPU. Initially, he used it for graphics like everyone else.
Buck has said that he and his cohort would use the chips to play video games such as "Quake" and "Doom," but eventually, he started asking himself what else his gaming setup could do.
He became fixated on proving that you could use GPUs for anything and everything. He received funding from Nvidia and the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, among others, to develop tools to turn a GPU into a general-purpose supercomputing machine. When the company saw Brook—Buck's attempt at a programming language that applied the power of GPUs beyond graphics, Nvidia hired him.
He wasn't alone. John Nickolls, a hardware expert and then director of architecture for GPU computing, was also instrumental in building CUDA. Buck may have been forever paired with Nickolls if the latter had not died from cancer in 2011.
"Both Nickolls and Buck had this obsession with making computers go faster in the way that a Formula 1 mechanic would have an obsession with making the race car go faster," Witt told BI. (The author said Huang expressed frustration that Nickolls doesn't get the recognition he deserves since his passing.)
Buck, Nickolls, and a small team of experts built a framework that allowed developers to use an existing coding language, C, to harness the GPU's ability to run immense calculations simultaneously rather than one at a time and apply it to any field. The result was CUDA, a vehicle to bring parallel computing to the masses.
The rise of CUDA as an essential element in the world of AI wasn't inevitable. Huang insisted on making every chip compatible with the software, even though hardly anyone was using it, despite it being free. In fact, Nvidia lost millions of dollars for more than a decade because of CUDA.
The rest is lore. When ChatGPT launched, Nvidia was already powering the AI computing revolution that is now the focus of trillions in infrastructure spending, much of which eventually goes to Nvidia.
King of the nerds
Buck's smarts do have limits. He joked to an eager audience at GTC in 2025 that quantum chromodynamics, a field of particle physics, just won't stick in his brain. But he thrives in Nvidia's notoriously rigorous environment.
Under Huang, the Santa Clara, California, company has maintained an intense culture that eschews one-on-one meetings and makes missteps and disagreements public. It might sound terrifying, but for those with the brains to keep up, the directness and the rigor are ideal.
For this report, Business Insider spoke with four people who have either worked directly with Buck at Stanford, Nvidia, or both. Those who know Buck personally describe him as gregarious and easygoing but capable of intensity when goals are on the line. He's focused on results rather than theory.
In his public remarks, at panels and in interviews on behalf of Nvidia, Buck volleys from rapid, technical lines of thought to slower, simple descriptions in layman's terms.
At a GTC press conference, he detailed the latest development in convolutional neural networks and then described proteins as "complicated 3D squigglies in your body." He describes the tiny, sensitive interconnects between parts of an Nvidia chipset like the Geek Squad explaining the back of a TV from memory — it's all in his head.
Harris said storytelling ability is particularly important in the upper ranks at Nvidia. Since the company essentially had a promising technology waiting for a market for years, Huang saw being early as a business strategy. He branded it "going after zero billion-dollar markets." The potential of AI, "AI factories," and the infrastructure spending that goes with them is a story Nvidia can't stop telling.
Buck's shilling skills have improved over the years. But even in 15-year-old footage, he's most animated when explaining the inner workings of Nvidia's technology.
"A lot of developers are amazing, but they say, 'Leave me alone. I'm going to write my code in the mountains somewhere," Paul Bloch, president of Nvidia partner DDN, told BI. Nvidia's leaders aren't like that, he said. Much of Nvidia's upper echelon may have the skills to match the reclusive set, but they don't choose between showmanship and code.
Ian Buck's next act
Ian Buck's work at Nvidia began with a simple mandate: make the GPU work for every industry. That mission is very nearly accomplished. There are hundreds of CUDA libraries targeting industries from weather forecasting to medical imaging.
"The libraries are really there to connect the dots so that every business doesn't have to learn CUDA," Harris said.
CUDA draws its strength from millions of developers, amassed over decades, who constantly innovate and improve on the platform. So far, no one has caught Nvidia's heels, but the competition is coming faster than ever.
Even as Buck spoke at GTC in 2025, developers across the world were trying to break through CUDA's dominance. The first night of the conference, a cast of competitors convened by TensorWave, an AI cloud company exclusively using chips from Nvidia's only US rival, AMD, held an event entitled "Beyond CUDA."
TensorWave cofounder Jeff Tatarchuck said it included more than "24 presenters talking about what they're doing to overcome the CUDA moat." New startups looking to crack CUDA are still fundraising, too.
AMD, which also presented at the event, is making an explicit effort to catch up on the software side of AI computing, but industry analysts say they're not there yet. And despite the rise of coding agents capable of writing CUDA kernels, demand for human CUDA engineers continues to grow. There have been more jobs requiring CUDA skills posted in 2026 than in 2025, according to the labor analytics platform Lightcast.
Harris told BI that Buck's team spends a lot of time speaking with researchers to stay on top. That's always been true, but the nature of the work has changed. A decade ago, Buck was convincing researchers to apply accelerated computing to their problems; now the tables have turned.
"One of the most challenging parts of my job often is to try to predict the future, but AI is always surprising us," Buck said at a Bank of America conference in 2025. Understanding what the smartest minds in AI need from Nvidia is paramount.
Many saw DeepSeek, the company that spooked markets last year with its ostensibly cheap reasoning AI model, as a threat to Nvidia since it achieved competitive results with less compute, not realizing that the team went deep into CUDA to squeeze out those gains. Buck described the Chinese team as "one of the best CUDA developers out there."
AI is entering a new phase as more companies commercialize their tools. Even with Nvidia's enormous head start, in part built by Buck, the pace is intense.
Talent is also a big part of how Nvidia is going to try to maintain its dominance, and another place where, Witt said, Buck has value beyond his technical skills. He's not exactly a household name, even at Stanford. But for a certain type of developer, the ones who can play in Buck's extremely complex sandbox, he is a draw.
"Everyone's trying to hire these guys, especially after DeepSeek," said Witt. "This was not a sexy domain in computer science for a long time. Now it is white hot." Huang's departure will make that side of his role even more important as several industry analysts have expressed concern that Nvidians may be more likely to leave the company now. Historically, Nvidia has had an extremely low rate of staff turnover.
Nvidia declined to make Ian Buck available for an interview with Business Insider and declined to comment on this report.
Who's Nvidia's next CEO?
Buck is more than a decade younger than Huang and has been part of the Huang succession discussion long before the current scandal.
Lip-Bu Tan, a semiconductor industry legend who became Intel's CEO in 2025, told BI that Buck was one of a handful of true collaborators for Huang, who has more than 60 direct reports.
"Jensen has three right-hand men," Tan told BI before he took over at Intel. Buck is one. Vice President of GPU Engineering Jonah Alben is another. And CFO Colette Kress, though clearly not a man, is the third, Tan said. Kress was appointed interim CEO by Nvidia's board Tuesday.
"Prediction markets have identified Rene Haas, former Nvidia VP and current CEO of Arm, as a potential external replacement, in addition to internal candidates Colette Kress and Ian Buck, head of Nvidia's AI efforts," said Brian Colello, Senior Equity Analyst at Morningstar, in an email Thursday.
"I don't think Ian spends a lot of time doing business strategy. He's more like the world's best mechanic," Witt said in 2025.

This image was AI-generated — OpenAI detected its own watermark on the image. However, the devastating flooding in Gaza is real, and there are dozens of authentic images illustrating the extent of the damage.
As winter flooding hit Gaza — where roughly 65% of the population, about 1.4 million people, lives in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the United Nations — a striking image circulated online in early November purportedly showing the magnitude of the flooding's damage.
Apparently shot at night, the image showed blue and white tents flooded by murky water, several buildings standing in the background as light from windows and streetlights appeared to reflect across the surface of the water.
Posts of the image shared across social media collectively gained millions of views and reactions, with hundreds of commenters appearing to believe the image was authentic. Prominent accounts, including British Parliament member Jeremy Corbyn, posted the image before deleting it (archived).
Although intense rainfall in Gaza early November has caused flooding and put thousands of people in danger as Israel continues to blockade crucial supplies — including 150,000 tents waiting just outside, according to the U.N. — this image was a fake.
The image contained multiple signs of being generated with artificial intelligrnace, including an OpenAI watermark that OpenAI's verification software identified. It's unclear precisely where it originated.
(OpenAI)
OpenAI reconstructs its images in a systemic grid pattern (autoregressive approach). Upon zooming in more closely, the pixel pattern of the image showed signs of a star-like grid, which digital forensics expert Hany Farid has described as a tell-tale sign of AI-generation.
(X user @ahmed_nashwan1 and Heny Farid, Snopes illustration)
The image displays other signs of AI generation, including unnatural light interruption, a mottled sky texture, and harsh lines between blurred pixels and textured pixels.
(X user ahmed_nashwan1, Snopes illustration)
Despite the fact that this image was AI-generated, there are hundreds of publicly available images showing the extent of the flooding destruction in Gaza.

Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.
The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.
A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.
Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.
At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.
Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.
The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.
The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

It’s been one week since Election Day, and Pete Hegseth is facing a different kind of war. Trump administration officials tell Inner Loop they knew the defense secretary would face a slew of investigations in the next Congress. Now, they think he is on track to be Democrats’ number one target—and Democrats are already planning to make their case as airtight as possible.
“Hegseth is now a passenger in whatever comes next,” says one source close to President Donald Trump. “And all the outcomes are potentially damaging.”
House Democratic aides tell Inner Loop that Democrats are likely to pursue an impeachment inquiry against Hegseth, and also work to narrow the charges against him to issues that Senate Republicans have also complained about, in an effort to attract their support.
Hegseth, who has championed the deeply unpopular and costly Iran war, has spent much of his controversial tenure upending various internal processes at the Defense Department, including firing generals and blocking promotions using criteria that disproportionately affected women and people of color. He has also become known for his notorious role in Signalgate and for military strikes against purported drug traffickers in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean.
Some of those topics have also previously been the subject of complaints from Republicans. The Senate Armed Services Committee chair Roger Wicker criticized Hegseth for the flag officer cuts and once reportedly threatened to block a Trump nominee unless the Pentagon handed over documents.
Last night, House Republicans managed to table an impeachment effort targeting Hegseth that was brought about by Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky. Massie, among other issues, accused Hegseth of waging the Iran war without approval from Congress and directing “extrajudicial killings.” But even though the effort failed, officials privately believe it is practically inevitable that Hegseth will be impeached again and face a Senate trial next year.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries suggested as much after the impeachment failed to progress, telling reporters he would consult with his top members on next steps.
“We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time, and that’ll be led by Adam Smith, soon to be chair of the Armed Services Committee, and Jamie Raskin, next chair of the judiciary,” Jeffries said.
Trump officials tell Inner Loop they still don’t expect Democrats to get enough GOP support to remove Hegseth—but they can’t shield him from wall-to-wall coverage of a trial.
The impeachment articles brought by Massie were seen by some Republicans as overly broad, which made officials think they could spare Hegseth an impeachment trial by having Senate majority leader John Thune dismiss all the charges in a straight-line vote.
But with Democrats taking over the Senate next year, that option is off the table.
It’s not going to be entirely simple, however. Hegseth’s biggest Republican detractors are all leaving Congress at the end of the year. Maine senator Susan Collins, North Carolina senator Thom Tillis, and Louisiana senator Bill Cassidy all lost reelection this midterm cycle, while Iowa senator Joni Ernst and Kentucky senator Mitch McConnell are stepping down after finishing their terms.
But even with his biggest detractors set to retire, at least five other Republican senators have complained about Hegseth’s performance—getting Democrats closer to the 67 votes needed to convict—like Wicker, South Dakota senator Mike Rounds, Kentucky senator Rand Paul, Alaska senator Lisa Murkowski, and Indiana senator Todd Young.
This is why the focus of the Democratic impeachment inquiry is going to have to be specific, and geared to Republican interests, so as to be unassailable.
Hegseth, for what it’s worth, doesn’t seem to want to go anywhere without a fight. In a televised appearance at the Pentagon earlier this week, Hegseth responded to a question about Vice President JD Vance blaming the Republican midterm losses on Iran, and said Vance was a “critical member of the team” and the war effort.
Hegseth then added, “I agree with what the president said, when he said ‘Hey, if I had to do this all over again, would we do it again? Absolutely.’”

House Republicans are poised to open an investigation into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's interactions with alleged Chinese spy and one-time tech executive Alice Huang, who is not related to the CEO.
The growing push for Congress to stand up its own investigation is set to put Republicans on a collision course with Trump, who has continued to publicly defend the CEO of the world's most valuable chip company.
During a congressional “Gang of Eight” briefing on Monday, officials including director of national intelligence Jay Clayton and CIA director John Ratcliffe gave only the broad brushstrokes of the classified intelligence surrounding Huang’s interactions, which left lawmakers deeply unsatisfied, sources say.

A few hours of exposure to firecracker smoke can be enough to trigger coughing, wheezing or breathlessness, particularly in people living with asthma or other respiratory conditions. The effects, however, are not limited to those with an existing diagnosis. High concentrations of particulate matter and gases can irritate the airways in anyone.
The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a numerical measure that converts the levels of different air pollutants into a single figure to indicate how polluted the air is and the likely health effects. India’s Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) calculates it using eight pollutants, including PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide.

How many SpaceX Starship rocket tests have failed?
The answer isn't so simple.
In late September 2026, SpaceX's Starship entered orbit for the first time, deploying 26 Starlink satellites in what was heralded as a major step for SpaceX's cosmic ambitions. However, the celebration was cut short when a failed engine forced the mission to end shortly after reaching orbit. The malfunction prevented the intended six-revolution trek through Earth's orbit, falling well short of its 10-hour goal.
This result is typical for Starship, as the company's "fail fast, learn fast" mindset recasts the program's failures — anywhere between four and 11 of 14 total launches, depending on how generous you are — as opportunities for growth. This has been true since its first test flight in April 2023, which exploded 65 miles short of its intended climb into Earth's atmosphere. As Musk tweeted after the fiery test, "Congrats @SpaceX team on an exciting test launch of Starship! Learned a lot for next test launch."
Given SpaceX's success to date, it is hard to argue with the company's logic. According to analytics firm BryceTech, SpaceX launched 85 percent of all spacecraft in 2025, including over half the world's orbital launches. To boot, Starlink's 9,800 active satellites currently account for over half of the world's total, according to satellite tracker Orbital Radar.
The largest and most powerful rocket ever assembled, Starship has a cargo capacity five times larger than SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket. This makes it essential for SpaceX's grander ambitions, including its million-satellite constellation, NASA's lunar missions and Musk's Mars colony dream. With another launch set for November 13, 2026, stakeholders will soon see whether the September launch represented progress or foreshadowed further additions to SpaceX's growing list of frustrations.
A checkered history
Gauging the success of the Starship project is difficult. Although some missions may fit within a binary success-failure matrix, most land somewhere in between. And while it has yet to deliver a fully-reusable rocket capable of missions to "Mars and beyond," progress was always going to be incremental. As such, its only fair to judge each mission against its own standards of progress.
Starship's start was turbulent. After its initial test combusted within minutes, its second flight saw the first-stage booster separate before the booster and vessel met fiery ends. Five months later, Starship's third test flight completed many of its objectives, reaching an altitude of 145 miles before disintegrating on its return. SpaceX then had two back-to-back successful launches, culminating in its launch tower successfully catching Starship's first-stage booster.
Unfortunately, another troubled period followed. Test six saw SpaceX call off its lauded mechanical arm before crashing the Super Heavy booster into the Gulf of Mexico. Two months later, Starship 7 exploded over the Bahamas just eight minutes after takeoff, sparking investigations by both the FAA and the Turks and Caicos government. The FAA launched another investigation after Starship's eighth test exploded in space, grounding planes across Florida. Starship 9 achieved minor improvements before spinning out of control, forcing SpaceX to cancel its planned deployment of 8 mock satellites.
Starship followed the disastrous run with a pair of its most successful tests. In August 2025, Starship released its first cargo of Starlink satellites. Two months later, SpaceX successfully launched and landed its 11th Starship rocket, fulfilling all major objectives.
Starship's twelfth test launched its upgraded Starship V3 rocket. While it accomplished several objectives, engine failures caused it to crash into the Gulf, triggering yet another FAA investigation. In July 2026, Starship 13 successfully deployed 20 of Starlink's new high-powered satellites before its first-stage booster failed to stick the landing. Considering its scattershot history, Starship 14's semi-successful run is par for the course.
Failing towards the stars?
Judging each mission against its stated objectives, most Starship launches have failed to meet expectations. SpaceX, however, would likely claim that its willingness to learn from mistakes puts its true failure rate closer to zero. The better question is whether the program is learning quickly enough to keep pace with its own meteoric ambitions.
If one takes Musk's proclamations as a measuring stick, Starship has underdelivered. In 2025, Musk predicted there was a 50 percent chance Starship would land on Mars in 2026. And with the once-every-26-months Mars launch window closing this November, you can guess which side of the coin SpaceX landed on. Of course, Musk is notorious for overpromising, so this is business as usual at Starbase.
Earlier this year, NASA announced that the program had fallen behind schedule by at least two years since the Agency selected SpaceX's rocket to carry its Artemis moon lander in 2021. With China aiming to reach the moon by decade's end, the pressure is mounting. NASA hopes to return to the moon in 2028; to do so, Starship must meet the Artemis III deadline in summer 2027.
Beyond being Musk's conduit to Mars, SpaceX's most ambitious projects depend on Starship to slash costs. SpaceX's proposed 1 million-satellite datacenter constellation Starmind, for example, is impossible without a high-capacity reusable rocket. The November 13 test should provide another data point to judge SpaceX's progress, especially given its ambitions. In a Q3 earnings call, Musk stated that SpaceX will attempt to catch both the rocket and its booster, making it the 
"first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered." During the event, Musk said the mission was "more likely than not" to succeed. Starship's history may say otherwise.

Well ahead of Black Friday, the MacBook Air is already $200 off, bringing down the price of the 13-inch model with an M5 chip, 16 GB of RAM, and 512 GB of storage to $1,099.
This is the lowest price the MacBook Air has been at since June, when Apple permanently hiked prices across its entire Mac lineup. Amazon frequently sells this MacBook Air for $1,149, but this even lower price is usually reserved for big sales events—the last being in October during Prime Day. And now it's back.
I probably don't need to expound too much on what makes the M5 MacBook Air such a fantastic, do-it-all laptop. It's extremely well-built, the performance and battery life are both top-notch, and it's still one of the thinnest laptops you can buy. There's a reason it tops my list of laptop recommendations—even after having tested dozens of new models this year.
Unlike the MacBook Neo, which makes compromises on memory and performance to achieve its low price, the MacBook Air does nearly everything right. And while a MacBook Pro may tempt you—whether the new M6 model or one of the more powerful touchscreen OLED models—most people won't actually feel the difference in performance. Unless content creation, media, or game development is a full-time gig for you, I think you'll be surprised by just how much the M5 MacBook Air can handle.
The only real question is what size is right for you. The 13-inch model plays to the strengths of the MacBook Air—offering an extremely portable laptop at a reasonable price without sacrificing performance. If you would appreciate a larger screen (and don’t plan to travel with the device as much), you might prefer the 15-inch model, which is also $200 off its retail price, currently selling for $1,299. Aside from the larger screen, the only other difference is a much more robust six-speaker audio system.
Either way, now remains a really good time to buy a MacBook Air. While prices were certainly lower in the first half of 2026, we’re still probably many months out from the inevitable M6 refresh. I don’t claim to have any insider knowledge, but based on pricing history, I can’t see these laptops coming down any lower in price over the next few months.

In November, right around Veteran's Day, posts online claimed to show former U.S. President Bill Clinton personally helping a homeless veteran outside The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in 1997.
According to the tale, Clinton offered the man, Marcus Williams, his coat, before asking him questions about his service. He then supposedly ordered a Secret Service agent to get Williams food, and personally contacted the Department of Veterans Affairs to help Williams get back on his feet.
The posts began:
"On a freezing December night in 1997, President Bill Clinton was leaving a holiday concert at the Kennedy Center when he noticed a homeless veteran sitting near the entrance. The man wore a thin jacket and was shivering in the cold. In his hands, he held a piece of cardboard with a simple message written on it: "Marine. Desert Storm. Hungry." What happened next caught the attention of people in the presidential motorcade. Clinton stopped, took off his own coat, placed it around the veteran's shoulders, and sat beside him on the icy concrete.
The veteran, 42 year old Marcus Williams, later told reporters that the President never questioned how he had ended up on the street or lectured him about his choices. Instead, Clinton asked about his military service, the battles he had experienced, and whether anyone had ever properly thanked him for what he had done. According to Secret Service agent Larry Cockell, who later wrote about the encounter, Clinton stayed with Marcus for nearly 25 minutes despite the freezing temperatures. When Marcus admitted that he had not eaten in two days, Clinton sent an agent to a nearby restaurant to get him food. He refused to leave until Marcus had finished his meal.
The posts were accompanied by images supposedly showing the two meeting as well as Williams holding a cardboard sign reading "Marine. Desert Storm. Hungry." Snopes readers contacted us to ask whether the story and images were real or fake.
We first uploaded the images into Google Lens to perform a reverse image search. Next, we used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo with phrases such as "Bill Clinton Marcus Williams Homeless Veteran" to see whether any reputable news outlets had documented the events. If the scene had occurred and the images were real, we would find evidence in newspapers and media archives like Getty Images. That was not the case. We did not locate any examples of credible outlets publishing the images, nor reporting on the alleged meeting.
We found that neither the story nor the images were real, and that they were generated using artificial intelligence tools. Therefore, we've labeled the claim false.
We uploaded the images accompanying the story into several tools that screen visual media for signs of AI: Sightengine, Hive Moderation, and Google's integrated SynthID detector. The first two found a high likelihood that the images were AI-generated, and the SynthID detector found the invisible watermark indicating Google's AI tools generated the images. We also ran the story through the AI text detection tool Pangram, which also determined that all of the text was written using a large language model such as ChatGPT.
Let us note here: These types of AI detection tools are fallible. Snopes cautions people against using them for definitive answers on media's authenticity without supporting evidence.
Detecting that the image was fake without using those tools was more difficult, given it was grayscale and grainy, but not impossible. We noticed that the writing on the cardboard sign looked too perfect, the cardboard itself looked unusually bright and the supposedly parallel sidewalk cracks didn't form straight lines or meet at a single vanishing point.
Our searches also uncovered a January article written by the fact-checking organization Lead Stories debunking the exact same story, though featuring a real archival image of Clinton instead of an AI-generated one. That fact-check also noted some factual errors in the text, most prominently that one of Clinton's Secret Service agents wrote about the encounter in a memoir. (No such memoir existed.) Because the exact claim was also previously been fact-checked almost a year ago, we concluded that users posting the claim in October and November were doing so in an attempt to make money.
The fictional story is an example of glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental." These types of low-quality posts often use standard or template language, making small tweaks in an attempt to game the social media algorithms. They rely on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories and hope to generate a profit from advertising revenue if the posts go viral.
Snopes previously explained the ongoing trend of politically motivated, AI-generated slop content similar to the claim debunked in this article.

Here is a thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama from director Nitesh Tiwari, with music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman, based on the ancient classical poem about Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. It has often been adapted for live-action and animated movies in the past, though surely not on this scale, the current three-hour blockbuster being only the first half. (There are no musical numbers though.) The idea of aristocrats submitting stoically and yet playfully to exile in the forest has something Shakespearean about it, and if you are suffering from Homer-withdrawal after Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, a story about the noble Prince Rama finally vowing to wage war on a distant city where his wife has been abducted might just fit the bill.
Ranbir Kapoor plays the mythical Rama, a noble warrior and statesman who has been brought into being in the city state of Ayodhya as a bodily representative of Vishnu, and from the first his sense of destiny is overwhelming. But what exactly is that destiny? In broad terms, his fate is to face off with Ravana (Naveen “Yash” Kumar), king of far-off Lanka, a figure whose former slave status once triggered in him such a cosmically intense prayer for justice that Lord Brahma offered him the superpower of athletic strength and indifference to pain.
In Ayodhya, Rama marries the sweetly devoted Sita (Sai Pallavi), he enjoys an intense bond of comradeship with his brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), and is the apple of his father’s eye; this is King Dasharatha (Arun Govil) who, careworn by affairs of state, is about cede the throne to Rama. But Rama’s stepmother Kaikeyi (Lara Dutta) furiously reminds Dasharatha that he promised the crown to Bharata (Adinath Kothare), the son they had together. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are banished to the forest.
Over in Lanka, a toxic stew of plotting against Ravana is being stirred by his slippery, smirking brother-in-law Vidyutjihva (played by Bollywood veteran Vivek Oberoi), whom Ravana ruthlessly slays in single combat; this man’s widow Shurpanakha (Rakul Preet Singh), who is Ravana’s sister, is banished to the same forest where Rama is humbly eking out his civilian existence. She falls in love with Rama, using her witchy wiles to trick and bamboozle the happily married man, and this is to lead to a cataclysmic confrontation between Rama and Ravana.
With its giant canvas and some truly beautiful sunset skyscapes, this very enjoyable film has a little of Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings and even Disney’s The Lion King (the latter surely influenced the animal-kingdom tableaux). The bizarre flying machine piloted by Ravana (who does not have the ability to fly as such) has something engagingly Gilliamesque about it. As so often with Indian cinema, this movie reminds you of the forthright, unselfconscious storytelling energy that popular Hollywood films had in the 1950s and 60s, the era of sword-and-sandal. It’s a rather amazing adventure.

FSN E-Commerce Ventures, the parent of online beauty retailer Nykaa, reported a 207% jump in consolidated net profit to Rs 101.2 crore for the second quarter ended September 2026 (Q2 FY27), compared with Rs 33 crore in the year-ago quarter. The growth was driven by higher sales across beauty and fashion businesses and better EBITDA margins.
Its operating revenue increased 28% to Rs 3,006 crore in Q2 FY27 from Rs 2,346 crore in the same quarter last year on the back of double-digit growth in both beauty and fashion segments.
On a quarter-on-quarter basis, profit surged 27% from Rs 79.8 crore, while operating revenue was up 8% from Rs 2,782 crore.
EBITDA came in at Rs 263 crore, up 65% year-on-year, while EBITDA margin expanded to 8.7% from 6.8% in Q2 FY26.
Nykaa’s gross merchandise value (GMV) grew 30% to Rs 6,151 crore during the quarter under review from Rs 4,744 crore in Q2 FY26.
Alongside the earnings announcement, the company’s board approved the acquisition of an 82% stake in Simply Nam, paving the way for Nykaa to enter the premium professional makeup segment.
Founded by celebrity makeup artist Namrata Soni and venture studio Bozzil Group, Simply Nam sells “100% vegan” premium beauty products. The company reported a turnover of Rs 17 crore in FY26, marking a 77% increase from Rs 9.6 crore in FY25.
Beauty remains the profitability anchor
Nykaa’s beauty segment generated Rs 2,699.7 crore in revenue in July-September 2026, up 27% from Rs 2,131.9 crore in the year-ago period. Profit before exceptional items from this segment skyrocketed 71% to Rs 180.2 crore during the quarter, compared with Rs 105.4 crore a year earlier.
Beauty GMV rose 25% YoY to Rs 4,454 crore in the September quarter of FY27, while net sales value (NSV) increased 28% YoY to Rs 2,536 crore. EBITDA jumped 51% to Rs 267 crore.
Nykaa attributed the growth to new customer acquisition, repeat customer engagement, and its expanding retail presence. Monthly average unique visitors (MAUV) rose 30% YoY to 54.1 million in Q2 FY27, while average order value (AOV) increased 5% to Rs 2,149. The company opened 14 new physical stores during the quarter, expanding its network base to 338 stores across 111 cities.
Over the past 12 months, the company has also added over 330 beauty brands to its portfolio, including French beauty brand Yves Rocher, luxury haircare brand Oribe and Korean skincare brand Mamonde.
Its quick commerce arm, Nykaa Now, expanded to 15 cities in Q2 FY27 from just three cities in Q1 FY26. The company is targeting more than 25 cities by the end of the ongoing fiscal year. Nykaa Now delivers an assortment of beauty, personal care and wellness products within 30–60 minutes.
Fashion vertical’s losses narrow in Q2
Nykaa’s fashion vertical contributed Rs 287.2 crore, or 9.5% of overall operating revenue, up 43% from Rs 201 crore in Q2 FY26. While the fashion business remained loss-making, losses before exceptional items narrowed 64% to Rs 7.7 crore during the quarter, compared with Rs 21.4 crore a year earlier.
The fashion business’s GMV soared 42% YoY to Rs 1,674 crore in Q2 FY27, while NSV surged 47% to Rs 509 crore. EBITDA came in at Rs 1 crore versus a negative EBITDA of Rs 12 crore in Q2 FY26.
The company attributed the growth to the continued addition of brands across categories and stronger customer acquisition.
In the fashion segment, Nykaa launched more than 250 new brands across categories in Q2, including UK-based streetwear brand Superdry, Swedish fashion house Totome, Indian home-comfort brand Sleepwell, and Chinese sportswear brand Anta, among others.
Visits to Nykaa’s fashion platform increased 25% YoY to 239 million, while annual unique transacting users rose 37% to 5.1 million. The platform also recorded 3.3 million orders during the quarter, up 38% YoY, with an AOV of Rs 4,378 crore.
Where did Nykaa spend?
In line with revenue, total expenses climbed 25% to Rs 2,867 crore in the July-September quarter of FY27, compared with Rs 2,297.6 crore in the corresponding quarter of the previous fiscal year. Sequentially, total expenses rose nearly 8% from Rs 2,662.2 crore.
- Procurement cost: This remained Nykaa’s largest cost center, rising 26% to Rs 1,624.3 crore in Q2 FY27 from Rs 1,292.4 crore in the year-ago quarter.
- Fulfilment expense: Surged 34% to Rs 304 crore from Rs 227 crore in Q2 FY26.
- Marketing and S&D cost: Increased 24% to Rs 457 crore in the September quarter of FY27 from Rs 368 crore a year earlier.
- Employee benefits expense: Stood at Rs 220 crore, up 20% from Rs 182.8 crore in Q2 FY26.
In June this year, Nykaa struck a multi-year deal with OpenAI to list its beauty and fashion storefronts as connected apps in ChatGPT, giving users product recommendations directly within the chat before being directed to Nykaa’s app or website to complete a purchase.

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

Online pharmacy startup PlatinumRx is in talks to raise around $32 Mn (over ₹300 Cr) in a funding round led by Belgium-based investment giant Sofina Ventures, as per sources familiar with the discussion. The proposed transaction is expected to value the Bengaluru-based startup somewhere in the range of $150-200 Mn (₹1,400-1,878 Cr). The proposed investment comes around a year after the startup raised $6 Mn in its Series A round. Stellaris Venture Partners and India Quotient backed the startup in its Series A round. The startup had previously raised around $800K in a seed round in April 2024, also led by India Quotient. Inc42 has reached out to the aforementioned investors to understand whether they will participate in the round. The September 2025 round had helped the startup strengthen its supply chain, expand fulfilment capabilities and build its product and technology teams. It had also outlined plans to add five fulfilment centres and improve sourcing efficiencies to make affordable substitute medicines more accessible. The discussions are understood to be ongoing, and the final terms of the transaction, including the valuation and investor participation, could change. Questions sent to PlatinumRx and Sofina Ventures didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story. If concluded, the funding round would mark a significant jump in PlatinumRx's valuation and provide it with the fresh capital required to strengthen its presence in India's online pharmacy market. Founded in 2023 by Ashutosh Pandey and Piyush Kumar, PlatinumRx operates an online pharmacy platform focused on helping consumers find affordable alternatives to prescribed medicines. The platform recommends substitute medicines with the same composition, allowing customers to access lower-cost options, particularly for recurring and chronic medication requirements. These medicines are sourced directly from pharmaceutical companies and offer alternatives with the same composition, addressing the price difference between branded medicines and their substitutes. It claims to have served over 10 Lakh customers till date. The proposed funding comes amid continued investor interest in specialised healthcare and pharmacy platforms. While quick commerce platforms are expanding into medicine delivery, online pharmacy startups are also attempting to build differentiated models around affordability, assortment and access. Broadly, the online pharmacy segment has continued to attract sizable investments. Quick medicine delivery startup Plazza raised $15 Mn in a Series A funding round in July 2026, co-led by Accel, Elevation Capital and Nexus Venture Partners, with participation from existing investors All In Capital and Better Capital. The Bengaluru-based startup operates a pharmacy-first quick commerce model focused on 15-30 minute medicine deliveries. On the other hand, last year, Truemeds had raised $85 Mn in funding to scale generic medicine delivery.

The British comedian Russell Brand is a major figure in health secretary Robert F. Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement. He regularly joined conference calls organized by the super PAC MAHA Action, on one occasion dialing in naked from a bath tub. He was a keynote speaker alongside Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz at the September 2026 MAHA Summit. He is also a convicted rapist who was just sentenced to 10 and a half years in jail.
During Brand’s trial, Tony Lyons, MAHA Action’s founder, was at the courthouse to support him. Lyons had argued that Brand was falsely accused, saying “he’s been vilified, persecuted, deplatformed, demonetized, censored, prosecuted.” On Tuesday, after the conviction came down, MAHA Action Inc.’s newsletter published a 3,700-word defense of Brand.
I’ve followed MAHA closely and I’m not at all surprised that the movement’s leadership is standing by Brand. There is a rot of toxic masculinity and violence at MAHA’s core.
Even before the prison sentence, MAHA happily palled around with Brand, despite the British police charging him in April 2025 and again in December 2025 with multiple counts of rape and sexual assault. The charges did not come out of nowhere: In 2023, three British outlets jointly published a special investigation into allegations against Brand.
National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya, who has said he wants the NIH to become “the research arm of MAHA,” shared billing with Brand at a November 2025 MAHA Summit. Earlier that year, Kennedy posted a photo of himself clutching a lizard, as Brand and a shirtless Oz put their arms around him, all smiles.
Perhaps most shocking of all, Oz chuckled at a joke about sexual consent that Brand made at the October 2026 MAHA Summit.
Oz told the audience that Brand was almost late because he was backstage “hugging the Secretary of Agriculture,” Brooke Rollins, to which Brand replied, “She initiated that contact, I should make clear, doctor!” I agree with Holly Baxter, senior reporter at The Independent, who said that of course the jocular exchange between Brand and Oz looks bad now, “but it should’ve looked bad then, when the court case was on the horizon, so let’s not expect much hand-wringing from Oz, MAHA-maven RFK Jr., and the other Trump health officials who embraced Brand over the past two years.”
The alliance between MAHA and Brand is not an aberration, it’s a pattern of befriending violent misogynists. MAHA made Mike Tyson, another convicted rapist who said in 1989 that he enjoyed hurting women, the face of its healthy eating campaign. Bhattacharya even posted a picture of himself with a Tyson face tattoo and the message “Be like Mike Tyson.” The New York Times reported that Donald Trump Jr., who championed the MAHA movement at Turning Point USA’s 2025 annual conference, “once called Andrew Tate a friend and publicly defended him against previous criminal allegations.” Tate is a leader of the manosphere who faces extradition to Britain on multiple charges including rape and sex trafficking.
You might think the shellacking that MAHA-allied candidates suffered in the midterm elections, despite major financial support from MAHA Action, would have led the MAHA bosses to rethink their allegiances. You’d be wrong.
On Nov. 6, for example, Kennedy celebrated Stephen Miller’s appointment as President Trump’s chief of staff, saying, “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken.” Miller is the man behind the inhumane family separation policy in Trump’s first term. He is also the architect of ICE’s brutal tactics during Trump 2.0. Kennedy has defended ICE tactics on Joe Rogan’s show and provided support for the horrific treatment of undocumented immigrants. Across the country, unaccompanied immigrant children as young as 3, who came to the U.S. to be reunited with their families, have faced sometimes tough interrogation by judges, nearly always having to represent themselves in court without a lawyer. Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services is legally required to care for them through its Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), and federal law requires these children be provided with legal counsel, fair hearings, and accommodation appropriate to a child’s age. But Kennedy, who has adopted harsh anti-immigrant rhetoric and who falsely argues that immigrants are disease vectors, refused to renew the contract to provide legal services for these children. And almost 90% of undocumented children are now being held in unlicensed ORR shelters in Texas, exempt from oversight and inspections.
Since the MAHA wipe-out in the midterms, there have been an endless slew of articles pondering how MAHA will change course. But MAHA’s rotten core of violence, including its love for Brand (who Lyons called “an incredible human being”), is one big reason why I’m deeply skeptical that “MAHA 2.0” will be any different. Beth Mole, senior health reporter at Ars Technica, notes that leaders of the grassroots wing of the MAHA movement remain “doggedly loyal” to Kennedy. They’re loyal to a man who has worked with Trump to roll out policies that I believe are inherently violent, who has espoused eugenicist views, and who shows zero signs of remorse.
There was violence in the MAGA/MAHA administration enacting policies that will throw 15 million people off health insurance, that cut off an estimated 2 million kids from food assistance, and that killed federal health research that could have improved the health of minoritized Americans. There is eugenics in the way that Kennedy blames the weak for their sickness, believes only “sick kids should die of measles,” and once said he wants to remove Black kids from their families and “reparent” them on government-run farms.
So when I think of MAHA’s future, there’s an old proverb that comes to mind: “The fish rots from the head down.” The head is, of course, Kennedy, MAHA’s supreme leader. Unless he radically changes his views and policy directions — which seems extremely unlikely — MAHA is destined to be that rotting fish in perpetuity.
Gavin Yamey is a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in Durham.

Haryana on Tuesday changed the leadership of two key civic bodies in Gurugram, transferring the chief executive officer of the Gurugram Metropolitan Development Authority (GMDA) and the Municipal Corporation of Gurugram (MCG) commissioner in a wider administrative reshuffle involving 14 IAS and HCS officers. The changes come months after severe monsoon waterlogging brought Gurugram to a standstill, leaving school buses carrying children stranded on flooded roads, and amid deteriorating air quality across Delhi-NCR. The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) has also invoked Stage III of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) across the region. According to a Haryana government order dated November 10, Phool Chand Meena, a 2004-batch IAS officer who was heading the GMDA and Faridabad Metropolitan Development Authority (FMDA), has been moved to the posts of Commissioner and Secretary in the state's Human Resources and General Administration departments. On August 24, intense showers inundated several arterial roads, underpasses and residential areas, disrupting traffic and leaving children travelling home from school stuck in buses for hours. Gurugram recorded around 75 mm of rainfall between 8 am and 5 pm that day, according to district administration data. The district administration subsequently invoked the Disaster Management Act and issued a standard operating procedure (SOP) to regulate school transport during heavy rainfall. 14 school buses had remained stranded for up to six hours during the August waterlogging.
