In a fresh legal challenge ahead of Cult.fit's proposed public listing, the Madras High Court (HC) has issued a notice on a petition seeking cancellation of the CULT trademark registration held by one of the company's subsidiaries. The rectification petition was filed by Deepak Poduval, who cofounded the CULT fitness business in Bengaluru in 2015. He has approached the court seeking cancellation of the trademark registration held by Cultfit Healthcare Pvt Ltd, a subsidiary of Cult.fit, alleging that the documents used to establish ownership of the brand were forged. The court issued notice in the matter (OP(TM) No. 51 of 2026) on October 12, 2026. During a hearing on November 5, it adjourned the proceedings to December 2, allowing Cultfit Healthcare to file its response. Separately, Poduval has approached the Commercial Court in Bengaluru, seeking to have the 2017 deeds that purportedly transferred the CULT brand declared void. He has alleged that the signatures on these documents were forged. The matter is scheduled for its next hearing on November 16. How The CULT Trademark Dispute Began The dispute over the CULT trademark dates back to 2015, when Poduval first applied for the 'CULT – The Workout Station' trademark in August that year. Cultfit Healthcare filed a separate trademark application in November 2016, claiming usage of the brand from May 1, 2015 — the same first-use date mentioned in Poduval's application. When the Trademark Registry raised objections citing Poduval's earlier application, Cultfit Healthcare did not produce the alleged assignment deeds. Instead, it claimed to be the prior user and owner of the trademark in its own right. Poduval has since challenged the validity of the 2017 assignment deeds that purportedly transferred the brand to Cultfit Healthcare. He alleges that his signatures on the documents were forged and has cited a privately commissioned forensic examination that, according to him, supports his allegations. Cult.fit, however, has denied the allegations, maintaining that Poduval signed the assignment deeds. In a statement, Poduval said the dispute concerns the ownership of a brand that has become central to a company preparing to go public. He added that investors deserve transparency about how Cult.fit acquired the trademark. Trademark Dispute Part Of Larger Cofounder Row The trademark challenge is part of a broader legal battle between CULT's cofounders, Deepak Poduval and Rishabh Telang, over the transfer of the fitness business's assets and intellectual property to the Mukesh Bansal-led startup. In August 2026, Poduval filed an FIR against Telang at Bengaluru's Bellandur Police Station, alleging forgery, cheating and criminal conspiracy in connection with the 2016 transfer of certain assets and intellectual property from Cult Fitness Pvt Ltd to Cultfit Healthcare Pvt Ltd. Poduval alleged that Telang forged his signatures on multiple documents used to wind up Cult Fitness, including board resolutions, shareholder consent documents and statutory filings. He also claimed that 50% of his shareholding in the company was extinguished without any consideration. Telang denied the allegations, maintaining that Poduval was involved in the transactions and the subsequent winding up of Cult Fitness. He further claimed that Poduval had received consideration for the transfer. Cult.fit also maintained that the transaction was carried out under appropriate contractual arrangements and that the consideration was duly paid and acknowledged by Poduval. The company added that neither it nor its subsidiary was an accused in the FIR. Following the FIR, Telang moved the Karnataka High Court seeking to quash the case. The court sought responses from Poduval and the state but did not stay the investigation. The latest petition before the Madras HC takes the dispute beyond the alleged transfer of assets, directly challenging the legal ownership of the CULT trademark held by Cultfit Healthcare. What The Dispute Means For Cult.fit's IPO The trademark challenge also raises questions about how Cult.fit has disclosed the ownership of the CULT brand in its draft IPO prospectus. In a written response dated October 14 to a complaint filed by Poduval with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), Cult.fit acknowledged that its draft prospectus did not correctly describe the ownership of the CULT trademarks. The company clarified that the trademarks are registered in the name of Cultfit Healthcare Pvt Ltd and not Cult.fit Ltd. It also undertook to correct the disclosure in its final prospectus. With the subsidiary's trademark registration now under challenge before the Madras HC, the dispute could become a point of scrutiny for prospective investors. Poduval has also questioned the company's treatment of the CULT acquisition in its IPO disclosures. According to his complaint, Cult.fit has described the acquisition as 'not material'. While the draft prospectus does not name the acquisition, the company has made the deeds relating to Fitness First, another brand acquired by the group, available for investor inspection. However, the corresponding deeds for CULT have not been made available, Poduval alleged. The challenge is significant given the extent to which Cult.fit uses the CULT brand across its operations. According to its draft IPO prospectus, hundreds of fitness centres operate under the brand. It also extends to Cult Neo gyms and the company's Cultgear products business. If the trademark challenge succeeds, it could potentially affect the group's rights to use, license or transfer the brand, raising questions about the implications for its operations and brand ownership. Cult.fit has filed its draft IPO papers for a proposed public issue. The company plans to raise up to ₹950 Cr through a fresh issue of shares, while existing investors are looking to offload up to 17.86 Cr shares through an offer for sale (OFS). The total IPO size is expected to be around ₹4,000 Cr.

New Zealand pacer Brett Randell earned his maiden international call up as he was included in the squad for the fourth and fifth ODIs against India to be played at the Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui.
The 31-year-old has 145 professional appearances, including five for the New Zealand A. He recently returned from a County Championship stint with Derbyshire.
Randell is also likely to make his debut in one of the remaining games.
All-rounder Josh Clarkson was also included in the squad.
“There’s been a few movements throughout the series so we’re fortunate to be able to bring in Brett and Josh,” New Zealand head coach Rob Walter said.
There’s also shuffling of the coaching staff with Northern Districts pathway coach Mitch Renwick and S&C coach Corey Mileys joined Walter and Martill Guptill for the ODIs.
Bowling coach Jacob Oram, batting coach Luke Ronchi, and S&C coach Chris Donaldson have left for Wellington for Test preparations.
India currently leads the five-match series 2-0 after no result was possible due to rain in the third ODI. The two-match Test series will start on November 19.

Game 4: Mitchell Santner (C), Finn Allen, Michael Bracewell, Kristian Clarke, Jacob Duffy, Matt Fisher, Dean Foxcroft, Mitch Hay (WK), Matt Henry, Kyle Jamieson, Nick Kelly, Brett Randell, Tim Seifert (WK), Will Young.

Pre-orders for some Apple Home Collection devices will open November 13
You can lock in orders for two LG cameras and a video doorbell.
On the same day that the Apple HomeView smart display and refreshed Apple TV 4K hit stores, pre-orders will open for some accessories in the Apple Home Collection. Apple confirmed to Engadget that you'll be able to pre-order the LG indoor camera, outdoor camera and video doorbell on November 13.
Those three devices, which Apple and LG collaborated on, will be the first Apple Home Collection accessories to ship. They're slated to arrive in December. Apple hasn't revealed exactly when other products in the lineup — including thermostats and door locks — will be available, but the company has said some will be available next month with the rest debuting in early 2027.
The indoor camera can capture 2.5K footage of what's going on in your home while you're away, giving you a way to keep an eye on your pets, for instance. It has low-light color night vision and infrared (IR) night vision support. The camera, which costs $200 and can detect people and pets, can tilt up when you're out and down when you're home — this can be managed automatically through the Home app or manually by pressing a button.
The outdoor camera can recognize faces, pets and deliveries. It too supports low-light color night vision, IR night vision and 2.5K video capture. The camera has IP65-rated protection from rain and dust and a two‑way talk function. As with the indoor camera, you'll get 10 days' worth of event video history via iCloud+. There's built-in storage too. The standard outdoor camera costs $300 and a version with a floodlight will run you $400.
As for the $250 video doorbell, that has a dual-camera design that can pick up (for instance) visitors and packages simultaneously — a 2.5K camera faces forward and a Full HD one points downward. You'll be able to view either feed separately in the Home app and chat to whoever's at your door using the two-way talk function. When someone rings the doorbell, HomeView and HomePod devices will sound a chime. You'll get notifications on other Apple devices too.
Again, there's low-light color night vision and IR night vision support, along with event video history in iCloud+ and built-in storage. The camera can detect people, pets, vehicles and packages and it has a dimmable spotlight.
Apple is making privacy a big selling point for these products, which offer end-to-end encryption (neither Apple nor LG will be able to access the data). Naturally, you can control them using your other Apple devices, such as your iPhone or HomeView, and view live video feeds.

The Trump administration’s fight to stop suspected leaks of top-secret military information on LinkedIn can’t sweep in “a vast number of confidential sources” of random journalists “who have no conceivable relationship” to the Department of Justice’s investigation, an appeals court ruled Tuesday.
The order came after the DOJ asked LinkedIn to turn over 18 months of communications from targeted journalists who collectively published more than 1,000 articles on many different topics over that time period. The request was not limited to journalists involved in a controversial report from a news outlet that Trump said exposed confidential military information in a foreign country. (The outlet is not being named to protect national security secrets.) Instead, the DOJ cast a wide net, requesting extensive LinkedIn data on journalists who had any possible link to the journalists around the time the report was drafted.
The majority of journalists have LinkedIn accounts and publish their contact information to encourage sources to connect on the platform, LinkedIn argued. So allowing that government overreach went beyond harming targeted journalists and threatened to undermine a critical platform where journalists frequently connect with confidential sources, judges ruled. Even more concerning, the Trump administration secured a secrecy order barring LinkedIn from telling anyone about the sweeping request for a year. That left journalists unaware for far too long that their First Amendment rights had been compromised, judges ruled.
Judge: Security and free speech can coexist
Penning the unanimous opinion from a three-judge panel, Ronald Reagan-nominated judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III rejected LinkedIn’s request to quash the order entirely and ordered the US district court to substantially narrow the order to avoid posing a grave threat to press freedoms.

Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says
- Published
Six people have been killed and about 30 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.
The hospital's director said two missiles hit a building containing surgical wards and intensive care units overnight, but that one of the missiles did not explode.
The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".
The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.
Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".
Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.
Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.
Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.
The Nasser Medical Complex is located in the city of Khan Younis and is the largest hospital in southern Gaza, serving almost one million people.
In a video posted on social media, a paramedic from the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency who arrived at the building after the strike early on Thursday said a missile penetrated the five-storey structure and hit a room in the surgical department.
Other footage shared by activists showed thick smoke inside the building and extensive destruction on the second floor, where medical equipment and beds had been scattered by an explosion.
The hospital's director, Dr Ahmed al-Fara, later told a news conference that Israeli forces had fired two missiles at the al-Yasin surgery building but that only one exploded.
"What's happened in Nasser Medical Complex is targeting the health sector mainly. We are talking about doctors, we are talking about civilians, we are talking about patients," he said.
"Also, there is... huge damage [to] the infrastructure inside the hospital."
Footage filmed by a freelance journalist working for the BBC showed extensive damage to an operating theatre, wards and a sleeping area for medics, as well as hallways and lifts.
News agencies also published photos that appeared to show an unexploded missile.
Dr Mohammed Qdeih, a general surgery specialist who was wounded in the head, said he and other medical staff had just finished work around 00:30 and had been preparing to go to sleep when there was an explosion.
"My whole body was trapped under the rubble. For a moment, I felt as if I was about to lose consciousness, or that I was about to die," he told the BBC.
"I started struggling to free myself and started calling out, 'Guys! Guys!' I began crawling, trying to pull my leg out from beneath the rubble. I managed to pull myself free. It was dark, there were no lights, nothing at all."
He said he had been lying in a bed near Dr Rizq Abu Shaira, who was killed. Another colleague suffered a broken leg.
"Dr Rizq was the kindest person in this department. He was very kind and always willing to help... And of course, he was a surgeon, one of the best among us."
He added: "Patients were killed as well. There were patients in the rooms next to us who were killed. A patient comes to the hospital seeking treatment and leaves carried on people's shoulders. I do not know what kind of humanity this is."
The Israeli military said in a statement that its "precise strike" had targeted the commander of Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade, who it named as Mohammed Abu Ismail, alongside other fighters who were "hiding inside" Nasser hospital.
"The terrorists were struck in order to remove the threat they posed after turning the Nasser hospital compound into a headquarters and operating from there to advance dozens of terrorist plots against our forces and restore the brigade's force," it alleged.
The military added that it had issued advance warnings before the strike and released an audio recording of what it said was one given to a senior Gaza health official. But Fara insisted the hospital had received no warning of an attack.
A Hamas statement rejected the Israeli military's accusations, calling them "a blatant attempt to justify a documented crime targeting a civilian medical facility whose function and purpose are well known".
"The nature of the targeted site and the casualties inflicted on patients, doctors and medical staff expose the falsity and weakness of this narrative," it said.
However, local activists circulated claims overnight that the strike may have targeted a senior Hamas security figure who was hiding inside the building.
Fara said this was the seventh time that Nasser hospital had been struck during the war. In August 2025, a double Israeli strike killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and health workers.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said it had documented a total of 1,056 attacks on healthcare in Gaza over the past three years, resulting in 1,010 deaths.
"Gaza's health facilities are lifelines for its people. They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked," warned Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the UN agency's director general.
Later on Thursday, at least four more Palestinians were reportedly killed in separate incidents in northern and central Gaza.
Medics said three were killed in Israeli air strikes in Gaza City, Jabalia and Deir al-Balah, while the fourth was killed by Israeli gunfire in Bureij refugee camp.
The Israeli military said it struck a "terrorist" in Deir al-Balah and another in Gaza City.
Israeli strikes on Gaza take place almost daily despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas in October last year.
More than 1,620 people have been killed in Gaza since then, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.
The humanitarian situation in Gaza also remains dire and has recently deteriorated further as a result of heavy rains last weekend that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

- The claim that Christians and MAGA supporters are planning to protest the 2026 midterm election results at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 3, 2027, is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from an event poster that advertises a "Peaceful protest & Christian unity against the rigged midterms" at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 3, 2027. The event's organizer is Jake Lang, a Jan. 6 Capitol rioter who spent four years in prison before being pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump.
- At the time of this writing, it is unclear whether Lang had permission to hold the protest at the Capitol and who would attend. Though the event poster includes Christian imagery and references, it is unclear whether the event has any connection to Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement. It is also unclear whether the event has the potential to devolve into a "sequel" to the Jan. 6 Capitol attacks, as some social media users and Snopes readers speculated.
- As was the case with the 2020 election, there is no evidence that widespread election fraud affected — or "rigged" — the results of the 2026 midterms.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have contacted the Capitol Police, which issues permits for protests at the U.S. Capitol, and Lang for more information about the protest and await replies to our queries.
In November, a claim (archived) circulated online that Christians and MAGA supporters were planning to protest the 2026 midterm election results at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 3, 2027.
One X user who posted about the alleged protest included what appeared to be a flyer for the event, titled, "The Million Crusader Cross March."
According to that flyer, the event described itself as "Peaceful protest & Christian unity against the rigged midterms" and encouraged attendees to "Bring your cross."
Posts about the alleged protest also circulated on Facebook and Instagram (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim. One reader asked whether the flyer showed that "there is another Insurrection planned at the Capitol on January 3rd 2027."
While the event flyer featured in the X post above did appear to advertise a real protest (archived) organized by Jake Lang, a Jan. 6 Capitol rioter who spent four years in prison before being pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump, it was unclear exactly who would attend or whether it had the potential to devolve into a "sequel" to the Jan. 6 Capitol attacks, as some social media users and Snopes readers speculated.
The event's connection to Christianity was clear from its use of Crusader and cross imagery and references in the event poster but it was unclear whether there was any connection to Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement. CNN reported in February 2021 that Lang did not vote in the 2020 election despite protesting to overturn the results months later. At the time of this writing, one of the listed speakers said on X (archived) that he would not be speaking at the event.
A Facebook page for the event that listed Lang as an organizer showed fewer than 200 attendees at the time of this writing.
We contacted the Capitol Police, which issues permits to protests held at the U.S. Capitol, to ask if Lang had applied for and received such a permit, and, if so, how many people he had estimated would attend. We asked Lang the same questions. We await replies to our queries.
In the meantime, because we could not confirm the size of the event, its likelihood of taking place or its exact connection to the MAGA movement, we leave this claim unrated.
It is important to note that, as was the case with the 2020 election, there was no evidence that widespread election fraud had affected — or "rigged" — the results of the 2026 midterms.
In a Nov. 10 article, the technology magazine WIRED investigated the possibility that activists on the far right would seek to lure disappointed Republican voters to embrace their groups and ideologies.
WIRED suggested Lang's protest was part of this movement, describing him as a "far-right activist."
Lang organized other protests across the U.S. with crusader imagery before the midterms.
For example, he hosted an anti-Muslim "Christian Crusade" in Dearborn, Michigan, on Aug. 18, in which Michigan Public reported protesters "gripped rifles, chanted 'U.S.A.' and argued with many local residents." Michigan Public reported that the Dearborn Police Department made 22 arrests in connection with the protest.
Lang also organized a protest in Bridgeview, Illinois, in October. The area is also known as "Little Palestine" because of its large Arab American population. NBC Chicago reported that Lang led a protest at the Palestine Fest event on Oct. 4 where protesters "wore military-style gear and held up anti-Palestinian messages."
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Lang crashed a Seattle cat convention to condemn furries.

Stephen Curry will miss at least two weeks for the Golden State Warriors because of a torn oblique muscle, an injury that comes with the NBA’s all-time 3-point leader on pace for one of the best seasons of his 18-year career.
The Warriors announced on Thursday that the 38-year-old Curry would be reevaluated in two weeks for the abdominal tear. An MRI exam revealed the injury, and it is something that can take longer to heal. Coach Steve Kerr called the concern level “high.”
Curry left early in Golden State’s loss against Houston Rockets on Wednesday night that ended an eight-game winning streak. He was in obvious discomfort, grabbing at his right side above the hip.

The two-week timetable means Curry will miss at least six games, starting with a matchup at San Antonio on Friday.

The Warriors are off to an 8-4 start but are 1-2 in games where Curry either doesn’t play or has to leave early because of injury.

Over the last hour or so, reports have come in from around the world that people can’t access their Outlook email, either through the web or apps. Microsoft has acknowledged the issue from its Microsoft 365 Status account, saying that “We’ve determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.”
Microsoft Outlook is down
Microsoft 365 issues are cutting people off from their email right now.
There were also some reports of problems with Teams, but most of the people reporting issues say Teams is still working now.
Now Microsoft says:
We’ve completed redistributing connection traffic across our worldwide infrastructure, and we’re moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure to further reduce load. We’re also restarting affected servers to return them to service. In parallel, we’re investigating whether the elevated traffic reflects a genuine increase in requests or a shift in how traffic is being routed across our infrastructure.
but it’s unclear how long it will take before access is restored, or if that will fix all of the issues people are seeing. On DownDetector, reports of issues with Outlook started to spike just before 1PM ET, and they have not completely gone away yet. It’s also probably not the best sign that we’re struggling to consistently load Microsoft’s own status pages to check on progress. If there are any more details, we will update this article.

Cardiologists have called for a review of a recent order issued by the Director General of Health Services (DGHS), strictly prohibiting the sterilisation and re-use of single-use devices and disposable surgical items used in critical specialties like cardiology and cardiothoracic and vascular surgery, citing issues of patient safety
At the annual conference of the Cardiological Society of India (CSI), Kerala chapter, here on Sunday, the CSI Kerala Chapter president Asokan P.K. said the association would seek a review of the order by DGHS as the exorbitant cost of medical devices and accessories would make crucial procedures such as angioplasty unaffordable and inaccessible to many.
Prathap Kumar N., organising chairman of the conference, said the rising cost of complex angioplasty, particularly procedures requiring multiple specialised devices, had become a major concern. Reimbursement package rates under government-funded health insurance schemes were often inadequate to cover the actual cost of advanced cardiac interventions.
With an increasing proportion of the population requiring advanced cardiac interventions, making complex procedures affordable to ordinary patients was a major challenge. Permitting the regulated re-use of select interventional devices, wherever scientifically proven safe, could help reduce treatment costs and extend the benefits of modern cardiac care to a wider section of the population, Dr. Prathap Kumar pointed out
He said cardiologists had sought a review to determine whether selected catheters, guidewires and other equipment could be safely re-processed under scientifically validated protocols and re-used for patients.
“Patient safety must remain paramount. Any proposal for re-use must be supported by scientific evidence, validated sterilisation, functional testing and strict regulatory oversight,” Dr. Prathap Kumar said.
He called for wider consultation among medical specialists, infection-control experts and regulatory authorities to develop an evidence-based policy regarding the sterilisation and re-use of medical devices, balancing affordability with patient safety.
The order by the DGHS said the practice of re-using single-use devices and disposable surgical items was a serious concern from the perspective of patient safety, infection prevention and control, regulatory compliance and healthcare expenditure. It said such re-use may also expose patients to significant risks, including cross-infection, device malfunction, loss of performance and other procedure-related complications
However, it is a fact that sterilisation and re-use of medical devices, ensuring the integrity of the devices and patient safety, is a common practice in both private and public sector hospitals across the country.
The Cardiological Society of India had in 2017 brought out a consensus document, “Guidance on reuse of cardio-vascular catheters and devices in India”, which clearly endorsed re-use, but set out certain requirements which had to be met for re-use to be safe and effective.
The devices, which can be reused, should be clearly defined, a meticulous process for disinfection and sterilisation followed and its functionality ascertained before use. Also, “an appropriate consent should be obtained where necessary” and the cost saving entailed should be directly passed on to the patient, the document said.
The CSI(K) conference also featured discussions on the evolving roles of drug-coated balloons and drug-eluting stents in coronary angioplasty, leadless pacemakers, laser-assisted coronary interventions, invasive coronary function testing, newer cholesterol-lowering therapies, complex valve procedures and advances in heart failure management.

Revised Maximum Retail Prices (MRPs) of 1,364 anti-cancer formulations have come into effect from Monday (November 9, 2026), a move projected to save consumers an estimated ₹3,540.38 crore annually, according to an official release.
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), functioning under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, capped trade margins on the MRP of 137 anti-cancer drugs based on recommendations submitted on October 17, 2026, by an Expert Committee constituted by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), Ministry of Health & Family Welfare.
Also read | Cancer care: Long battle for affordable treatment
According to the Ministry, 85 pharmaceutical companies have reported revised MRPs for 1,364 anti-cancer formulations across 121 drugs as of November 8, 2026.
Price reductions of over 50% have been reported for 679 brands, with the highest price cut recorded at 96.45%, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers: Department of Pharmaceuticals said in the release.
The Ministry stated that no chemist or hospital pharmacy is permitted to charge more than the revised MRP.
Consumers can verify medicine rates via the revised MRP printed on packs, the 'Pharma Sahi Daam' mobile application, or the official NPPA website (nppa.gov.in), it said.
Consumers can lodge complaints against instances of overcharging or other pricing-related issues through the Pharma Jan Samadhan portal or contact the NPPA helpline at 1800-111-255, the release added.

Lupus patients struggling with the debilitating disease are lining up to try experimental CAR-T therapies even after the recent deaths of four patients in clinical trials for a variety of autoimmune diseases, according to doctors who treat the life-threatening condition.
The trials remain halted and full details of the deaths — three linked to Novartis and one to Bristol Myers Squibb — have not been released.
Still, patients are willing to take the risk, compelled by accounts of people with advanced disease who were able to stop all medications and reclaim normal lives.
“I have patients that are literally waiting to get in,” said Dr. Anca Askanase, chief of rheumatology at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York, who has enrolled patients in the Bristol Myers CAR-T trials.
Systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE, the most common and severe form of lupus, causes agonising joint pain and raises the risk of stroke, heart attack and kidney disease. Current treatments, which range from steroids to immunosuppressants and targeted biologics, often fail to control the disease. Some 10% to 15% of people with lupus die prematurely.
Brittan Kopittke, 27, who works for the University of North Carolina helping to counsel patients considering CAR-T, was diagnosed with lupus at age 22. SLE, which affects about 300,000 people in the US, typically develops between the ages of 15 and 44.
What began as a rash on her chest rapidly progressed to crippling joint pain, mouth sores and crushing fatigue. Steroids to reduce inflammation and the antimalarial drug hydroxychloroquine to tamp down antibodies attacking her healthy cells and tissues failed.
“My mouth sores were rampant. I was struggling to eat. I was struggling to drink. I was just very, very miserable,” she said.
Despite trying a cocktail of medicines, her disease advanced, attacking her kidneys, heart and lungs.
“I had reached the end of the line with treatments,” she said.
In June 2024, Kopittke went to UNC-Chapel Hill for a trial testing CAR-T, a personalised immunotherapy successfully used to treat blood cancers. It involves removing blood cells called T cells, genetically reengineering them to attack rogue immune cells, and reinfusing them with the aim of growing new, healthy immune cells.
Kopittke developed two dangerous reactions: cytokine release syndrome, which causes systemic inflammation, and a life-threatening, high-grade neurological complication called ICANS that left her unresponsive for three days.
Now, some two years into remission, Kopittke said she does not “sugarcoat” the risks when advising patients. “But I do say that I would do this again.”
150 trials underway
Novartis, Bristol Myers, and other companies with approved CAR-T cancer therapies, such as Johnson & Johnson and Gilead, are currently testing the technology against other hard-to-treat diseases.
There are about 150 trials underway pursuing CAR-T for lupus, as well as many others for myasthenia gravis, scleroderma, myositis, multiple sclerosis and stiff-person syndrome.
“There’s billions and billions of dollars pouring into this space,” said P.J. Utz, a Stanford Medicine autoimmunity researcher.
The risks became clear when Novartis in late August said it halted eight trials of its experimental rap-cel CAR-T therapy in autoimmune and neurological disorders after three patients died from a rare but known hyperinflammatory complication called IEC-HS.
Novartis, in an emailed statement, said it is working with multiple investigators and external academic experts to understand the root cause of the deaths and will share its findings “once the analysis is completed and the results can contribute to furthering patient care.”
Bristol also paused enrollment in its CAR-T autoimmune trials, citing temporary inflammatory events in patients. On October 23, it announced the death of a multiple sclerosis patient in one of the trials but said it had identified the cause of the safety issue and hopes to resume testing in 2027.
Piecing together what happened
The revelation of deaths in the Novartis trials surprised doctors eager to try CAR-T, buoyed by the success of Georg Schett of the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg. In 2022, Schett published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine showing five lupus patients achieved remission with CAR-T. Subsequent studies showed lasting remission.
The Novartis deaths have left doctors in the dark, Schett said. The company needs to disclose what diseases the patients had, how well controlled their diseases were and what emergency treatments they received, Schett added.
Without those details, he said, doctors enrolling patients in other trials are left to speculate. “This is very sad for the community.”
Schett said he and CAR-T inventor Carl June of the University of Pennsylvania have tried to piece together what happened in the Novartis trials for an article they have submitted to NEJM.
He attributes the rare hyperinflammatory events in part to Novartis’ compressed manufacturing process, which reduces the time it takes to produce the cells from more than 10 days to fewer than two.
With this process, patients receive cells in an immature form, which Schett suggests is triggering a severe inflammatory response as cells expand in patients’ bodies. “We don’t see that in other programs,” he said.
He and others were less concerned about the more familiar side effects reported by Bristol Myers.
“We have treated high-grade inflammatory events that have been reversible with treatment,” said Kopittke’s doctor, Saira Sheikh, of the University of North Carolina, who chairs a network of nearly 70 lupus clinical trial centres.
Dr. Cuoghi Edens, a rheumatologist at the University of Chicago Medicine, which treats more than 100 paediatric lupus patients, said her hospital has had great success with a CAR-T therapy from Cabaletta Bio, which uses a more traditional manufacturing process.
Cabaletta has started testing its treatment in patients as young as 12. Edens said she walked through the informed consent process with a 15-year-old late last month.
“When the potential long-term impact of your diagnosis is death,” Edens said, “I don’t know if (treatment risks are) going to make that big of a difference to these patients.

A post is being widely circulated on social media (here, here) claiming that Members of Parliament (MPs) in India are exempt from GST on purchases of cars, air conditioners, and flight tickets. It also claims that MPs are entitled to toll tax exemptions and free train travel. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Indian MPs are exempt from GST on purchases of cars, air conditioners, and flight tickets. They are also entitled to toll tax exemption and free train travel.
Fact: MPs are entitled to free train and air travel, as well as toll fees exemption. However, they are not exempt from paying GST on purchases of cars and air conditioners. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
First, according to the details of benefits available to MPs on the official Parliament website (here and here), each MP is entitled to 34 free single air journeys per year anywhere within India. They can use these tickets to travel with their spouse, relatives, or friends.
Additionally, MPs are entitled to free first-class AC or executive-class train travel anywhere in the country. Their spouse or another accompanying person can also avail of this facility. An accompanying assistant is entitled to a free AC two-tier (2-Tier) train pass.
According to the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) regulations (here and here), vehicles used by MPs are exempt from paying toll fees on national highways. MPs are also entitled to toll-exempt FASTags for two vehicles during their tenure.
However, there is no evidence to suggest that MPs are exempt from paying GST on cars, air conditioners, or other items they purchase. Neither the Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954, which outlines the benefits and entitlements of MPs, nor any official government notification mentions such a GST exemption.
To sum up, while MPs are entitled to certain travel benefits, they do not receive any GST exemption on the cars, air conditioners, or other items they purchase.

In Mexico, journalists face threats from attackers — and from the system meant to protect them, too
Created in 2012, Mexico’s Protection Mechanism for Human Rights Defenders and Journalists has struggled to guarantee the safety of those it was designed to protect, operating largely in response to attacks rather than preventing them

Three years ago, Alberto Amaro was sitting at home when he heard two gunshots. His son, playing in the garden, ran inside in terror. When Amaro reached the front gate, he saw two armed men running down his street.
Amaro, 38, a journalist in the central Mexican state of Tlaxcala, says he immediately reported the shooting to the federal agency responsible for protecting journalists and requested emergency measures. “More than 48 hours passed without a response,” he says. Amaro eventually turned to a court, which ordered security for his family.
His is not an isolated case. What happened to Amaro was one of multiple frightening encounters that exposed shortcomings in Mexico’s federal Protection Mechanism for Human Rights Defenders and Journalists, a program created in 2012 to safeguard people threatened because of their work.
Between 2017 and 2022, eight journalists were killed while enrolled in Mexico’s federal Protection Mechanism, according to a joint investigation by Amnesty International and the Committee to Protect Journalists.
Amaro joined the Mechanism in 2019, shortly after founding his outlet. Since then, he has lived through more than 30 violent or menacing encounters, including death threats, detention, gunfire and intimidation linked to his reporting on police, government officials and organized crime.
In 2023, after he reported receiving direct death threats from a mayor, the Mechanism classified Amaro as being at high risk and assigned him bodyguards.
The agency later sought to withdraw his protection despite acknowledging that he remained at high risk. Amaro went to court and a judge ordered authorities to conduct a comprehensive risk assessment.
“I worry about what I publish, whether I’ll be killed when I leave home or make it back that day,” says Amaro, who founded the digital news outlet La Prensa de Tlaxcala in 2019. “I also have to worry about making sure they don’t take away my protection measures.”
A decade fighting for protection and justice
Mexico remains one of the world’s most dangerous countries for journalists outside of active war zones. CPJ has documented six journalist killings in the country in 2026, five of them in just over two months.
Priscila Pacheco, 34, the eldest daughter of journalist Francisco Pacheco, has spent more than a decade fighting for protection since her father was shot dead outside his home in Taxco, in the Mexican state of Guerrero, in 2016. An investigative journalist who reported on local government corruption, he founded El Foro de Taxco with his wife, Verónica, in 1998.
“I think the hardest thing for me was having to choose a coffin for my father,” says Priscila, the last person to see him alive.
After more death threats, Priscila, her mother and two siblings fled days after the murder, abandoning their home and printing press. More than a decade later, they remain displaced and the killing remains unsolved.
Propuesta Cívica, a Mexican civil society organization that provides legal support to journalists and their families, estimates that 98% of journalist homicides remain unpunished. “The deeper structural problem is that the Mechanism has been given a responsibility that belongs to the state as a whole," says Vanessa Carrillo, Propuesta Cívica's codirector.
Despite ongoing threats, Priscila said the Mechanism has denied her personal protection because she works as a public employee. She works for the state-level Protection Mechanism in Toluca, in the State of Mexico.
The security measures provided to her family have been unreliable, she says. Their panic button does not always work, and Priscila has none she can carry herself. Security equipment installed at the family’s home, including cameras, locks and lights, is not properly maintained, she says, and police patrols are often skipped or conducted only after a formal written request.
At annual risk reassessments, Priscila has to repeatedly ask more than 20 officials not to withdraw the limited protection her family still receives.
“It seems they need you to receive a direct threat, or for someone to actually come and do something to you,” she says.
The family has no plans to return to Taxco while violence persists. “We will never feel safe. Security is something that has been taken from us,” she says. “It has become something utopian for us, because it is the authorities themselves who have failed us.”
The struggle to keep reporting safely
Jonathan Cuevas, 38, spent three years displaced from his home in Iguala, Guerrero, after threats linked to his reporting on organized crime and local officials.
In 2020, Mexico’s Protection Mechanism arranged for him to live in a safe house in Mexico City, but the threats continued. He was transferred between three safe houses during his displacement.
“My return to Iguala wasn’t the result of any government action,” Cuevas says. “It happened simply because the groups agreed to a truce.”
An agreement between two rival criminal groups fighting for control of the area allowed Cuevas and other displaced journalists to return in 2023.
But after he returned, Cuevas says two people warned him to stop publishing stories about the local prosecutor’s office, threatening to kill him if he continued. He eventually stopped reporting on those issues. Cuevas says the Mechanism documented the attacks he reported but failed to coordinate with federal prosecutors.
The protection measures also proved inconsistent and often ill-suited to his work, he says. The panic button he received does not work in communities without cell service, where he often reports, while security patrols are irregular.
Cuevas has refused bodyguards, saying that moving around with armed men would make him an easier target. He believes the system prioritizes keeping journalists in safe houses over allowing them to continue working. Although displacement can offer greater security, it separates local journalists from their families, communities and sources.
“What happens," Cuevas asks, "to those of us who want to keep working and practicing journalism?”
A reactive system, not a preventive one
The Inter-American Commission for Human Rights has emphasized that the state must prevent attacks and reduce risks, not simply investigate them. “The system’s success," Carrillo says, must also be measured by “its ability to reduce risks, prevent further attacks and allow journalists to continue their work freely and safely.”
According to Propuesta Cívica, Mexico’s federal Protection Mechanism is hampered by bureaucratic delays, insufficient staffing and a reactive approach. Protection measures are often inadequate, risk assessments delayed and safeguards withdrawn despite ongoing threats.
In 2025, President Claudia Sheinbaum said the Protection Mechanism could receive additional funding if needed, but Reporters Without Borders (RSF) says the government has made little progress in fulfilling its press freedom commitments, including a promised review of the Mechanism.
The Associated Press contacted Mexico’s Protection Mechanism for Human Rights Defenders and Journalists several times seeking an interview. A senior official declined to be interviewed, and the agency has not responded to subsequent requests.
After spending a year in Spain with his family because of threats, Alberto Amaro underwent another assessment. It classified him as facing a high risk but found that his family did not. In 2025, authorities sought to withdraw his family’s bodyguards and eventually restricted some of their movements. Amaro challenged the decisions in court and won.
In one recent threat, Amaro received a call from an unknown number. The caller claimed to be a senior operative with the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and warned him to watch what he writes.
Despite having two bodyguards with him around the clock, Amaro says he still does not feel safe.
“If I come across four people," he says, “they have already beaten us.”

Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
- Published
A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run.
Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires.
His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded.
Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa.
He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements.
Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary.
When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained.
Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper Clarín.
However, the experts found that while Bertulazzi had tampered with the device, he had done so to prevent the alarm from sounding once he removed it.
A nationwide manhunt is now under way.
Italian media say that his extradition to Italy had been imminent after his last appeal was rejected.
Bertulazzi was first arrested after using a false passport to cross into Argentina from neighbouring Chile in 2002.
However, he was granted refugee status in 2004 and lived freely in the South American country until his re-arrest in 2024, when the current right-wing president, Javier Milei, took office.
Milei's government said at the time that "Bertulazzi is responsible for crimes that undermined democratic values and the lives of many victims".
He was a member of the Red Brigades, which kidnapped and killed a number of state officials in the 1970s and '80s.
Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades' Genoa section that kidnapped Pietro Costa on the street and then held him for 81 days before receiving a big ransom.
The money it made from the kidnapping was then used to buy a flat in Rome, which was used in 1978 for the Red Brigades' most notorious crime, the kidnap and murder of Italian former Prime Minister, Aldo Moro.
Moro was abducted when his car was ambushed on the way to the opening of parliament. He was held in the flat for 54 days before he was shot and his body abandoned in the boot of a Renault car in the centre of Rome.

Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling
In northern Ethiopia, conflict pushes a strained healthcare system to the brink
"It was a mess, it was chaos, and that continued for almost seven, eight days. Without (cell) network, without electricity," recalls a surgeon in Ethiopia.
On September 24, a two-year ceasefire between rebels and the Ethiopian government began to collapse. As injured people streamed in from the countryside, this surgeon and his colleagues treated as many as they could at a hospital in Mekele, the capital city of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Fearing repercussions for treating rebel fighters, the surgeon asked NPR not to publish his name.
"The whole emergency (room) was flooded with war trauma patients," he recalls. "The floors were all filled up, there was no place to step."
For the past several weeks, the violence has continued at a steady pace, raising concerns that Ethiopia could again face a civil war. The Ethiopian military has accused Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea of backing Tigrayan militants, who have aligned themselves with seven rebel groups in Ethiopia with the goal of ousting Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
After drone strikes in late October killed at least 15 people, including children, the director-general of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, posted on X that the violence in northern Ethiopia "is pushing an already fragile health system closer to collapse."
During the initial outbreak of violence in September, the surgeon in Tigray says he spent days operating on victims of gunfire, drone attacks, and mortar shells. Some were clearly civilians, but others were fighters in uniform. Complicating matters, he recalls, there was no way to know how many patients were coming because cell service and the internet were cut.
"We don't know where they're from — you just go ahead and do whatever you can, you know?" he told NPR.
There had been signs that the war between Ethiopia's federal government and rebel groups could reopen. In May, Tigrayan rebels ousted regional leaders and installed their own. In response, Ethiopia's federal government cut funds to Tigray — including to hospitals run by the regional administration. Doctors, he says, haven't been paid in months.
"It's an open wound, which was never closed, you know. Left for healing and never healed," he says. "I guess now it's infected."
For Tedros of WHO, the situation is deeply personal. He is Tigrayan and previously served as Ethiopia's minister of health. In his social media post, he wrote that hospitals are facing shortages of workers, medicine and ambulances, and that WHO and the U.N. are working to deliver medical supplies to the affected regions.
"As fighting continues, more people are likely to lose access to essential healthcare … civilians must be protected," Tedros wrote. "The most courageous choose peace."
A worldwide worry
Public health experts say targeted attacks on healthcare —– generally considered a war crime —– have become a growing concern in conflict zones around the world.
So far in 2026, attacks on health care facilities and workers in 19 countries led to more than 960 deaths, according to data collected by WHO. While the largest mass casualty event occurred in a Pakistani airstrike on a drug rehabilitation center in Afghanistan, hundreds of people have died in attacks on healthcare settings in Sudan, Lebanon, and Ukraine.
Complicating matters are funding cuts to global health initiatives, including the dismantling of USAID shortly after Donald Trump took office in 2025.
"The continual attack against healthcare is eroding the norm of healthcare being a protected part of conflict," says Lindsey Green, a researcher focused on Ethiopia for the U.S. nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights.
The Tigray war lasted two years, killing an estimated 600,000 people. The majority of Tigray's health facilities were only partially functional, as the Ethiopian government imposed an aid blockade on the region — home to more than 7 million people.
Attacks continued, despite a peace agreement
The government struck a peace agreement with Tigrayan rebels in 2022, ending most hostilities, but attacks on healthcare continued. In August of this year, Physicians for Human Rights worked with the Organization for Justice and Accountability in the Horn of Africa to publish a report detailing these attacks.
Of more than 600 health workers surveyed across three regions of northern Ethiopia, 63% reported attacks on ambulances, some as they tried to reach injured patients, and 57% reported witnessing an armed takeover of their clinic or hospital between 2020 and 2024. One health worker in Mekele recalled Ethiopian forces occupying a hospital and placing the uniforms of Tigrayan rebels on the floor and forcing staff to step on them. "Nonsense stuff," he said.
"Armed groups were occupying facilities to take resources or to destroy resources, to destroy machines and equipment, really with the goal of making healthcare harder to access," Green says.
In the report, researchers confirmed targeted attacks on health care workers perpetrated by both rebels and government forces – often as retribution for a community's perceived alliances or against doctors who treated an enemy. But there has been no way for victims to seek justice from either party.
"It's very clear that this ongoing pattern of attacks on healthcare links back to impunity for these violations," Green says.
NPR reached out to Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry and Office of the Prime Minister, but did not receive a response.
Doctors in northern Ethiopia say the one-two punch of a war that specifically targeted healthcare, followed by foreign aid cuts, have left the region without a chance to recover.
A health worker in Tigray counted more than 100 women who died in childbirth over the past year. He attributed their deaths to the dire state of the health system. He spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity, due to fear of being targeted for speaking out.
"They died during delivery because of a lack of medicine, lack of health care providers, a lack of fuel. So the ambulances are not functional," he said.
An independent review of birth data during the Tigray war from 2020 - 2022 showed that the maternal mortality rate per 100,000 live births increased fivefold, compared to prewar data. Researchers in 2022 found that 83% of clinics and hospitals were no longer able to serve pregnant women. Additionally, systemic rape and sexual violence were regularly used as a weapon of war.
"They told us, the people should be punished, because we are supporters of the TPLF (Tigrayan rebels)," the health worker says.
Ayoda Werede, a California-based physician with the nonprofit, Health Professionals for Tigray, says that since the latest outbreak of violence, the Ethiopian military has not targeted health centers. But other unidentified groups have stolen supplies, "including medication, equipment, even mattresses off of patient's beds," Werede says. "This was just the opportunistic vacuum space that was created because of this conflict."
Her fear is that Ethiopia's healthcare system is already stretched beyond its capacity — and as the conflict reignites, injured people will have nowhere to go. The surgeon in Mekele has similar concerns. Many of Tigray's doctors, he says, have already left the country.
"We've lost our sense of being secure," he says. "It's a repeat of what's happened in the past."

Open earbuds are the big new thing in headphone land. Unlike in-ear variants, open earbuds are like tiny speakers that rest on the ear and let outside sound in naturally, so you can fully hear the world around you. Some use a hook style that wraps around the back of your ear, while others are clip-ons that look more like statement-piece earrings. Style aside, they are excellent for anyone who finds traditional earbuds uncomfortable or wants full environmental awareness for activities like running, biking, or even just doing chores around the house.
I’ve tested dozens of models since 2022, and while I still recommend having a pair of noise-canceling earbuds, I also love open earbuds for specific use cases.
For more headphone recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Earbuds, Best Workout Headphones, and Best Wireless Headphones.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Open Earbuds Overall
Anker Soundcore AeroClip 2 Specs
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0 | 
| Battery life | 8 hours, 32 with case | 
| Water/dust resistance | IP57 | 
| Wireless charging | Yes | 
These are truly take-everywhere, do-anything headphones I would recommend to anyone looking for great open earbuds. They are exceedingly comfortable and easy to use all day, so much so that I sometimes forgot I was wearing them.
They’re clip-ons that wrap around the earlobe, with the speaker end resting at the ear canal opening and the other end behind the ear. Importantly, the top of your ear is free for glasses, sunglasses, or hats. Like nearly all open earbuds, they let in sound from your surroundings, so don’t expect them to be a great companion for long-haul flights or daily gym sessions.
There are other open earbuds that are nearly as good as these, and some surpass them in areas like sound quality. But it’s a combination of small details that puts the AeroClip 2 at the top. The physical button controls on each earbud are much easier to use than touch-sensitive alternatives, especially when running or exercising outdoors. The charging case is surprisingly small, smaller than most other options on this list. And, importantly, the call quality is great. These buds use the same AI-powered chip as the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro, and while they don’t sound quite as good, they are noticeably better than other open earbuds, especially in noisy environments.
The best part? They cost less than many similar competitors I tested.
Runner-Up
Shokz OpenDots 2 Specs
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.1 | 
| Battery life | 10 hours, 40 with case | 
| Water/dust resistance | IP57 | 
| Wireless charging | Yes | 
My former top pick, and still a great option, especially if you value battery life. These earbuds do most of what the Soundcore AeroClip 2 does, just a little larger and a little pricier. The buds are exceedingly comfortable and stable for all-day wear, even during outdoor workouts.
What sets them apart from the AeroClip 2 is battery life. They are best in class—10 hours on a single charge, and 40 hours total with the charging case. They also have an IP57 dust and water-resistance rating, the same as premium, flagship earbuds like Apple AirPods Pro 3 and Samsung Galaxy Buds4 Pro. I’ve worn them in the rain, on the beach, and fully submerged them in water multiple times without issue.
They are a bit pricey, though. Shokz recently launched the lower-priced Shokz OpenDots Air and Shokz OpenFit Air 2—I may update this recommendation depending on how my testing goes.
Best Premium Open Earbuds
Bose Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) Specs
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.3 | 
| Battery life | 6 hours, 24 with case | 
| Water/dust resistance | IPX4 | 
| Wireless charging | Yes | 
The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds were a big deal when they launched in 2024—a brand-new design from Bose and one of the biggest swings from a major brand in clip-on open earbuds. Two years later, the brand launched the second-generation version, and they are a solid, if expensive, option. That’s mainly because of sound quality—these earbuds sound clearer and more defined than most competitors. Another differentiator is physical button controls on each bud, which I find easier to use than touch alternatives, especially when running or biking.
Like the Soundcore and Shokz earbuds, they are very comfortable, so much so that I sometimes forgot I am wearing them. This gen-two version has a more distinct, two-tone material design that is certainly eye-catching, especially in the white colorway. They also now support wireless charging, a big omission in the first generation. But they are much pricier by comparison, and only worth it if you want the best sound quality in this clip-on form factor.
Best Cheap Open Earbuds
Soundpeats PearlClip Pro Specs
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.3 | 
| Battery life | 7.5 hours, 30 with case | 
| Water/dust resistance | IPX5 | 
| Wireless charging | No | 
It can be a little nerve-wracking to spend big bucks on a concept (open earbuds) you aren’t totally convinced by. That’s one reason I love this $50 option—the PearClip Pros aren’t super pricey and are a great way to find out if you even like open earbuds in the first place, especially the kind that clip onto the outside of your ear.
They are far less refined than Shokz or Soundcore. Things like the app and touch controls can be a little finicky. But that’s common at this super-low price point, and you can always upgrade to a more premium earbud if you fall in love with the clip-on form factor.
Best Open Ear Headphones
Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 Specs
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.3 | 
| Battery life | 12 hours | 
| Water/dust resistance | IP55 | 
| Wireless charging | No | 
The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are more like headphones than earbuds—with a wraparound headband, long battery life, great sound quality (for open headphones), and no charging case. They use a combination of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver clearer sound than most smaller open earbuds, especially in noisy environments. That combination of technologies is why these are some of my favorite earbuds for outdoor fitness activities like running and biking.
I do wish these headphones were a little cheaper. I’m currently testing the recently released, more affordable Shokz OpenRun Air 2, and I’m hopeful they can be a budget-friendly alternative.
Honorable Mentions
Apple AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging Case for $149: Apple AirPods 5 are semi-open earbuds—they still go in your ears, but don’t have rubber eartips that block outside noise, meaning you can still hear the world around you pretty clearly. Because they go in your ear somewhat, they have better sound quality and automated noise-canceling than nearly all of my top picks. Fit, however, is a big issue. While nearly all of my top picks are excellent workout companions, the AirPods 5 are quite the opposite—they can fall out often during exercise and are tricky to control mid-run.
Nothing Ear (Open) for $99: Former WIRED editor Adrienne So loves these earbuds and uses them for almost all her outdoor activities. They are very slim (19-mm wide) and lightweight. They fit slightly inside your ear and, like most Nothing headphones, have a distinct transparent design. The case doesn’t clamp shut very firmly, so be careful, but at this price, that’s forgivable.
CMF Clip Pro for $99: If you want something a little nicer and a little more comfortable than our budget pick (the Soundpeats PearClip Pro), these CMF open earbuds are a solid option. Sure, they’re a big step up in price, but for under $100, I found them more comfortable and easier to use thanks to the physical button control on each earbud (similar to my top picks).
JLab Epic Open Sport for $100: JLab’s Epic Open Sport stands out for its controls: the JLab emblem is a touch sensor, and each earbud also has physical buttons on top, making it a breeze to control. What holds the Epic Open Sport back is audio quality—the sound isn’t very detailed and is generally boring to listen to.
Other Open Earbuds I’ve Tested
EarFun Clip for $70: For around $70, these are a solid pick for anyone on a budget. Former WIRED reviewer Waniata found the overall package punches above its price point, with a snappy, compact case, a comfortable fit, push-button controls, and reliable multi-device Bluetooth connections. The problem is our budget pick, the Soundpeats PearlClip Pro, often sells for less and offers a similar overall experience. Don’t dismiss these earbuds if you find them heavily discounted.
Shokz OpenFit Pro for $250: The Shokz OpenFit Pro has a great premise: open earbuds with noise canceling. Hear the world around you as you would without headphones, and turn on noise-canceling when you don’t, just like regular earbuds. And while they do cancel some noise, it’s not much. The bigger issue is price: for $250, you could get open earbuds and great noise-canceling earbuds that do a better job for each task.
Suunto Wing 2 for $179: These open-ear headphones are designed for endurance athletes—they have a long 12-hour battery life and come with a wireless power bank you can take on the go. Dock the headphones in the power bank for up to 36 hours of total battery life. There’s nothing inherently wrong with these headphones, but I don’t see a world where I would recommend them over the Shokz Openrun Pro 2, which retails for the same amount and offers more comfort, a sleeker design, better sound, and a more robust app.
Suunto Spark for $179: The Suunto Spark has a similar story to the Suunto Wing 2: it's built for athletes and syncs with Suunto fitness watches, but the similarly priced Shokz Openfit 2 outclasses it in the areas that matter (comfort, sound quality, battery).
What Are Open Earbuds and How Do They Sound?
At a glance, open earbuds seem a lot like typical wireless earbuds. The big difference is that, instead of going inside your ear canal, they rest somewhere on the outside of your ear, leaving it open so you can easily hear the world around you. I use them all the time for outdoor exercise like running or biking, where I want my music but also need to hear other runners, bikers, and cars to stay safe.
Because they leave your ears open and the sound comes from farther away (outside your ear rather than inside), audio performance isn’t as clear, intimate, or bassy as regular earbuds. They also typically lack noise-canceling features, so they are not a great fit for the office or air travel.
When or Where Would I Use Open Earbuds?
Open earbuds are perfect for outdoor activities or when you want to talk to other people without taking off your headphones. When I run or go for a bike ride, I only use open earbuds so I can hear my surroundings and stay safe. I also like using them around the house when I am cooking or doing laundry.
What About Semi-Open Earbuds?
Semi-open earbuds, like Apple’s AirPods, sit inside the ear but don’t have eartips that create a sound seal. They can offer better audio quality than other open earbuds because the speakers and microphones are closer to your ear and mouth. Semi-open earbuds are comfortable, but they’re usually pretty loose—they can fall out easily and may be a poor option for fitness activities.
How Do I Test Open Earbuds?
I test open earbuds like I test any pair of headphones: in the real world, in my daily life. I wear each pair for at least a few weeks to test comfort, battery life, ease of use, and onboard controls. I listen to podcasts, watch TV shows, jam out to my favorite playlists, and call friends.
With open earbuds in particular, I also wear them on jogs, bike rides, and errand runs to get a better feel for how stable they are on my ears. I don’t expect them to cancel any noise, so I don’t test them on airplanes or loud commutes—they aren’t really made for that. My main audio source is Spotify Lossless, but, when possible, I test other formats and codecs as well.
