Apple TV 4K (4th gen) review: Still great, but drastically more expensive
The $150 price increase is hard to swallow.
The Apple TV 4K has been our pick for the best premium streaming device since the third-gen model arrived in 2022. In terms of pure performance, it was undoubtedly the best you could buy, thanks to the combination of picture quality, speed and features you wouldn't find on any of the more affordable competition. That was true four years ago and it's still true now.
Unfortunately, the global tech landscape has changed massively over the last two years. Nearly every device is more expensive, especially if it needs RAM or its own processor. Apple's streaming box didn't escape that fate. For the 4th-generation Apple TV 4K, Apple made big upgrades to performance and added a slew of new features, and of course, it carved out a more prominent place for Siri AI in your living room. The compact streaming box is a lot more expensive than the previous generation cost at launch, though, and the new $299 price tag certainly dulls its shine.
What's new on (and good about) the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K?
If you were hoping for a new design, there are only subtle tweaks to report. The most evident is that Apple moved the light on the front of the box from the right to the center. If you dive into the spec sheets, you'll discover the new model is slightly larger than the previous version. I'm talking 0.24mm bigger in width and depth, and 3 grams heavier. You'll be forgiven for not noticing. The Siri Remote, however, is exactly the same size at 1.4 inches x 5.4 inches x 0.36 inches.
Apple upgraded the processor from the A15 Bionic to the A19 chip. In iPhone terms, that would be like going from an iPhone 13 to an iPhone 17, so the computing power increase here is significant. The company says that the A19 chip is capable of 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to 2x faster GPU performance than the previous Apple TV 4K. I don't have the tools to quantifiably check those claims, but I can tell you the device is super responsive, navigation is speedy and overall the UI is noticeably more fluid. Plus, the A19 delivers a dedicated AV1 decoder for HDR rendering efficiency.
Of course, the A19 offers a boost to Siri AI, which is playing a bigger role in the living room thanks to the new Apple TV 4K. For starters, the streaming box now has three far-field microphones built in, so you no longer have to use the remote to interact with the assistant. You can simply speak your queries while watching TV and Siri is off and running. Like before, Apple's AI can help with finding and playing live TV, movies, shows and sports from your go-to apps. But with Siri's recently expanded capabilities, it can now pull in personal context from Messages and other apps too. So when you want Siri to "play the show Jack texted me about," the assistant knows just what to do. Additionally, audio captured from the far-field mics is processed within the Secure Exclave on the A19, so neither the apps, the OS nor Apple get access to any of the data.
The new feature that will get the most use at my house is Precision Finding for the remote in the Find My app. I have two kids who are constantly leaving the remote in undisclosed locations, so the added ability to play a sound has already greatly reduced the amount of time I spend searching for it. And when I can't hear it, Precision Finding is better than the previous method for locating the remote with an iPhone. With the built-in mics for Siri though, a lost remote is much less frustrating since you can just tell the Apple TV 4K what to do.
There's also a noteworthy audio upgrade on the Apple TV 4K. Before, you could only use two HomePod or HomePod mini speakers as a stereo pair. Now you can use up to four of those, so long as they're second-gen HomePods or HomePod mini 2s, for a more complete home theater surround sound system. The only additional requirement is that the two front speakers and two rear speakers have to match. So you can have two HomePods in the front and two HomePod mini 2s in the back, which is the configuration I tested. If you have four of the same speaker, that works too.
Once you have all of the HomePods in place, you'll hear a series of tones as the Apple TV 4K locates the speakers and tunes the audio for the room. I suspected that a combination of HomePods and HomePod minis is the ideal setup and my testing proved me right. The HomePods provide the added bass needed for action scenes, or really just for a fuller soundstage most TV viewing will eventually require. The HomePod minis can't do that on their own, but they do well as rear speakers, providing dimensional backup to the larger speakers at the front. I think having four HomePods would be overkill, not to mention expensive. I also heard a four-mini configuration during a demo last month, and while it's certainly a boost compared to TV speakers, it's not nearly as potent as the arrangement I tested at home.
I'll also note that there's a feature called Whole Room Audio that will be great for parties and gatherings. This allows for all four speakers to play the same sounds, rather than the fragments each might deliver in a surround sound setup. This ensures that everyone hears everything, from vocals to guitars, or even the commentators of an F1 race. Whole Room Audio is also easy to activate as it's accessible from the Speaker Mode option in the Control Center.
Like it has in the past, the new Apple TV 4K can function as a smart home hub. This allows you to control HomeKit and Matter accessories like cameras, locks and thermostats, and Apple says "thousands" of such devices are compatible. Thanks to the HomeKit Secure Video, you can expect secure local processing on the streaming box, which encrypts clips before they're stored in iCloud. Apple Intelligence provides captions for camera feeds and you can control everything from the Control Center.
Siri voice control is available as well, as is the ability to run scenes from the Home app in the Control Center. If you have a HomeKit or Matter compatible camera (I don't), you can get a live view of those in the top right corner of your TV screen. If someone rings the doorbell, you can also choose to be automatically notified on the display you're already looking at. If needed, you can chat with them and unlock the door without leaving your seat.
What's not so good about the new Apple TV 4K?
My biggest complaint about the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K is the price. At $299, this model is $150 more than the equivalent version of its predecessor was at launch. Sure, Apple increased the price of the third-gen Apple TV 4K from $149 to $249 earlier this year, and a lot has happened since that model debuted in 2022. However, even with rising memory and component costs, tacking on another $50 to the already inflated price tag is adding insult to injury. It especially stings when you consider the company actually decreased prices when it launched these models in 2022.
To pour more salt in the wound, Apple got rid of the cheaper Wi-Fi-only option that also offered less storage space (64GB). In 2022, that version of the third-gen Apple TV 4K launched for $129, though it eventually went up to $199 this year. If you'll allow me to dig even deeper into Apple TV 4K history, that $129 model was not only $50 cheaper than the W-Fi-only version before it, but even doubled the 32GB onboard storage. Its original price was a drop from the $179 that the comparative version preceding it cost. Meanwhile, the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K only comes in one configuration and it has 128GB of storage; that's the same capacity as the priciest model of the previous generation.
After living with the Apple TV 4K's new home theater setup with four HomePods, I'm starting to question how many people will actually use it. Not only does it require you to have four of Apple's speakers, but you'll also have to put all four of them in the same space. When you consider one of the primary functions of a HomePod is to serve as a direct line to Siri, permanently putting all four in your living room seems like a waste. Not to mention you'll miss out on multiroom audio and features like Intercom, which are more helpful if your HomePods are spread around the house. After some testing, it seems to me like the quad-Pod speaker arrangement is a neat bonus — something you temporarily pull together for movie night or parties — rather than a substitute for a soundbar or traditional home theater setup.
I have another gripe that is more of a frustration with tvOS as a whole, but it's worth mentioning as it relates to the new Apple TV 4K. Even if you've added the streaming box to the Home app and assigned it to a room, the Home icon won't appear in the Control Center until you've either added a camera or created a Scene. So if you fire up your Apple TV and can't find your non-camera devices, that's probably why.
I appreciate the fact that camera feeds will be the most useful on a TV. But I think it's silly that I have to create a Scene (manually triggered saved settings) in order to see things like a thermostat or lights on a device that's advertised as a "smart home hub." At the very least, I want there to be a shortcut in the Control Center for Rooms I've set up in the Home app on iOS, where I can then access individual devices if needed. I should also mention that tvOS doesn't have a dedicated Home app; everything to do with controlling your smart home requires digging into the Control Center on an Apple TV. Or, of course, you could fire up the full app on your phone.
Wrap-up
In terms of performance, the Apple TV 4K remains the best streaming box you can buy. That's been true for a while now, and the upgrades the company made for this version only cements its position at the top of the premium heap. However, with the current state of global technology, specifically the price of anything that uses RAM or a chip like the A19, Apple's streaming device isn't as easy to recommend as it once was.
If you're rocking with a third-gen model, I'd urge you to stay put. And if you're looking to invest in an Apple TV for the first time, try to hold out for a sale or catch one on the refurbished market. Heck, I'd even keep my eye out for a used third-gen model. Yes, you'll miss out on the newest features in that scenario, including the convenience of an always-listening Siri device that isn't a HomePod, but the core of what makes an Apple TV a great device is still there. And in late 2026, there's something to be said for saving significant money on a tech purchase.

On 02 November 2026, three BSF personnel, including an Assistant Commandant, were injured after a group of people allegedly attacked them during an anti-smuggling operation in Ashabari, Boxanagar, Tripura. The attackers allegedly assaulted the personnel, damaged their vehicle, and snatched a service weapon. By 08 November 2026, police had arrested 21 people, including two key accused, Rabiul Hossain and Mahabul Hossain. Chief Minister Manik Saha also chaired a security review meeting and directed strict action against those involved. Subsequently, authorities launched land demarcation and ownership verification near the Ashabari Border Outpost, while security agencies intensified identity checks and patrols along the India-Bangladesh border (here, here, and here).
Following the incident, several videos are being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming to show BSF personnel retaliating against the attackers by identifying and assaulting them, along with bulldozer action against their properties. Let’s verify the truth behind these videos in this article.
Claim: The video shows BSF personnel in Tripura retaliating against those involved in the attack by assaulting them.
Fact: The videos do not show BSF personnel retaliating against those involved in the 2 November 2026 attack in Tripura. The first video dates back to a lathi charge during local election counting in Tripura’s Khowai district on 5 October 2026. The second shows police action against garment workers protesting in Mirpur, Bangladesh, on 1 November 2026. The third is from a protest against a proposed land port in Jaigaon-Gotibari, West Bengal, on 3 November 2026. The fourth shows an eviction drive in Baburhat, Chandpur, Bangladesh, during which illegal structures were demolished. None of these videos are related to the BSF attack in Ashabari, Tripura. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1 & 2
In our investigation, we found that the first video, which shows security personnel lathi-charging people as they run away, dates back to 5 October 2026. It shows an incident during the vote-counting process for local elections in Tripura’s Khowai district. According to local media reports (here, here), the video was recorded near a counting centre in the Champahawar area, where workers from several political parties had gathered to hear the Gram Sabha election results. Tensions escalated during the counting process, prompting security personnel to use lathis to disperse the crowd. One person reportedly died in the ensuing stampede.
The second video, which shows a man being assaulted by security personnel, is also unrelated to the BSF attack in Tripura. We found that it shows police chasing and assaulting garment workers during a protest in Mirpur, Dhaka, Bangladesh (here, here, and here). According to local media reports, garment workers in the Mirpur-10 and Mirpur-11 areas staged protests on 1 November 2026, demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka. Police used batons and tear gas to disperse the protesters, leading to clashes, stone-pelting, and chases between the two sides. A police vehicle was also reportedly set on fire near the Mirpur-11 metro station (here, here, and here).
Video 3
In our investigation, we found (here, here, and here) that the video is from a protest held in the Jaigaon-Gotibari area of Alipurduar district, West Bengal, on 03 November 2026. Local tribal residents were protesting against a proposed land port, demanding rehabilitation and compensation. The situation escalated when police arrived to clear the road blockade, resulting in clashes between the protesters and police. Following the incident, police arrested 11 people.
Video 4
In our investigation, we found that the video shows an eviction drive in Baburhat, Chandpur, Bangladesh, during which more than 200 illegal structures were demolished. According to media reports (here, here, and here), local authorities launched a joint eviction campaign to remove illegal structures along the Chandpur-Comilla highway, between Khajuria and Border Bazar. Officials had issued prior warnings and public announcements before carrying out the demolition drive, which was scheduled to continue for three days, with the possibility of extension. The Roads and Highways Department and district administration also planned to plant trees in the cleared areas and construct a dedicated traffic intersection to ease congestion. Police and administrative personnel were deployed to maintain law and order during the operation.

The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 combines a stylish translucent design with smooth linear switches, a compact 75% layout, multi-device connectivity, and excellent battery life. It’s great for everyday typing, but limited customization, closely packed keys, and a premium price may put some buyers off.
ASUS has a wide range of product categories, and its mechanical keyboards are quite popular among gamers.
ASUS also offers standard mechanical keyboards for regular users. The company recently sent us its recently announced Jelly75 keyboard for review. It features a 75% layout, a unique translucent design, and multi-device connectivity. The keyboard also comes with a slightly higher price tag of Rs 7,999 (US $129.99)
I have been using this keyboard for the past several days, and in this review, you will learn everything about the keyboard, including the good and the bad things, and also learn if this Jelly75 keyboard is worth the price for what it offers.
Table of Contents
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Review: Design, Typing Experience, and Everyday Use
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Unboxing
You get a fairly simple package when you unbox the ASUS Jelly75 KD201. Inside, you find the keyboard, a USB-A to USB-C cable, a 2.4GHz wireless receiver, a quick start guide, and warranty documentation.
However, ASUS doesn’t provide a keycap puller or even a switch puller out of the box.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Design and Build Quality
The ASUS Jelly75 keyboard is available in two colors: Volt Green and Orange Meadow. I received the Volt Green variant of the Jelly75, which comes with a translucent chassis and a combination of white, black, and mint green keys. This color combination makes it very attractive for a vibrant and unique desktop setup.
If you don’t like contrasting looks, the Orange Meadow color variant, which offers muted colors and a retro-looking design, is the best choice, which I personally prefer.
But the Volt Green variant also looks good in person and stands out more than the regular black-and-white finishes on most mechanical keyboards.
The standout feature on both variants is the translucent design, so you can see parts of the internal keyboard structure through the casing.
However, the body and keys are made of polycarbonate, but it’s solidly built, and the weight adds extra rigidity.
The steel plate inside the keyboard adds to its weight, bringing it to about 1.19 kg.
While the weight helps the keyboard stay stable during typing, it can be inconvenient if you plan to carry it often.
Since the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard uses a 75% layout, it measures about 326.2 x 142.1 x 39.5 mm, which takes up less space than traditional full-size keypads but more than smaller percentage keypads.
If you are not familiar with keyboard percentages, here is a detailed visual guide we created to help you understand different keyboard layouts.
The keys are densely packed together, and there is not much space between them; also, there is no gap between functional keys and the regular keys, especially around the arrow key cluster, where, until you get used to this layout, there is a high chance that you can accidentally mispress the other keys.
Also, the keyboard doesn’t have any knobs, which would have been a nice addition for direct volume control. Additionally, the Caps Lock key doesn’t come with any light indication to show it’s active.
The rubber pads on the bottom help it stay stable and in place without sliding on a smooth desk surface.
The keyboard also comes with adjustable kickstands that let you set three typing-angle positions.
While the design is attractive, the translucent, lighter-colored keycaps make dirt more visible. It also supports a wireless receiver, but the keypad doesn’t have a dedicated compartment to store it, which is inconvenient, especially if you plan to carry it between workspaces. It won’t be much of a concern if you plan to connect it via Bluetooth, but it’s something you should know.
Continuing with the design, you will find the ASUS logo on the bottom right, a toggle to switch between connection types on the top, and a USB-C charging port on the top left.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Keyboard Layout and Ergonomics
The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 uses a 75% keyboard layout, which is a sweet spot between portability and functionality.
Unlike smaller 60% or 65% layouts, it includes a function row at the top and navigation keys on the right.
However, it doesn’t include a separate number pad, which full-size keyboards often have.
This compact layout has all essential keys and doesn’t miss anything, especially if you are coming from notebooks or a Mac.
This layout works for writing, programming, office work, and even standard gaming.
Although you get a dedicated number row below the function keys, a dedicated number pad is still more convenient, especially if your work involves entering numbers regularly.
However, the keys are densely packed, with negligible gaps between them.
ASUS has also included a dedicated Copilot key near the arrow key cluster, which could accidentally launch Windows Copilot, especially until you get used to this densely packed layout.
In terms of key design, ASUS used tall, squarish-rounded keycaps instead of the flatter options found on many keyboards.
While this makes them look unique, it may take time to get used to, especially if you are switching from a MacBook or another low-profile keyboard.
Since these keys are taller, I recommend a separate wrist rest, especially if you plan to use the keyboard lying flat.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Switches, Keycaps and Typing Experience
Typing experience is one of the most important things to consider when buying a mechanical keyboard, since you spend several hours every day writing, coding, or working on documents.
The ASUS Jelly75 comes with linear mechanical switches that offer 4mm of total key travel.
However, you won’t get tactile feedback when you press the keys. Unlike tactile switches, which have a noticeable bump when pressed, the Jelly75’s linear mechanism presses the keys gently, creating a smooth typing experience.
I personally prefer tactile feedback because I am used to my MacBook keyboard, but many also prefer smooth switches for longer typing sessions.
ASUS also rates the switches at 50 million keystrokes, which should last longer with regular use.
The keyboard also offers a gasket-mounted structure. ASUS calls it Uni-cushion technology, where it uses cushioning between the internal keyboard layout assembly and the outer body to help absorb vibrations.
This is especially useful if you press the keys harder, as the chassis absorbs vibration and stays steady overall.
The keycaps have a rigid feel. You won’t get rattling, wobbling, or uneven keypresses even on the larger keys like the spacebar.
As a mechanical keyboard, the ASUS Jelly75 offers hot-swappable switches, so you can remove and replace individual switches without soldering.
If you prefer tactile switches, you can also replace linear switches with tactile options.
However, ASUS doesn’t include a switch puller in the box, so you will need to buy it separately if you plan to swap the keys.
The ASUS Jelly75 keyboard comes with a white backlight instead of RGB backlighting. It keeps the keyboard looking cleaner.
You can adjust the white backlighting to four brightness levels using the dedicated keys on your keyboard, including Fn + F9 shortcuts.
You can also turn off the backlight completely, which can help extend battery life further.
However, the backlight illuminates the area around the keys and doesn’t illuminate the letters and symbols printed on the keys; instead, it glows around them.
This won’t be an issue if you are already used to this keyboard layout and type without looking at the keyboard, but if you look at the keys while typing, the lighting may not be as helpful in low light.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Connectivity and Multi-Device Switching
Another big advantage of the ASUS Jelly75 KD201 keyboard is its connectivity. If you use multiple devices, such as a Windows PC, MacBook, or iPad, you can connect this keyboard to all of them wirelessly and switch between them easily.
The Jelly75 keyboard supports three connectivity options: Bluetooth, 2.4GHz wireless, and a wired USB connection, and it can connect up to five devices using all three connection types.
The Jelly75 keyboard supports Bluetooth 3.0 and 5.0, and it can remember up to three Bluetooth devices.
To pair your devices, switch the keyboard to Bluetooth mode and hold Fn + 1, 2, or 3 for more than three seconds.
Once paired, you can easily switch between devices using the corresponding shortcuts.
You can pair up to three devices via Bluetooth. It also supports a 2.4 GHz wireless connection using the included USB receiver. ASUS says the wireless range is about 10 meters.
You can also connect the keyboard using the USB cable provided in the box.
The USB cable is long and suitable for any desktop layout, and its braided design lets you fold it easily and keeps it tngle-free.
However, as I said before, the main limitation is that it lacks a dedicated compartment for storing the 2.4GHz receiver if you plan to carry the keyboard between workplaces.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Customization
You won’t get much customization on the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard. Instead, ASUS kept it simple with a plug-and-play design.
It supports dedicated shortcuts to switch between Windows and MacBook layouts and offers several function-key shortcuts.
You can use Fn + F1, F2, and F3 to mute or adjust the volume, and F6-F8 to control music playback. It also includes shortcuts for switching between applications, searching, and launching Launchpad on macOS and Windows Search and Spotlight on macOS.
The keyboard also includes a dedicated Microsoft Copilot key, which lets you launch Copilot directly from your keyboard.
However, one noticeable downside is that, unlike other mechanical keyboards, it doesn’t include dedicated software for advanced key-mapping customization, so you can’t set custom shortcuts.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Battery Life
The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 has a 4000mAh rechargeable battery. ASUS rates the keyboard as lasting up to 8500 hours on a single charge with the backlight off, which translates to roughly 354 days.
It can last days without needing to charge. I used this keyboard with the backlight on throughout the entire two-week review period. I didn’t have to charge it once.
Regarding charging, the Jelly75 uses a USB-C port and includes a USB-A to USB-C cable in the box. It supports up to 5W charging. You can also charge the keyboard by connecting it directly to your device. It also includes a useful wired USB mode, which can be convenient if you suddenly run out of battery.
The keyboard uses battery light indicators to show the remaining battery. When the battery level drops to 20%, the status light slowly flashes red and reminds you to charge it. While charging, the indicator flashes, and when it’s fully charged, the light turns solid white. You can also check the remaining battery life in the Bluetooth settings for the connected device.
Asus MD105 Wireless Mouse Review
Along with the Jelly75 keyboard, ASUS also sent the MD105 wireless mouse, which pairs well with it. Interestingly, it comes in two color variants: Volt Green, which perfectly matches your keyboard if you picked up the Volt Green variant, and Milky White, which suits the Orange variant.
In terms of design, the MD105 mouse looks like a conventional mouse with a slightly wider body, and it comes with a dedicated thumb rest designed for right-hand users that offers great support, especially if you are a creator and plan to use the mouse for several hours a day.
It feels very light and weighs just 66 grams without a battery, and although it’s slightly wider, it isn’t as travel-friendly as other compact mice.
One feature I particularly like is the silent-click mechanism, which reduces clicking noise. This can be especially useful in shared offices and libraries, or when you’re working late at night.
The MD105 uses an optical sensor with three adjustable DPI settings, including 1200, 1600, and 2400. You can switch between them using the DPI button. Lower DPI settings offer more controlled cursor movement, while higher settings let you move the cursor faster.
For my big hands, the mouse feels perfectly compact, and my right finger rests comfortably on the support, making it comfortable to use.
Since it is lightweight, it is also quickly responsive and easy to move. For connectivity, the MD105 supports Bluetooth 5.0 and also offers 2.4 GHz wireless through the included USB receiver.
You can pair up to three devices: two via Bluetooth and one via the wireless receiver.
It also offers a wireless compartment in the mouse. If you are planning to use it with Bluetooth, you can safely store the wireless receiver in the compartment.
Since it supports multiple devices like the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard, it is also useful for switching between Windows and Mac computers.
A few months ago, I switched to a mouse with a built-in battery, but the MD105 comes with a single AA battery included in the box.
You need to replace it whenever you want, without waiting for the mouse to recharge. However, I prefer a rechargeable mouse, as mine also comes with a battery level indicator, so I can charge it.
If you can, this MD105 mouse suggests you need to keep an AA battery on hand in case it suddenly runs out of battery
The ASUS MD105 mouse is priced at Rs 1,699, which is a good value considering the ergonomics, comfort, and portability it offers.
It also has dedicated left-side switches for extra shortcuts, and its quiet operation, adjustable sensitivity, and multi-device connectivity make it a great buy if you are planning to get it alongside the Jelly75 keyboard.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Review Verdict
At Rs 8,999 (US$129.99), ASUS faces stiff competition from brands like AULA, Royal Kludge, and Keychron, which offer feature-packed mechanical keyboards with hot-swappable switches, RGB lighting, and dedicated volume knobs.
Some keyboards, like Royal Kludge, also offer a small dedicated display that shows useful information such as battery status and connection mode.
However, ASUS Jelly75 bets on its design, with colorful, translucent, rounded keycaps that make it one of the most distinctive-looking keyboards.
The gasket-mounted construction, linear switches, and multi-device connectivity also make it a great everyday companion with a simple plug-and-play device for a productive and attractive-looking desktop setup. However, if you want a fully customizable keyboard experience with a dedicated knob and customizable software, this might be a limitation.

LONDON — Millions of people would have their obesity diagnoses flipped — from having obesity to not, and vice versa — if an alternate way of defining the disease supplanted the standard body mass index measure, according to a new study that argues such an approach could lead to better care for patients.
The study, published Wednesday in the journal Nature, is the latest volley in a debate about the limitations of the body mass index, and what could possibly replace it. BMI is deeply entrenched as a metric, dictating everything from regulatory decisions to insurance coverage to who is eligible for certain medical treatments. But it is a blunt measure that fails to take into account other health issues and differences in body composition, such as where fat is stored.
The new research stems from an effort to come up with a different diagnostic framework. Last year, a Lancet commission proposed a pathway that aimed to identify people whose health is currently being hurt by their weight and who are more likely to have dire outcomes going forward.

As Delhiites burst firecrackers well past the 10 p.m. deadline set by the Supreme Court for Deepavali night, air pollution shot up to over 150-200 times World Health Organisation (WHO) limits in parts of the city, but fell through the early morning hours of Monday (November 9, 2026) due to better weather conditions, show official data.
At the peak of pollution, following the bursting of firecrackers on Sunday night, crucial air quality data were missing from several monitoring stations managed by government authorities. Experts say missing data on peak values of air pollution will artificially show better air quality than the reality.
Though the Supreme Court allowed only green firecrackers during fixed windows on November 7 and 8, traditional firecrackers, which are more polluting, were also available in the markets of Delhi.
As per the Delhi government’s Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) data, the level of PM2.5 (a major pollution) in Patparganj of East Delhi was 2,597 micrograms per cubic metre at 1 a.m. on Monday — about 173.13 times the WHO permissible limit of 15 micrograms per cubic metre for a 24-hour period.
Similarly, the level of PM2.5 in NSUT West Campus was 3,008.4 micrograms per cubic metre at 5 a.m. on Monday — about 200.5 times the WHO permissible limit. PM2.5 (Particulate matter 2.5) are fine inhalable particles, which can get into lungs and bloodstream and lead to a range of respiratory and other diseases.
Favourable wind
Gufran Beig, chair professor, National Institute of Advanced Studies, said though the air pollution spiked around 12 midnight on Sunday to 5 a.m. on Monday due to bursting of firecrackers on Deepavali, both wind direction and speed were very favourable for faster dispersion of air pollution.
“The wind direction was earlier north westerly, originating from stubble burning areas in Punjab and Haryana. But around Sunday afternoon, it changed to easterly and south easterly and also picked up speed by Sunday evening. The reversal of wind direction led to almost negligible effect of stubble burning in Delhi,” said Mr. Beig, who is also the founder-director of the Central government’s SAFAR (System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting Research).
The 24-hour average overall Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi stood at 344 (“very poor”) at 4 p.m. on Monday, lower than 376 (“very poor”) a day earlier, according to the CPCB’s daily bulletin, which is considered the day’s AQI. A higher AQI means worsening of air quality. The overall AQI of Delhi which stood at 370 (very poor) at 9 a.m. on Monday, improved through the day to reach 344 by 4 p.m.
Meanwhile, both the AAP and the Congress attacked the BJP government over the missing data, with the former alleging that it was “data fraud”. Hitting back, Delhi Labour Minister Kapil Mishra alleged there was a “conspiracy” by AAP-governed Punjab to set stubble on fire on Sunday evening.
Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.
Stubble burning in Punjab
Meanwhile, Punjab recorded 1,152 stubble burning incidents on Sunday — the highest this paddy harvest season, according to the Indian Agricultural Research Institute’s (IARI) daily bulletin. But it dropped to 198 on Monday, taking the total this harvest season to 4,657, the second lowest since 2020 (till November 9), the data show.
The contribution of stubble burning in neighbouring States to PM2.5 (a chief pollutant) in Delhi on Sunday was 5.1%, according to the Union Ministry of Earth Sciences data.

Until recently, Cameroon had been one of the most consistent sides from Africa to feature in the FIFA World Cup. Between 1982 and 2014, across nine editions, it played in seven of them.
But in the last three editions, it has missed the berth twice. Its legend, Samuel Eto’o, has made headlines for the wrong reasons as president of the Cameroon FA, and the Indomitable Lions find themselves lost in the savannah, looking for a stage to roar again.
“It’s not only about Cameroon. Heavyweights like Italy didn’t play in the last World Cup. It’s about seizing the moment. When you play qualifiers, you have to capitalise … We didn’t get the points we were supposed to,” laments former Cameroon international Raphael Messi Bouli.
Messi Bouli played for Cameroon in the African Nations Championship (CHAN) and was also part of the national team setup for the 2018 World Cup qualifiers.
“The federation and the new coach are trying to build a new team with young players. This is good. It’s a new policy. They played well in the last Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), and now they are playing in the qualifiers,” he adds.
A fertile hub for football talent
Cameroon is the second-most successful team in the AFCON, with five titles, and plays Namibia on Thursday in the 2027 AFCON qualifiers. The African nation, needless to say, is a fertile land for nurturing some of the icons of the game – the magic of Patrick Mboma (whom Messi Bouli admires), the goals of Samuel Eto’o and the celebrations of Roger Milla.
But it has also exported talent, some of the best in recent times — Samuel Umtiti (a 2018 World Cup winner with France) and Breel Embolo (a FIFA World Cup 2026 quarterfinalist), while the roots of some trace back to the Central African Nation, like Kylian Mbappe (a two-time World Cup finalist) and Aurelien Tchouameni (a UEFA Champions League winner and a World Cup runner-up).

Does that hurt Cameroon’s footballing ambitions? “I don’t think so. You cannot blame them because they have the opportunity to play there. They are also giving back,” Messi Bouli insists, citing examples of Mbappe’s Inspired by KM (IBKM) or Umtiti’s Umantiti, both of which work on humanitarian projects in Cameroon.
“That’s something I’m also proud of. Football is not only what you see, but it’s also what you cannot see behind,” Messi Bouli says.
With great power comes great responsibility
Football has the power to unite people and transform them into heroes overnight. But with great power comes great responsibility. Eto’o, Cameroon’s record goalscorer and a European treble winner with two different clubs, moved into administration after retirement, after hanging up his boots in 2019.
But his leadership, as president of the Cameroonian Football Federation (FECAFOOT), has been marred by match-fixing allegations (2023-24), disciplinary sanctions by FIFA (2024) and, most recently, embezzlement allegations relating to payments by Russia in 2023.
But Messi Bouli believes the former Barcelona and Inter Milan striker at the top of the football body is a step in the right direction. “I think he’s doing well. … not everything is good, but we can see the improvement. And the only thing he needs now is support,” the forward, who now plays for Punjab FC in the Indian Super League, says.
Under Eto’o’s presidency, FECAFOOT invested extensively in resources – financial and infrastructural – to develop grassroots and professionalise clubs, which saw the men’s Under-20 team win gold at the 2023 Francophonie Games, while the women’s U-20 team qualified for the 2024 FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup.
“When you reach somewhere, with the name he has, people expect you to give more, and change things automatically. It’s not like that. Every process takes time. He’s trying to come up with his philosophy to improve Cameroonian football. You have to be patient with him,” Messi Bouli adds.
Cameroon qualified for the World Cup in Eto’o’s first year of presidency, and Messi Bouli believes that when all pieces of the puzzle of development come together, the Indomitable Lions will find their way back to the World Cup four years later.
In the current round, the team has moved on from older veterans like Eric Maxim Choupo-Moting (37), Nicolas Nkoulou (36) and Vincent Aboubakar (34) to younger prospects like Angel Yondjo (19), Geovanni Ndjee (19) and Harouna Djibirin (20).
“There is a good team, a new team with new players. Let’s see. I think we will play in the next World Cup. There is no doubt about that. But we have to work and try to keep going,” Messi Bouli says.

The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150 mph (240 km/h), with winds gusting over 185 mph (296 km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100 mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150 mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

It’s been nearly a decade since Bethesda’s MachineGames released Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus in 2017, and now Xbox is ready to announce a sequel from the studio. Wolfenstein 3 was officially announced today, just days after Bethesda also confirmed that the next Elder Scrolls game will be called The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel.
Xbox announces Wolfenstein 3
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma revealed a new entry in the Wolfenstein series with a brief tease.
In a post, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced the name and a photo of a script. “Looking forward to sharing more,” she said. MachineGames also announced the game in a post, saying the game is “in production” and sharing a photo from a motion-capture session. IGN reports that Brian Bloom (who plays protagonist William Joseph “BJ” Blazkowicz) and Debra Wilson (who plays Grace Walker) are reprising their roles, and they appear to be the featured actors in the photo.
The last mainline entry, Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus, launched in 2017 and continued the story of Blazkowicz in an alternate 1960s where Nazi Germany had won the Second World War. Wolfenstein: Youngblood also debuted in 2019 as a co-op spinoff, starring Blazkowicz’s twin daughters.

Trump truly said the words "nobody has died" regarding the Iran war. However, the brief videos that people shared omitted what Trump said immediately after that remark, including, "This war, seven months, 18 people killed. That includes Venezuela, 18," as well as, "Eighteen is too much." His comments during the interview, as well as during other recent speaking occasions, reflected his effort to draw comparisons between the low number of U.S. casualties during the Iran war and significantly larger figures in past U.S. conflicts.
On Nov. 6, U.S. President Donald Trump sat down for an interview with "60 Minutes" correspondent Ross Douthat. The interview covered a wide range of topics, including Republicans' losses in the midterm elections, the wars in Iran and Ukraine and the economy.
CBS News published a transcript and the edited broadcast version of the Trump sit-down on Nov. 8, as well as a full transcript and unedited interview. The broadcast segment lasted 27 minutes, whereas the full interview spanned 52 minutes.
That same evening, the Democratic Party's rapid response X account, FactPost (@factpostnews), posted (archived) a 14-second video with the caption, "Trump on the Iran War: Nobody has died. It's not a war." The video shows Trump saying: "Nobody has died. You know, when you call it a war, it's not a war. If you look at what's happened with Iran, in the last six months, five months, six months, we haven't lost one soldier. You know, I wrote one thing down. I think it's intere—."
The Democratic National Committee later posted a shortened version of that same clip on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and other platforms, omitting the last several seconds. The posts were overlaid with the text, "Trump blatantly lies about Iran war: 'Nobody has died.'"
Snopes readers asked us whether Trump made the remark as presented in the videos.
Because Trump truly said "nobody has died" while speaking about the Iran war, we've rated this claim a correct attribution. However, the brief videos shared on social media omitted what he said immediately after that remark, including, "This war, seven months, 18 people killed. That includes Venezuela, 18," as well as, "Eighteen is too much."
Those remarks about the number of deaths did not appear in posts making the claim on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and other platforms.
Trump's comments from that portion of the interview, as well as during other recent speaking occasions, reflected his effort to draw comparisons between the low number of U.S. casualties during the Iran war and significantly larger figures in past conflicts. His remarks also advanced the talking point that the deaths that did occur happened near the beginning of the war and not during the more-recent five or six months.
Snopes contacted the DNC to ask why it omitted Trump's subsequent remarks from its post, as well as the White House to request comment. The DNC declined to comment. We will update this article if we receive further information.
Casualties during Iran war
The Defense Department's Defense Casualty Analysis System website, which hosts information about service members who died or were wounded in action, reported 15 deaths — seven hostile and eight non-hostile — as well as 417 injuries, all hostile, during "Operation Epic Fury," the U.S. military's name for the Iran war.
According to the data, 14 of those deaths occurred in March, in Iraq, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. The remaining death is reported as happening in the Arabian Sea in July, making false Trump's claim that "nobody has died" in the last five or six months.
The same website also listed eight deaths (only six displaying names), four hostile and four non-hostile, and 450 injuries, all hostile, categorized under "overseas operations" for the entire year, including in Iraq, Jordan, Qatar and United Arab Emirates.
We located further data about 21 deceased service members on Military.com. We contacted the Defense Department to ask questions, including about the status of the two missing names, and will update this story if we receive a response.
The U.S. casualties were only a very small percentage of the many thousands of deaths reported across the Middle East during the war, including hundreds of children.
Transcript of Trump's comments
In the full interview, Trump spoke about crime in Washington, D.C., then transitioned to the Iran war and military action in Venezuela, saying, "And, by the way, nobody has died" (bolded emphasis shows comments from the FactPost video):
TRUMP: They love me, and, by the way, speaking of that, the crime rate in Washington, D.C., is down 89%. It's the safest, and when I was here it was a killing field, three murders a week. Now we haven't had a murder in a long time. And, by the way, nobody has died. You know, when you call it a war, it's not a war. If you look at what's happened with Iran, in the last six months, five months, six months, we haven't lost one soldier. You know, I wrote one thing down. I think it's interesting. I just wrote it. I just looked at it this morning. So we've been in Iran seven months, maybe eight months. There have been 18 people, and that includes Venezuela, two wars. Venezuela where, by the way, we've taken out 50 times what the war has cost already. To the victor belong the spoils. But listen just one second.
DOUTHAT: Yeah, I'm listening.
TRUMP: Afghanistan, 20 years, thousands of people killed. Iraq War, nine years, 5,000 people killed. Vietnam, 21 years, 60,000 people killed. The Korean War, four years, 40,000 people killed.
DOUTHAT: This is, this is a good segue …
TRUMP: This war, wait …
DOUTHAT: Yeah?
TRUMP: This war, seven months, 18 people killed. That includes Venezuela, 18. Now, now, I, I, I want to just …
DOUTHAT: This is a good segue to my last question.
TRUMP: OK, but just sec.
DOUTHAT: Yeah, I, I hear you. I hear you …
TRUMP: Eighteen is too much, but you're talking about 40,000, 50,000, 60,000.
DOUTHAT: I, I agree that the Iran war has had many fewer casualties than past American wars.
TRUMP: And, but what did we get? What did we get? No nuclear. We won, and there will be no nuclear. And they didn't get anything. Those wars were lost. And they lost 60,000.
The above remarks begin at the 47:07 mark in the unedited "60 Minutes" interview YouTube video.
Trump's past remarks about casualties
In similar remarks, Trump spoke to members of the media in Palm Beach, Florida, on Nov. 8, saying, "Again, we haven't lost anybody. No soldiers been lost. If you look at Vietnam and if you look at all these others, there were for many years with thousands, tens of thousands of people killed, soldiers with us. So, we've gone two wars."
The DNC's FactPost account highlighted those remarks in a video post (archived), again ending the trimmed clip just before Trump continued commenting about losing 18 soldiers and that one loss "is too many."
Speaking about Iran and Venezuela, he continued (at 5:01), "We've lost, and by the way, one is too many. But we've lost 18 soldiers in two wars. And the one war is seven months. The other one was 58, 48 minutes."
On Nov. 9, Trump once again spoke about the low number of casualties in the Iran war during a news conference at the White House, specifically citing a number of deaths.
In September, Trump also corrected his own commerce secretary about the number of service members who died during the Iran war, posting on Truth Social, "Sec. Lutnick had Venezuela on his mind when he said nobody was killed. 18 people were killed in Iran!"
For further reading, we previously reported about a false rumor claiming Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed made a remark on "60 Minutes" about young girls seeing male genitals in locker rooms.

One in three students across the globe experiences bullying every month, while one in 10 faces cyber bullying, the UNESCO said, warning that AI is accelerating new forms of technology-facilitated violence (TFV).
UNESCO's new policy brief, ‘Connected and Safe’, shows that nudification apps, voice cloning, automated harassment and AI companion apps used for grooming are now surfacing in school-based incidents across multiple regions.
The United Nations agency has called upon countries to invest in digital safety measures, teacher preparation, and mental health support for students, in coordination with technology companies.
According to Khaled El-Enany, director-general of UNESCO, one in three learners experience bullying every month, while one in ten face cyber bullying. Behind these figures are millions of children whose education, health and well-being are at risk, with consequences that can extend far beyond the classroom.
"Online and technology-facilitated violence (TFV) is no longer a peripheral concern for education systems. It is part of the reality of school life for many learners, with direct consequences for safety, well-being, participation and learning. Around one in ten learners worldwide has experienced cyber bullying, and across 44 countries in Europe, Central Asia and North America, prevalence rose from 12 to 15 per cent between 2018 and 2022, among both boys and girls," the policy brief said.
"Some learners are more exposed than others. Girls, learners with disabilities, learners of diverse sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, and those marginalised by socio-economic status or geography face distinct and often more severe forms of harm," it said.
In the context of bullying, data shows that girls are just as likely as boys to experience bullying, although the types of bullying differ.
"Boys are generally more exposed to physical bullying and violence, while girls are more exposed to psychological bullying, particularly through cyber bullying and appearance-based bullying. Sexual bullying (sexual jokes, comments and gestures) affects boys and girls at similar rates.
"Physical sexual violence (assault, harassment and rape) can affect both boys and girls, but girls are more likely to experience this form of violence. Corporal punishment and all forms of violent discipline are also influenced by gender, with boys more likely to experience physical corporal punishment than girls and learners likely to be punished to reinforce expectations regarding behaviours deemed socially appropriate for each gender," the brief said.
UNESCO argued that responsibility for safer digital environments for students must be shared between governments, technology companies, platforms and regulators, as schools alone cannot face this issue.
"Safer schools require sustained investment in teacher preparation, mental health and psychosocial support, reporting and response systems, digital safety measures, and coordinated action across education, child protection, health and technology sectors.
"UNESCO recently launched the process towards a new global recommendation on young people and digital environments in the age of AI, to ensure that these technologies protect children's rights and well-being, strengthen critical thinking and empower them to shape their own future," it said.
