Srinagar– The Jammu and Kashmir Cabinet will meet on Friday to take a final call on several proposals submitted by different government departments.
Sources said that Chief Minister Omar Abdullah will chair the meeting at 3:30 pm.
The meeting comes against the backdrop of dissent among a section of NC legislators following the October 27 Cabinet expansion, with several MLAs seeking a comprehensive reshuffle and raising concerns over ministerial representation and the functioning of the government.
The legislators had also sought the removal of the Chief Minister’s adviser, greater coordination between ministers and elected representatives, and time-bound implementation of the party’s election promises.
In a recent move to address the concerns, NC president Farooq Abdullah has initiated the process of forming informal advisory groups of MLAs for each minister. The groups are expected to act as a bridge between the party and the government.
This will be the first Cabinet meeting since the Darbar Move shifted the government offices to Jammu for the winter months.
Further details about the agenda were not immediately available.

An eight-year-old boy diagnosed with Type II achalasia – a rare disorder that affects the ability to swallow food and liquids – has undergone a Perora-l Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM) procedure at Rela Hospital.
Achalasia affects the nerves controlling the muscles of the oesophagus, causing the lower oesophageal sphincter – a muscular valve connecting the food pipe to the stomach – to remain abnormally tight. This prevents food and liquids from passing normally into the stomach. The condition is estimated to affect 0.1 to 0.18 children per 100,000 annually.
The child had progressively worsening difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids. Following the procedure, he was able to resume consuming clear liquids and subsequently, a soft diet, within 24 hours.
POEM involves passing an endoscope through the mouth and creating a small tunnel within the oesophageal wall to reach and divide the muscle fibres causing the obstruction. Unlike conventional surgery, the procedure does not require external incisions or stitches.
S.N.K. Chenduran, senior consultant and endoscopic surgeon, Department of Medical Gastroenterology, performed the procedure, which took about 50 minutes. He said performing POEM in children required particular precision because of the smaller dimensions of the oesophagus and the delicate tissues.
Dinesh Jothimani, director, Hepatology and Medical Gastroenterology, said persistent swallowing difficulties, regurgitation, vomiting, and unexplained weight loss in children warranted medical evaluation.

Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when the Ecuadorian journalist was shot dead.
Beltrán ran a Facebook page with news about Calceta, a small city in the province of Manabí, whose Pacific coastline has made it a key flashpoint in the gang warfare over drug trafficking routes that has transformed one of Latin America’s safest countries into one of its most violent.
Police and the public prosecutor’s office have not said much about the case, and little was known about the killers except that they were armed and then fled the scene. It was also unclear whether the crime was linked to Beltrán’s work, though he had previously reported allegations of corruption involving local authorities.
Regardless, many press freedom groups already cite his murder as the latest example of how conditions for journalists have deteriorated dramatically in Ecuador. Six journalists were killed in the country last year alone.
Artur Romeu, Reporters Without Borders’ Latin America director, said in a statement that months ago Beltrán had told the organisation “about his fears and the threats he was receiving”.
“We took part in efforts to get him to safety,” he said, adding that Beltrán had been placed in a protection programme run by the public prosecutor’s office, although it was not known whether that protection was still in place when he was killed.
“Reporters Without Borders calls on the public prosecutor’s office to investigate as a priority whether there is a link to his journalistic work, identify any possible masterminds and protect his family and colleagues,” said Romeu.
The Ecuadorian civil society organisation Fundación Periodistas Sin Cadenas (FPSC) reported that at least 19 journalists have had to go into exile since gang violence exploded in 2023. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, it has become a major trafficking hub, particularly through the Pacific.
Journalists have received death threats with photographs of their homes and details of their routines and families.
“Practising journalism in Ecuador is now an extremely high-risk job,” said María Fernanda Almeida, a project coordinator at FPSC, adding that all of last year’s killings of journalists “remain completely unpunished”.
“And one of the many terrible effects of this violence is self-censorship: at least in the coastal provinces, colleagues no longer want to report on violence,” she added.
Almeida said another problem for journalists has been the stance of the government of the far-right president Daniel Noboa, who has responded to the surge in crime with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, repeatedly declaring states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces in measures that have been widely criticised by human rights groups.
While covering military operations, reporters have had their phones confiscated, a search warrant was executed at a reporter’s home and a journalist was threatened by soldiers simply for filming them stopping university students.
There have also been several reports that Noboa, one of US president Donald Trump’s key allies in Latin America, has pressured media organisations to dismiss journalists critical of him, including the columnist Roberto Aguilar, who said he was fired from the newspaper Diario Expreso after the government reportedly threatened private advertisers with audits if they continued advertising with the outlet.
Noboa’s administration did not respond to requests for comment.
“I don’t think there is complete freedom of expression in Ecuador today,” said Almeida. “And that is very worrying because the more violence and silencing there is, the more journalism is needed.”

Phage therapy, which uses bacteriophages to selectively eliminate harmful bacteria, holds significant potential in combating antimicrobial resistance (AMR), said Dr. Kalyan Chakravarthy Koganti, sepsis and infectious diseases specialist at SHRI Hospital, Guntur.
He said this while sharing his research experience during a press release, after presenting his team's scientific findings at an international symposium jointly organised by the Chinese University of Hong Kong and reputed biomedical research journals.
Dr. Kalyan said his team's research presentation on phage therapy received appreciation from participants at the symposium. Dr. Sutharsan Govindarajan, associate professor and phage biologist, SRM University-A.P., also presented research conducted by the team.
He described the event as an enriching learning experience, particularly the discussions on the wider applications of bacteriophages in diagnostics and therapy, including cancer research. Chuanbin Mao, chair of the symposium, has been researching bacteriophages for 25 years and has contributed extensively to scientific literature, he said.
Dr. Kalyan noted that bacteriophages selectively target disease-causing bacteria without harming human beings, making them promising alternatives when antibiotics fail.
His team has administered phage therapy to a few patients at its centre with encouraging results. In collaboration with SRM University-A.P. and Szeged University, Hungary, the team has been working to advance its availability in India.

Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
- Published
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.
It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.
The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.
Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.
Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.
Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.
It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.
Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.
On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.
Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.
Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.
His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.
Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.
Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.
Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.
All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.
On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

United is restricting AI agents from booking flights
The airline believes AI poses security risks and may violate DOT and FAA rules.
United Airlines has announced it will change ticking policies to restrict AI agents' from booking flights through its website, third-party travel agencies and flight aggregators. The airline joins a growing number of businesses, including JPMorgan Chase and Amazon, which block agents from using their products to avoid the security and privacy issues associated with them.
Giving something like your payment details or log-in credentials to an agent can expose sensitive information and lead to "unintended purchases, account changes or use of MileagePlus miles," United says. Allowing an AI agent to complete a booking could also violate existing airline regulations from the Department of Transportation and Federal Aviation Administration. For example, United says only a human can acknowledge that their bag doesn't contain explosives during flight check-in.
United would like to avoid association with any agent-based embarrassments, for instance when Meta's Muse leaked a user's address online. Like other companies, it also wants to keep AI from getting in the way of its relationship with customers. The Wall Street Journal reports that United CEO Scott Kirby has been open about the company's reluctance to jump into agentic commerce. "To be honest, I don't want to create another middleman," Kirby said at an event on Tuesday. Not every airline feels the same way: Southwest created a plugin so users can book flights with ChatGPT.
Luckily for United and other companies blocking AI agents, agentic commerce might not be taking off with regular people. During its recent third-quarter earnings call, Uber shared that it handled 320 million trips and deliveries during the week of Halloween; of those, AI agents were responsible for 500 Uber Eats orders and only four rides. Those aren't exactly industry-destroying numbers.
Handing an AI your credit card is very different from handing it your email login, and both are different from just asking it to send you a news summary every morning. Even if a large number of people are downloading apps like Muse, it seems like letting an agent shop for you isn't as frictionless or foolproof as it needs to be to catch on.

Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
- Published
Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.
Some 1,800 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported receiving a similar threat to one that created chaos in Italy on Wednesday - even though no devices have been found anywhere.
The Italian government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated".
Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.
On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.
The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.
Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.
Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".
Some officials say it originated in Taiwan.
A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.

John D. “Jay” Rockefeller IV, the progeny of one of America’s most famous and wealthiest families, who during three decades in the U.S. Senate sought expanded healthcare for the poor and excoriated President George W. Bush’s handling of the Iraq War, died on Friday (November 6, 2026) at his home in Washington, the Washington Post reported. He was 89.
His family did not provide a cause, the newspaper added.
Mr. Rockefeller, a tall, soft-spoken Democrat with liberal views, was elected in 1984 to the first of his five six-year terms representing West Virginia in the Senate after two terms as Governor of the poor coal-mining State.
Mr. Rockefeller voted in 2002 in favour of the Republican Bush’s measure authorising the Iraq war, which began with a U.S.-led invasion in 2003. He later expressed regret over that vote and, as head of the Senate intelligence committee, accused Mr. Bush of taking the nation to war on “false premises.”
He was a great-grandson of oil tycoon John D. Rockefeller and the scion of a family that formed a political dynasty that included his uncle, New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller.
Initiatives in public office
New York-born Jay Rockefeller’s life changed direction after he graduated from Harvard and served in a national service program in impoverished rural West Virginia from 1964 to 1966.
When he was put in public office, he worked to increase healthcare access, fight poverty, provide health benefits to coal miners and assist military veterans. As a senator, he had a role in shaping the programme created in 1997 under which the U.S. government helps States provide medical coverage for millions of uninsured children.
Mr. Rockefeller backed Democratic President Bill Clinton’s failed proposal for near-universal health insurance coverage in the 1990s and then fought for Democratic President Barack Obama’s successful quest for a healthcare overhaul law, signed in 2010.
In the debate over Mr. Obama’s measure, Mr. Rockefeller unsuccessfully sought to have the federal government offer a medical insurance program to the general population — in addition to existing programs for the poor and elderly — as an alternative to private insurance plans that could be costly and exclusive.
“Championing those most in need has been my life’s calling and I will never stop fighting to make a difference for the people who mean so much to me,” Mr. Rockefeller said in 2013 when he announced at age 75 he would not seek a sixth Senate term.
On the Iraq war
Before the Iraq invasion, Mr. Bush’s administration built the case for war by touting intelligence indicating Iraq owned an arsenal of weapons of mass destruction — they actually did not exist — and alleged ties between Iraqi leaders and the al Qaeda network responsible for the September 11, 2001, attacks on the U.S.
“If I had known then what I know now, I would have voted against it,” Mr. Rockefeller told the Charleston Gazette newspaper in 2004, referring to the 2002 war authorization measure.
“I think the intelligence was shaped,” he continued. “And I think the interpretation of the intelligence was shaped. You had a president who we now know was determined to go to war.”
‘Fundamentally misleading’
A report from the intelligence committee issued in 2008, when he served as its chairman, asserted that Mr. Bush, Vice President Dick Cheney and other leading officials exaggerated intelligence findings and ignored disputes within U.S. intelligence circles about Iraq’s weapons and the hotly disputed ties to al Qaeda.
The report rejected pre-war statements by Mr. Bush and Cheney that Iraq might give al Qaeda weapons of mass destruction.
“Representing to the American people that the two had an operational partnership and posed a single, indistinguishable threat was fundamentally misleading and led the nation to war on false premises,” Mr. Rockefeller said as the report was released.
During his Senate tenure, he also headed the Commerce, Science, and Transportation and Veterans Affairs committees.
Wealthy family
Mr. Rockefeller was born on June 18, 1937, weeks after the death of his great-grandfather, who had been America’s richest man.
The Rockefeller name came with high expectations. His father was a famous philanthropist. His uncle Nelson served as U.S. vice president, as well as Governor of New York. His uncle David Rockefeller headed Chase Manhattan Bank and uncle Winthrop Rockefeller was governor of Arkansas.
He was elected to West Virginia’s legislature in 1966 before age 30, then elected West Virginia’s Secretary of State in 1968.
He lost a bid to become Governor in 1972, then served as a college president before being elected Governor in 1976. Mr. Rockefeller, who became one of the wealthiest members of the U.S. Congress, spent millions of dollars of his own money to bankroll his successful campaign for the US Senate in 1984.
Mr. Rockefeller sometimes found himself overshadowed by his State’s other senator, Robert Byrd, who died in 2010 at age 92 as the longest-serving member of Congress in U.S. history.
He usually backed his State’s coal and steel industries but angered coal executives in 2012 by fighting Republican efforts to prevent regulation of emissions from coal-fired power plants.
He was married to public television executive Sharon Percy Rockefeller, with whom he had four children.

- Rockstar Games has officially joined Douyin, China's version of TikTok, to promote GTA 6.
- Its first video promotes GTA 6 pre-loading ahead of the November 19, 2026, launch.
- Rockstar previously joined Bilibili in 2023 and is now expanding its presence on Chinese social media.
Rockstar Games is expanding its GTA 6 marketing campaign in China. The company has reportedly joined Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, ahead of the game’s November 19, 2026 release. Its first video promotes the game’s upcoming launch and pre-loading availability on both PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.
According to a November 12 report by GamerSky, Rockstar’s Douyin account is officially verified under the name “ROCKSTAR INTERNATIONAL LIMITED,” with its IP location listed as Shanghai, China. The account is still relatively new, with a small follower count and just one video posted so far.
The video has been adapted into a vertical format to suit Douyin’s short-video platform and features GTA 6 protagonists Jason and Lucia. The timing also lines up with the start of GTA 6 pre-loads on November 10 for players who pre-ordered the game. The download requires up to 212 GB of available storage, depending on the console.
This is not Rockstar’s first entry into Chinese social media. The company previously joined Bilibili in 2023, where it has promoted games from the Grand Theft Auto Online and Red Dead Redemption franchises. Its arrival on Douyin gives Rockstar another major platform to reach Chinese gaming audiences.
Rockstar has also been promoting GTA 6 through massive billboards and murals across major cities worldwide. The company recently partnered with West Coast Customs to bring the in-game Grotti Cheetah to life as a custom-built supercar. The vehicle is currently on display at Selfridges in London, with a price tag of £1 million.
Despite its growing presence on Chinese social media, Rockstar has not announced an official mainland China release for GTA 6. Previous titles in the franchise also lacked official releases in the country. Chinese players could still access the games on PC through the international version of Steam or on consoles through imported copies.

Robertson set to make history, but hero Dalglish will always be King
- Published
Andy Robertson says it gives him "goosebumps" any time he thinks about it.
Friday at Hampden, North Macedonia the visitors, a 102nd cap to be won and, when it is, he'll be level in the pantheon with Sir Kenny Dalglish, the football man he loves more than any other.
On Monday in St Gallen, Switzerland - all being well - Robertson will break the great man's record, a mark that has stood for 40 years.
The Tottenham left-back is sitting in the boardroom at Queen's Park in the shadow of Hampden with a phone in his hand and eyes fixed on his 19-year-old self coming off the bench in Warsaw on 5 March, 2014.
"Nervous, excited, living the dream, not knowing what road I was on," he smiles as he looks at the moment he takes his first touch in international football.
"As I was going on, Gordon [Strachan, Scotland manager] said to me, 'remember why you're here, play like you play at Dundee United, don't play safe'. The first ball, when it came to me, I just drove forward about 30, 40 yards.
"I had pretty much every emotion that day. My mum and dad were there. My brother. My aunt and uncle. My other uncle. There's a picture of me and my brother [Stephen] at the airport after the game. He had a big Poland hat on and a half-and-half scarf. He was well oiled by that point."
'I've never actually been confident'
Robertson says he'd have laughed out loud had you told him then what lay ahead of him - two Premier Leagues, two League Cups, an FA Cup, a Champions League, a Super Cup, a Club World Cup, soon-to-be the most capped male Scottish players in history and, by a mile, the one with the most games as captain of the men's team.
"I've never actually been confident," he says, which is a surprise admission given everything he's done.
Maybe what he means is that he always had a quiet belief in his own ability but found that constantly questioning himself was who he was and who maybe who he still is.
"I've always doubted myself and that's always got the best out of me. I've always tried to prove people wrong and prove myself wrong. The one thing I didn't do was look too far ahead. I always just lived in the here and now and that's served me well."
In the room where he's talking there are a dozen normal chairs and away to the side, detached from the rest, is an elaborate seat. A high-backed, ornate, somewhat regal affair.
It looks fit for a king and, given the history Robertson's about to make, maybe he should plonk himself in it. And that brings us back to the man whose record he's about to match and surpass.
"There are normal seats but there's one throne and Kenny Dalglish should be sat on it," he says. "Friday night's not about me. Friday night's about the greatest player of all time in our country, and for me, that will always be Kenny.
"He's had this record for so long. He deserves it. If he played in a different era, he would probably have played a number of games that wouldn't have been able to be caught.
"Sometimes - not as a criticism - as a country we're maybe not good at recognising how good people we've got are. For me, he's the best player to ever play with Scotland and arguably Britain.
"We have to appreciate that man because I certainly do, my family certainly do and, I think on Friday, I'll have him at the front of my mind, the back of my mind and I'm not really bothered about myself."
It's a lovely thing, that. Robertson, about to draw level with Dalglish, is only thinking about Dalglish.
The depth of feeling comes tumbling out of him when he starts telling stories about what King Kenny means to his family and how he seemingly created a miracle by momentarily curing Robertson's beloved late grandfather's hearing.
"I always remember my agent talking to me about the first time he met Liverpool," Robertson says of a time when he was still with Hull but about to move to Anfield.
"He met the chief scout and sporting director and all of a sudden Kenny 'accidentally' walked into the room. It was 100% planned, I know it was planned.

"One of the things right at the top of the list for me was the fact [by joining Liverpool] I got to meet Kenny in person and I've actually got to have a relationship with him and his family, because his family are special.

"Bear in mind his grandson's just qualified for another Champions League final and he basically barged me out of the way and shook Kenny's hand.
"My grandad had hearing aids. He couldn't really hear much of us but he heard everything Kenny said, so it did open a lot of questions in the family as to how bad the ear problem was with my grandad. He's no longer with us but to see how happy he was… Kenny was his hero."

On the pitch and off, the transfer to Liverpool as a 23-year-old was the greatest move he could have possibly made.
In reflective mood, on the cusp of Scottish football history, Robertson talks about his mother and father and his brother. "They're as proud of my brother as they are of me," he said. "The exact same, whatever achievements we have. But I think they're more proud of the men we've become. That was always most important for me.
"Anyone who knows me, my family, my friends, I always want them to like the person first, the footballer second. Anyone that only wants to know me as the footballer, then I don't let them get too close but if they want to know me as the person first and foremost, then they're the people that are really in my close circle.
"I've still got the same friends I went to nursery with at three years old. Three of my best friends."

Robertson says he often thinks about the game in Scotland and whether young kids today are getting the kind of opportunities he got. "We talk about that - my story, John McGinn's story, Ryan Christie's story," Robertson said.

"It's about trying to protect the 15, 16, 17-year-olds just now and we all have a duty to help with that. We always want the young players to come in and I just love their energy, I love how excited they are. Findlay Curtis just bounces about all the time.
"These are the kids that are going to bring the country forward. They're all sitting at the other end of the table playing games we don't even know about but it's great for us to sit back and go, 'OK, we're part of this squad, but when we leave, then hopefully Scotland will be in a good place."

National Drugs Act's stringent restrictions cannot override personal liberty, says Supreme Court
The court noted that the accused, Arshdeep Singh, had been in custody since May 2020, and although charges were recently framed, the trial was yet to commence.
Keeping an accused behind bars for more than six years without the trial even beginning amounts to “punishment in itself”, the Supreme Court has held, terming the state of affairs “unacceptable” and reminding courts that even the rigours of special laws must yield to the constitutional right to personal liberty.
“Keeping an accused incarcerated without trial for more than six years itself amounts to punishment, which is unacceptable,” said a bench of justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu in a recent order, as it granted bail to a man arrested in a narcotics case.
The bench was categorical that the stringent restrictions under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act cannot override the constitutional guarantee of personal liberty.
Court takes note of case
The court noted that the accused, Arshdeep Singh, had been in custody since May 16, 2020, and although charges were recently framed, the trial was yet to commence. It also noted that he had no prior criminal antecedents. It pointed out that in such a case, the rigours of Section 37 of the NDPS Act must yield to Article 21 of the Constitution, which protects the right to personal liberty.
Setting aside an Allahabad High Court order from July 28, 2025, which had rejected Singh’s second bail application, the apex court directed his release on bail subject to conditions imposed by the trial court.
Section 37 of the NDPS Act imposes stringent twin conditions for granting bail in cases involving commercial quantities of narcotic substances. Where the prosecution opposes bail, the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the accused is not guilty and is unlikely to commit an offence while on bail. The provision is designed to make bail difficult in drug-trafficking cases. However, the Supreme Court’s intervention underscores that these restrictions cannot become a justification for indefinite pre-trial incarceration.
Interception of the accused by NCB
Singh was arrested by the Narcotics Control Bureau on May 16, 2020, after a truck in which he was travelling was intercepted on GT Road. Investigators claimed to have recovered 31kg of opium concealed in plastic bags in the truck. The prosecution alleged that the contraband was in his conscious and constructive possession, while Singh maintained that he was merely driving the vehicle and had no knowledge of the substance allegedly concealed in it.
His first bail application was rejected by the high court in July 2022. When he approached the court again, he argued, among other things, that the mandatory procedure under Section 52A of the NDPS Act, governing the disposal and documentation of seized narcotic substances, had not been followed.
The high court rejected this argument, relying on a Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling, which held that delayed compliance or non-compliance with Section 52A, by itself, would neither vitiate a trial nor constitute a standalone ground for granting bail. It also found no fresh ground warranting reconsideration of Singh’s plea, apart from the period of incarceration.

Apart from emphasising the quantum of recovery and that Singh was allegedly in conscious possession of the contraband, the high court also relied on the statutory restrictions under Section 37 and rejected his plea.
The Supreme Court, however, considered the prolonged incarceration and the absence of progress in the trial decisive, underscoring that the severity of an accusation cannot, by itself, justify keeping an undertrial in prison for years without bringing the case to trial.
The bench also made Singh’s liberty conditional on his diligent attendance at trial and directed that any breach of bail conditions, including attempts to influence witnesses, could lead to cancellation of bail.

As Delhi continues to battle toxic air, one home in the national capital is drawing attention for maintaining an indoor Air Quality Index (AQI) of around 10-15. The residents, Peter Singh and Neeno Kaur, have created a green living space with approximately 15,000 plants, filtered air and an aquaponics-based farming system. The couple's home has come into focus again amid worsening pollution in Delhi-NCR, where restrictions under Stage III of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) remain in force. According to an India Today report, the couple have developed a clean-air ecosystem inside their home, using air filtration, extensive greenery and a system that allows them to grow much of their own food. Peter Satwant Singh, 81, and his wife Neeno Kaur, 72, are Delhi-based urban farmers who live in Sainik Farms, South Delhi. The couple moved to the locality in 1989, after Neeno was diagnosed with chronic leukaemia and needed treatment at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), according to The Week. Their journey towards sustainable living began with Neeno's health struggles. After chemotherapy affected her lungs, the couple explored ways to improve their living environment and adopted an organic lifestyle. They later developed an extensive home-based farming system using aquaponics, which combines fish farming with soil-free plant cultivation. Singh holds a PhD in topology in mathematics from Delhi University’s St Stephen’s College, as per Hindustan Times. The couple describe themselves as urban farmers and also conduct online classes to share their knowledge of aquaponics, growing vegetables and composting. The couple's home in South Delhi's Sainik Farms has around 15,000 plants, which form a major part of its green ecosystem. Their approach combines traditional construction techniques, indoor greenery and systems designed to reduce dependence on external resources. A report by The Better India in 2024 stated the house maintained an AQI reading of around 15. It also highlighted the couple's use of aquaponics, a method that combines fish farming with soil-free plant cultivation. Their aquaponics arrangement includes four large fish tanks. Water containing nutrients from the fish tanks is circulated to the plants, which absorb the nutrients and help filter the water before it returns to the tanks. The system reportedly uses around 1,000 litres of water daily, with water being recycled. The couple also grow vegetables, maize and herbs at home. Kitchen waste is converted into organic fertiliser, while rainwater harvesting and greywater recycling help reduce water wastage. Neeno's health concerns were among the reasons behind the couple's decision to change their lifestyle. The Better India reported that the initiative began after she was diagnosed with cancer. The couple subsequently focused on creating a healthier environment and growing organic food. "We want to show that this is how we live. If we can do it, anyone can do it," Neeno told The Better India. The couple's clean-air home stands in contrast to the pollution situation across Delhi-NCR. On Thursday, Delhi recorded an AQI of 321 at 7 am, placing it in the 'very poor' category, according to Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data cited by ANI. Several monitoring stations recorded readings above 350. The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) invoked Stage III of GRAP across the entire NCR on November 6, after Delhi's daily average AQI reached 382. The commission said forecasts from the India Meteorological Department and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology indicated that air quality was likely to deteriorate into the 'severe' category in the following days. Stage III measures include restrictions on non-essential construction and demolition activities, in addition to measures under the first two stages. The CAQM also urged residents to use cleaner transport, combine journeys, avoid coal and wood for heating, and follow work-from-home and hybrid-schooling directions where applicable. Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): A huge learning gap among students in state government schools from Classes 2 to 5 has been exposed in an internal assessment of the Rajya Shiksha Kendra (RSK), which found that only around 20 per cent of children are performing at the learning level expected for their respective classes.
This means nearly 80 per cent of students assessed are yet to achieve grade-appropriate competencies, raising concerns over students being promoted to higher classes without acquiring basic skills in reading, writing and mathematics. Approximately 27 lakh students study in Classes 2 to 5 in government schools.
The RSK issued directives to district project coordinators regarding this on November 10. The directives state that the learning levels of children were found to be below the expected class-wise standards in the assessment. A special programme will be conducted for students. Class 1 students have been excluded because their school learning begins at the foundational level and they are already being covered through the regular foundational learning process.
Special 90-day programme will be held
In response to the poor learning outcomes, the RSK has directed schools to launch a special 90-day learning reinforcement programme for students of Classes 2 to 5. The initiative, scheduled to run from November 16 to February 16, will focus on strengthening basic competencies in Hindi, English and mathematics.
Focus on listening, speaking, reading and writing in English
The English reinforcement module focuses on all four language skills: listening, speaking, reading and writing. It suggests activities to improve children s familiarity with letters, letter sounds, words, sentence formation and basic reading.
Teachers cautioned against scolding or comparing students
The State Education Centre has also issued instructions on classroom behaviour during the programme. Teachers have been asked not to scold or embarrass children, compare their performance with that of classmates, or put pressure on them to complete all learning targets in a single day. They have been directed to begin teaching from each child s current learning level, appreciate small improvements, ensure active participation and maintain a positive classroom environment.

Australia captain Pat Cummins has described as “utter nonsense” claims from ex-teammate Usman Khawaja that he knew about using sandpaper to tamper with a ball in a 2018 cheating scandal that rocked cricket.
Cummins held an extraordinary news conference Friday (November 13, 2026) to address allegations made in Usman Khawaja's autobiography, published this week, hours ahead of Australia's home-season opening one-day international against England in Perth.
Khawaja has said he published his account, which the whole team knew about, of the plot to support the three players who received unprecedented, lengthy bans from the sport as a result of the so-called Sandpapergate scandal.
He's had support from one of them — his longtime friend and fellow top-order batter David Warner, who posted on social media that the Cricket Australia investigation at the time was rushed and botched.
Cummins, who was part of the bowling attack in that test at Cape Town against South Africa, rejected it and accused Khawaja of being “casual” and “flippant” with his claims.
“When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he’s 100% wrong,” Cummins told a packed news conference in Sydney. “I’ve said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.
“But I think Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper.
“That’s complete and utter nonsense.”
Cummins said he was prepared to answer questions all day if required, because he didn't want the topic to be dredged up again every time a book was published or another claim made.
After an hour, a cricket administrator suggested the news conference wind down, but Cummins again invited all questions to continue for as long as needed.
Steve Smith and Warner — the captain and vice-captain in that series eight years ago — were each banned for 12 months by Cricket Australia following an investigation into the cheating plot.
Cameron Bancroft, who was caught on TV footage using sandpaper on the ball during the test match, was banned for nine months.
Cricket Australia, team management and other players have rarely commented on the saga. The bowling group has rejected claims that everyone was in on the plot to use sandpaper to help make the ball “reverse” — or swing unconventionally through the air.
But in his autobiography, Khawaja said he was sitting beside Bancroft in the locker rooms at one stage and learned of a plot to tamper with the ball and urged caution.
Cummins on Friday turned the scenario back on Khawaja, who retired from the test team earlier this year.
“I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out that Usman admitted that he told Cam to be careful when using sandpaper,” he said.
“That’s not the Usman that I know. It’s not the Usman that I think has been part of a team that’s helped rebuild the Australian cricket culture over the last eight years,” he said. “And the one that would have stopped that from happening there and then.”

Two days after Diwali was celebrated across India, on November 10, Tuesday, the nation woke up to grim newspaper headlines and reports highlighting the sharp deterioration of air quality across major cities. According to reports, 93 Indian cities appeared among the world’s 100 most polluted locations, several parts of Delhi reportedly witnessed a staggering Air Quality Index (AQI) of 3,000+, and six cities recorded an AQI above 1,000 at 9 pm on Diwali night.
Newspaper reports suggested that despite bans and restrictions, the bursting of firecrackers remained untethered across states, resulting in not only a severe surge in air pollution, but major fire accidents, noise pollution, and several people, stray animals and birds suffering burn injuries.
The front page of the Delhi edition of The Times of India on Tuesday led with a report headlined ‘Delhi pollution on Diwali rockets to worst in 5 yrs’.
“Delhi saw its most polluted Diwali day in five years, with AQI touching 376 at 4pm Nov 8, the worst since 2021. The city, however, narrowly escaped its worst post-Diwali pollution day in five years, with Monday’s AQI touching 370 at 11am before improving to 344 by 4pm, better than 2025’s post-Diwali air quality,” the report read, while highlighting that “several monitoring stations failed to report crucial AQI data”.
The front page also carried reports on the death of 10-year-old Rishi Garg in Delhi’s Narela after suffering a deep injury on his chest while bursting a firecracker; the hourly PM2.5 concentration at Jahangirpuri surging to 4,985 µg/m³ on Diwali night, which is 83 times the daily national ambient air quality standard; and X “locking” the account of TOI photojournalist Anindya Chattopadhyay after he posted visuals of smog in Delhi, citing violation of its rules.
The Mumbai edition of the paper on Tuesday reported “a record number of firecracker accidents” across the city on Diwali, with the headline ‘390 fires caused by crackers across Mum region on Diwali’. The report highlighted that the local train services on the Western line were disrupted due to a fire damaging signalling cables between Virar and Nalasopara. It noted that over 60 people suffered burns across Mumbai Metropolitan Region and over 30 stray animals and birds sustained burn injuries due to crackers, among various other major accidents and mishaps across MMR.
Similarly, the Kolkata edition led with a story on firecracker-related noise complaints. With the headline, ‘This Diwali, city seeks max number of noise complaints’, the report highlighted the widespread bursting of banned high-decibel firecrackers across the city, well beyond the permissible hours, making Sunday night one of the noisiest in recent years. Kolkata’s air quality deteriorated sharply over the same period, with readings lying between the “very poor” and “severe” categories from Sunday night to the intervening morning, and PM2.5 rising from 74 to 409 in Ballygunge and 115 to 444 in Salt Lake within a span of 2 hours, the report highlighted.
The front page Delhi edition of The Indian Express on Tuesday carried the lead story on pollution with the headline ‘Delhi wakes up to toxic post-Diwali air, 8 stations in ‘severe’ zone’. It reported that the capital had recorded its “worst” Diwali-day air quality in the last five years. Pollution levels rose sharply after sunset and remained elevated into the following morning, with PM2.5 concentrations touching nearly 5,000 µg/m³ at some monitoring stations. India’s 24-hour national ambient air quality standards prescribe a safe limit of 60 µg/m³ for PM2.5 and 100 µg/m³ for PM10.
The lead story of the Hindustan Times carried the headline, ‘Delhi pollution monitors went dark as AQI surged on Diwali’. According to the report, 43 of Delhi’s 59 air quality monitoring stations went “blank” on Diwali night just as PM2.5 readings surged towards 1,000 µg/m³. The data gaps reportedly affected the calculation of the capital’s daily AQI, raising questions about the reliability of pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours.
The front page also featured reports on Punjab recording nearly 200 stubble burning incidents on November 9, Monday; the sale of firecrackers continuing in Delhi despite a Supreme Court ban; and the rampant bursting of firecrackers leading to an increase in ambient noise levels across most monitoring stations in Delhi.
The Telegraph featured a collage showing the contrast of visibility of Delhi’s India Gate before and after Diwali, with photographs taken on October 30 and November 9 respectively. With the lead headline reading ‘Diwali cocktail of cacophony’, the front page reports covered the aftermath in both Delhi and Kolkata, highlighting data gaps in Delhi’s pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours and administrative inaction in Kolkata.
“Slackness in the seizure of banned fireworks. Stalls selling crackers at almost every neighbourhood. Lackadaisical police response to noise complaints. Political endorsement at the highest level in the name of religion. Several factors made this Diwali the most deafening in years, according to environmentalists, former pollution control board members, Opposition politicians and ordinary Calcuttans,” the report read.
The Telegraph reported that this Diwali celebration was Delhi’s most polluted Diwali in five years. It noted that, over 18 hours, from 10 pm on Sunday to 4 am on Monday, 59 air quality stations in the national capital should have recorded 1062 hourly readings; however, around 24% are missing from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data.
On Kolkata’s exceeding noise pollution levels, the report stated that “even a minister and an MLA from the BJP complained of the “unbearable” noise…However, asked about the rampant violation of noise pollution norms, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari politicised the issue, saying it was the “communists” and those unnerved by the “stupendous rise of Sanatan” that were complaining.”
ALSO READ: Suvendu calls firecracker critics communists as Kolkata chokes on Diwali pollution
The Hindu on Tuesday carried a standalone image of thick smog enveloping Rashtrapati Bhavan on Monday morning with the caption ‘Pollution unlimited’. On Page 6, it further reported that air pollution levels in Delhi had spiked to 200 times the World Health Organization’s recommended limits during Diwali.
Hospitals Report Burn Patients; Doctors Raise Concerns
“I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival,” Dr Vijay Hadda, professor, department of pulmonary medicine and sleep disorders at AIIMS, told ANI on Monday.
He said that the green crackers reduced emissions by only 30 per cent, but as far as the particulate matter was concerned, 70 per cent of the emissions remained the same as conventional firecrackers. He raised concerns over people breathing this ‘poisonous’ smoke and said, “You should understand that you are simply inhaling poison and exhaling it.”
#WATCH | Delhi: On air pollution, Dr Vijay Hadda, Professor, Department of Pulmonary Medicine & Sleep Disorders, AIIMS, says, “These green crackers reduce emissions by only 30%. As far as the gases and particulate matter are concerned, 70% of the emissions remain the same as those from conventional firecrackers. The AQI, which used to be in three digits, has now reached four digits. If you compare Delhi’s air quality with that of other cities, you will find that there is almost a 50% difference. Obviously, life is not going to be easy for the people living here. You keep inhaling this poisonous smoke, breathing it in continuously. Every minute, you breathe at least 20 times, taking in at least half a litre of air with each breath. I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival. I am absolutely certain that as time passes, we will begin to see its effects. Many of my colleagues who are otherwise completely healthy have been calling me and saying, “I am unable to get rid of this irritation. It feels as though something is stuck in my throat.” We saw patients during our last OPD session, and they have returned again today. This happens every year, but somehow, we all forget. The general public forgets, and even policies remain somewhat in a grey area, making it difficult to understand how they should be interpreted. Overall, the situation is not good at all. You should understand that you are simply inhaling poison and exhaling it…”
— ANI (@ANI) November 9, 2026
In the aftermath of Diwali, doctors in Delhi began reporting an alarming number of juvenile patients, including newborns, arriving with breathing difficulties, even as hospitals are witnessing a significant rise in respiratory illnesses. According to reports, 397 patients with Diwali-related injuries were treated at four major hospitals in Delhi. The cases included burns, firecracker injuries and eye trauma.
AIIMS reported 42 burn injury cases by 11 am on November 9. Of these, 37 were caused by firecrackers. Eleven patients sustained major injuries, while 31 had minor injuries. Eight were admitted, including one in critical condition. Moreover, 18 of the 42 patients were under 18, including six below the age of 10. An eight-year-old child at AIIMS was in critical condition after sustaining burns over 45 per cent of their body surface area. Safdarjung Hospital recorded 135 burn injury cases. Of these, 129 were attributed to firecrackers and six to traditional diyas. Seven patients sustained major burns requiring hospital admission. The hospital also treated 35 children with firecracker-related injuries in its outpatient department.
Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital treated 41 patients with burn injuries from 9 am on Saturday. 18 of these injuries were reportedly caused by firecrackers, with two patients requiring admission. Eight patients were hospitalised overall, while approximately 10–12 of those treated were children. Guru Tegh Bahadur Hospital reported 172 patients with firecracker burns and other Diwali-related injuries within 24 hours. Among them were 25 children and 56 women. Thirty-four patients also suffered eye injuries.
The toll was not limited to burn injuries. The Dr Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences at AIIMS received nearly 110 patients with eye injuries on Sunday and during the early hours of Monday, most of them with firecracker-related ocular injuries. 18 patients suffered corneal perforations or lacerations and underwent surgical intervention.
In Pali, Rajasthan, sparks from firecrackers being burst on a road reportedly reached a firecracker shop near Swarn Mandir in Falna town, gutting three shops and killing two people. One person sustained burn injuries and three others were initially reported missing.

Musk says it would be ‘an honor’ to hire scandal-struck Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
World’s richest man expresses support for under-fire executive, who could be forced out of the chipmaker he founded after its share value dipped 9 percent

Already a member? Log in
Elon Musk has said it “would be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang, at risk of being fired as Nvidia’s CEO after reports he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy tanked the chipmaker’s share price.
The world’s richest man replied to a post on his social media platform X from a financial blog called Zerohedge appealing to him to take on Huang, 63, if he is ultimately let go by the company he founded in 1993, whose products are powering the current global AI boom.
“That would be an honor,” the SpaceX and Tesla boss wrote in response.
Musk and Huang have reportedly known each other for at least a decade, with Nvidia supplying chips for the former’s Tesla Model S and X vehicles and its hardware powering that company’s self-driving technology, as well as xAI. The two men have also collaborated on space-based data centers.
The forner paid tribute to the Nvidia boss on X just last month, saying that they were “old friends are the best friends,” adding: “Jensen rocks.”
Huang previously discussed his trillionaire friend (he is a humble billionaire by comparison) during an appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience last December, crediting him as being the “first customer” for his DGX-1 deep-learning supercomputer in 2016 when “nobody in the world wanted it,” giving his business a huge boost.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board of directors was meeting late Wednesday to decide Huang’s fate following the reports about his personal life. The company’s shares fell approximately 9 percent in after-hours trading Wednesday, knocking approximately $350 billion from its value.
The executive sent a memo to Nvidia employees Sunday admitting he had been unfaithful to his wife and saying he was “deeply sorry” for the hurt he had caused without going into details.
U.S. intelligence warned former Megaspeed director Alice Huang — who is no relation but with whom the tech boss has been pictured on a number of occasions — was a suspected spy for China.
China has denied the claims that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was recruited by its Ministry of State Security for corporate espionage purposes, calling them “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”
The infidelity was first reported by The New York Times, which has since alleged that the executive had another relationship with Kimberly Powell, his company’s vice president of healthcare, who is also married.
Nvidia’s board responded to the initial affair by launching an internal investigation into the revelations led by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.
Huang’s potential exit would create a leadership vacuum at the $4 trillion chipmaker, which has found itself at the heart of the big tech arms race between the U.S. and China.
The fallout from the scandal has also reached Washington, where it has been reported that Trump was “warned” about Huang’s compromised position by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in May as the executive joined their visit to Beijing, despite his saying earlier this week he had been blindsided by the news.
Republican leaders of three House committees called for Huang to deliver closed-door testimony on his interactions with the alleged intelligence asset while North Dakota GOP Sen. Kevin Cramer has openly called for him to resign “as a matter of his own conscience.”
Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have also written to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to demand that all company records relating to Nvidia’s dealings with China be preserved.

Keeping up with UP| In the Lord’s name: A religious row with a political twist
Dhirendra Krishna Shastri’s remarks contrasting Lord Ram and Lord Krishna have triggered a row, exposing tensions among religious leaders and political parties.
In the 1990s, when the Ram temple movement was at its peak, people took serious offence to derogatory public utterances about Hindus having several gods and goddesses for the simple reason that worshipping multiple gods and goddesses was never a contentious issue. Regardless of many Hindus having a specific “aradhya dev” (beloved or tutelary deity), they revered all gods—Ram, Krishna, Shiva and Maa—who were often called by different names in different regions.
It was, therefore, shocking when the head priest of the Bageshwar Dham, Dhirendra Krishna Shastri, drew a divisive contrast between Lord Ram and Lord Krishna during a religious discourse in Madhya Pradesh recently. Shastri not only framed Ram as “hamare (our) Ram” and Krishna as “tumhare (your) Krishna” but also appeared to ridicule Krishna’s iconic three-fold posture, called “tribhangi”.
“Hamare Ram stands straight, looks straight and his name is also spelt straight while your Krishna is bent in three places,” Shastri said.
The derogatory tone and tenor appeared aimed at eulogising Lord Ram over Lord Krishna. Shastri had also asked Krishna devotees to raise their hands, conceding they would be hurt by his observation. He later apologised for his comment, but by then, his comments had created a furore. Many Krishna devotees, including the Yaduvanshis, were outraged. Samajwadi Party national president Akhilesh Yadav immediately demanded a ban on Shastri’s religious discourses in the state. Many others, including Union minister Chirag Paswan, also condemned the statement. “He has always been against dividing society in the name of religion and caste, but here, he is creating a rift in the name of our “bhagwan” (God),” Paswan said.
Some backed Shastri but Bharatiya Janata Party leaders maintained their distance from the controversy. This was perhaps because some in the party leadership had earlier lauded Shastri’s efforts to promote Hindu unity. Shastri is no stranger to controversies but his dismissive remark must have triggered unease within the BJP, whose politics revolves around “Sanatan and development.”
The issue also has a demographic dimension.
Krishna devotees form a powerful community in Gujarat, the land of Dwarka, and West Bengal, where the legacy of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu runs deep. These devotees have a strong connection with Vrindavan and Mathura. ISKCON followers are also spread around the globe.
The controversy has come at a time when the movement in Krishna Janmasthan in Mathura is gaining momentum, with the tacit support of Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath. The religious dispute over the temple and an adjoining mosque is in court, but it has become a poll issue.
The situation escalated when former Uttar Pradesh minister Raghuraj Pratap Singh alias Raja Bhaiya decided to proceed with Shastri’s three-day Ram Katha, from November 17 to 19, in his stronghold of Kunda in Pratapgarh, despite the growing row. Large-scale preparations with the support of the state government are underway.
Singh heads a party, the Jansatta Dal (Loktantrik), with two lawmakers. A Rajput leader with money and muscle power, Singh was put behind bars under POTA (Prevention of Terrorism Act) by then chief minister Mayawati over two decades ago. He has navigated various political parties and has maintained cordial relations with the CM.
Though he also enjoyed good ties with former CM Mulayam Singh Yadav, who withdrew the POTA charges against him within 24 hours of assuming power in 2003, Singh’s relationship with Mulayam’s son, Akhilesh Yadav, has not been cordial.
Singh has operated in the region with money and muscle power. He is a political influencer who helped form the Kalyan Singh government by mobilising MLAs from other parties and, in return, received a cabinet berth. But Kalyan Singh had once branded him “Kunda ka goonda (the thug of Kunda)”.
The recent war of words between Akhilesh Yadav and Singh, and their supporters has inflamed Rajput-Yadav tensions, with provocative statements flowing thick and fast. The Rajputs are seen leaning towards the BJP and the Yadavs towards the SP. Who will the row help politically?
Poll time
In an era of religious renaissance, where crowds increasingly flock to spiritual congregations, politicians are also seeking the services of social-media-savvy gurus. Politicians want crowds, and people seeking succour from the burden of their daily lives are drawn to these self-styled religious figures.
“When the desire for attention, recognition and self-importance overtakes genuine wisdom, silence and discernment, even the most revered figures begin to speak recklessly, contradict themselves and expose the hollowness beneath their public persona.This is particularly evident among some self-proclaimed Hindu spiritual leaders, who seem to mistake visibility for wisdom and popularity for spiritual authority. The constant need to remain in the spotlight often leads them to make sweeping statements, indulge in unnecessary commentary and eventually descend into absurdity,” said Sandeep Singh, author of two books on Temple Economics, a Decade for Mandir
The question arises: Are such figures promoting ‘Sanatan Dharma’ or spreading misinformation and superstition?
Political parties once relied on local muscle power or mafia dons to mobilise voters. But they later decided to take over the operation themselves even as the Election Commission struggled with reforms to check the criminalisation of politics. Could the self-styled emissaries of God – equipped with money and muscle power, private armies and blind followers – follow the same trajectory? Instead of mobilising crowds for others, they could claim power for themselves.
